Used (1) to reassure someone: "Tutto andrà bene" = "Everything will be fine," and (2) to say something will be suitable/acceptable for a purpose: "Questo/questa andrà bene?" = "Will this work / Is this OK?" You can also use it about time plans: "Ogni giorno andrà bene" = "Any day will be fine."
target_language_example: Va bene anche domani, ma se preferisci sabato, andrà bene lo stesso.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is fine too, but if you prefer Saturday, that will be fine as well.

meaning: “Everything will be fine / it’ll all be okay.”
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or express optimism about the future. It’s the future tense of “andare” (“to go”): literally “everything will go well,” but it’s usually translated as “everything will be fine/okay.” Often said as encouragement (“Avanti, andrà tutto bene”) or with “penso/credo” (“I think/I believe everything will be fine”).
target_language_example: Tranquillo: andrà tutto bene, ci penso io.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything will be fine, I’ll take care of it.

additional_notes: Uses the passato remoto form of “andare” (andò = he/she went). Common in storytelling, books, news reports, and in some regions of Italy for past events. It’s followed by “a” before a destination (a Boston, a Kyoto) or a place like “a letto” (to bed).
target_language_example: Ieri sera andò a casa molto tardi.
native_language_example: Last night he/she went home very late.

additional_notes: Past historic (passato remoto) of "andare a casa" (to go home). Common in written narratives and storytelling; in everyday conversation many speakers use "è andato/a a casa" instead. The subject is usually understood from context (e.g., Tom, he, she).
target_language_example: Dopo la riunione, andò a casa subito.
native_language_example: After the meeting, he/she went home right away.

additional_notes: Passato remoto (simple past) of “andare a letto” = “to go to bed,” often used in storytelling, books, or to talk about a completed action in the past (especially in some regions). With a time: “andò a letto alle dieci” = “went to bed at ten.” Note: “andare a letto con qualcuno” can also mean “to sleep with someone” (often implying sex), depending on context.
target_language_example: Dopo cena, andò a letto presto.
native_language_example: After dinner, he/she went to bed early.

additional_notes: Past tense using the passato remoto of andare (andò = “he/she went”), common in written storytelling and in some regions when speaking. Used literally for going/attending school; it can be expanded (e.g., “andò a scuola di legge” = “he went to law school”).
target_language_example: Da bambino, Marco andò a scuola in centro.
native_language_example: As a child, Marco went to school downtown.

additional_notes: "Andò" is the passato remoto (remote past) of "andare" and is common in stories, news, and historical narration (especially in central/southern Italy). In everyday conversation, people often use "è andato/a" instead. "Al" = "a" + "il" and is used with masculine singular places: "andò al museo", "andò al lavoro".
target_language_example: Ieri Marco andò al cinema con gli amici.
native_language_example: Yesterday Marco went to the cinema with friends.

meaning: “he/she went to (into)” (past tense of andare + in).
additional_notes: Used to say someone went to a place in the past. It’s the passato remoto form of “andare” (andò = he/she went), common in storytelling and in some regions; in everyday speech you often hear “è andato/a in…”. Use “in” especially with countries/continents (in Italia, in America), cities as “in città”, and certain places like “in una moschea”.
target_language_example: Ieri andò in Francia per lavoro.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she went to France for work.

additional_notes: Used for the ring given when a couple gets engaged. Often appears with possessives (il mio/il suo anello di fidanzamento) and verbs like dare (to give), comprare (to buy), perdere (to lose), portare (to wear).
target_language_example: Ha comprato un anello di fidanzamento per la sua ragazza.
native_language_example: He bought an engagement ring for his girlfriend.

meaning: pet (a domestic animal kept at home).
additional_notes: Used to refer to an animal kept as a companion in the home (e.g., dog, cat, rabbit, parrot). Common questions: "Hai un animale domestico?" (Do you have a pet?) or "Che tipo di animale domestico...?" (What kind of pet...?). Plural: "animali domestici".
target_language_example: Hai un animale domestico?
native_language_example: Do you have a pet?

additional_notes: Used to talk about animals kept at home (like cats and dogs). In signs and rules (e.g., hotels, apartments), it often means “pets are allowed/not allowed.” Singular: "animale domestico".
target_language_example: In questo appartamento sono ammessi gli animali domestici.
native_language_example: Pets are allowed in this apartment.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *avere* (to have) to talk about age. Most commonly appears in questions like **Quanti anni ha?** = 'How old is he/she?' or formally 'How old are you?'. With *tu* (you, informal) you usually say **Quanti anni hai?**. The subject pronoun is often omitted in Italian (so *ha* can refer to 'he/she' or formal 'you').
target_language_example: Quanti anni ha tua sorella?
native_language_example: How old is your sister?

additional_notes: Used to say who something is owned by. It’s the 3rd-person singular form of the verb "appartenere" + "a" (to): "X appartiene a Y" = "X belongs to Y". Often used in questions: "Appartiene a te?" (Does it belong to you?).
target_language_example: Questo zaino appartiene a Marco, non a me.
native_language_example: This backpack belongs to Marco, not to me.

meaning: “belongs to her” or “belongs to you (formal, to a woman)”.
additional_notes: From the verb *appartenere* (“to belong to”). *Lei* can mean “her” or formal “you” (used with strangers or in polite situations); if addressing a man formally, you still say *Lei* (same word). Often used to talk about ownership of objects: *Questo/Questa ... appartiene a lei?* = “Does this ... belong to her/you (formal)?”
target_language_example: Mi scusi, questa borsa appartiene a lei?
native_language_example: Excuse me, does this bag belong to you?

additional_notes: Used to say that something is your property/possession. "Appartiene" is the 3rd person singular of "appartenere" (to belong), so it matches singular things: "questo/quella cassa/questa automobile". For plural, use "appartengono a me" (they belong to me). Often you can also just say "È mio/a" (it’s mine) depending on the noun’s gender.
target_language_example: Scusi, questo zaino appartiene a me.
native_language_example: Excuse me, this backpack belongs to me.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (e.g., sono/sei/è appena arrivato) to say someone arrived a moment ago. The adverb appena means “just/barely,” and the past participle arrivato agrees with the person (appena arrivata for a woman; appena arrivati/arrivate for plural). Often used as a quick update when you’ve just gotten somewhere.
target_language_example: Scusa il ritardo: sono appena arrivato alla stazione.
native_language_example: Sorry I'm late: I just arrived at the station.

meaning: "Open your eyes"; also "wake up / face reality".
additional_notes: Imperative (tu form) of "aprire" + "gli occhi". It can be a literal command (e.g., after someone has their eyes closed) or a figurative one meaning "stop being naive" or "realize what’s really going on." Often said with urgency or frustration; adding a name makes it more direct ("Apri gli occhi, Diane").
target_language_example: Apri gli occhi: ti sta mentendo.
native_language_example: Open your eyes: he’s lying to you.

additional_notes: A direct command using the tu form of aprire (apri). Use it with friends, family, kids, or someone you address as tu. To be more polite, add per favore or per piacere. With Lei (formal), you would say: "Apra la porta".
target_language_example: Scusa, apri la porta un attimo?
native_language_example: Sorry, can you open the door for a moment?

meaning: to open one’s mouth; (often) to speak / say something.
additional_notes: Often used to mean “to speak,” especially in negative forms like “non ha aperto bocca” = “he/she didn’t say a word.” You can also use it literally when talking about opening your mouth (e.g., at the dentist).
target_language_example: Durante la riunione, non voleva aprire bocca.
native_language_example: During the meeting, he/she didn’t want to say a word.

meaning: to open your eyes; (figuratively) to realize / wake up to the truth.
additional_notes: Often used in the imperative or with dovere/potere (Devi aprire gli occhi; Puoi aprire gli occhi) either literally (open your eyes now) or figuratively to tell someone to stop being naive and notice what’s really happening. With "adesso" it’s typically literal: "Puoi aprire gli occhi adesso!"
target_language_example: Devi aprire gli occhi: non ti sta dicendo la verità.
native_language_example: You have to open your eyes: he’s not telling you the truth.

meaning: to open fire; to start shooting.
additional_notes: Used mainly in military/police or news contexts to mean starting to shoot with firearms. It can also be used more broadly to mean initiating hostilities or an attack (typically not metaphorical in everyday conversation).
target_language_example: I soldati hanno deciso di aprire il fuoco contro il nemico.
native_language_example: The soldiers decided to open fire on the enemy.

additional_notes: Used for physically opening a window to let in air/light. Common with modal verbs like dovere (devo/deve) and with instructions using di + infinitive (mi ha detto di aprire...). You can also use the polite request: Può aprire la finestra?
target_language_example: Puoi aprire la finestra, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you open the window, please?

additional_notes: Used for physically opening a door (by turning the handle, pushing/pulling, etc.). You’ll often see it with modal verbs like riuscire a (to manage to) or with requests like Puoi aprire la porta? (Can you open the door?).
target_language_example: Puoi aprire la porta, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you open the door, please?

additional_notes: Used for physically opening a box/container (e.g., a package). In many situations Italian also uses the shorter phrase "aprire la scatola" simply meaning "open the box"; you can add an object pronoun if needed (e.g., "Aprila!" = "Open it!").
target_language_example: Puoi aprire la scatola, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you open the box, please?

meaning: to open the doors; (figuratively) to open up opportunities / allow access.
additional_notes: Literal: opening actual doors (e.g., a building, shop, or venue). Figurative: giving someone access, permission, or a chance to do something (similar to English “open doors”). Often used with "a" + person/thing: "aprire le porte a qualcuno/a qualcosa" = "to open the door to someone/something."
target_language_example: Questo corso può aprire le porte a molte opportunità di lavoro.
native_language_example: This course can open the door to many job opportunities.

meaning: “open the door” (command to more than one person, or formal ‘you’).
additional_notes: Imperative of aprire used for: (1) talking to a group (“you all”), or (2) formal/polite ‘you’ to one person (Lei). Often said urgently with subito (“right now”) or softened with per piacere (“please”). Negative command: Non aprite la porta! = “Don’t open the door!”
target_language_example: Scusate, aprite la porta, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you open the door, please?

additional_notes: "Aprì" is the passato remoto of "aprire" (to open), used especially in narratives and (in many regions) for actions completed in the distant past. In everyday conversation many Italians often use passato prossimo instead: "ha aperto la porta". It can also appear with an indirect object: "aprì la porta a Maria" = he/she opened the door for Mary (or opened the door to Mary).
target_language_example: Quando suonarono, aprì la porta e salutò tutti.
native_language_example: When they rang the doorbell, he/she opened the door and greeted everyone.

additional_notes: General term for a weapon that shoots bullets using gunpowder/explosive force (e.g., a pistol or rifle). Often used in formal contexts like police reports or medical/legal descriptions (e.g., "ferite da arma da fuoco" = gunshot wounds).
target_language_example: La polizia ha trovato un’arma da fuoco nell’auto.
native_language_example: The police found a firearm in the car.

meaning: angry with me (said about a woman).
additional_notes: Uses the adjective “arrabbiato/a” (“angry”) + “con” (“with”) to say someone is angry with someone else: “arrabbiata con me/te/lui/lei…”. “Arrabbiata” agrees with a feminine subject; for a man, use “arrabbiato con me”. You can intensify it with “molto” (very): “molto arrabbiata con me”.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace: sei arrabbiata con me?
native_language_example: I’m sorry: are you angry with me?

additional_notes: "Arrabbiato" is the masculine singular form (for a man). For a woman, use "arrabbiata": "Sono arrabbiata con lui." The person you’re angry with is introduced by "con" + pronoun/name: "arrabbiato con me/te/lei/loro", "arrabbiato con Marco". Common question: "Perché sei arrabbiato con lui?" = "Why are you angry with him?"
target_language_example: Non sono più arrabbiato con lui.
native_language_example: I’m not angry with him anymore.

additional_notes: Use **essere arrabbiato/a con [someone]** to say you’re angry *with* someone. Change the ending for gender/number: **arrabbiato** (male), **arrabbiata** (female), **arrabbiati/e** (plural). The pronoun can change too: **con te** (with you), **con lui/lei** (with him/her), **con noi/voi** (with us/you all), **con loro** (with them). You can add a reason with **per**: *arrabbiato con me per...* (“angry with me for...”).
target_language_example: Sei ancora arrabbiato con me?
native_language_example: Are you still angry with me?

meaning: to get home; to arrive home.
additional_notes: Used for reaching your home (or the place you’re staying). Common in questions about how/when you’ll get home (e.g., in macchina, a piedi, in autobus) and with time expressions (e.g., tardi, alle otto). In the past tense you’ll typically see it conjugated (e.g., sono arrivato/a a casa), but the base multi-word term is "arrivare a casa".
target_language_example: A che ora pensi di arrivare a casa?
native_language_example: What time do you think you’ll get home?

additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of "arrivare a casa" (to arrive home). Common in narratives, books, news reports, or storytelling; in everyday conversation Italians often use "è arrivato/a a casa" (passato prossimo) instead. "Arrivò" agrees with the subject only by context (it can mean he or she).
target_language_example: Quando arrivò a casa, trovò un messaggio sul tavolo.
native_language_example: When he/she got home, he/she found a message on the table.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. Use it after verbs like piacere (Mi piace ascoltare la musica) or amare (Amo ascoltare la musica). You can add a genre after musica (musica pop/rock/jazz) or use soprattutto (“especially”) to say your favorite type.
target_language_example: Mi piace ascoltare la musica mentre studio.
native_language_example: I like listening to music while I study.

additional_notes: Repetition of the imperative aspetta (“wait”) to sound more urgent or to interrupt and get someone to pause. Very common in spoken Italian; often followed by a short request like solo un attimo/un minuto/un secondo, or by a correction/added thought (e.g., “ascolta…”).
target_language_example: Aspetta, aspetta: ho dimenticato le chiavi!
native_language_example: Wait, wait—I forgot the keys!

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to pause briefly while you do something or think. Common in spoken Italian; you can also hear it repeated for emphasis (“Aspetta un attimo, aspetta”) or used as a quick interruption (“Aspetta un attimo!”).
target_language_example: Aspetta un attimo, devo rispondere a questo messaggio.
native_language_example: Wait a moment, I have to reply to this message.

additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb essere (or sometimes stare) to say someone did not go to school: “Sono/ero/è assente da scuola.” You can add a reason with “per” or “per via di” (e.g., “per via della malattia” = due to illness).
target_language_example: Oggi Giulia è assente da scuola perché ha la febbre.
native_language_example: Today Giulia is absent from school because she has a fever.

additional_notes: Used to say you are with someone (same place, doing an activity, living/working) or doing something jointly. It’s a common variant of "insieme a" (same meaning). Often followed by a person/pronoun: "assieme a me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro" or a noun: "assieme a Maria".
target_language_example: Stasera vado al cinema assieme a un amico.
native_language_example: Tonight I'm going to the movies together with a friend.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is similar in appearance or characteristics to someone/something else. It’s the verb assomigliare (to resemble) + a (to). Common pattern: [subject] assomiglia a + person/thing (e.g., Mia sorella assomiglia a mia madre).
target_language_example: Mia sorella assomiglia a mia madre.
native_language_example: My sister looks like my mother.

additional_notes: Used for position or movement near/around a person or thing: "attorno a lei" = "around her". It can also mean "around" in the sense of approximately with times: "attorno a mezzanotte" = "around midnight". In some contexts it implies being nearby or hanging around someone/somewhere.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo attorno alle otto?
native_language_example: Shall we meet around eight?

additional_notes: Used for going from one side of a street/road to the other (on foot or generally). Often appears after verbs like "guardare" (to look) or with warnings like "È pericoloso..." (It’s dangerous...). In Italian, "strada" can mean both "street" and "road" depending on context.
target_language_example: Scusi, dov’è l’attraversamento pedonale per attraversare la strada?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the crosswalk to cross the street?

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun (il). It can mean moving from one side to the other ("through the desert/country"), looking through something ("through the microscope"), or indicating a means/channel ("through mutual respect", "through the Quran", "transmitted through a kiss"). For feminine singular use "attraverso la"; for plural "attraverso i/le".
target_language_example: Ho imparato l'italiano attraverso il lavoro.
native_language_example: I learned Italian through work.

meaning: back and forth; to and fro.
additional_notes: Used to describe repeated movement in one direction and then the opposite (walking, carrying something, going between places). Often used with verbs like camminare/andare (to walk/go) or portare (to carry/bring). It can describe pacing (e.g., in a room) or going back and forth over time.
target_language_example: Ho passato la mattina ad andare avanti e indietro tra casa e l’ufficio.
native_language_example: I spent the morning going back and forth between home and the office.

meaning: entitled to; having the right to.
additional_notes: Used in formal/official contexts (laws, benefits, tickets, discounts) to indicate a person who qualifies for something. Often used as a legal/administrative modifier after a noun (e.g., "soggetto avente diritto") or as a set plural expression "gli aventi diritto" (= those entitled/eligible). It can be followed by "a" + noun/infinitive (e.g., "avente diritto al rimborso", "avente diritto a votare").
target_language_example: Il soggetto avente diritto può richiedere il rimborso entro 30 giorni.
native_language_example: The entitled person may request a refund within 30 days.

meaning: “to have done” (past infinitive, used after modal/auxiliary verbs).
additional_notes: It’s the past infinitive of **fare**: **avere + fatto**. Very common after modal verbs like **dovere/potere/volere** to talk about a past action in an uncertain, hypothetical, or regretful way: **devi/potrebbe/non può/vorrei aver fatto...** = “you must have done / might have done / can’t have done / I wish I had done...”.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace non aver fatto in tempo a chiamarti.
native_language_example: I’m sorry I didn’t manage to call you in time.

meaning: to have to do with; to be related to; (also) to deal with (someone/something)
additional_notes: Structure: subject + conjugated form of "avere" + "a che fare con" + noun/pronoun. Commonly used to say something is (or isn’t) connected to something else: "Non ho niente a che fare con..." (= I have nothing to do with...). It can also mean having dealings/contacts with someone: "Non voglio avere a che fare con lui." (= I don’t want to deal with him / have anything to do with him).
target_language_example: Questo problema può avere a che fare con il lavoro.
native_language_example: This problem may have to do with work.

additional_notes: Literally means "to have need of." Use it with di before a noun or an infinitive: avere bisogno di una pausa = "to need a break," avere bisogno di riposare = "to need to rest." The verb avere normally changes depending on the subject (ho bisogno di, hai bisogno di, etc.), but the fixed dictionary form is avere bisogno di.
target_language_example: Mary sembra avere bisogno di una vacanza.
native_language_example: Mary seems to need a vacation.

additional_notes: Usually followed by di + noun/pronoun: avere cura di qualcuno/qualcosa (“to take care of someone/something”). It focuses on responsibility, attention, and caring (family, children, animals, possessions). Similar in meaning to prendersi cura di, often interchangeable.
target_language_example: Puoi avere cura del gatto mentre sono via?
native_language_example: Can you take care of the cat while I’m away?

meaning: to have an effect; to work (e.g., a medicine or remedy).
additional_notes: Used to say that something produces a result or works as intended. Often followed by “su” + person/thing affected: “avere effetto su di me/su qualcosa”. For medicines, Italians also commonly say “fare effetto” (same idea, often more natural in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Questo farmaco sembra non avere effetto su di me.
native_language_example: This medicine doesn’t seem to have any effect on me.

additional_notes: Literally “to have hunger,” but it’s the normal Italian way to say “to be hungry.” In conjugated form it’s very common: ho fame (I’m hungry), hai fame? (are you hungry?). The exact infinitive “avere fame” is used after modal/other verbs (e.g., dovere, potere, sembrare) or in reported speech/thought: sembra/potrebbe/dovrebbe avere fame; mi ha detto di avere fame.
target_language_example: Tom sembra avere fame, quindi possiamo mangiare subito.
native_language_example: Tom seems to be hungry, so we can eat right away.

additional_notes: Literally “to have cold.” In Italian you use avere (to have) + a sensation/need: avere caldo (to be hot), avere fame (to be hungry), avere sete (to be thirsty). It conjugates with avere: ho freddo, hai freddo, ha freddo, abbiamo freddo, avete freddo, hanno freddo.
target_language_example: Quando esco senza giacca, inizio ad avere freddo.
native_language_example: When I go out without a jacket, I start to feel cold.

additional_notes: Used especially in announcements, schedules, and formal writing to indicate when an event, meeting, ceremony, or process starts. Commonly appears with a time or date (e.g., "alle 9", "il 3 maggio"). Similar in meaning to "iniziare" / "cominciare" but more formal. Note: it often conjugates the verb "avere" (e.g., "avrà inizio"), but the fixed expression is "avere inizio".
target_language_example: La conferenza deve avere inizio alle nove.
native_language_example: The conference must begin at nine.

meaning: to have your hands tied (to be unable to act).
additional_notes: An idiom used when you can’t do what you want because of rules, lack of authority, a promise, or circumstances. Often followed by a reason: "Ho le mani legate: non posso..."
target_language_example: Vorrei aiutarti, ma in questo momento devo avere le mani legate: non posso decidere io.
native_language_example: I’d like to help you, but right now my hands are tied: it’s not up to me.

additional_notes: Used mainly in formal or written Italian (news, notices, official communication) to say that an event happens. It’s commonly followed by a time or place expression: “La riunione avrà luogo domani” (time) / “avrà luogo a Roma” (place).
target_language_example: La conferenza deve avere luogo venerdì alle 18 in sala A.
native_language_example: The conference must take place on Friday at 6 p.m. in room A.

meaning: to be afraid; to be scared
additional_notes: Literally means "to have fear," but in English it is usually translated as "to be afraid" or "to be scared." It is often followed by di or articulated forms such as del, della, etc. to say what someone is afraid of: avere paura del futuro = "to be afraid of the future."
target_language_example: Non dovreste avere paura del futuro.
native_language_example: You shouldn't be afraid of the future.

meaning: to keep in mind; to be aware of.
additional_notes: Used to say you remember something and are actively considering it while deciding or acting. Common in phrases like “Devi avere presente che…” (“You have to keep in mind that…”) or “Ho presente…” (“I’m aware / I remember”). Often followed by a clause introduced by “che”.
target_language_example: Devi avere presente che domani i negozi sono chiusi.
native_language_example: You have to keep in mind that the shops are closed tomorrow.

additional_notes: A very common Italian expression used to say that someone is correct. Literally it means "to have reason," but the usual English translation is "to be right." It often appears in forms like "hai ragione" ("you're right"), but the dictionary form is "avere ragione."
target_language_example: Pensi che Tom potrebbe avere ragione?
native_language_example: Do you think Tom might be right?

meaning: to make sense; to be meaningful; to be worth it/there to be a point.
additional_notes: Used to say something is logical, understandable, or worthwhile. Common in questions/negatives: “Ha senso?” (Does it make sense?), “Non ha senso” (It doesn’t make sense). It can also mean “to be worth doing”: “Non ha senso farlo” (There’s no point in doing it).
target_language_example: Non credo che abbia senso discutere adesso: ne parliamo domani.
native_language_example: I don’t think it makes sense to argue now: we’ll talk about it tomorrow.

additional_notes: In Italian you literally say “to have thirst” (avere + sete). Very common in everyday situations. You can add intensity: avere molta sete (very thirsty), avere poca sete (a little thirsty).
target_language_example: Dopo la corsa, inizio ad avere sete: posso avere un bicchiere d’acqua?
native_language_example: After the run, I’m starting to get thirsty: can I have a glass of water?

meaning: to be sleepy; to feel like sleeping.
additional_notes: Used with the verb avere (“to have”) to describe a state: Ho sonno (I’m sleepy). You can also specify degree: Ho molto/poco sonno (I’m very/a little sleepy), or ask: Hai sonno? (Are you sleepy?).
target_language_example: Dopo pranzo, comincio ad avere sonno e vado a letto presto.
native_language_example: After lunch, I start to feel sleepy and I go to bed early.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb avere and followed by the noun successo. It can refer to achieving a goal (Il piano è destinato ad avere successo) or being generally successful in life/work. Common with verbs like sperare di (to hope to), augurare di (to wish to), and expressions like essere destinato a (to be destined to).
target_language_example: Se lavori con costanza, puoi avere successo.
native_language_example: If you work consistently, you can succeed.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s opinion, judgment, or statement is incorrect. Often contrasts with "avere ragione" (to be right). You can use it with different tenses and modals: "può avere torto" (may be wrong), "potrebbe avere torto" (might be wrong), "sapevo di avere torto" (I knew I was wrong).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, credo di avere torto.
native_language_example: Sorry, I think I’m wrong.

additional_notes: Used when avere (“to have”) is followed by a singular masculine noun: un drago, un figlio, un amico. It is not a fixed idiom, just a very common combination. Before some masculine nouns, Italian uses uno instead (for example uno studente); with feminine nouns, use una or un'.
target_language_example: Vorrei avere un cane.
native_language_example: I'd like to have a dog.

meaning: to have a/an (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns: avere una visione (a vision), una teoria (a theory), una tazza (a cup), una fine (an end), una moglie (a wife). In conversation it can be a request/question: “Potrei avere una…?” = “Could I have a…?”. Compare: avere un (masculine), avere un’ (before a vowel).
target_language_example: Posso avere una bottiglia d’acqua, per favore?
native_language_example: Can I have a bottle of water, please?

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of comprare: avete (you have) + comprato (bought). Used with “you” plural (you all) or polite/formal “you” (Lei/Loro, depending on context). In questions, intonation or context can make it mean “Did you buy…?”
target_language_example: Avete comprato anche il pane?
native_language_example: Did you buy bread too?

meaning: "you met" / "have you met" (you plural or polite).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *conoscere* with **voi** (you all) or formal **Lei** (you). It’s used when asking or saying when/where you first met someone: *Dove avete conosciuto…?* In some contexts it can also mean “got to know” someone, but in questions like these it usually means “met.”
target_language_example: Dove avete conosciuto Laura?
native_language_example: Where did you meet Laura?

meaning: "you gave" / "you have given" (to give — 2nd person plural or formal).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of the verb "dare" (to give): "voi/Lei (pl.) avete dato". Used with a direct object (Avete dato una chiave), often with an indirect object introduced by "a" (Avete dato una chiave a qualcuno; Avete dato loro quel cane). Common pattern: "dare da mangiare" = "to feed" (literally “to give to eat”). Another common use is "dare del/della + insult/label" = "to call someone ..." (Mi avete dato della codarda = You called me a coward).
target_language_example: Mi avete dato un consiglio molto utile.
native_language_example: You gave me very useful advice.

meaning: "you said that" (addressing more than one person).
additional_notes: Uses passato prossimo of dire: "avete detto" = "you (plural) said" / "you have said." It’s followed by "che" to introduce what was said. "Avete" is the voi form, used when speaking to a group (not the polite singular "Lei," which would be "ha detto che").
target_language_example: Avete detto che la riunione iniziava alle tre, giusto?
native_language_example: You said that the meeting started at three, right?

additional_notes: Past tense of "fare" addressed to "voi" (you all) or formal "you" in some contexts. It’s used to talk about actions completed in the past ("You did...") or with a link to the present ("You have done..."). Often followed by a noun (avete fatto i compiti = you did the homework) or by something/anything/nothing (avete fatto qualcosa/niente). In questions it’s very common: "Perché avete fatto...?" = "Why did you do...?"
target_language_example: Avete fatto una prenotazione per stasera?
native_language_example: Did you make a reservation for tonight?

additional_notes: Used with "voi" (you plural), either to address more than one person or, in some regions, as a polite form. It commonly appears in questions about whether something has been done yet (e.g., "Avete già + past participle?"). For one person formally, you’d usually say "Ha già..." (Lei). Word order can change with pronouns: "L’avete già trovata?" = "Have you already found her/it?"
target_language_example: Avete già finito di mangiare?
native_language_example: Have you already finished eating?

meaning: “Have you ever eaten…?” (asking about someone’s past experience).
additional_notes: Used to ask one or more people (voi) if they have ever eaten/tried something at any point in their life. It uses the present perfect (avere + mangiato) and often introduces a food you’re curious about: Avete mai mangiato + [food]? You can answer with: Sì, l’ho mangiato / No, non l’ho mai mangiato.
target_language_example: Avete mai mangiato il sushi?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten sushi?

meaning: "Have you ever seen...?" (asking if someone has ever seen something at any time).
additional_notes: "Avete" is the 2nd person plural (voi) of "avere" in the present tense, used for addressing multiple people or as a polite/formal "you". It’s typically followed by a person/thing + an infinitive ("Avete mai visto Tom ballare?") or a noun ("Avete mai visto un orso?"). Often used with "prima" to mean "before" ("... prima?").
target_language_example: Avete mai visto questo film?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen this movie?

meaning: "Have you ever seen a …?" (to more than one person).
additional_notes: Used to ask a group (or one person politely with "voi") if they have ever seen something. "mai" = "ever" and usually goes between the auxiliary and the past participle: "avete mai visto…?" Change the article as needed: "un" (masc. singular), "uno" (before s+consonant, z, gn, etc.), "una" (fem. singular). With one person informally: "Hai mai visto un/una…?".
target_language_example: Avete mai visto una lucertola così grande?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a lizard this big?

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "mangiare" for "voi" (2nd-person plural). Use it when talking to more than one person: "Avete mangiato?" = "Have you eaten?" In a statement it means "You ate..." / "You have eaten...". (In some contexts "voi" can be used as a polite form, but the most common polite singular is "Lei ha mangiato".)
target_language_example: Avete mangiato qualcosa oggi?
native_language_example: Have you eaten anything today?

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "prendere" used with "avere": "voi" + "avete" + past participle "preso". Used for many meanings of "prendere": taking (medicine, an object), getting/buying something ("Dove avete preso...?" = Where did you get it?), and in set phrases like "prendere parte" (to take part/participate). Word order changes with questions: "Avete preso...?" = Have you taken...?.
target_language_example: Avete preso i biglietti online?
native_language_example: Did you get the tickets online?

meaning: "have you heard" / "did you hear" (you all / formal you).
additional_notes: Second-person plural of "sentire" (to hear). It can mean literally hearing a sound/words, or more generally "to hear about" news (often with "di": "Avete sentito di...?" = "Have you heard about ...?"). Used for speaking to a group, or as the polite/formal "you" in some regions/contexts.
target_language_example: Avete sentito che domani scioperano i treni?
native_language_example: Have you heard that the trains are on strike tomorrow?

additional_notes: Second-person plural of the passato prossimo of trovare (“to find”). Used when speaking to more than one person (voi) or as a polite/formal “you” (especially in some regions) to ask if someone has found something, like a job.
target_language_example: Avete trovato una soluzione?
native_language_example: Have you found a solution?

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of vedere for voi (2nd person plural): avere (avete) + past participle (visto). Used both in questions (Avete visto…? = “Have you seen…?”) and statements (Voi avete visto… = “You have seen…”). Can mean “have you watched” with movies/series: Avete visto quella serie? = “Have you watched that series?”
target_language_example: Avete visto le mie chiavi da qualche parte?
native_language_example: Have you seen my keys anywhere?

additional_notes: Form of "avere bisogno di" (to need). "Avete" is for "you" plural (you all) or formal "you" (e.g., speaking to customers). It’s followed by "di" + an infinitive (Avete bisogno di aggiornare…) or "di" + a noun with an article (Avete bisogno di un dizionario?). In questions, intonation or a question mark makes it “Do you need…?”
target_language_example: Avete bisogno di aiuto con la prenotazione?
native_language_example: Do you need help with the booking?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has certain items or people (e.g., in a shop, hotel, restaurant, or talking to a family). "Avete" is 2nd-person plural (you all) and is also used as the polite/formal "you" in some regions. "Dei" is a partitive meaning "some/any" before a masculine plural noun; the feminine plural form is "delle" (Avete delle camere?), and for plural nouns starting with s+consonant, z, ps, gn, etc., it becomes "degli" (Avete degli asciugamani?). Often in English it translates as "any" in questions.
target_language_example: Scusi, avete dei biglietti per oggi?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have any tickets for today?

meaning: “do you (plural/formal) intend to…?” / “are you planning to…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s intention or plan. It’s the verb phrase "avere intenzione di" (to intend/plan to) conjugated for "voi" (you all) or formal "you" in some contexts, followed by an infinitive (e.g., cominciare, ritornare).
target_language_example: Avete intenzione di venire con noi domani?
native_language_example: Are you planning to come with us tomorrow?

meaning: 'are you afraid of' / 'are you scared to'.
additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person ("voi"), asking if they’re afraid of someone/something or afraid to do something. If it’s followed by a verb, use "di" + infinitive: "Avete paura di dirlo?" (= Are you afraid to say it?). If it’s followed by a noun/pronoun, it means "afraid of": "Avete paura di me?" (= Are you afraid of me?).
target_language_example: Avete paura di fare una domanda?
native_language_example: Are you afraid to ask a question?

meaning: “you have a …” / “do you have a …?” (to a group).
additional_notes: "Avete" is the 2nd-person plural of "avere" (to have), used when speaking to two or more people ("you all"). With rising intonation or a question mark, it’s a common way to ask if someone has something available: "Avete un…?" = “Do you have a…?”. "Un" is the masculine singular article (“a/an”); for feminine you use "una" (e.g., "Avete una penna?").
target_language_example: Scusi, avete un tavolo libero?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have a free table?

meaning: "do you have a…?" / "you have a…" (addressing you-plural or polite).
additional_notes: From the verb "avere" (to have). "Avete" is 2nd-person plural: used when speaking to more than one person (you all), and also commonly as a polite/formal way to address one person (e.g., a customer, receptionist, waiter). "Una" is "a" for feminine singular nouns, so it’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., una prenotazione, una stanza).
target_language_example: Scusi, avete una penna?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have a pen?

additional_notes: Imperfect past (3rd person singular) of “avere bisogno di” (to need). Used for an ongoing or habitual need in the past, or to provide background description. It can refer to a person (he/she) or a thing/situation (it): e.g., “Il bagno aveva bisogno di…”. Follow it with a noun/pronoun (“aveva bisogno di lei/noi”) or with an infinitive construction such as “aveva bisogno di essere + participle” (needed to be cleaned/done).
target_language_example: Il bagno aveva bisogno di essere pulito.
native_language_example: The bathroom needed to be cleaned.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **avere** (“to have”) with **fame** (“hunger”) to talk about being hungry. **Aveva** is the **imperfetto** (imperfect past) form of *avere* for **lui/lei** (“he/she”), often used for background situations or ongoing states in the past (e.g., *stamattina* = “this morning”).
target_language_example: Dopo la passeggiata, aveva fame e ha mangiato un panino.
native_language_example: After the walk, he was hungry and ate a sandwich.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of "avere paura di" (to be afraid of / to be afraid to do). Use "aveva paura di" to talk about a past, ongoing state of fear. It can be followed by an infinitive to mean “was afraid to (do something)” (e.g., "andare", "dire"), or by a noun/pronoun to mean “was afraid of (someone/something)" (e.g., "di Sami").
target_language_example: Da bambino, aveva paura di dormire da solo.
native_language_example: As a child, he was afraid to sleep alone.

additional_notes: From the expression **avere ragione** (“to be right”). **Aveva** is the imperfect tense of *avere* and typically means someone “was” right in the past (sometimes “used to be” right, depending on context). You can add **riguardo a / su** to specify what they were right about: *aveva ragione riguardo a lui* = “he/she was right about him”; *aveva ragione su di lei* = “he/she was right about her.” Note: **avere ragione di + infinitive** means “to have reason to…”: *Non aveva ragione di essere arrabbiato* = “He had no reason to be angry.”
target_language_example: Lo sa che Tom aveva ragione.
native_language_example: You know that Tom was right.

additional_notes: "Avere torto" means "to be wrong". "Aveva" is the imperfect tense, used for an ongoing state in the past, background description, or reported speech. It often corresponds to English "was wrong" or sometimes "used to be wrong" depending on context. You can also ask: "Chi aveva torto?" = "Who was wrong?"
target_language_example: Mary mi disse che aveva torto.
native_language_example: Mary told me that she was wrong.

additional_notes: Imperfetto of "avere" + "un". Used to say someone/something had (or used to have) something in the past, often describing a state or ongoing situation/background: "Aveva un problema" (He/She had a problem), "Il latte aveva un cattivo sapore" (The milk had a bad taste). "Aveva" can mean he, she, or it depending on context; with feminine nouns it becomes "aveva una".
target_language_example: Da bambino aveva un cane.
native_language_example: As a child, he had a dog.

additional_notes: Used when talking about (usually criminal) investigations to say someone could prove they were elsewhere at the time. You can change the verb/person: ho un alibi (I have an alibi), hai un alibi? (Do you have an alibi?), aveva un alibi? (Did he/she have an alibi?). Often followed by a time expression: per quella notte / per ieri sera.
target_language_example: Non poteva essere lui: aveva un alibi per quella sera.
native_language_example: It couldn’t have been him: he had an alibi for that evening.

additional_notes: From avere (to have) in the imperfetto: aveva = “he/she had / used to have / was having.” It’s followed by a feminine singular noun with una (“a”). The subject is often understood from context (e.g., Tom aveva una… = “Tom had a…”).
target_language_example: Quando era piccolo, aveva una bicicletta rossa.
native_language_example: When he was little, he had a red bike.

additional_notes: Past tense (imperfetto) of “avere bisogno di” = “to need.” Used for ongoing/repeated need in the past, or to describe a past situation/background. Structure: avere bisogno di + noun (avevano bisogno di aiuto/denaro) or + pronoun (avevano bisogno di voi).
target_language_example: Quando erano piccoli, avevano bisogno di molta attenzione.
native_language_example: When they were little, they needed a lot of attention.

meaning: “you had said that …” (talking about what someone previously said).
additional_notes: Used to remind someone of a past statement or to point out what they previously claimed. It’s the past perfect of dire: avevi detto = “you had said/told”. Often followed by che + a clause. In questions/negatives (Non avevi detto che…?) it can mean “Didn’t you say that…?”
target_language_example: Avevi detto che saresti arrivato alle otto.
native_language_example: You had said you would arrive at eight.

meaning: "you were right" (informal singular), in the past.
additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tu) that they were correct about something, often after you realize it later. Common with prepositions: avevi ragione a + infinitive ("you were right to..."); avevi ragione riguardo a / su ("you were right about..."). In the plural/formal you’d say: avevate ragione (you all were right) / aveva ragione (he/she was right) / aveva ragione (Lei was right).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace: avevi ragione su tutto.
native_language_example: I’m sorry: you were right about everything.

additional_notes: Past tense (imperfetto) of "avere bisogno di" + noun/infinitive, used to say you needed something (often as background, ongoing, or not tied to one single moment). "Di" is required: avevo bisogno di cibo / di dormire. Common variants: "ho bisogno di" (I need), "avevi/aveva/avevamo... bisogno di".
target_language_example: Ieri avevo bisogno di dormire presto.
native_language_example: Yesterday I needed to go to sleep early.

meaning: I was planning to / I meant to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to say you had an intention in the past, often something you planned but may not have done. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., andare, chiamare, aiutare). Note the tense: "avevo" is imperfect, so it often implies an ongoing intention or background plan.
target_language_example: Avevo intenzione di studiare, ma poi mi sono addormentato.
native_language_example: I was planning to study, but then I fell asleep.

meaning: "I was afraid of" / "I was afraid to".
additional_notes: Imperfetto of "avere paura" (to be afraid), used to describe an ongoing or habitual fear in the past. Use "di" + noun (avevo paura di mio padre = I was afraid of my father) or "di" + infinitive (avevo paura di prendere un raffreddore = I was afraid of catching a cold).
target_language_example: Da bambino avevo paura di parlare in classe.
native_language_example: As a child, I was afraid to speak in class.

additional_notes: Imperfetto of the expression "avere ragione" (to be right). Used to say you were correct about something in the past, often with emphasis like "E avevo ragione io" = "And I was the one who was right." You can add what you were right about with "su" (e.g., "Avevo ragione su di te").
target_language_example: Te l’avevo detto: avevo ragione.
native_language_example: I told you: I was right.

meaning: "I felt like" / "I wanted to" (in the past).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a desire/urge you had at a particular moment in the past. It’s often closer to “I felt like…” than a firm plan. The verb after di stays in the infinitive (di parlare, di urlare). Related forms: ho voglia di (present), avevi voglia di (you had), aveva voglia di (he/she had), avevamo voglia di (we had).
target_language_example: Ieri sera avevo voglia di restare a casa.
native_language_example: Last night I felt like staying at home.

meaning: “should have” / “ought to have” (past advice, criticism, or missed obligation).
additional_notes: Conditional perfect of *dovere* (“to have to / must”). Used to say that someone did not do something in the past, but it would have been the right or expected thing to do. Pattern: **avrebbe dovuto + infinitive**. Often carries a sense of regret, reproach, or hindsight (“he should have… but he didn’t”).
target_language_example: Avrebbe dovuto dire la verità.
native_language_example: He should have told the truth.

additional_notes: Conditional perfect of dovere + essere: expresses regret, criticism, or an expectation that didn’t happen in the past. Used with a noun/adjective ("avrebbe dovuto essere un problema" = it should have been a problem) or with a past participle to form the passive ("avrebbe dovuto essere fatto/preso/punito" = should have been done/taken/punished). Often implies "but it wasn’t / didn’t happen".
target_language_example: La riunione avrebbe dovuto essere ieri, ma è stata rimandata.
native_language_example: The meeting should have been yesterday, but it was postponed.

meaning: “would have done / would do” (conditional past of “fare”).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that was expected, hypothetical, or reported as something someone said they would do. It’s the conditional past of fare: avrebbe (he/she/it would have) + fatto (done/made). Often appears in indirect speech after a past verb (e.g., disse che avrebbe fatto...), and with expressions like “avrebbe fatto meglio a...” = “he/she would have been better off (to)...”. It can also mean “it would be (weather)” in phrases like “avrebbe fatto freddo” = “it would be cold.”
target_language_example: Non sapevo cosa avrebbe fatto al mio posto.
native_language_example: I didn’t know what he/she would have done in my place.

meaning: “could have / would have been able to” (past conditional of *potere*).
additional_notes: Used to express a past possibility or ability seen from a hypothetical/conditional point of view (often implying regret, criticism, or an alternative outcome). Typically followed by an infinitive: *avrebbe potuto dire/fare/andare*. Negative: *non avrebbe potuto* (“couldn’t have / wouldn’t have been able to”). Note: it agrees with the subject in person/number via the auxiliary (*avrei/avresti/avrebbe/avremmo/avreste/avrebbero potuto*).
target_language_example: Avrebbe potuto dirmelo prima.
native_language_example: He/She could have told me earlier.

meaning: “I should have” / “I ought to have” (in hindsight).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something you now think was the right thing to do, but you didn’t do it. It’s the conditional past of dovere (“to have to / should”), often followed by an infinitive: avrei dovuto + dire/fare/andare… Negative: non avrei dovuto (“I shouldn’t have”). Questions are common for second-guessing: Non avrei dovuto dirlo? (“Shouldn’t I have told him/it?”).
target_language_example: Avrei dovuto studiare di più per l’esame.
native_language_example: I should have studied more for the exam.

meaning: "I should have done" / "I was supposed to do" (but didn’t).
additional_notes: This is the conditional past of *dovere* + *fare*. It’s used to talk about a missed duty/expectation, often with regret or criticism. You can change the subject: *avresti dovuto fare* (you should have done), *avrebbe dovuto fare* (he/she should have done), *avremmo dovuto fare* (we should have done). Often followed by what you should have done: *Avrei dovuto fare di più* (I should have done more).
target_language_example: Avrei dovuto fare una domanda prima di firmare.
native_language_example: I should have asked a question before signing.

additional_notes: Conditional perfect of "potere" (avere + potuto). Used to talk about a possibility/ability in the past that didn’t happen, or was only hypothetical: "I could have..." / "I would have been able to...". Common in questions like "Come avrei potuto saperlo?" (= "How could I have known?") and in hypothetical sentences with "se" + imperfect subjunctive: "Se fossi..., avrei potuto..." (= "If I were/had been..., I could have...").
target_language_example: Avrei potuto aiutarti, ma non lo sapevo.
native_language_example: I could have helped you, but I didn’t know.

meaning: "I would have liked" / "I would have wanted".
additional_notes: Past conditional of "volere" (io). Used to express a wish or preference about the past (often with regret: you wanted something but it didn’t happen). Common patterns: (1) "avrei voluto" + infinitive: "Avrei voluto venire." (2) "avrei voluto che" + subjunctive (often past subjunctive for past events): "Avrei voluto che tu fossi venuto." It can also sound softer/more polite than a direct "volevo" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Avrei voluto chiamarti ieri, ma ero troppo stanco.
native_language_example: I would have liked to call you yesterday, but I was too tired.

meaning: "you should have" / "you ought to have" (talking about something in the past).
additional_notes: This is the conditional perfect of "dovere" ("to have to / must"). It’s used to say what someone was expected to do in the past, often with a tone of advice, criticism, or regret. "Avreste" is 2nd person plural ("you all"), and it can also be used as a polite form in some contexts.
target_language_example: Avreste dovuto dirmelo prima.
native_language_example: You should have told me earlier.

meaning: “you should have” / “you ought to have” (but you didn’t).
additional_notes: Conditional perfect of dovere: avresti (you would have) + dovuto (had to/should). Used to express regret, criticism, or advice about a past action not done. Usually followed by an infinitive: Avresti dovuto + verbo (es. dire, fare, rifiutare).
target_language_example: Avresti dovuto chiamarmi prima di uscire.
native_language_example: You should have called me before going out.

meaning: “you could have” (past possibility/ability; often implying regret or criticism).
additional_notes: Formed by the conditional of avere (avresti) + past participle potuto. Used to talk about something someone had the chance/ability to do in the past but didn’t: Avresti potuto dirlo = “You could have said it.” It can sound like a reproach (“you should have”) depending on tone/context. Commonly followed by an infinitive: avresti potuto fare/chiedere/dire…
target_language_example: Avresti potuto avvisarmi prima.
native_language_example: You could have warned me earlier.

additional_notes: Future tense of avere successo (“to succeed”). Used after a subject (explicit or implied): Tom avrà successo = “Tom will succeed.” It can also refer to things (an idea, a plan, a business): Il progetto avrà successo = “The project will be a success.”
target_language_example: Sono sicuro che la tua idea avrà successo.
native_language_example: I’m sure your idea will succeed.

meaning: had some problems; had trouble (doing something).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have) to say you experienced difficulties. Often followed by "a" + infinitive: "abbiamo avuto dei problemi a entrare" = "we had trouble getting in." The "dei" means "some" (not specific problems).
target_language_example: Ho avuto dei problemi a trovare parcheggio.
native_language_example: I had trouble finding parking.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with the verb "avere" in the passato prossimo: "ha avuto successo" (he/she/it was successful), "hanno avuto successo" (they were successful). Common with people, projects, plans, missions, etc.: "La missione ha avuto successo."
target_language_example: Il progetto ha avuto successo grazie al tuo aiuto.
native_language_example: The project was successful thanks to your help.

meaning: a rowboat; a boat you row with oars.
additional_notes: Used for a small boat propelled by rowing (using oars), not a motorboat or sailboat. Often appears after verbs like andare in (to go by) or avere (to have).
target_language_example: Siamo andati al lago in barca a remi.
native_language_example: We went to the lake in a rowboat.

meaning: "as long as" / "provided that"; also "all you have to do is".
additional_notes: Introduces a condition that is enough to make something acceptable or true. Very common in spoken Italian. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "basta che tu venga" = "as long as you come"), though in informal speech you may also hear the indicative.
target_language_example: Puoi prendere la mia macchina, basta che me la riporti stasera.
native_language_example: You can take my car, as long as you bring it back tonight.

additional_notes: Used in medical/health contexts to talk about the heart’s beating, especially whether it’s regular/irregular or present. Common with verbs like “sentire” (to feel/hear) and adjectives like “regolare” (regular). In everyday Italian you may also hear “battito del cuore.”
target_language_example: Il medico controlla il battito cardiaco e la pressione.
native_language_example: The doctor checks the heartbeat and blood pressure.

additional_notes: An English loanword used in Italian for the sport played on sand. Typically used with "giocare a" (to play): "Gioco a beach volley". It’s usually masculine: "il beach volley".
target_language_example: D'estate giochiamo a beach volley in spiaggia.
native_language_example: In summer we play beach volleyball at the beach.

meaning: "Well then," / "Well, so…" (reacting and drawing a conclusion).
additional_notes: Common conversational filler used at the start of a reply to show you’re reacting to what was just said (surprise, acceptance, mild disagreement) and often to introduce a conclusion or next step. As a question ("Beh, allora?") it can mean "Well, then?" / "So?"—asking what happens next, sometimes with impatience.
target_language_example: Beh, allora andiamo: è tardi.
native_language_example: Well then, let’s go: it’s late.

meaning: "Well, I..." (used to introduce what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Used as a conversational opener before giving your opinion, reacting, hesitating, or slightly changing topic. Often followed by a statement about yourself ("io..."). In writing it’s usually followed by a comma: "Beh, io...".
target_language_example: Beh, io non so cosa dire.
native_language_example: Well, I don’t know what to say.

meaning: "Well, (no/not…)"—used to introduce a negative reply or disagreement.
additional_notes: “Beh” is a very common spoken interjection (like “well…”). With “non” it often softens or sets up a correction, refusal, or negative opinion. It’s typical in conversation and can sound a bit informal/colloquial.
target_language_example: Beh, non sono d'accordo.
native_language_example: Well, I don't agree.

additional_notes: "Bei" is the plural of "bel" (meaning "beautiful/nice") and is used before a plural noun (like "fiori"). It’s an adjective + noun phrase used to compliment flowers, often with "molti" (many) or in phrases like "grazie per...".
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei bei fiori per tua madre.
native_language_example: I bought some beautiful flowers for your mother.

meaning: “Nice shot!” / “Good one!” (a great move, hit, or success).
additional_notes: Used to congratulate someone after a good action (a shot in sports, a clever idea, a successful attempt). Literally “nice hit/blow,” and it can also describe an achievement or a well-executed move: *È stato un bel colpo* = “That was quite a feat / a great success.”
target_language_example: Bel colpo! Hai risolto il problema in un attimo.
native_language_example: Good one! You solved the problem in no time.

meaning: a good impression; to come across well.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like fare/farsi ("fare bella figura", "fare una bella figura") meaning to look good, impress others, or behave appropriately in a situation. It can be said seriously (hoping to impress) or sarcastically when things go badly ("che bella figura stiamo facendo!").
target_language_example: Con quel discorso hai fatto davvero bella figura.
native_language_example: With that speech you really made a good impression.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate or praise someone for something they did (often as an exclamation on its own: “Ben fatto!”). You can intensify it with “molto”: “Molto ben fatto.” As an adjective describing a noun, it can agree in gender/number (ben fatto, ben fatta, ben fatti, ben fatte), but as a standalone compliment it’s commonly kept as “Ben fatto!”
target_language_example: Ben fatto! Hai fatto un ottimo lavoro.
native_language_example: Well done! You did a great job.

additional_notes: In modern Italian it is usually written as one word: "benvenuto". As a greeting/exclamation you will most often see the fused form, but the spaced form "ben venuto" may appear in older, poetic, or stylized writing. It agrees with the person/people welcomed: "ben venuta" (female), "ben venuti" (plural masc./mixed), "ben venute" (plural fem.). Also used in phrases like "Sei il benvenuto" = "You’re welcome here / You’re welcome (to come)."
target_language_example: Ben venuto a casa mia!
native_language_example: Welcome to my home!

additional_notes: Used at the end of a statement to check or confirm something you believe is true, similar to an English tag question. Literally it’s “well, true?”, but it’s normally translated as “right?” / “isn’t it?” / “didn’t you?” depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Domani ci vediamo alle 10, bene, vero?
native_language_example: We’re seeing each other tomorrow at 10, right?

additional_notes: Used after a verb (often "parlare") to say you do something well in French: "parlare bene il francese" = "to speak French well". You can also intensify it with "così" (so) or "davvero" (really): "parlare così/davvero bene il francese".
target_language_example: Parlo bene il francese, ma non lo scrivo molto bene.
native_language_example: I speak French well, but I don’t write it very well.

meaning: “Okay, then,” / “Well, then,” (used to move things along or conclude).
additional_notes: Common conversational connector. Use it to react to what was just said and then state your next action, decision, or question. Often followed by what you’ll do next (Bene, allora vado…) or by a prompt (Bene, allora cosa facciamo?). Commas are common in writing; intonation carries the meaning in speech.
target_language_example: Bene, allora ci vediamo domani alle otto.
native_language_example: Okay, then, see you tomorrow at eight.

meaning: to drink something (often: to have something to drink).
additional_notes: Common, polite everyday phrase used when offering or suggesting a drink. "Qualcosa" means "something" and can be followed by an adjective or "di + adjective" to specify what kind: "qualcosa di fresco" = "something cold/refreshing". Often used with "vuoi/vuole" (do you want?) or "vieni" (do you want to come?) to invite someone for a drink.
target_language_example: Dopo la passeggiata, andiamo a bere qualcosa?
native_language_example: After the walk, shall we go have something to drink?

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo of bere (“to drink”): ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno + bevuto. "Del" means “some” (an unspecified amount), so "ho bevuto del caffè" = “I drank some coffee / I had some coffee.” You can also say "ho bevuto caffè" (more general: “I drank coffee”).
target_language_example: Non ho bevuto del caffè oggi.
native_language_example: I didn’t drink any coffee today.

additional_notes: Used for a card with your name and contact details, especially in professional contexts. Often with verbs like avere/dare/lasciare (to have/give/leave) and with possessives: il mio biglietto da visita (my business card). Figuratively, it can mean a “calling card” or something that represents you/your work (e.g., È il nostro biglietto da visita = It’s our calling card).
target_language_example: Le lascio il mio biglietto da visita.
native_language_example: I’ll leave you my business card.

additional_notes: Used with the structure "avere bisogno di" + noun/pronoun: "(avere) bisogno del mio aiuto" = "(to) need my help." "del" is the contraction of "di + il". You’ll often see it after "ha/hai/aveva/avete bisogno..." and in questions like "Perché hai bisogno del mio aiuto?"
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno del mio aiuto, dimmelo.
native_language_example: If you need my help, tell me.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di + [noun]" = "to need + [noun]". Here: "(avere) bisogno del nostro aiuto" = "(to) need our help". You can add "ancora" to mean "still": "Hai ancora bisogno del nostro aiuto?". With people: "ho bisogno del tuo/suo/nostro aiuto" = "I need your/his/her/our help".
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno del nostro aiuto, chiamaci.
native_language_example: If you need our help, call us.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" ("avere bisogno di..." = "to need..."). "Suo" here is the formal/polite form meaning "your" (to one person you address with Lei). In context it often appears as "(avere) bisogno del suo aiuto" = "(to) need your help."
target_language_example: Mi scusi, ho bisogno del suo aiuto.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need your help.

additional_notes: Used after the verb "avere" (to have): "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo bisogno del tuo aiuto" = "I/you/he/she/we need your help." You can put it in the future with "avrò bisogno..." (I will need...), or make it negative: "non ho più bisogno del tuo aiuto" = "I don't need your help anymore."
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma ho bisogno del tuo aiuto oggi.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, but I need your help today.

additional_notes: "Avere bisogno di" means “to need.” "Del" = "di" + "il" (“of the”), and "vostro" is the formal/plural way to say “your” (to one person politely, or to more than one person). Very common with different tenses: "ho/avrò/abbiamo bisogno del vostro aiuto".
target_language_example: Scusi, ho bisogno del vostro aiuto per compilare questo modulo.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need your help to fill out this form.

additional_notes: Usually used in the expression avere bisogno di, which means "to need." It is followed by a noun (ho bisogno di aiuto = I need help) or by an infinitive (ho bisogno di dormire = I need to sleep).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di parlare con te.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di aiuto" = "to need help." You can change the verb for tense/person: "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/hanno bisogno di aiuto" (present), "avevo/avevi/aveva... bisogno di aiuto" (past/imperfect). Often used to offer or ask for assistance: "Hai bisogno di aiuto?"
target_language_example: Scusa, ho bisogno di aiuto con questo modulo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need help with this form.

additional_notes: Used for money or funding awarded to someone to study (often based on merit, need, or sports). Common with verbs like ricevere/ottenere/avere una borsa di studio, and you can add the field or destination: una borsa di studio di calcio; una borsa di studio per la Germania.
target_language_example: Ha ricevuto una borsa di studio per studiare all’università.
native_language_example: He/She received a scholarship to study at university.

additional_notes: Used to describe a bag by its color. Often heard in questions to identify who a bag belongs to (è tua? = is it yours?; è sua? = is it his/hers?).
target_language_example: Scusi, questa borsa nera è sua?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is this black bag yours?

additional_notes: Used when buying, recommending, or bringing wine. The partitive structure “di” indicates the contents: a bottle containing wine. You’ll often hear it with an adjective (e.g., “una buona/bella bottiglia di vino”) or in questions in shops/restaurants (“Quale bottiglia di vino consiglia?”).
target_language_example: Per la cena ho comprato una bottiglia di vino rosso.
native_language_example: For dinner I bought a bottle of red wine.

additional_notes: Used when talking about a quantity of beer measured in bottles, often with a number (e.g., due/tre/quattro bottiglie di birra). Singular: una bottiglia di birra.
target_language_example: Per la festa abbiamo comprato sei bottiglie di birra.
native_language_example: For the party we bought six bottles of beer.

meaning: right arm; (figurative) right-hand man/most trusted assistant.
additional_notes: Literally “right arm” (braccio = arm, destro = right). Used both for the physical body part (Alza il braccio destro) and figuratively to mean someone’s main helper or trusted aide (Essere il braccio destro di qualcuno). Agreement: braccio destro / braccia destre (fem. plural in Italian), but the adjective stays masculine singular with the singular noun: il suo braccio destro.
target_language_example: Giulia è il braccio destro del direttore.
native_language_example: Giulia is the director’s right-hand woman (most trusted assistant).

additional_notes: Used to say someone has ability/skill in the French language. "Bravo" changes to match the person: bravo (male), brava (female), bravi (mixed/plural), brave (female plural). Often used with other subjects too: "bravo in matematica" = good at math.
target_language_example: Tom è bravo in francese, ma non è bravo in tedesco.
native_language_example: Tom is good at French, but he isn’t good at German.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or talk about unpleasant information. Often said with verbs like avere/portare/dare (“to have/bring/give”) and with per to say who the news is for (e.g., brutte notizie per lui).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma ho brutte notizie per te.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, but I have bad news for you.

additional_notes: A common Christmas greeting used from the holiday season through Christmas Day. You can say it when you meet someone, in messages/cards, or as a toast. Often written with a capital N (Buon Natale).
target_language_example: Ti auguro un buon Natale e un felice anno nuovo!
native_language_example: I wish you a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year!

additional_notes: Used as a New Year’s greeting, often expanded to “Buon anno nuovo!” You can say it when greeting someone around New Year’s Day or in messages/cards. In other contexts it can also be literal (“a good year”), as in “È stato un buon anno.”
target_language_example: Auguri e buon anno!
native_language_example: Best wishes and Happy New Year!

additional_notes: Used as a polite wish before someone starts eating (said by the host, server, or anyone at the table). You can also say it on its own: “Buon appetito!” Note: in sentences like “ha un buon appetito,” it means “to have a good appetite” (to be hungry / eat well), not the mealtime wish.
target_language_example: Il pranzo è pronto: buon appetito!
native_language_example: Lunch is ready: enjoy your meal!

additional_notes: Used as a birthday greeting. Often followed by the person’s name or said on its own. You may also see the same idea as “Tanti auguri!” (more general: “best wishes”).
target_language_example: Buon compleanno! Ti auguro una bellissima giornata.
native_language_example: Happy birthday! I wish you a wonderful day.

additional_notes: Used as a friendly wish when someone is about to do something enjoyable (a party, trip, show, night out). It can be casual on its own (“Buon divertimento!”) or more formal with a polite phrase like “Le auguro buon divertimento” (“I wish you have fun”). Similar structure to “buona notte/buon viaggio/buon appetito.”
target_language_example: Vai al concerto stasera? Buon divertimento!
native_language_example: Are you going to the concert tonight? Have fun!

additional_notes: A polite, standard greeting used during the daytime, especially in the morning and early afternoon. Often written as one word: "buongiorno". You can use it when greeting someone directly (e.g., with a name or a friendly term like "vicino" = neighbor).
target_language_example: Buon giorno, come sta?
native_language_example: Good morning, how are you?

meaning: "Good work" / "have a good day at work"; also "a good job" (employment).
additional_notes: Used as a greeting/wish to someone who is about to work or is working (like saying “Have a good shift” / “Have a good one at work”). It can also describe employment: “un buon lavoro” = “a good job” (a good position). Agreement: buon lavoro (masc. sing.); but with the article it’s “un buon lavoro”.
target_language_example: Buon lavoro! Ci vediamo stasera.
native_language_example: Have a good day at work! See you tonight.

additional_notes: A polite greeting used from early afternoon until early evening (after lunch, before "buona sera"). Often followed by "a tutti" (everyone) or used when addressing a group (e.g., "signore e signori").
target_language_example: Buon pomeriggio, come posso aiutarla?
native_language_example: Good afternoon, how can I help you?

additional_notes: Used to talk about practical, reasonable thinking. Often appears with verbs like avere (to have), mancare (to lack), or expressions like un briciolo di (a bit of): avere buon senso, manca il buon senso, senza un briciolo di buon senso.
target_language_example: Serve un po' di buon senso per risolvere questo problema.
native_language_example: It takes a bit of common sense to solve this problem.

additional_notes: Used to say someone feels cheerful/positive. Common in phrases like “essere di buon umore” (to be in a good mood) and “mettere di buon umore” (to put someone in a good mood).
target_language_example: Oggi sono di buon umore.
native_language_example: Today I’m in a good mood.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone well before they leave on a trip or journey. You can say it directly (“Buon viaggio!”) or with verbs like augurare/fare: “Ti auguro buon viaggio” (I wish you a good trip), “Fai buon viaggio” (have a good trip).
target_language_example: Domani parti per Milano? Buon viaggio!
native_language_example: Are you leaving for Milan tomorrow? Have a good trip!

additional_notes: Used to wish someone well before an exam, job, trip, or any challenging situation. Often followed by “con/col + noun” (Buona fortuna con l’esame!) or used on its own as an exclamation. Can be formal (con il suo...) or informal (con il tuo...).
target_language_example: Hai un colloquio domani? Buona fortuna!
native_language_example: Do you have an interview tomorrow? Good luck!

additional_notes: Used as a polite greeting or, more commonly, as a farewell (like “Have a good day”). It can also be used literally to describe that today is a good day (often with “una”: “una buona giornata”). As a greeting, it’s more formal than “ciao” and similar in tone to “buona giornata, signore/signora”.
target_language_example: Grazie per l’aiuto, buona giornata!
native_language_example: Thanks for the help, have a good day!

additional_notes: Used to say something is a good suggestion/plan (È una buona idea?) or to agree with someone’s proposal (Sì, buona idea.). Often used with the article: una buona idea (“a good idea”).
target_language_example: Andiamo in treno: è una buona idea.
native_language_example: Let’s go by train: it’s a good idea.

meaning: Good night (said when going to sleep).
additional_notes: Used as a nighttime farewell, typically when you or the other person is going to bed. You can say it to one person or a group (e.g., family, kids). Often contrasted with "buona sera" (good evening), which is used earlier in the evening.
target_language_example: È tardi, vado a dormire: buona notte!
native_language_example: It’s late, I’m going to sleep: good night!

additional_notes: A polite greeting used from late afternoon through the evening. Common in both formal and neutral situations, often followed by a name or title (e.g., "Buona sera, signora"). It can also be used when entering a place (shops, restaurants) or starting a conversation.
target_language_example: Buona sera, avete un tavolo per due?
native_language_example: Good evening, do you have a table for two?

additional_notes: Plural feminine form. Use it when the friends are women/girls (or an all-female group): "Siamo buone amiche" = "We’re good friends." For a mixed group or male friends, use "buoni amici"; for two women, you can also say "due buone amiche".
target_language_example: Siamo buone amiche da tanti anni.
native_language_example: We’ve been good friends for many years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone being well-mannered (or ironically, if their actions contradict it). Often appears with verbs like "avere" (to have): "Ha delle buone maniere". You can also use it when talking about teaching etiquette to children.
target_language_example: Cerchiamo di usare buone maniere a tavola, per favore.
native_language_example: Let’s try to use good manners at the table, please.

additional_notes: Common way to announce or introduce something positive. Often used after verbs like avere/portare (to have/bring): “Ho delle buone notizie (per te/voi)” = “I have good news (for you).” Can also stand alone as an announcement: “Buone notizie!” Note: “notizia” is singular; “notizie” is plural.
target_language_example: Ho buone notizie per te: domani non lavoriamo.
native_language_example: I have good news for you: we’re not working tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say two or more people have a friendly relationship. Often with "essere" (to be) or "diventare" (to become): "Siamo buoni amici" = "We’re good friends." You can add "dei" before it when it follows "sono" to mean "some"/"(they are) good friends of yours": "Sono dei tuoi buoni amici."
target_language_example: Siamo buoni amici da molti anni.
native_language_example: We’ve been good friends for many years.

additional_notes: A strong insult used to say someone is lazy, incompetent, or worthless. It’s often said with "essere" (e.g., "Sei/Lui è buono a nulla"). Can also be used as a noun insult: "un/una buono/a a nulla" (plural: "buoni a nulla"). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Non ascoltarlo: ti chiama "buono a nulla" solo per offenderti.
native_language_example: Don’t listen to him: he calls you a “good-for-nothing” just to insult you.

additional_notes: Common food item. You can also say “burro d’arachidi” (with d’ before a vowel) in normal speech/writing. Often used with verbs like “comprare” (to buy), “mangiare” (to eat), or “spalmare” (to spread) and with “su” + food: “spalmare il burro di arachidi sul pane” (to spread peanut butter on bread).
target_language_example: Vorrei un panino con burro di arachidi e marmellata.
native_language_example: I’d like a sandwich with peanut butter and jam.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "bussare" (to knock) + "a" + an object/surface (most commonly "alla porta"). It’s literal (someone knocks on a door) and is often followed by whose door it is: "bussare alla porta di qualcuno". Common in polite contexts before entering.
target_language_example: Prima di entrare, devo bussare alla porta.
native_language_example: Before going in, I have to knock on the door.

meaning: to throw to the ground; to knock down.
additional_notes: Used for physically tossing or dropping something onto the ground (intentionally or accidentally). It can also mean to knock someone/something down (e.g., in a fight, an accident, or strong wind). Often interchangeable with "buttare per terra" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Non buttare a terra il bicchiere: si rompe!
native_language_example: Don’t throw the glass on the ground: it’ll break!

meaning: to throw out; to kick out (expel).
additional_notes: Used both literally (remove and throw something outside) and figuratively (force a person to leave a place, e.g., a bar/club). Often followed by what is removed ("buttare fuori la spazzatura") or by a person + da ("buttare fuori qualcuno dal locale"). Related noun: "il buttafuori" = the bouncer.
target_language_example: Hanno deciso di buttare fuori un cliente dal bar perché faceva troppo rumore.
