additional_notes: “Del” = “di + il” and is used after many verbs/adjectives to mean “about/of.” “Suo” can mean “his” or “her” depending on who it refers to. Common with verbs like parlare/discutere (“to talk/discuss about”) and adjectives like fiero/orgoglioso/stufo (“proud/tired of”).
target_language_example: Non parla mai del suo lavoro a casa.
native_language_example: He/She never talks about his/her work at home.

additional_notes: "Del" is the partitive (di + il) and is used when you mean an indefinite quantity of something uncountable, like coffee: "del caffè" = "some coffee". In everyday English you might also just say "coffee". Often used with verbs like bere (to drink), preparare/fare (to make), offrire (to offer), volere (to want).
target_language_example: Vuoi del caffè o del tè?
native_language_example: Do you want some coffee or some tea?

additional_notes: Partitive article: "del" = "di" + "il" and is used with uncountable masculine singular nouns like "cibo" to mean an unspecified amount (“some/any”). In many contexts English omits “some”: "Ho comprato del cibo" = “I bought food.” For feminine nouns you’ll often see "della" (e.g., "della pasta").
target_language_example: Ho preso del cibo da asporto.
native_language_example: I got some takeout food.

additional_notes: "Del" is a partitive article (di + il) used to mean an unspecified amount of something uncountable or plural. So "mangiare del gelato" = “to eat some (ice cream)” (not a specific portion). You can also hear "mangiare il gelato" when talking about the ice cream in general or a specific one.
target_language_example: Vorrei del gelato, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like some ice cream, please.

meaning: some milk (an unspecified amount of milk).
additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (di + il = del) with an uncountable noun: *latte*. Very common for talking about an indefinite quantity, especially with verbs like *bere* (to drink) and *versare* (to pour). In English it often translates as “some” or is omitted (“Tom drinks milk”). Literally it’s “of the milk,” but the meaning is “some milk.”
target_language_example: Vorrei del latte, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like some milk, please.

meaning: "some bread" (partitive: an unspecified amount of bread).
additional_notes: Del = di + il. With uncountable nouns like pane (“bread”), it’s commonly used to mean “some” in general: comprare del pane = “to buy some bread.” In other contexts it can also literally mean “of the bread” (referring to a specific bread).
target_language_example: Per favore, prendi del pane mentre torni a casa.
native_language_example: Please pick up some bread on your way home.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (di + il = del) to mean an unspecified amount: “some” or “any” tea, especially when talking about drinking, pouring, or serving. With an amount you’d usually use a measure instead (e.g., “una tazza di tè” = “a cup of tea”).
target_language_example: Vuoi del tè caldo?
native_language_example: Do you want some hot tea?

meaning: "of the forest/woods" (used to describe where someone/something is from or associated with).
additional_notes: It’s the contraction of "di + il" → "del" plus "bosco" (forest/woods). Very common in titles, names, and roles: "la Strega del Bosco" = "the Witch of the Woods"; "gli Elfi del Bosco" = "the Forest Elves." Often capitalized when it’s part of a name or title.
target_language_example: Ho incontrato un lupo del Bosco durante la passeggiata.
native_language_example: I met a wolf from the woods during the walk.

additional_notes: Combination of "di" + "il" → "del". Used to specify that something belongs to or refers to the whole world, very common in set phrases like "la mappa del mondo" (the world map).
target_language_example: Vorrei comprare una mappa del mondo.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy a world map.

additional_notes: Uses the contraction **del** (= **di** + **il**) before a masculine singular noun. Often seen in names and titles (e.g., **Via del Sole**, **Tempio del Sole**). **Sole** is often capitalized in names, but it can also be lowercase (**del sole**) in normal text.
target_language_example: Abitiamo in Via del Sole.
native_language_example: We live on Via del Sole (Sun Street).

meaning: “about the case” / “of the case” (referring to a specific investigation or matter).
additional_notes: Used with a specific case name or identifier (e.g., “del caso Fuller”) to mean information, details, documents, or archives related to that case. Grammatically it’s the contraction of “di + il” → “del” (“of the”).
target_language_example: Ho letto tutti i rapporti del caso Bianchi.
native_language_example: I read all the reports about the Bianchi case.

meaning: "of the body" (sometimes "of the corpse/body" depending on context).
additional_notes: It’s the contraction of **di + il** → **del**. Used to talk about body parts or anything related to the body: **parti del corpo** (parts of the body), **la salute del corpo** (the health of the body). In **guardia del corpo / guardie del corpo**, it means **bodyguard(s)** (literally “guard(s) of the body”). In some contexts **corpo** can also mean a **dead body** (“corpse”), e.g. **Che ne hai fatto del corpo?** = “What did you do with the body?”
target_language_example: La salute del corpo è importante.
native_language_example: The health of the body is important.

meaning: "of the heart" (literal), or "dear/close" in set phrases.
additional_notes: Literally "di + il cuore" = "of the heart." Used both in a physical/anatomical sense (e.g., "più in alto del cuore" = "higher than the heart") and in common expressions about feelings and closeness: "amici del cuore" = very close friends; "dal (più profondo) del cuore" = from the (very) bottom of my heart / sincerely.
target_language_example: Grazie dal profondo del cuore per il tuo aiuto.
native_language_example: Thank you from the bottom of my heart for your help.

additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “di + il” and is used before a masculine singular noun (il film). You’ll see it after verbs and expressions that take “di” (e.g., pensare/parlare di: “Cosa ne pensi del film?” = “What do you think about the film?”) and with nouns that describe something related to the film (e.g., la durata del film = the film’s duration, il manifesto del film = the film poster).
target_language_example: Parliamo del film dopo cena.
native_language_example: Let’s talk about the film after dinner.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something of the same type/kind as what’s being talked about. Often follows a noun: "un errore del genere" (= an error like that / of that kind). Very common with "qualcosa": "qualcosa del genere" (= something like that).
target_language_example: Non dire una cosa del genere!
native_language_example: Don’t say something like that!

additional_notes: Used to link something to the government (ownership, responsibility, or connection): e.g. "istituzioni del governo" (government institutions), "propaganda del governo" (government propaganda). It’s the contraction of "di" + "il" → "del". Similar forms: "dello" (di + lo), "della" (di + la), "dei" (di + i), "degli" (di + gli), "delle" (di + le).
target_language_example: Non mi fido delle promesse del governo.
native_language_example: I don’t trust the government’s promises.

additional_notes: Contraction of "di + il" ("of/about the"). Used to specify something related to a book (e.g., the title, a copy, your opinion). Often follows questions/verbs like "che ne pensi del..." = "what do you think about the...?"
target_language_example: Non ricordo il nome dell’autore del libro.
native_language_example: I don’t remember the name of the author of the book.

additional_notes: Most often used with the verb "fare": "fare del male (a qualcuno)" = to hurt someone / to harm someone (physically or emotionally). With "a" to name who is harmed: "fare del male a una mosca" is an idiom meaning someone is very gentle and wouldn’t hurt even a fly.
target_language_example: Non voglio farti del male.
native_language_example: I don't want to hurt you.

additional_notes: A fragment rather than a complete expression by itself. It is the contraction of di + il mio, and it is used before a masculine singular noun: del mio libro, del mio problema, del mio cavallo. Depending on the verb or adjective, it can correspond to 'of my', 'about my', or sometimes natural English uses like 'with my' (e.g. contento del mio lavoro = happy with my work).
target_language_example: Non voglio parlare del mio problema.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk about my problem.

additional_notes: Most often used after a superlative to mean “in the world”: il più X del mondo = “the most X in the world” (migliore/più bello/più profondo, etc.). It can also be used more generally to sound emphatic or dramatic: la fine del mondo (“the end of the world”), il re del mondo (“king of the world”).
target_language_example: Questo è il gelato più buono del mondo.
native_language_example: This is the best ice cream in the world.

additional_notes: Contraction of "di" + "il nostro" (= "of our"). Used to show possession or connection to something: "le date del nostro viaggio" (the dates of our trip), "in segno del nostro apprezzamento" (as a sign of our appreciation). In the common expression "fare del nostro meglio", it means "to do our best" (literally "to do of our best").
target_language_example: Faremo del nostro meglio per arrivare in tempo.
native_language_example: We’ll do our best to arrive on time.

meaning: anyway; besides / for that matter (also: “of the rest”).
additional_notes: Often used as a sentence add-on to comment on what you just said, meaning “besides/anyway/for that matter” (e.g., listing another example: “O Glenn Gould, del resto.”). In more literal contexts with "il resto" it can mean “of the rest,” as in "Per non parlare del resto" = “not to mention the rest.”
target_language_example: Non mi sorprende, del resto: lo conosci bene.
native_language_example: It doesn’t surprise me, anyway: you know him well.

additional_notes: Used before a man’s surname to show possession or reference: il figlio del signor Rossi = “Mr. Rossi’s son”; i film del signor Bianchi = “Mr. Bianchi’s films.” It’s a contraction of di + il + signor. Often used in more formal contexts; in writing you may also see Signor abbreviated as Sig.
target_language_example: Potrei parlare con la segretaria del signor Conti?
native_language_example: Could I speak with Mr. Conti’s secretary?

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (often with più/meno or prima/dopo) to compare something to what normally happens: prima del solito (earlier than usual), più felice del solito (happier than usual). Very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Oggi ho finito il lavoro più tardi del solito.
native_language_example: Today I finished work later than usual.

additional_notes: Usually followed by a masculine singular noun, as in del suo lavoro. del is the contraction of di + il, and suo can mean his, her, its, or your (formal), depending on context. In sentences, di can mean things like 'of' or 'about'.
target_language_example: Abbiamo parlato del suo progetto ieri.
native_language_example: We talked about his/her project yesterday.

additional_notes: Formed by **di + il → del** + **suo** (his/her/its) + **lavoro** (job/work). It’s used after verbs/adjectives that take **di** (e.g., *parlare di* “to talk about”, *essere fiero di* “to be proud of”, *essere stufo di* “to be fed up with”). **Suo** agrees with *lavoro* (masculine singular), so *del suo lavoro* can refer to either “his” or “her” job—context tells you which.
target_language_example: Sono orgoglioso del suo lavoro.
native_language_example: I’m proud of his/her work.

additional_notes: Used after verbs/adjectives that take **di** (e.g., *essere sicuro/certo di...* “to be sure/certain of...”, *vantarsi di...* “to boast about...”). **Del** = *di* + *il* (“of the”). **Suo** can mean “his”, “her”, “its”, or “your” (formal), depending on context.
target_language_example: Non dubito del suo successo.
native_language_example: I don’t doubt his/her success.

additional_notes: Del = di + il (“of the”). With tempo it can mean (1) “of time” in a general or sci‑fi/historical sense (confini dello spazio e del tempo; corridoio del tempo; del tempo di Luigi…), and (2) “about the weather” especially after verbs like parlare/discutere: “Parliamo del tempo” = “Let’s talk about the weather.”
target_language_example: Parliamo del tempo: domani piove?
native_language_example: Let’s talk about the weather: will it rain tomorrow?

additional_notes: Contraction of "di + il tuo". Used before a masculine singular noun to mean "of your" (possession/connection) or, with verbs like "parlare/dire", "about your". It changes with gender/number: "della tua" (fem. sing.), "dei tuoi" (masc. pl.), "delle tue" (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Parlami del tuo lavoro.
native_language_example: Tell me about your job.

additional_notes: Used to intensify a statement, meaning “completely/fully.” Very common with negatives: "non del tutto" = “not completely / not entirely.” It can also appear with agreement/disagreement: "del tutto in disaccordo" = “completely disagree.”
target_language_example: Non sono del tutto sicuro di aver capito.
native_language_example: I’m not entirely sure I understood.

meaning: of the village; from the village.
additional_notes: "Del" = "di + il" and shows possession/association ("the village's...") or origin ("someone from the village"). It’s used before a singular masculine noun (villaggio). Often translates as "of the village" or "in the village" depending on context (e.g., "la gente del villaggio" = "the village people / the people in the village").
target_language_example: Il bar del villaggio è chiuso oggi.
native_language_example: The village bar is closed today.

additional_notes: Used with the partitive article (del = di + il) to mean an unspecified amount of coffee. In questions it often corresponds to “any coffee?” in English (e.g., “Vuoi del caffè?” = “Do you want some/any coffee?”).
target_language_example: Vuoi del caffè dopo pranzo?
native_language_example: Do you want some coffee after lunch?

additional_notes: "Del" is a partitive article (di + il) used to mean “some” with uncountable nouns like cibo (“food”). In English you often just say “food” without “some.” It can also literally mean “of the food” in certain contexts, but in everyday sentences like the examples it usually means “some food.”
target_language_example: Abbiamo comprato del cibo per il viaggio.
native_language_example: We bought some food for the trip.

additional_notes: “Del” = “di + il” and is used as a partitive article to mean “some” with an uncountable noun (food). Common in offers, orders, and requests: “Vuoi del couscous?” / “Ho ordinato del couscous.” You can also see “del” change with gender/number: “della pasta”, “dei biscotti”, “dell’acqua”.
target_language_example: Per cena prendiamo del couscous e delle verdure.
native_language_example: For dinner let’s have some couscous and some vegetables.

additional_notes: Partitive form (di + il = del) used when you mean an unspecified amount of money. Common with verbs like dare (to give) and dovere (to owe): “dare del denaro” = to give someone some money; “dovere del denaro (a qualcuno)” = to owe someone money.
target_language_example: Non ho del denaro da prestarti oggi.
native_language_example: I don’t have any money to lend you today.

additional_notes: `del` is the partitive article (di + il) and is used to talk about an unspecified amount of something you can’t easily count (like ice cream, water, bread). It often translates as “some” or is left untranslated in English: *Vuoi del gelato?* = “Do you want (some) ice cream?” You can also hear *del* used in questions meaning “any”: *Vende del gelato qua?* = “Do they sell ice cream here?”
target_language_example: Prendiamo del gelato dopo cena.
native_language_example: Let’s get some ice cream after dinner.

additional_notes: "Del" is the partitive article (di + il). With uncountable nouns like latte, it often means “some” (an unspecified amount) and is very common when talking about buying, drinking, pouring, etc. In English you may simply say “milk” rather than “some milk,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Vorrei del latte nel caffè, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like some milk in my coffee, please.

additional_notes: Most often used in the phrase “fare del male (a qualcuno)” = “to harm/hurt (someone)”. It commonly appears with indirect object pronouns: “farmi del male” (hurt me), “farti del male” (hurt you), “gli/le fare del male” (hurt him/her), “farvi del male” (hurt you all/you formal).
target_language_example: Non voglio farti del male.
native_language_example: I don’t want to hurt you.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (del = di + il) to mean an unspecified quantity of an uncountable noun: “some bread / (any) bread.” Common with food and drink. In questions it often means “any”: “Hai del pane?” = “Do you have any bread?” With a specific bread already mentioned, “del” can also be closer to “of the bread,” but most beginner uses are simply “some.”
target_language_example: Vorrei del pane, per favore.
native_language_example: I'd like some bread, please.

additional_notes: "Del" is a partitive article (di + il) meaning “some” or “any” with a masculine singular mass noun. Used when talking about an unspecified quantity of fish (e.g., buying, selling, eating, cooking). Often paired with alternatives like "carne o pesce?"
target_language_example: Prendo del pesce e un po' di verdure.
native_language_example: I’ll have some fish and some vegetables.

additional_notes: "Del" is partitive: di + il = del. It’s used to talk about an unspecified quantity of something uncountable or plural (like rice). In English you often just say “rice,” or “some rice.” Used with verbs like mangiare (to eat), comprare (to buy), fare (to make/cook).
target_language_example: Per cena preparo del riso con le verdure.
native_language_example: For dinner I’m making some rice with vegetables.

meaning: some blood (an unspecified amount of blood).
additional_notes: Uses the partitive article "del" (= di + il) with an uncountable noun: "sangue". It often translates as "some/any blood" in English, especially when talking about finding/seeing blood ("c'è del sangue") or donating blood ("donare del sangue"). Literally it’s "of the blood," but in everyday use it means an unspecified quantity.
target_language_example: C'è del sangue sulla camicia.
native_language_example: There is some blood on the shirt.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article **del** (= **di + il**) to talk about an unspecified quantity of something uncountable or treated as uncountable. With foods you often use it to mean “some/any”: **mangiare del sushi** = “to eat (some) sushi.” In comparisons, it can be repeated: **Io ho ordinato del sushi e John del tempura** (“I ordered some sushi and John (ordered) some tempura”).
target_language_example: Prendiamo del sushi da asporto stasera.
native_language_example: Let’s get some sushi to take away tonight.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (di + il = del) to mean an unspecified amount of time. Very common with verbs like richiedere/servire (“to require/to need”) and with expressions like avere ancora del tempo (“to still have some time”). Often translates naturally as “some time” or just “time,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Dammi del tempo e ti rispondo domani.
native_language_example: Give me some time and I’ll reply to you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has free time available. "del" is the partitive article (like “some”), so it often suggests an unspecified amount of free time rather than a specific time slot. Common with verbs like "avere" (to have): "Hai del tempo libero?"
target_language_example: Hai del tempo libero stasera?
native_language_example: Do you have some free time tonight?

meaning: some wine (an unspecified amount of wine).
additional_notes: "Del" is the partitive article (di + il) used with uncountable nouns like vino to mean “some/any” rather than a specific quantity. It’s common with verbs like bere (to drink), comprare (to buy), avere (to have). In negatives, Italian often uses "non ..." without the partitive (e.g., "Non ho vino" = "I don't have any wine"), though "non ho del vino" can sound more like “I don’t have (any) of that wine.”
target_language_example: Vuoi del vino o dell'acqua?
native_language_example: Do you want some wine or water?

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article "del" (di + il) to mean an unspecified amount of something. In English it’s usually translated as “some” (not “of the”). Common in questions and everyday statements: "Hai del vino rosso?" = “Do you have any red wine?”
target_language_example: Vorrei del vino rosso, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like some red wine, please.

meaning: “of his/her/its” (referring to a feminine singular noun); sometimes “about his/her …” after verbs like dire/parlare.
additional_notes: Formed by **di + la + sua**. Used before a **feminine singular** noun: *della sua casa* (“of his/her house”), *della sua medicina* (“of his/her medicine”), *della sua relazione* (“of his/her relationship”). The possessive **sua** agrees with the thing owned (feminine singular), not with the owner. After verbs like **dire/parlare/raccontare/rivelare**, **di** often means “about”: *disse a Mary della sua macchina nuova* (“he told Mary about his new car”).
target_language_example: Non parlare della sua vita privata.
native_language_example: Don’t talk about his/her private life.

meaning: about her/his family; of her/his family.
additional_notes: "Della" = "di + la". With verbs like "parlare/dire/raccontare" it often means "about" (e.g., "parlare della sua famiglia" = "to talk about his/her family"). It can also show possession/relationship ("la visita della sua famiglia" = "his/her family's visit"). "Sua" agrees with what is owned (famiglia), not with the owner; it can mean either "his" or "her" depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi ha parlato della sua famiglia durante la cena.
native_language_example: He/She talked to me about his/her family during dinner.

additional_notes: Used to mean an unspecified amount of music (not specific songs). Very common after verbs like ascoltare (to listen to), sentire (to hear), and suonare (to play). Formed from di + la = della + musica; in negatives you’ll often hear non + verb + (molta) musica instead of della musica.
target_language_example: Vuoi ascoltare della musica mentre cuciniamo?
native_language_example: Do you want to listen to some music while we cook?

additional_notes: "Della" is a partitive article (di + la) used to talk about an unspecified amount of something. With food, it often means “some” (not a whole pizza). Similar forms: "del pane" (some bread), "dell’acqua" (some water), "dei biscotti" (some cookies).
target_language_example: Vuoi della pizza o preferisci la pasta?
native_language_example: Do you want some pizza or do you prefer pasta?

meaning: “of the (female) cat” / “belonging to the cat”; also used as a surname or place/business name.
additional_notes: Grammatically it’s the preposition+article combo **di + la = della** (“of the / belonging to the”), plus **gatta** (“female cat”). If you see it capitalized (**Della Gatta**), it may be a **proper name** (e.g., a last name, street name, restaurant name) rather than referring to an actual cat.
target_language_example: Questa ciotola è della gatta.
native_language_example: This bowl belongs to the cat.

meaning: "of Reason" / "of the Reason" (often used in names, e.g., buildings or institutions).
additional_notes: This is the preposition+article combination "della" (= di + la, “of the”) plus "ragione" (“reason”). You’ll often see it capitalized as part of a proper name (for example, in place names like "Palazzo della Ragione"). In normal sentences you more commonly see it in lowercase: "della ragione".
target_language_example: Ci vediamo davanti al Palazzo della Ragione.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in front of the Palazzo della Ragione.

meaning: “of the city” / “in the city” (referring to something belonging to or within a city).
additional_notes: It’s the preposition articolata made from di + la = della. Used to link something to the city: the governor of the city (governatore della città), the biggest mosque in the city (la moschea più grande della città), the best lasagna in the city (le migliori lasagne della città). Often appears with superlatives like più grande / migliore to mean “in the city.”
target_language_example: È uno dei parchi più belli della città.
native_language_example: It’s one of the most beautiful parks in the city.

additional_notes: Used with nouns to show something belongs to or relates to a family group. Often followed by a surname or name (e.g., "della famiglia Rossi" = "of the Rossi family"), or used in general ("il resto della famiglia" = "the rest of the family"). It’s the contraction of "di" + "la".
target_language_example: Parliamo della famiglia di Marco stasera.
native_language_example: Let’s talk about Marco’s family tonight.

additional_notes: “della” is the contraction of **di + la** (“of the”) and is used to link something to “the war”: *il dio della guerra* (“the god of war”), *il pericolo della guerra* (“the danger of war”). It also appears after some expressions like **prima della** (“before the”) and in comparisons after **meglio/peggio**: *La pace è meglio della guerra* (“Peace is better than war”).
target_language_example: Spero che non si parli più della guerra.
native_language_example: I hope people don’t talk about the war anymore.

meaning: “of the car” / “the car’s” (feminine singular: di + la).
additional_notes: Used to show possession or a relationship with something: la chiave della macchina (the car key), il motore della macchina (the car’s engine), il prezzo della macchina (the car’s price). It’s the preposition "di" + feminine singular article "la" → "della". Often interchangeable with the English ’s or “of the …” depending on what sounds natural.
target_language_example: Ho perso le chiavi della macchina.
native_language_example: I lost the car keys.

additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to or happened during your life. Very common after superlatives or time expressions: “il giorno migliore/peggiore della mia vita” (the best/worst day of my life), “i tre giorni più lunghi della mia vita” (the three longest days of my life). You may also see it in expressions like “a rischio della mia vita” (“at the risk of my life”).
target_language_example: È stata la decisione più importante della mia vita.
native_language_example: It was the most important decision of my life.

additional_notes: Contraction of "di + la morte". Used to link something to death, often after a noun: "il pensiero della morte" (the thought of death), "la paura della morte" (fear of death). It can also be used in dramatic/figurative labels or names like "il pianeta della morte" (the planet of death).
target_language_example: Ho paura della morte, ma cerco di non pensarci troppo.
native_language_example: I'm afraid of death, but I try not to think about it too much.

additional_notes: It’s the preposition+article combo **di + la = della** followed by the possessive **nostra** (“our,” feminine singular). Used before a feminine singular noun: **della nostra scuola** (of our school), **della nostra epoca** (of our era), **della nostra comunità** (of our community). For masculine singular you’ll often see **del nostro**; plural forms include **delle nostre / dei nostri**.
target_language_example: Questa è una tradizione della nostra famiglia.
native_language_example: This is a tradition of our family.

meaning: 'of the police' / 'police' (used to describe something belonging to or connected with the police).
additional_notes: It’s the contraction of **di + la** (“of the” + feminine singular). It’s used after a noun to specify a connection/possession, e.g. **la protezione della polizia** (“police protection”), **il cane della polizia** (“police dog”), **gli archivi della polizia** (“police records/files”), **a disposizione della polizia** (“at the police’s disposal / available to the police”).
target_language_example: Hanno chiesto l’aiuto della polizia.
native_language_example: They asked for the help of the police.

additional_notes: "Della" is the contraction of "di + la". It’s used to indicate possession or relationship ("of the school") and sometimes origin/source ("from the school"), depending on context. It agrees with a feminine singular noun like "scuola" (la scuola).
target_language_example: La segreteria della scuola è aperta fino alle 16:00.
native_language_example: The school office is open until 4:00 p.m.

additional_notes: Literally “of the his/her family.” Uses **di + definite article** (**della** = di + la) to mean “about/of” depending on the verb. Common patterns: **sapere qualcosa di** (to know something about), **non sapere niente di** (to know nothing about), **avere bisogno di** (to need), **importare di** (to care about). **Sua** can mean “his” or “her” based on context.
target_language_example: Non voglio parlare della sua famiglia adesso.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about his/her family right now.

additional_notes: Used after verbs that take the preposition di, like convincere qualcuno di qualcosa (to convince someone of something) and approfittare di qualcuno/qualcosa (to take advantage of someone/something). Della = di + la. Sua can mean "his" or "her" depending on context.
target_language_example: Non sono sicuro della sua innocenza.
native_language_example: I'm not sure of his/her innocence.

additional_notes: Used after verbs/adjectives that take the preposition di (which combines with la → della), e.g. essere fiero/orgoglioso/convinto di (“to be proud/convinced of”) or rispondere di (“to vouch for / be accountable for”). Sua agrees with the feminine noun onestà, and can mean “his,” “her,” or formal “your,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Non dubito della sua onestà.
native_language_example: I don’t doubt his/her honesty.

additional_notes: Contraction of **di + la** plus **tua**. It’s used before a **feminine singular** noun: *la tua età* → **della tua età** (“of your age”), *la tua esperienza* → **della tua esperienza** (“of your experience”). With some verbs and expressions that take **di** (e.g., *fidarsi di*), it can mean “to trust **your** …”: *fidarmi della tua parola* = “trust your word.”
target_language_example: Non dubitare della tua capacità di farcela.
native_language_example: Don’t doubt your ability to do it.

meaning: “of your life” / “in your life” (talking about your life).
additional_notes: Used with nouns and expressions to refer to your life in general (“the rest of your life”, “the happiest moment of your life”), or with verbs like fare/che cosa fare to mean “what to do with your life.” It’s the combination of di + la (“della”) + tua (“your”, informal singular) + vita (“life”).
target_language_example: È la decisione più importante della tua vita.
native_language_example: It’s the most important decision of your life.

additional_notes: Combination of di + la (= della) + vita. Often used in set phrases like i piaceri della vita (“the pleasures of life”), lo scopo della vita (“the purpose of life”), and il costo della vita (“the cost of living”). In expressions about living conditions, it’s usually translated as “of living” rather than literally “of life.”
target_language_example: Il costo della vita qui è molto alto.
native_language_example: The cost of living here is very high.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article "della" (di + la) to mean an unspecified amount of an uncountable noun. Common after verbs like "bere" (to drink), "comprare" (to buy), and "volere" (to want). Literally it looks like "of the beer," but in everyday English you usually translate it as "some beer" (or just "beer" depending on context).
target_language_example: Per la festa abbiamo preso della birra e delle bibite.
native_language_example: For the party we got some beer and some soft drinks.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified quantity of meat. It’s made of di + la (= della) + carne, and is common when ordering food or describing what someone ate. In questions/offers you’ll often hear it contrasted with another option: "della carne o del pesce?"
target_language_example: Per cena prendiamo della carne alla griglia.
native_language_example: For dinner we’ll have some grilled meat.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (di + la → della) to mean an unspecified amount of an uncountable food item (fruit). Often used when offering, buying, or talking about eating fruit in general (not specific pieces).
target_language_example: Per colazione prendo della frutta e un caffè.
native_language_example: For breakfast I have some fruit and a coffee.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (di + la → della) with an uncountable noun. It often means “some/any music” rather than “of the music,” especially with verbs like ascoltare (to listen to), sentire (to hear), and suonare (to play). In questions/negatives it can mean “any music.”
target_language_example: Vuoi della musica italiana?
native_language_example: Do you want some Italian music?

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (di + la → della) to mean an unspecified amount of a mass food item. Common with verbs like prendere/mangiare/ordinare when you don’t specify quantity (vs. "una pizza" = a whole pizza).
target_language_example: Vuoi della pizza o preferisci la pasta?
native_language_example: Do you want some pizza or do you prefer pasta?

additional_notes: "Delle" is the partitive article (di + le) used to mean "some" with feminine plural nouns. "Cose" is a very common, general word meaning "things" (objects, tasks, matters, events). Often used when you don’t want to be specific: "devo controllare delle cose" = "I have to check a few things."
target_language_example: Prima di uscire, devo comprare delle cose per la cena.
native_language_example: Before going out, I have to buy some things for dinner.

additional_notes: Used when you mean an unspecified number of questions. Common in polite contexts like meetings, lessons, or customer service: “Avete/Ha delle domande?” = “Do you have any questions?” Note: “delle” is a partitive article (di + le) meaning “some.”
target_language_example: Se avete delle domande, chiedete pure.
native_language_example: If you have any questions, feel free to ask.

additional_notes: "Delle" is the partitive article (di + le) used to mean “some” with plural feminine nouns. In everyday speech, "Ho delle foto" can simply mean “I have photos,” without emphasizing “some.” "Foto" is short for "fotografie" and is feminine plural here.
target_language_example: Hai delle foto del viaggio?
native_language_example: Do you have any photos from the trip?

additional_notes: “Delle” is a partitive article (di + le) used to mean an unspecified quantity: “some”. It’s common with plural count nouns like “mele” (apples), especially when buying, eating, giving, or having an unspecified amount. In negative sentences you often use “non … (delle)”, and very often “non … mele” without the partitive (e.g., “Non ho mele”).
target_language_example: Vorrei delle mele, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like some apples, please.

additional_notes: Partitive article + adjective: **delle** (= “some”) + **nuove** (= “new”, feminine plural). Used before a **feminine plural noun**: *delle nuove macchine / delle nuove persone / delle nuove amicizie / delle nuove frasi*. Similar patterns: **dei nuovi** (masc. plural), **delle nuove** (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Ho comprato delle nuove scarpe.
native_language_example: I bought some new shoes.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article "delle" (di + le) to mean an unspecified quantity: "some" (plural, feminine). In contexts like "Vogliamo delle risposte", English often drops "some" and simply says "We want answers" to sound natural.
target_language_example: Vorrei delle risposte subito.
native_language_example: I want some answers right now.

additional_notes: Used when you mean an indefinite quantity: usually “some shoes” or “a pair of shoes,” without specifying which ones. "Delle" is the partitive article (di + le) and often corresponds to English “some/any.” In negatives it often becomes "non ... delle" (e.g., "ma non delle calze").
target_language_example: Mi servono delle scarpe comode per camminare.
native_language_example: I need some comfortable shoes for walking.

additional_notes: "Delle" is a partitive article meaning “some” (an unspecified quantity). "Delle uova" is used when you don’t mean a specific, exact number of eggs. If you mean specific eggs, you’d say "le uova" (the eggs); if you mean a set number, use a number: "due uova" (two eggs).
target_language_example: Devo comprare delle uova per la frittata.
native_language_example: I have to buy some eggs for the omelet.

additional_notes: "Delle" is a partitive article meaning "some" (di + le). It’s used with plural feminine nouns like "verdure" to talk about an unspecified quantity. Often in English you may simply say "vegetables" without "some" (e.g., "You should eat vegetables").
target_language_example: Vorrei comprare delle verdure per la cena.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy some vegetables for dinner.

additional_notes: This is the preposition **di** + the plural feminine definite article **le** (“the”), contracted to **delle**. It often means **“of the women”** (possession/comparison: *più potere delle donne* = “more power than women”) or **“about women”** after verbs like *pensare/parlare di* (*Cosa pensi delle donne?* = “What do you think about women?”). In other contexts, **delle donne** can also mean **“some women”** (partitive), e.g. *Ci sono delle donne qui.*
target_language_example: Parliamo delle donne nella storia italiana.
native_language_example: Let’s talk about women in Italian history.

additional_notes: This is the contraction of **di + le mie**. It’s used with feminine plural nouns (often omitted because it’s understood): **una delle mie (cose/amiche/specialità)** = “one of my …”. It also appears after verbs that take **di** (e.g. **rispondere di**) to mean “to be responsible/accountable **for**”: **rispondere delle mie azioni** = “to answer for my actions.”
target_language_example: Questa è una delle mie canzoni preferite.
native_language_example: This is one of my favorite songs.

meaning: "of the people" / "of some people"; also "than people" after comparatives.
additional_notes: It’s the combination of **di + le persone**. Most often it means **“of the people”** (e.g., *i gatti delle persone ricche* = “the cats of rich people”; *prendersi cura delle persone anziane* = “take care of elderly people”). After comparatives (*più/meno*), **di** means **“than”**, so *più delle persone* = “more than people.”
target_language_example: Ho parlato con alcune delle persone del mio corso.
native_language_example: I spoke with some of the people in my class.

meaning: 'of her' / 'of his' / 'of its' / 'of your (formal)' (with feminine plural nouns).
additional_notes: Made of **di + le = delle** (“of the / some of the”) + **sue** (feminine plural of the possessive *suo*). It’s used before a **feminine plural noun**: *delle sue amiche* = “of her friends”. Often appears after verbs/adjectives that take **di** (e.g., *essere sicuro di…* → *sicura delle sue idee* = “sure of her ideas”) or in expressions like *ridere di…* (“laugh at…”) and *cadere vittima di…* (“fall victim to…”). The exact person (his/her/its/your formal) comes from context.
target_language_example: Ho parlato con alcune delle sue sorelle.
native_language_example: I spoke with some of her sisters.

meaning: “of your” (feminine plural), often in phrases like “one of your …” or “enough of your …”
additional_notes: “Delle” = di + le (“of the”, feminine plural). “Tue” is the feminine plural of “your” (tuo/tua/tui/tue). It’s used with feminine plural nouns (e.g., regole, studentesse, cazzate) and very commonly after expressions like “una delle tue …” (“one of your …”) or “abbastanza delle tue …” (“enough of your …”).
target_language_example: Non voglio sentire altre delle tue scuse.
native_language_example: I don’t want to hear any more of your excuses.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive plural article **delle** (di + le) + **cose** (“things”) to mean an indefinite amount: “some things / a few things.” Common with verbs like **dire** (“to say/tell”): *Devo dirti delle cose* = “I need to tell you some things.” Literally it can also mean “of the things,” but in everyday speech it often just means “some.”
target_language_example: Prima di partire, devo dirti delle cose importanti.
native_language_example: Before leaving, I have to tell you some important things.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (di + le → delle) to mean an unspecified number/amount of letters. Common with verbs like scrivere (“to write”): Scrivo delle lettere = “I write some letters / I write letters.” In questions it can mean “any”: Ha delle lettere? = “Do you have any letters?”
target_language_example: Ti mando delle lettere quando posso.
native_language_example: I’ll send you some letters when I can.

additional_notes: "Delle" is the partitive article (di + le) meaning "some" with feminine plural nouns. It’s used when the quantity isn’t specified. Here it introduces the plural noun "mele" (apples). In negatives, Italian often uses "non ... (alcuna)" instead of the partitive: "Non ho mele" / "Non ho alcuna mela."
target_language_example: Vorrei comprare delle mele, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy some apples, please.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive plural article "delle" (di + le) to mean an indefinite quantity: "some". It’s commonly used with verbs like "scrivere" (to write): "scrivere delle poesie" = "to write some poems". In many cases you can also say just "scrivo poesie" with a similar general meaning ("I write poetry / I write poems").
target_language_example: Ti ho scritto delle poesie.
native_language_example: I wrote you some poems.

additional_notes: "Delle" is the partitive article (di + le) used with feminine plural nouns to mean an unspecified quantity: "some" or sometimes simply plural "eggs" in English. It’s common after verbs like preparare (to prepare), comprare (to buy), vendere (to sell), mangiare (to eat), trasportare (to carry/transport). Singular equivalents: "dell’uovo" (some egg) and plural masculine: "dei" / "degli". In the phrase "bacon e uova", Italian often uses the partitive for the eggs: "del bacon e delle uova".
target_language_example: Compro delle uova al supermercato.
native_language_example: I’m buying some eggs at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used when talking about an unspecified quantity of sugar (not “the sugar” in general). It’s made of the partitive article "dello" (di + lo) + "zucchero" and is common with food/drinks: "Vuoi dello zucchero?" = “Do you want some sugar?”
target_language_example: Mi dai dello zucchero, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you give me some sugar, please?

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happens inside a specific feminine singular place/thing. It’s made of dentro + the definite article la. For masculine singular, use “dentro il/lo” (often “dentro il” becomes “dentro al” in everyday Italian). Often interchangeable with “in” in some contexts (e.g., “dentro la moschea”), but “dentro” emphasizes being physically inside.
target_language_example: C'è un regalo dentro la borsa.
native_language_example: There’s a gift inside the bag.

meaning: “having said/told her that …” / “(I/they) told her that …”.
additional_notes: A fragment often used to introduce reported speech or an explanation. It combines the past participle detto (“said/told”) with che (“that”) and a lei (“to her”). In full sentences you’ll often see something like: “Le ho detto che …” (I told her that …) or “Detto che a lei …, …” (Having told her …, …).
target_language_example: Le ho detto che a lei non posso promettere nulla.
native_language_example: I told her that I can’t promise her anything.

additional_notes: Used when reporting what you told someone about another person (or 'you' informally). It’s built from: (ho) detto = 'I said/told', che = 'that', eri = 'you were' (imperfect of essere, used for a past state). Often preceded by an indirect object pronoun like gli ('to him') or le ('to her'): Gli ho detto che eri… = 'I told him you were…'. Adjectives may agree in gender: impegnato/occupato (male), impegnata/occupata (female).
target_language_example: Le ho detto che eri stanco e che saresti arrivato più tardi.
native_language_example: I told her you were tired and that you would arrive later.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech after verbs like dire (“to say/tell”). It introduces what someone said about you: (ha) detto che ero + adjective/noun/phrase. Note that ero is the imperfect of essere (“to be”), commonly used after che in indirect speech (e.g., “he said that I was sick”).
target_language_example: Mi hanno detto che ero in ritardo.
native_language_example: They told me that I was late.

meaning: “said/told that to him/them” (often part of a longer sentence).
additional_notes: This is usually not a standalone phrase, but a fragment you’ll see inside a sentence. "detto" is the past participle of **dire** (to say/tell), "che" introduces a clause (“that …”), and **gli** is an indirect object pronoun meaning **to him** (and sometimes **to them** in informal/colloquial Italian). Often used after an auxiliary verb: *ho detto che gli…* / *avevo detto che gli…*
target_language_example: Gli ho detto che gli mando un messaggio più tardi.
native_language_example: I told him that I’ll send him a message later.

additional_notes: Past form of "dire di no" (to say no, to refuse). Very common with object pronouns to show who you refused: "Le ho detto di no" (I said no to her), "Mi ha detto di no" (He/She said no to me), "Ti ho detto di no" (I said no to you). Often used with "già" to mean "already" ("I already told you no").
target_language_example: Gli ho detto di no perché non potevo.
native_language_example: I told him no because I couldn't.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "dire" (to tell/say) + "di" + infinitive to report an instruction/advice: "dire a qualcuno di non fare qualcosa" = "to tell someone not to do something". In the passive, you’ll often see it as "è stato detto di non farlo" (was told not to do it). "Farlo" means "to do it" (fare + lo).
target_language_example: Mi hanno detto di non farlo, ma l’ho fatto lo stesso.
native_language_example: They told me not to do it, but I did it anyway.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "dire" in the past: "ha detto la verità" (he/she told the truth), "mi ha detto la verità" (he/she told me the truth). It refers to telling what is true rather than lying or hiding information. In sentences with a doubt/opinion verb (e.g., "penso che", "pensi che"), Italian often uses the subjunctive: "abbia detto la verità".
target_language_example: Finalmente mi ha detto la verità.
native_language_example: At last he told me the truth.

additional_notes: Used with the negation **non**: **non ho detto niente** = “I didn’t say anything.” Italian commonly uses double negation (**non ... niente**) where English uses a single negative. You can change the indirect object: **non gli ho detto niente** (“I didn’t tell him anything”), **non mi ha detto niente** (“she didn’t tell me anything”).
target_language_example: Non ti ho detto niente perché non lo sapevo.
native_language_example: I didn’t tell you anything because I didn’t know.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is required/obliged to leave or go somewhere. Often followed by a destination introduced by "a" (e.g., "deve andare a casa") or set phrases like "fuori" (outside), "in galera" (to jail/prison), "a letto" (to bed). Can be used in questions and with formal "Lei" (e.g., "Lei deve andare ora?").
target_language_example: Lei deve andare ora?
native_language_example: Do you have to go now?

additional_notes: Used to express either a strong guess/deduction ('it must be...') or necessity/obligation ('it has to be...'), depending on context. It is often followed by a noun or adjective, and it can also be used in the passive, as in 'deve essere sostituito' = 'has to be replaced'. With a past participle phrase like 'deve essere stato', it means 'must have been'.
target_language_example: Deve essere molto tardi.
native_language_example: It must be very late.

meaning: 'must be very…' / 'she/he must be really…' (making a guess).
additional_notes: Used to make a strong assumption or inference based on what you see/know (not an obligation). It’s followed by an adjective: e.g., deve essere molto stanca/stanco (very tired). The adjective usually agrees with the person: affamata (female), affamato (male). Often you can add a time word like adesso (now).
target_language_example: Dopo il viaggio, deve essere molto stanco.
native_language_example: After the trip, he must be very tired.

meaning: "must have been" (a guess/inference about the past).
additional_notes: Used to express a strong assumption about how something was in the past, based on clues or what seems likely. It’s the present of "dovere" (deve = must) + infinitive "essere" + past participle "stato". It changes for gender/number: "deve essere stata" (she/it [f.] must have been), "devono essere stati" (they [m./mixed] must have been), "devono essere state" (they [f.] must have been). Negative: "non deve essere stato" = "it must not have been" / "it can’t have been."
target_language_example: Deve essere stato un periodo difficile per te.
native_language_example: It must have been a difficult time for you.

additional_notes: Means someone is required/obliged to work. "Deve" is the 3rd-person singular of "dovere" (must/have to), used with an infinitive like "lavorare". The subject can be said (e.g., "Lei deve lavorare") or understood from context.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma oggi deve lavorare fino a tardi.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but today he/she has to work until late.

additional_notes: Uses the verb dovere (devi = “you must/have to,” 2nd person singular) + andare (“to go”). It can mean you need to leave (“Do you have to go?”) or that you must go somewhere/do something (“You have to go upstairs,” “You have to go on foot”). Often followed by a destination with a/da/in/su, or by an adverb phrase like a piedi (“on foot”), di sopra (“upstairs”), fino in fondo (“all the way / to the end”).
target_language_example: Tu devi andare?
native_language_example: Do you have to go?

additional_notes: "Devi" is the present tense of "dovere" (to have to / must) for "tu" (you). It’s followed by an infinitive like "fare" (to do/make): "devi fare X" = you must do X. Often used to give instructions, obligations, or advice; in questions it can mean "what do you need to do with it?" (e.g., "che diavolo ci devi fare?").
target_language_example: Devi fare attenzione quando attraversi la strada.
native_language_example: You have to be careful when you cross the street.

meaning: 'you must/need to be' or 'you must/need to stay'.
additional_notes:
Used to give a strong instruction or necessity ("you have to..."). Very common with:
- adjectives: "Devi stare calmo" (you must be calm), "Devi stare sveglio" (stay awake)
- places/positions: "Devi stare fuori" (stay outside)
- distance: "Devi stare lontano/a" (stay away)
- "stare a" + infinitive: "Devi stare a sentire" (you have to listen).
"Devi" is 2nd person singular (tu).
target_language_example: Devi stare qui finché torno.
native_language_example: You have to stay here until I come back.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an honest admission, often something you didn’t expect, don’t really want to say, or are acknowledging after thinking about it. Common in both spoken and written Italian. You can also hear it as “devo ammettere” without “che” when the sentence continues in another way.
target_language_example: Devo ammettere che avevi ragione.
native_language_example: I must admit that you were right.

additional_notes: First-person singular of dovere + andare. Used to say that you need to leave or go somewhere. It can be followed by a destination (devo andare in stazione) or by another verb, often with a, to express purpose (devo andare a lavorare).
target_language_example: Scusa, devo andare adesso.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go now.

additional_notes: Used with either (1) a place: "devo andare a una conferenza" = "I have to go to a conference", or (2) "a" + infinitive to express purpose/what you need to go and do: "devo andare a dirglielo" = "I have to go tell him/her/you." In everyday English, this often translates as "I have to go (and) ..." even if Italian keeps "andare a".
target_language_example: Scusa, devo andare a prendere i bambini.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go pick up the kids.

additional_notes: First-person singular of dovere + dire. It is used when the speaker says they need or are obliged to say/tell something. In context, dire can mean either "say" or "tell" in English.
target_language_example: Devo dire la verità.
native_language_example: I have to tell the truth.

meaning: “I must be / I have to be.”
additional_notes: Used to express necessity/obligation about your state, location, or behavior: *Devo essere qui* (“I have to be here”), *Devo essere onesto* (“I must be honest”). It’s often followed by an adjective or phrase. The adjective agrees with the speaker: masculine *contento/sicuro/sincero*, feminine *contenta/sicura/sincera*. It can also introduce an opinion politely: *Devo essere sincero…* (“I have to be honest…” / “I must say…”).
target_language_example: Scusa, devo essere a casa entro le otto.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to be home by eight.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity. It’s the verb phrase "dovere" (to have to/must) + "fare" (to do/make). The object is often a verb in the infinitive (e.g., "devo fare", "devo studiare"). With pronouns, you can place them before "devo" ("Lo devo fare") or attach them to the infinitive ("Devo farlo"); both mean “I have to do it.”
target_language_example: Scusa, devo fare una telefonata.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to make a phone call.

additional_notes: Used to say you are obligated to work (because of your job, a duty, or a necessity). It can be followed by details like who you work with (con Tom) or when (stasera). Often said as an excuse or to complain: “Ma io devo lavorare!”
target_language_example: Scusa, non posso venire: devo lavorare domani.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have to work tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you must/need to talk to someone. It’s made of: devo (“I must/I have to”) + parlare (“to speak/talk”) + con (“with”). The person you want to talk to comes after con (e.g., con lui/lei/te/voi, con Tom). Often followed by details like in privato (“in private”) or riguardo a… (“about/regarding…”).
target_language_example: Devo parlare con la professoressa dopo la lezione.
native_language_example: I need to talk to the teacher after the lesson.

meaning: “I have to find” / “I need to find.”
additional_notes: Used when you must locate something/someone (“Devo trovare la chiave”) or when you must figure out/get something (“Devo trovare un modo…”, “Devo trovare un altro lavoro”). Often followed by a noun or by “un modo per + infinitive” (a way to do something).
target_language_example: Devo trovare un modo per arrivare in tempo.
native_language_example: I need to find a way to arrive on time.

meaning: “they must be / have to be” (also “they must have…” as a guess).
additional_notes: Formed by dovere (must/have to) + essere (to be). Used either for obligation/requirement (things/people are required to be something or to be done) or to make a strong assumption about a situation (like “They must have gone crazy”). The subject is “they” or a plural noun.
target_language_example: Per entrare, i biglietti devono essere validi.
native_language_example: To enter, the tickets must be valid.

additional_notes: Literally means “of (a) woman.” In everyday Italian you’ll often see it in labels and shopping contexts to mean “women’s,” especially with clothing and accessories: e.g., "abbigliamento di donna" (women’s clothing), "scarpe di donna" (women’s shoes). When it refers to a specific woman, it can also mean “(belonging) to the woman,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Sto cercando un cappotto di donna.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a women’s coat.

meaning: “of May” (used as part of a last name).
additional_notes: In Italian names, di/Di + a word can be part of the surname (e.g., “Nihad di Maggio”). In this use, you normally keep it as-is and don’t translate it. It may be written with a lowercase or uppercase D depending on the person’s preference and official documents.
target_language_example: Ha detto di chiamarsi Luca Di Maggio.
native_language_example: He said his name is Luca Di Maggio.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something connected to the sea. Very common in set phrases like: frutti di mare (seafood), pesce di mare (saltwater fish), aria di mare (sea air), città/paese di mare (seaside town).
target_language_example: Vorrei un piatto di frutti di mare.
native_language_example: I’d like a seafood dish.

additional_notes: Most commonly used after a noun to specify that something is related to life (e.g., qualità di vita = quality of life; stile di vita = lifestyle; speranza di vita = life expectancy). In some fixed phrases it can mean 'for life' (e.g., condannato all’ergastolo, in carcere a vita = in prison for life).
target_language_example: È importante avere una buona qualità di vita.
native_language_example: It’s important to have a good quality of life.

additional_notes: "Di" + infinitive is very common in Italian after certain verbs to introduce what someone is asked/told/decides to do. For example: "chiedere a qualcuno di aiutare" (to ask someone to help), "decidere di aiutare" (to decide to help), "dire a qualcuno di aiutare" / "essere detto di aiutare" (to tell someone to help / to be told to help). In English this is usually just "to + verb" (to help), not "of helping."
target_language_example: Mi ha chiesto di aiutare con i compiti.
native_language_example: He/She asked me to help with the homework.

meaning: to help her (or to help you, formal).
additional_notes: Used as "di" + infinitive after many verbs (e.g., cercare di…, chiedere di…, avere tempo di…, offrirsi di…) to mean “to …”. "Aiutarla" = aiutare + "la" (her / you, formal).
target_language_example: Ho promesso di aiutarla domani.
native_language_example: I promised to help her tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used after the verb "essere" (to be) to say something/someone is helpful: "È di aiuto" = "It’s helpful" / "It helps." You’ll also see "di aiuto" after nouns like "richiesta" or "offerta" to mean "for help" (e.g., "richiesta di aiuto" = "request for help").
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno, sarò di aiuto.
native_language_example: If you need it, I’ll be of help.

additional_notes: Used as di + infinitive after many verbs and adjectives, where English often just uses 'to' + verb. For example: dire a qualcuno di andare = 'to tell someone to go', permettere di andare = 'to allow someone to go', essere libero di andare = 'to be free to go'.
target_language_example: Mi ha detto di andare subito.
native_language_example: She told me to go right away.

meaning: 'to go home' (infinitive phrase, often after another expression).
additional_notes: Used after verbs/adjectives/nouns that take "di + infinitive" (e.g., "avere fretta di..." = to be in a hurry to..., "essere liberi di..." = to be free to..., "è tempo di..." = it’s time to...). "A casa" means "home" and "andare" means "to go".
target_language_example: Sono contento di andare a casa presto.
native_language_example: I’m happy to go home early.

additional_notes: Used when an infinitive clause is introduced by "di" after many verbs (e.g., chiedere di… = to ask to…, pregare di… = to beg/request to…, pensare di… = to plan/think of…). "Andare via" is a common way to say 'leave' (a place/situation). In polite requests you may see: "La prego di andare via" = 'Please leave.'
target_language_example: Mi hanno detto di andare via subito.
native_language_example: They told me to leave right away.

meaning: to leave; to go away (often: to go away from a place/situation).
additional_notes: Used after many verbs that take **di + infinitive** (e.g., *dire, chiedere, pregare, scegliere, decidere*): **"Digli di andarsene"** = "Tell him to leave." The core verb is **andarsene** (pronominal: *andare + si + ne*), often implying leaving a place or situation, sometimes with a stronger tone like "go away." Common related forms: *me ne vado* (I’m leaving), *vattene* (go away), *se n’è andato/a* (he/she left).
target_language_example: Per favore, gli dica di andarsene.
native_language_example: Please, tell him to leave.

meaning: 'to wait' (used with an infinitive after another verb, e.g., 'tell someone to wait').
additional_notes: Often follows verbs like dire/chiedere (to say/ask), as in "dire a qualcuno di aspettare" = "to tell someone to wait". Here "di" introduces the infinitive "aspettare". Note: "aspettare" can look like English "to expect"—but it usually means "to wait".
target_language_example: Ti chiedo di aspettare qui un momento.
native_language_example: I’m asking you to wait here a moment.

meaning: 'to have' after a verb (in an infinitive clause), often meaning 'that (someone) has…'.
additional_notes: Used when a verb is followed by an infinitive clause introduced by "di" (common after verbs like dire, ammettere, negare, accusare, ringraziare). "Avere" is the infinitive "to have"; with "di" it often corresponds to English "to have" or "that (I/you/he/she/they) have". Example: "Dice di avere finito" = "He says he has finished." In everyday speech, you may also hear "di aver" (shortened form of "di avere").
target_language_example: Spero di avere abbastanza tempo per finire.
native_language_example: I hope I have enough time to finish.

additional_notes: Used after many verbs to link them to the infinitive avere. In English it is often just 'to have', but after verbs like pensare or dire it may be translated more naturally as 'that I have', 'that she has', etc. Usually the subject is understood from the main verb.
target_language_example: Penso di avere abbastanza tempo.
native_language_example: I think I have enough time.

meaning: 'for having done it' / 'to have done it'.
additional_notes: Used with "di" + infinitive past (aver fatto) + object pronoun (lo = "it") to talk about an action that happened before the main verb. Common after verbs/adjectives like ringraziare (to thank), ammettere (to admit), negare (to deny), essere felice/contento (to be happy/glad): e.g., "Grazie di averlo fatto" (Thanks for doing it). "Averlo" = "avere" + "lo" (to have it/done it), and "fatto" is the past participle of "fare".
target_language_example: Mi dispiace di averlo fatto.
native_language_example: I'm sorry I did it.

meaning: "to have (done something) to you" / "of having (done something) to you".
additional_notes: Used with the past infinitive: di + aver + object pronoun (ti → becomes -ti attached: averti). It refers to an action completed before the main verb (e.g., "Sono felice di averti visto" = I’m happy to have seen you). Common after expressions like felice di..., mi dispiace di..., piacere di..., credevo/pensavo di....
target_language_example: Mi dispiace di averti disturbato così tardi.
native_language_example: I’m sorry to have bothered you so late.

additional_notes: Often used with nouns to mean “basic/fundamental” (e.g., significato di base, teoria di base, problema di base). It can also describe where someone is mainly located: “Sono di base a/su…” = “I’m based in…” (common with cities/areas).
target_language_example: Di base, sono d'accordo con te, ma abbiamo bisogno di più tempo.
native_language_example: Basically, I agree with you, but we need more time.

additional_notes: Often used in casual conversation, especially in the question "Cosa fai di bello?" meaning “What are you up to (that’s nice/interesting)?” In answers it can mean “nothing special” ("Di bello niente"). In other contexts it keeps a more literal meaning: "qualcosa di bello" = “something beautiful/nice.”
target_language_example: Allora, cosa c’è di bello stasera?
native_language_example: So, what’s happening tonight (anything fun)?

meaning: 'of beer' / 'beer' (used after a quantity or container).
additional_notes: Used with measurements, containers, or amounts to specify the drink: una pinta di birra (a pint of beer), una lattina di birra (a can of beer), una cassa di birra (a case of beer). It can also appear in the expression pancia di birra, meaning a “beer belly.”
target_language_example: Prendo una bottiglia di birra, grazie.
native_language_example: I’ll have a bottle of beer, thanks.

meaning: really badly; seriously/a lot (as an intensifier). Also: “something bad” in “qualcosa/niente di brutto”.
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- **qualcosa / niente di brutto** = “something / nothing bad” (literally “of bad/ugly”).
- With verbs, **di brutto** works as an **informal intensifier** meaning “a lot / hard / badly”: *litigare di brutto* (fight badly), *dormire di brutto* (sleep hard).
- **fuori di brutto** is slangy: “really out of it / crazy / way beyond normal.”
Meaning depends on context, but it generally adds the idea of “really” + something negative/strong.
target_language_example: Ieri notte ho dormito di brutto e non ho sentito la sveglia.
native_language_example: Last night I slept really hard and I didn’t hear the alarm.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "essere" (to be): "sono/sei/è di buon umore". Often contrasted with "di cattivo umore" (in a bad mood). "Buon" is a shortened form of "buono" before a noun ("umore").
target_language_example: Dopo la vacanza, ero di buon umore e avevo tanta energia.
native_language_example: After the vacation, I was in a good mood and had lots of energy.

meaning: “of coffee” / “some coffee” (coffee as the thing being measured or described).
additional_notes: Uses the preposition di (“of”) to link a quantity/container to what it contains: un litro di caffè (a liter of coffee), tre tazze di caffè (three cups of coffee), due tazzine di caffè (two small espresso cups). It can also describe a person or thing connected to coffee: un bevitore di caffè (“a coffee drinker”).
target_language_example: Vorrei una tazza di caffè, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a cup of coffee, please.

additional_notes: “Di” means “of.” With food/nutrition it often means “rich in” (ricco di calcio = rich in calcium). With sports it means “of” the sport (partita di calcio = soccer match; giocatore/giocatrice di calcio = soccer player).
target_language_example: Mio fratello gioca a calcio e io guardo le partite di calcio.
native_language_example: My brother plays soccer and I watch soccer matches.

meaning: made of paper; paper (as a material).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say what it’s made of (e.g., "un biglietto di carta" = a paper ticket). With abstract nouns like "consumo", it indicates consumption/usage of paper in general ("consumo di carta"). Related: "fatto di carta" / "fatto di carta riciclata" = made of (recycled) paper.
target_language_example: Preferisco i sacchetti di carta a quelli di plastica.
native_language_example: I prefer paper bags to plastic ones.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize certainty, often as a short answer (“Di certo.” = “For sure.”). Very common in negative replies: “No di certo!” / “Io no di certo.” = “Certainly not!” / “Not me, for sure.” It can also introduce a statement: “Di certo, …” = “Certainly, … / For sure, …”.
target_language_example: Non è di certo colpa tua.
native_language_example: It’s certainly not your fault.

additional_notes: Used to ask the color of something. Often followed by the noun: “Di che colore è + [object]?” If the thing is explicit you can also ask “Di che colore è?” alone (it = the thing you’re talking about).
target_language_example: Scusa, di che colore è questa maglietta?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what color is this T-shirt?

additional_notes: Used to ask what the topic is (“about what?”) or what something is made of/consists of (“of what?”). Often appears with verbs like parlare (to talk), discutere (to discuss), and with è fatto (is made). You may also hear the shorter synonym “di cosa?”.
target_language_example: Di che cosa avete bisogno?
native_language_example: What do you need?

meaning: 'Whose is this?' / 'Whose ... is this?' (asking who something belongs to).
additional_notes: Used to ask who an item belongs to. "Di chi" = "whose" (literally "of whom"), and you change the demonstrative to match the noun: "di chi è questo?" (masc. singular), "di chi sono questi?" (masc. plural), "di chi sono queste?" (fem. plural). Often followed by the noun: "Di chi è questa borsa?"
target_language_example: Scusa, di chi è questa giacca?
native_language_example: Sorry, whose jacket is this?

meaning: “Whose is this?” / “Who does this belong to?”
additional_notes: Used to ask who the owner is. The pattern is: “Di chi è questo/questa + noun?” (masc. questo, fem. questa). You can also use plurals: “Di chi sono questi/queste…?” In more formal contexts you may see “Mi dica…” before the question.
target_language_example: Scusi, di chi è questo ombrello?
native_language_example: Excuse me, whose umbrella is this?

meaning: to call me (as part of a verb + “di” + infinitive structure).
additional_notes: “Di chiamarmi” literally means “of calling me,” but in English it’s usually “to call me.” It’s used after many verbs/expressions that require **di + infinitive**, such as **chiedere di** (to ask to), **avere bisogno di** (to need to), and **smettere di** (to stop). The **-mi** ending means “me.”
target_language_example: Non dimenticare di chiamarmi stasera.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to call me tonight.

meaning: “than anyone else” / “than anybody else” (after a comparison); sometimes “from anyone else”.
additional_notes: Used with comparisons, especially after "più"/"meno" (more/less): "più forte di chiunque altro" = "stronger than anyone else." In some contexts it can mean "from anyone else" (e.g., "da/di chiunque altro"), emphasizing that any other person would be an acceptable/possible source.
target_language_example: Sono più veloce di chiunque altro in squadra.
native_language_example: I’m faster than anyone else on the team.

additional_notes: Literally means “of color.” With objects it often refers to color/pigment (e.g., “tracce di colore”). When used about people (“una persona di colore”), it’s a dated euphemism and can sound awkward or offensive; in many contexts Italians prefer more direct wording like “una persona nera” (a Black person) or more specific terms (e.g., “afrodiscendente”) depending on the situation.
target_language_example: Attento: la maglietta bianca si è macchiata di colore.
native_language_example: Careful: the white T-shirt got stained with color/dye.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or changes very quickly and unexpectedly. It often goes near the verb (e.g., “Di colpo si spense…”, “Sei cambiato di colpo?”).
target_language_example: Di colpo ha iniziato a piovere.
native_language_example: All of a sudden it started to rain.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the effect or outcome of a previous action or situation. It often comes at the beginning of a sentence ("Di conseguenza, ...") or between commas ("..., di conseguenza, ..."). In the imperative "Scrivi di conseguenza!", it means "write accordingly" (adjust what you write based on what was just said).
target_language_example: Non hai studiato e, di conseguenza, hai preso un brutto voto.
native_language_example: You didn’t study and, as a result, you got a bad grade.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very frequently or without interruption. Common with verbs like "fare", "dire", "chiedere", "lamentarsi" (e.g., "mi chiama di continuo"). Slightly formal/neutral; similar to "continuamente" or "in continuazione".
target_language_example: Mi scrive di continuo, anche quando sono al lavoro.
native_language_example: He/she texts me constantly, even when I'm at work.

additional_notes: Used like an adverb to describe doing something quickly or rushing (often after verbs of movement: venire/andare/arrivare/avvicinarsi di corsa). It can also be used more generally to mean “always rushing” (e.g., Sempre di corsa = Always in a hurry).
target_language_example: Scusa il ritardo: sono arrivato di corsa.
native_language_example: Sorry I'm late: I got here in a hurry.

additional_notes: Used when Italian needs the preposition di before cosa, often after verbs or adjectives like parlare di, preoccuparsi di, or essere capace di. In English it is often translated more naturally as "what ... about" or simply "what," depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Di cosa stai parlando?
native_language_example: What are you talking about?

meaning: “What are you talking about?” / “What is he/she talking about?”
additional_notes: Literally “about what are you speaking.” Used to ask what the topic is, often when you’re confused or want clarification. Change the subject with the verb: “di cosa stai parlando?” (you, informal), “di cosa sta parlando?” (he/she/you formal: “lei”). Can be neutral or sound impatient depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Scusa, di cosa sta parlando esattamente?
native_language_example: Sorry, what exactly are you talking about?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone means or what topic they’re referring to. Often expresses confusion, surprise, or disbelief depending on tone (and can sound confrontational in arguments). You can also use it as part of a longer sentence: “Non so di cosa stai parlando” = “I don’t know what you’re talking about.”
target_language_example: Scusa, di cosa stai parlando?
native_language_example: Sorry, what are you talking about?

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something previously mentioned, especially after verbs/adjectives that take the preposition "di" (e.g., "parlare di" = to talk about, "preoccuparsi di" = to worry about). It often translates to "(that) ... about" / "(that) ... of" in English: "la cosa di cui parlavo" = "the thing (that) I was talking about."
target_language_example: Questo è il problema di cui ti parlavo ieri.
native_language_example: This is the problem I was talking to you about yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to express strong, sincere feeling, especially in set phrases like “Grazie di cuore” (thank you very much, sincerely) or “Ti ringrazio di cuore.” It can also describe doing something with genuine emotion: “ridere di cuore” = to laugh heartily. In some fixed expressions it keeps its literal sense of “heart,” e.g. “attacco di cuore” = heart attack.
target_language_example: Ti ringrazio di cuore per il tuo aiuto.
native_language_example: Thank you from the bottom of my heart for your help.

additional_notes: Used especially with verbs like **togliere** (to take/remove) to mean removing something from someone’s body or stopping someone/something from bothering or clinging to them. Common patterns: **togliere [something] di dosso (a qualcuno)** = take [something] off (someone); **togliersi di dosso** = get off me / get out of my way; **non togliere gli occhi di dosso (a qualcuno)** = not take your eyes off (someone).
target_language_example: Finalmente mi sono tolto di dosso quel pensiero.
native_language_example: I finally got that thought out of my head / off me.

additional_notes: Used when a verb requires **di** before an infinitive, e.g. *permettere di...* (to allow to...), *chiedere di...* (to ask to...). It often corresponds to English “to + verb,” even though Italian uses **di**.
target_language_example: Mi hanno chiesto di entrare subito.
native_language_example: They asked me to go in right away.

additional_notes: di + essere is a common infinitive pattern after another verb. After verbs like pensare, credere, dire, or permettere, it often means simply 'to be', though English may sometimes use a clause like 'that someone is/was' instead. The subject of essere is usually understood from the main clause or a nearby person mentioned.
target_language_example: Credevo di essere pronto.
native_language_example: I thought I was ready.

meaning: to be careful / to be cautious.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like dire (to tell), chiedere (to ask), consigliare (to advise), cercare (to try) to express “to be careful.” It’s the infinitive phrase “di essere” + adjective. Common patterns: “Dissi a Tom di essere prudente” = “I told Tom to be careful”; “Cerco di essere prudente” = “I try to be careful.” You can change prudente to agree with the person: prudente (singular), prudenti (plural).
target_language_example: Per favore, cerca di essere prudente quando guidi.
native_language_example: Please, try to be careful when you drive.

meaning: of hunger; from hunger (used with verbs like "to die/starve" and "to be starving").
additional_notes: Most common with "morire di fame" (to starve to death / to die of hunger) and "morire di fame!" as an exaggeration meaning "I’m starving." You can also pair it with other causes, e.g. "morti di fame e di freddo" (died from hunger and cold).
target_language_example: Dopo l’escursione, morivo di fame.
native_language_example: After the hike, I was starving.

additional_notes: Used when fare follows another verb or expression that takes di + infinitive. In English, this often corresponds to just 'to do/make' after verbs like cercare di (try to) or chiedere di (ask to), but after smettere di it is usually translated as 'doing' ('stop doing'). Here di is grammatical and usually not translated as 'of'.
target_language_example: Ho deciso di fare una pausa.
native_language_example: I decided to take a break.

additional_notes: A very common pattern: di + infinitive. Here, farlo = fare + lo, so it means “do it.” After many verbs and expressions (like chiedere, dire, proibire, permettere, essere capace), Italian uses di before the infinitive, where English often just uses “to.”
target_language_example: Ha promesso di farlo domani.
native_language_example: He promised to do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or emphasize what is true in reality, sometimes to correct a misconception or add a clarifying point. It can also be used as a short confirmation (e.g., “Di fatto, sì.” = “Actually, yes.”). Often set off by commas at the start of a sentence: “Di fatto, …”.
target_language_example: Di fatto, non abbiamo abbastanza tempo per finire oggi.
native_language_example: In fact, we don’t have enough time to finish today.
