"Disse" is a narrative/literary past form of dire, so you will see it often in books and stories; in everyday spoken Italian, "ha detto che era" is more common. "Era" can mean he/she/it was, and the context or the following adjective usually makes it clear.
target_language_example: Disse che era stanco dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: He said that he was tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Used in storytelling and reported speech, usually in the past (disse = “said”). "Che" introduces what was said (“that”), "era" = “was”, and "davvero" intensifies the adjective that follows (“really”). The subject (he/she) is often understood from context and not stated.
target_language_example: Disse che era davvero stanco dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: He said he was really tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about themselves or someone else. "disse" is the passato remoto of "dire" (said/told), common in narratives and written Italian; in conversation you’ll often hear "ha detto" instead. "che" = "that" introduces reported speech. "era" (imperfect of "essere") sets the description in the past. You usually add an adjective after "molto" (e.g., "molto stanco", "molto felice").
target_language_example: Disse che era molto stanco dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: He said that he was very tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Used in the past to report what someone said about their state or feelings. “Disse” is the simple past of *dire* (“to say”), common in storytelling and written narration. In speech you may also hear *ha detto che era veramente…* with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Marco disse che era veramente stanco dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: Marco said that he was really tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Past-tense reporting phrase. "Disse" is the passato remoto of "dire" (to say), common in narratives/stories and some regions; in everyday speech many people use "ha detto che non era" instead. "Non era" is the imperfect of "essere" (to be), often used to describe a state/condition at that time: "disse che non era sposata" = he/she said she wasn't married.
target_language_example: Luca disse che non era pronto per l’esame.
native_language_example: Luca said that he wasn’t ready for the exam.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech to introduce two layers of what someone said and what they believed/thought. It’s made of: disse (passato remoto of dire, “said”) + che (“that”) + pensava (imperfetto of pensare, “was thinking/thought”) + che (“that”). After pensare che, Italian often uses the subjunctive in the next clause (e.g., fosse, sembrassi).
target_language_example: Disse che pensava che fosse troppo tardi.
native_language_example: He/She said that he/she thought it was too late.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about how they were feeling. "disse" is a past tense of "dire" (he/she said), and it’s followed by "che" (that) plus a verb in the imperfect ("si sentiva") to describe the state/feeling at that time. "si sentiva" is literally "felt (oneself)" and is commonly used with adjectives (affamato/a, deluso/a, disperato/a, ecc.).
target_language_example: Luca disse che si sentiva stanco dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: Luca said that he felt tired after the trip.

additional_notes: A common narrative pattern in indirect speech. disse is the passato remoto of dire, often seen in books and storytelling; in everyday spoken Italian, ha detto che voleva is more common. The subject is usually understood from context, so in English you often add he or she.
target_language_example: Luca disse che voleva partire subito.
native_language_example: Luca said that he wanted to leave right away.

additional_notes: Past narration: "disse" is the simple past (passato remoto) of "dire" (to say), common in stories, books, and news reports (especially in some regions). "che" means "that" and introduces what was said. "voleva" is the imperfect of "volere" (to want), often used to report someone’s desire/intention in the past. In everyday conversation, many speakers replace "disse" with "ha detto" (passato prossimo).
target_language_example: Disse che voleva parlare con il direttore.
native_language_example: He said that he wanted to speak with the manager.

meaning: “(he/she) said that (he/she) had …” (reported speech in the past).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said, with the verb in the past (disse = “said”). After disse, Italian often uses di + infinitive; with a completed action you use the past infinitive: aver + past participle (e.g., aver visto = “to have seen”, aver trovato = “to have found”). It can refer to a man or a woman depending on context: “lui disse…” / “lei disse…”.
target_language_example: Lei disse di aver dimenticato le chiavi a casa.
native_language_example: She said that she had forgotten her keys at home.

additional_notes: "Disse" is the passato remoto of *dire* (“to say”), often used in narratives and news-like storytelling. "di avere" introduces what someone said they had done or experienced; it’s commonly followed by a past participle (e.g., *avere sentito/trovato/vinto/mangiato*). In everyday conversation, you’ll often hear *ha detto di avere...* instead of *disse di avere...*.
target_language_example: Disse di avere visto qualcuno vicino alla porta.
native_language_example: He/She said (that) he/she had seen someone near the door.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of "dire" (disse = "he/she said"), used often in storytelling, books, news reports, or formal narration. It introduces reported speech with "di" + infinitive ("essere"). In everyday conversation, Italians often use "ha detto di essere" instead. The subject is usually understood from context; you can add it for clarity (e.g., "Lui disse di essere...").
target_language_example: Il testimone disse di essere fuori città quella notte.
native_language_example: The witness said he was out of town that night.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) reporting what some people said in the past. "Dissero" = "they said" (remote past, common in storytelling and in some regions); "che" introduces the clause; "avevano" is imperfetto of "avere" (= "had"), often used for states/conditions in the past (fear, thirst, need, etc.). In everyday conversation many speakers prefer "hanno detto che avevano...".
target_language_example: Dissero che avevano perso le chiavi.
native_language_example: They said they had lost the keys.

additional_notes: Used to report what a group of people said in the past. "Dissero" is the remote past (passato remoto) of "dire" (to say), common in written narratives and in some regions; in conversation you’ll often hear "hanno detto che erano". Follow it with an adjective or phrase (e.g., "depressi", "pronte ad andare").
target_language_example: Dissero che erano stanchi, ma continuarono a camminare.
native_language_example: They said they were tired, but they kept walking.

additional_notes: Used to report what a group of people said about themselves or others. **Dissero** is the *passato remoto* (literary/narrative past) of *dire* (“to say”); in everyday speech you often hear **hanno detto che erano molto…**. After **molto**, you add an adjective that agrees in gender/number with the people described (e.g., *annoiate/annoiati, malate, pover(e), scettici*).
target_language_example: Dissero che erano molto stanchi dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: They said they were very tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Used to report what a group of people said about how they were feeling. "Dissero" is passato remoto (past historic) of *dire* = “they said,” common in narratives and writing (in conversation you’ll often hear *hanno detto*). *Si sentivano* comes from *sentirsi* (“to feel”), and is often followed by an adjective: *forti* (strong), *nervose* (nervous), *soli* (lonely).
target_language_example: Dopo la visita dal medico, dissero che si sentivano meglio.
native_language_example: After the doctor’s visit, they said they felt better.

additional_notes: Uses the simple past (passato remoto) of dire: "dissero" = "they said" (common in storytelling, books, and in some regions; in everyday speech you often hear "hanno detto"). Followed by "che" + imperfect "volevano" to report what someone wanted in the past. With an object pronoun: "mi dissero che volevano" = "they told me they wanted".
target_language_example: Dissero che volevano partire subito.
native_language_example: They said they wanted to leave right away.

additional_notes: "Dissi" is the passato remoto (remote past) of *dire* (“to say/tell”), common in written stories, news, and in some regions when speaking about completed past actions. It’s followed by **a + person** (the person you spoke to): *Dissi a Tom...*. Often used with **che** + sentence (*dissi a Tom che...*) or **di** + infinitive for commands/requests (*dissi a Tom di fermarsi*).
target_language_example: Dissi a mia sorella che sarei arrivato tardi.
native_language_example: I told my sister that I would arrive late.

additional_notes: "Dissi" is the remote past (passato remoto) of "dire" (to say/tell), used mainly in written Italian and in some regions for completed actions in the distant past. "loro" = "to them" and "che" introduces what you told them. In everyday conversation many speakers would use "ho detto loro che" instead.
target_language_example: Dissi loro che non potevo restare.
native_language_example: I told them that I couldn’t stay.

additional_notes: Said to express hope that something will go well, or to wish someone luck. Often used on its own as an exclamation (e.g., "Dita incrociate!") or with "per" + noun ("Dita incrociate per l’esame").
target_language_example: Dita incrociate per il colloquio di domani!
native_language_example: Fingers crossed for tomorrow’s interview!

additional_notes: Used to give a command/request to more than one person (or as a polite/formal "you" in some contexts): "Dite a [person] che..." = "Tell [person] that...". It can also be followed by a noun with "di/del/della...": "Dite a Tom del concerto" = "Tell Tom about the concert."
target_language_example: Dite a Marco che arriviamo tra dieci minuti.
native_language_example: Tell Marco that we’ll arrive in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (politely or formally, or when speaking to more than one person) to pass a message on to other people. In everyday informal speech to one person you’ll often hear “di’ loro che …”. The “che” introduces what you want them to say.
target_language_example: Per favore, dite loro che arrivo tra dieci minuti.
native_language_example: Please tell them that I’ll be there in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to give an instruction or request directed at “them” (loro), followed by an infinitive verb (di + infinitive): dite loro di aspettare, di venire, di fare, etc. "Dite" is the imperative (command form) of "dire" for "voi" (you all) and also the formal plural "you".
target_language_example: Dite loro di aspettarmi qui, per favore.
native_language_example: Tell them to wait for me here, please.

additional_notes: From the verb "diventare" (to become). "Divenne" is the remote past (passato remoto), common in stories, biographies, and more in southern Italy; in everyday speech many people use "è diventato/a" instead. Use "un" before a masculine singular noun (un insegnante, un cittadino); for feminine use "divenne una" (e.g., divenne una dottoressa).
target_language_example: Dopo anni di studio, divenne un medico.
native_language_example: After years of studying, he became a doctor.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a goal or career choice. It often follows verbs like pensare di (to think about), consigliare di (to advise), piacerebbe (I’d like), and volere (to want). You can change the article/gender: diventare un insegnante (male/unspecified), diventare un’insegnante (female).
target_language_example: Da piccolo volevo diventare un insegnante.
native_language_example: When I was little, I wanted to become a teacher.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "diventare" (to become) in the passato remoto (simple past), common in storytelling, history, and written narration. "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article, used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., "un insegnante"). For feminine nouns, you’d use "diventò una" (e.g., "diventò una dottoressa").
target_language_example: Da grande diventò un medico famoso.
native_language_example: When he grew up, he became a famous doctor.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly (more than once). It can refer to a specific situation (e.g., the phone rang several times) or to a general frequency (e.g., several times a week).
target_language_example: Te l’ho spiegato diverse volte, ma non mi ascolti.
native_language_example: I’ve explained it to you several times, but you don’t listen.

meaning: we must act / we need to take action.
additional_notes: Used to express urgency or necessity. "Dobbiamo" = "we must/have to" (from dovere), and "agire" = "to act". Often followed by an adverb like "subito" (right away) or "in fretta" (quickly).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo agire prima che sia troppo tardi.
native_language_example: We must act before it’s too late.

meaning: "We have to leave" / "we must go away (from here)."
additional_notes: Uses the verb "dovere" (dobbiamo = we have to) + "andarsene" (to leave/go away). The little word "ne" adds the idea of leaving from a place ("from here/from there"), so it often sounds like "we need to get out of here." Common with urgency words like "subito" (right away) or "presto" (soon).
target_language_example: È tardi: dobbiamo andarcene adesso.
native_language_example: It’s late: we have to leave now.

additional_notes: Used to say that it’s necessary to leave or to go somewhere (often because of time, rules, or urgency). You can add a destination (e.g., "dobbiamo andare lì") or time ("dobbiamo andare adesso"). As a question ("Dobbiamo andare?") it asks if it’s necessary to go/leave.
target_language_example: Scusa, dobbiamo andare subito.
native_language_example: Sorry, we have to go right away.

meaning: we have to go to / we need to go to (and do something).
additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity: "dobbiamo" = "we must/we need to" + "andare a" = "go to". It can be followed by a place ("andare a Boston") or by an infinitive to say "go to do" something ("andare a bere", "andare a vederli"). In questions it often sounds like "Why do we have to go... ?".
target_language_example: Dobbiamo andare a comprare il pane.
native_language_example: We have to go buy bread.

additional_notes: Formed by dovere (to have to/must) in the 1st person plural present (dobbiamo = we must/have to) + essere (to be). Used to say a necessity/obligation about a state, quality, or behavior: dobbiamo essere prudenti (we must be careful), preparati (prepared), pazienti (patient). It can also be used about being in a place: Dobbiamo essere a Boston? (Do we have to be in Boston?). The adjective typically agrees with the group: onesti (mixed/masc. plural), oneste (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo essere puntuali domani mattina.
native_language_example: We have to be on time tomorrow morning.

meaning: "we have to do / we must do" (sometimes "we have to make").
additional_notes: Uses the verb "dovere" (to have to/must) + an infinitive. "Dobbiamo" is the "we" form: "we have to". It’s followed by an action verb like "fare" (to do/make): "Dobbiamo fare qualcosa" = "We have to do something." Note: Italian "fare" usually means "do/make" (not English "fare" as in "bus fare").
target_language_example: Dobbiamo fare una scelta oggi.
native_language_example: We have to make a decision today.

additional_notes:
Literally “we must talk” (dovere + parlare). Often used to introduce an important or serious conversation, especially when said on its own with emphasis: “Dobbiamo parlare!” You can add details with:
- “dobbiamo parlare di …” = “we need to talk about …”
- “dobbiamo parlare prima” = “we need to talk first / beforehand.”
target_language_example: Aspetta un attimo: dobbiamo parlare di quello che è successo ieri.
native_language_example: Wait a moment: we need to talk about what happened yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "dovere" (to have to/must) in the "noi" form: "dobbiamo" = "we have to" + the infinitive "trovare" (to find). It can mean obligation (must) or practical necessity (need to). Object pronouns can go before "dobbiamo" (e.g., "Le dobbiamo trovare" = "We have to find them" referring to feminine plural).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo trovare un taxi subito.
native_language_example: We need to find a taxi right away.

additional_notes: Used to talk about plans, appointments, or actions happening in the morning of the next day. Often placed at the end of the sentence, but it can also be moved earlier for emphasis (e.g., “Domani mattina va bene.”).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo domani mattina alle nove.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow morning at nine.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen tomorrow in the afternoon (roughly after lunch until early evening). Often used without a preposition: “Ci vediamo domani pomeriggio.” You can also specify a time: “alle due domani pomeriggio.”
target_language_example: Ho un appuntamento dal dentista domani pomeriggio.
native_language_example: I have a dentist appointment tomorrow afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to talk about plans or events happening tomorrow in the evening (typically after work/school) and often extends into the night. Common in invitations and scheduling (e.g., asking if someone is free, booking a taxi).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo domani sera alle otto?
native_language_example: Shall we see each other tomorrow evening at eight?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the Sunday coming up (the Sunday after today). Often used with the future tense or with the present to talk about a scheduled event: "È domenica prossima" / "Sarà domenica prossima."
target_language_example: Ci vediamo domenica prossima alle 10.
native_language_example: See you next Sunday at 10.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the most recent Sunday before today. It’s a common time expression; you can put it at the beginning or end of the sentence. Agreement: use scorsa (feminine singular) because domenica is feminine (la domenica).
target_language_example: Domenica scorsa ho pranzato con i miei amici.
native_language_example: Last Sunday I had lunch with my friends.

additional_notes: Means “women and children” as a group. Often used in safety/emergency contexts to indicate priority or restriction (e.g., “Prima donne e bambini!” = “Women and children first!”, “Solo donne e bambini!” = “Women and children only!”). Note: the correct plural is "donne" (not "donne").
target_language_example: In caso di emergenza, prima donne e bambini.
native_language_example: In an emergency, women and children first.

additional_notes: Used to say that one action happens after another. It’s followed by a past infinitive (aver + past participle): dopo aver pranzato, dopo aver perso, dopo aver fatto, dopo aver visto, dopo aver scritto. Often corresponds to English “after (doing/having done) …”.
target_language_example: Dopo aver finito i compiti, esco con gli amici.
native_language_example: After finishing my homework, I go out with friends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you do later in the evening, once you’ve finished eating dinner. It can go at the start of the sentence (Dopo cena...) or later (… dopo cena).
target_language_example: Dopo cena guardiamo un film.
native_language_example: After dinner we watch a movie.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause describing something that happened earlier in time: “after” + subject + verb. Often followed by the indicative (e.g., dopo che è morto) for past facts; it can also be followed by the subjunctive in some contexts, especially when the action is viewed as not yet completed or is in the future (e.g., dopo che un dottore ti avrà visitata / after a doctor has examined you).
target_language_example: Andiamo a cena dopo che finisci di lavorare.
native_language_example: We’ll go to dinner after you finish working.

additional_notes: Used as a polite way to invite someone to go first (e.g., through a door, into an elevator, or ahead in line). It can be repeated back and forth as a courteous “no, after you.”
target_language_example: Prego, dopo di te: entra pure.
native_language_example: Go ahead, after you: come in.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens later than a specific event/time. It’s the preposition "dopo" (after) + the masculine singular definite article "il". Often corresponds to English “after the …”. With other articles you’ll get: dopo lo, dopo l’, dopo la, dopo i, dopo gli, dopo le.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo dopo il pranzo.
native_language_example: See you after lunch.

meaning: after work (after finishing your job for the day).
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens once the workday is over. Common with plans and routines: “Dopo il lavoro vado in palestra” (After work I go to the gym). Often refers to your regular job, and can also be used with specific places/types of work (e.g., “dopo il lavoro in banca”).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo dopo il lavoro per un caffè?
native_language_example: Shall we meet after work for a coffee?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the time period once the school day ends (often for plans, activities, or what someone does later that day). It can be used on its own or with verbs like fare, andare, venire, giocare, etc.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo dopo la scuola.
native_language_example: See you after school.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than 12:00 a.m. Often with past tenses to describe when you arrived, woke up, etc. You can also say "dopo la mezzanotte" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Il treno parte dopo mezzanotte.
native_language_example: The train leaves after midnight.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause referring back to events, efforts, or experiences already mentioned or understood from context. Often expresses surprise, disappointment, or emphasis (e.g., “after all we’ve done/been through…”). Usually followed by a verb phrase: è successo, abbiamo fatto, ho fatto per te, ha passato, etc.
target_language_example: Dopo tutto quello che abbiamo fatto per aiutarti, non vuoi nemmeno ringraziarci?
native_language_example: After everything we’ve done to help you, you don’t even want to thank us?

additional_notes: Used to add a final point that changes or sums up what was said before. Common for: (1) “actually/it turns out” when a previous idea was wrong (Si sbagliava dopo tutto.); (2) “in the end” when someone decides to do something (Ha deciso di farlo dopo tutto.); (3) “after all” to remind someone of an important fact (Mi hai protetto, dopo tutto.). Often set off by commas in speech and writing.
target_language_example: Non è poi così difficile, dopo tutto.
native_language_example: It’s not that difficult, after all.

additional_notes: Used to ask or say someone’s place of residence. It’s “dove” (where) + “abita” (lives), from the verb “abitare.” “Abita” can mean he/she lives or the formal “you live” (Lei): e.g., “Dove abita?” = “Where do you live?”
target_language_example: Scusi, dove abita lei?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where do you live?

additional_notes: Used to ask where someone bought something. "Avete comprato" is passato prossimo (literally "have bought"), commonly translated as simple past in English ("did you buy"). "Avete" is used for: (1) speaking to more than one person (you all), or (2) the polite/formal "you" (Lei) would normally be "ha comprato" instead.
target_language_example: Scusi, dove avete comprato questa borsa?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where did you buy this bag?

meaning: "where the hell" / "where on earth" (shows strong irritation or surprise).
additional_notes: Used in questions to add emphasis and express annoyance, impatience, or disbelief. It’s stronger than plain "dove" and can sound rude depending on tone and context. Similar in meaning to "dove cavolo" (usually a bit milder).
target_language_example: Dove diavolo hai messo le chiavi?
native_language_example: Where the hell did you put the keys?

additional_notes: Used to ask the place or store where someone bought something. "Ha comprato" is the passato prossimo of "comprare" (to buy) and can mean "bought" or "have bought" in English. "Ha" is used with Lei (formal "you") and with lui/lei (he/she).
target_language_example: Scusi, dove ha comprato questa giacca?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where did you buy this jacket?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the place where someone learned how to do something. It uses the formal past tense (Lei/third person) "ha imparato"; with "tu" you’d say "Dove hai imparato a…?". You can also add a name/topic: "Tom, dove ha imparato a…?".
target_language_example: Dove ha imparato a guidare così bene?
native_language_example: Where did you learn to drive so well?

additional_notes: Used to ask where someone put something. It’s in the passato prossimo: ha (has) + messo (put). The subject can be omitted if it’s clear (e.g., “Dove ha messo il giornale?”) or added for clarity (“Tom, dove ha messo…?”). “Ha” is for he/she or polite “you” (Lei); for “you” informal (tu) it becomes “dove hai messo…”.
target_language_example: Scusi, dove ha messo i biglietti?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where did you put the tickets?

additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo of prendere (ha preso = "got/took"). It can ask about the origin of something ("Where did you get it?") or where someone took it from ("Where did he take it from?"). With a name (e.g., "Tom"), it usually means "Where did Tom get ...?". In a question, you’ll often see the subject after the verb: "Dove ha preso Tom... ?" or "Tom, dove ha preso ...?"
target_language_example: Scusi, dove ha preso questa borsa?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where did you get this bag?

additional_notes: Used to ask where someone found something. "Ha trovato" is the passato prossimo of "trovare" with the formal subject "Lei" (third-person singular), common when speaking politely to one person (e.g., a stranger, customer, older person). In informal speech to a friend you’d usually say: "Dove hai trovato ...?"
target_language_example: Dove ha trovato questa chiave?
native_language_example: Where did you find this key?

additional_notes: Used to ask where someone hid a person or thing. It’s made of: dove (where) + hai (you have) + nascosto (hidden, past participle of nascondere). Addressed to one person (tu). Often followed by a noun: "Dove hai nascosto la chiave?". In reported speech it can appear inside another sentence: "Vuole sapere dove hai nascosto la chiave.".
target_language_example: Dove hai nascosto le chiavi?
native_language_example: Where did you hide the keys?

meaning: "Where did you get ...?" / "Where did you pick up ...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask where someone obtained something (an object, food/drink, cigarettes, etc.). It can also mean where someone got information or an idea (“Where did you get that note/that information?”). With a person, it can mean “Where did you find (this person)?” and can sound rude depending on the noun and tone (e.g., “questo idiota”).
target_language_example: Dove hai preso questa giacca?
native_language_example: Where did you get this jacket?

additional_notes: Used to ask where someone found an object. Literally “where you have found”: dove (where) + hai trovato (you found / you have found). Commonly followed by a noun, often with a demonstrative like questo/questa (“this”) or questi/queste (“these”).
target_language_example: Dove hai trovato il tuo portafoglio?
native_language_example: Where did you find your wallet?

meaning: “Where did you/he/she … them?” (feminine plural “them” in the past tense).
additional_notes: Used to ask where an action happened in the passato prossimo: dove (where) + le (them, feminine plural) + ha (has). The subject is often implied by context: ha = “he/she has” or formal “you (Lei) have.” It’s typically followed by a past participle: “Dove le ha comprate?” = “Where did you/he buy them?” If the items are masculine plural, you usually use “dove li ha …?” instead.
target_language_example: Dove le ha trovate, queste chiavi?
native_language_example: Where did you/he find these keys?

meaning: "where did you ... them?" (to a female plural object).
additional_notes: Used to ask where someone put/left/did something with a feminine plural object that was already mentioned (le = “them”, feminine plural; hai = “you have”). It’s the start of a question and is followed by a past participle (e.g., messe, lasciate, buttate via). In full form it’s often “Dove le hai + past participle?”.
target_language_example: Dove le hai messe le chiavi?
native_language_example: Where did you put the keys?

additional_notes: Used to ask in which place something happened to “them” (li = “them,” masculine plural object pronoun, often used for mixed groups too). It’s typically followed by a past participle in the passato prossimo (avete + buttati/lucidati/pesati, etc.). “Avete” is 2nd person plural (“you all”) or the polite plural in some contexts.
target_language_example: Dove li avete trovati?
native_language_example: Where did you find them?

meaning: “Where did you/he/she … them?” (question starter before a past participle).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the place where an action was done to a masculine plural object (li = “them”). The verb is in the passato prossimo: dove + li + ha + past participle (e.g., comprati, rotti). “Ha” is third-person singular (“he/she has”) and also the formal “you” (Lei). For feminine plural, use “dove le ha … ?”.
target_language_example: Dove li ha trovati?
native_language_example: Where did you/he/she find them?

additional_notes: Used to start a question in the passato prossimo: "Dove li hai + past participle?" The pronoun "li" is a direct-object clitic meaning “them” (masculine plural: e.g., i libri, i soldi, i ragazzi). For feminine plural use "Dove le hai...". In English you usually put “them” after the verb, but in Italian the pronoun comes before the auxiliary: "li hai" (= “you have them”).
target_language_example: Dove li hai messi?
native_language_example: Where did you put them?

meaning: “where did you put/do them?” (literally: “where have you [plural/formal] … them?”).
additional_notes: Used to ask where something happened or where someone placed/used something. "li" = “them” (masculine plural, or mixed group). "avete" is the "you" form for "voi" (you all) or polite plural (e.g., speaking to a group). It’s typically followed by a past participle to complete the action: "Dove li avete messi?" (Where did you put them?).
target_language_example: Dove li avete messi i documenti?
native_language_example: Where did you put the documents?

additional_notes: Used to start a question in the passato prossimo. "Dove" = where, "li" = them (direct object, masculine plural; for feminine plural you’d use "le"), "ha" = has (auxiliary "avere"). It’s typically followed by a past participle (e.g., "mandati" = sent).
target_language_example: Dove li ha messi?
native_language_example: Where did you put them?

meaning: “where did you… them?” (asking where you did something to them).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the place where an action happened. "Dove" = where, "li" = them (masculine plural direct object), "hai" = you have (auxiliary for the past tense). You typically add a past participle after it: "Dove li hai aiutati?" (Where did you help them?), "Dove li hai preparati?" (Where did you prepare them?).
target_language_example: Dove li hai comprati?
native_language_example: Where did you buy them?

additional_notes: Used to ask where you are able/allowed to do something. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb: “dove posso + fare/andare/trovare…”. For extra politeness you can also say “dove posso… per favore?” or use “dove potrei…?” (where could I…?).
target_language_example: Scusi, dove posso comprare un biglietto?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where can I buy a ticket?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the place/store where you can purchase something. Often followed by the item you want, e.g. "dove posso comprare un biglietto?" (a ticket). You can add "qui" for emphasis: "Dove posso comprare... qui?"
target_language_example: Scusi, dove posso comprare una SIM?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where can I buy a SIM card?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the location of something. Often followed by a noun (lo zucchero) or by "un/una" + noun (una cabina telefonica). In a store you can add "in negozio" (in the store).
target_language_example: Scusi, dove posso trovare la fermata dell’autobus?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where can I find the bus stop?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s location. It can also be followed by an adjective or a past participle to ask about a state or a past action that uses "essere" as the auxiliary: e.g., "Dove sei ferito?" (Where are you injured?), "Dove sei salito sul treno?" (Where did you get on the train?).
target_language_example: Scusa, dove sei? Non ti vedo.
native_language_example: Sorry, where are you? I can’t see you.

additional_notes: Used to ask where someone has been, often because they were absent or hard to reach. It’s the passato prossimo of "essere" (sei stato = you have been/were), and it’s addressed to one person (tu). You can add a time phrase: "Dove sei stato questa settimana?" = "Where have you been this week?"
target_language_example: Ehi, dove sei stato? Ti ho chiamato ieri.
native_language_example: Hey, where have you been? I called you yesterday.

meaning: “where is it located?” / “where can I find…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for the location of a place or thing. Literally “where is it found/located,” with the impersonal/passive-style si trova (“is located”). Often followed by a noun with an article: Dove si trova il bagno? You can also use it inside a longer sentence: Sai dove si trova…? (Do you know where … is?)
target_language_example: Scusi, dove si trova la stazione?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the station?

additional_notes: Used as a direct question to ask your current location ("Dove siamo?"). It can also be used in an indirect clause meaning “where we are” (e.g., "Non so dove siamo" = “I don’t know where we are”). "Siamo" is the "we" form of "essere" (to be), and you can add "noi" for emphasis: "Dove siamo noi?"
target_language_example: Scusa, non so dove siamo: puoi controllare la mappa?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know where we are—can you check the map?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "siete" (2nd person plural of "essere", to be), so it’s said to more than one person (“you all”). It can be a direct question ("Dove siete?" = "Where are you?") or part of a longer sentence as an indirect question ("Devo sapere dove siete" = "I need to know where you are").
target_language_example: Scusate, dove siete adesso?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where are you now?

additional_notes: Used to ask where people or things are. Since Italian often drops the subject pronoun, dove sono? can also mean "where am I?" or "where are they?" depending on context.
target_language_example: Dove sono le chiavi?
native_language_example: Where are the keys?

meaning: “where are my …?” (asking where your things are).
additional_notes: Used to ask where your belongings (or other items you refer to with a feminine plural noun) are. It’s usually followed by a feminine plural noun, e.g., le mie chiavi (my keys), le mie cose (my things), le mie medicine (my medicines). For masculine plural nouns, use “Dove sono i miei …?”.
target_language_example: Dove sono le mie chiavi?
native_language_example: Where are my keys?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s destination. Literally “where is going,” and it commonly uses the present continuous in Italian: "stare" (sta) + gerund (andando). You can add a subject or name after it (e.g., "Dove sta andando Tom?"). With "Lei" it can be formal/polite; with "voi" it addresses multiple people.
target_language_example: Scusi, dove sta andando il treno?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the train going?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (informal singular “tu”) where they are headed, often right now. Common with add-ons like “adesso/ora” (now) and “esattamente” (exactly). For the formal/polite version (Lei), say: “Dove sta andando?”
target_language_example: Scusa, dove stai andando adesso?
native_language_example: Sorry, where are you going now?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the destination (literally “where we are going”). Often said with surprise, worry, or confusion: “But where are we going?” You can add “esattamente?” (“exactly?”) to sound more specific.
target_language_example: Scusa, dove stiamo andando adesso?
native_language_example: Sorry, where are we going now?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s destination. Literally “where” (dove) + “you go” (vai). Can be neutral or sound concerned/surprised depending on tone/context (e.g., “And now, where are you going?”). Often followed by a question mark; you can add a name or term of address: “Marco, dove vai?”
target_language_example: Scusa, dove vai così di fretta?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where are you going in such a hurry?

additional_notes: Used in direct questions (Dove vive Tom? = Where does Tom live?) and in indirect questions after verbs like sapere/scoprire/capire (Non so dove vive. = I don’t know where he lives.). In a direct question, Italian often uses the same word order as a statement (no 'do/does' like English).
target_language_example: Non so dove vive tua sorella.
native_language_example: I don’t know where your sister lives.

additional_notes: "Dovete" is the present tense of dovere (to have to / must) for voi (plural "you" or formal "you" in some regions), and "essere" means "to be". It’s used to make a strong assumption or conclusion about someone’s state (e.g., preoccupati, stanchi) or to express obligation depending on context.
target_language_example: Dopo tutto quel lavoro, dovete essere esausti.
native_language_example: After all that work, you must be exhausted.

additional_notes: Formed by **dovere** (to have to/must) in the **present tense, voi** form (**dovete**) + an infinitive (**fare**, “to do/make”). Used to tell or ask what a group must do (or to speak formally to one person using **voi** in some contexts). With an object pronoun, it can go before the verb (e.g., **Lo dovete fare** = “You must do it”).
target_language_example: Dovete fare attenzione quando attraversate la strada.
native_language_example: You must be careful when you cross the street.

meaning: 'was supposed to be' / 'was meant to be' (or 'had to be').
additional_notes: Past tense (imperfetto) of dovere + essere: it often expresses an expectation, plan, or intention that something would be a certain way (sometimes with disappointment or irony: “It was supposed to be fun?”). It can also express necessity in the past (“had to be …”), especially in passive structures: “Doveva essere detto” = “Something had to be said.” Agreement: use the correct form of dovere (dovevo/dovevi/doveva/dovevamo/dovevate/dovevano) depending on the subject.
target_language_example: Doveva essere una serata tranquilla, ma è finita tardi.
native_language_example: It was supposed to be a quiet evening, but it ended late.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of dovere (“dovrebbe” = “should”) + andare (“to go”) to give advice, a recommendation, or say what would be best/expected. The subject is often implied by context (io/lui/lei). Common variants: “dovresti andare” (you should go), “dovrebbero andare” (they should go). You can add a place with “a/in” (e.g., “in palestra”, “a letto”) or use “andarsene” to mean “go away/leave” (e.g., “se ne dovrebbe andare”).
target_language_example: Dovrebbe andare dal medico domani.
native_language_example: He/She should go to the doctor tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Dovrebbe" is the conditional form of "dovere" (to have to / must). "Dovrebbe essere" is used to express what is recommended, expected, or considered the right thing (often like English "should be"). It can also be used for polite/soft obligation or a logical assumption ("It should be there" = you expect it to be there).
target_language_example: Il documento dovrebbe essere pronto domani.
native_language_example: The document should be ready tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of dovere (dovrebbe) + infinitive (fare) to give advice, express what is expected, or say what someone is supposed to do. Often refers to what a third person (he/she/it) should do, and it can appear in questions (“Cosa dovrebbe fare...?”). Negative: “non dovrebbe fare” = “shouldn’t do.” You can replace fare with another verb: “dovrebbe andare” (should go), “dovrebbe chiamare” (should call).
target_language_example: Tom dovrebbe fare una pausa.
native_language_example: Tom should take a break.

meaning: “they should be” / “they ought to be” (conditional form).
additional_notes: Formed from the conditional of dovere (“should/ought to”) + essere (“to be”). It’s used to give advice, express what is expected, or make a cautious assumption (often like “they should be…” meaning “they’re probably…”). The subject is usually “they” (or a plural noun), but it can also refer to a formal “you” (voi) in some contexts.
target_language_example: Le chiavi dovrebbero essere sul tavolo.
native_language_example: The keys should be on the table.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of dovere (“should/ought to”) + andare (“to go”). Often expresses advice, a sense of obligation, or that it’s probably the right thing to do. Common for leaving or excusing yourself: “Ora dovrei andare…” You can add a place with a + (il/lo/la) or da + person: “dovrei andare a scuola / a letto”, “dovrei andare da solo.”
target_language_example: Scusa, dovrei andare adesso: è tardi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I should go now: it’s late.

meaning: "should I give" / "would I have to give".
additional_notes: From dovere (to have to/should) in the conditional tense + dare (to give). It’s often used in questions to ask why you should give something (money, a chance, a tip) or how much you should give. Note: Italian dare means “to give” (not the English verb “to dare”).
target_language_example: Scusa, quanto dovrei dare di mancia al ristorante?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how much should I tip at the restaurant?

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of dovere (dovrei) to express advice, duty, or what you feel is the right thing to do. It’s followed by dire and then the person introduced by a (= to). What you tell them can come after (often with che/cosa/quello che) or as an infinitive with di (e.g., dire a Tom di provare...).
target_language_example: Dovrei dire a Luca che domani non posso venire.
native_language_example: I should tell Luca that tomorrow I can’t come.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of dovere (“to have to / must”) + essere (“to be”) to express what you think is expected, appropriate, or logically true. It can be a real obligation (“I’m supposed to be there helping her”) or a rhetorical/ironic comment (“Io dovrei essere così fortunata!” = “Yeah, I’m supposed to be so lucky!”).
target_language_example: Dovrei essere a casa entro le otto.
native_language_example: I should be home by eight.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of dovere (“to have to / should”) + infinitive andare (“to go”) to suggest or advise an action. It can also be a polite way to ask if something is the right thing to do. In questions and negatives it becomes: Dovremmo andare? (“Should we go?”) and Non dovremmo andare? (“Shouldn’t we go?”).
target_language_example: È tardi: dovremmo andare a casa.
native_language_example: It’s late: we should go home.

meaning: “we should do” / “we ought to do” (often: “what should we do?”).
additional_notes: "Dovremmo" is the conditional of "dovere" (to have to), used to make suggestions or ask for advice more politely/softly than "dobbiamo" (“we must/we have to”). "Fare" can mean “do” or “make,” so the exact translation depends on context (e.g., "dovremmo fare una pausa" = “we should take a break”).
target_language_example: Secondo me dovremmo fare una lista prima di decidere.
native_language_example: I think we should make a list before deciding.

meaning: 'you should talk to / speak with' (polite advice).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of *dovere* (*dovreste* = “you should/you ought to”) to give advice or a recommendation, often politely. It’s followed by the person you should talk to: *con lei* (with her), *con lui* (with him), *con loro* (with them), *con me* (with me).
target_language_example: Dovreste parlare con il medico prima di partire.
native_language_example: You should talk to the doctor before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to give advice, a recommendation, or a gentle (sometimes firm) suggestion. It’s the conditional form of "dovere" (to have to), so it can sound softer and more polite than "devi andare" (you must go). In "te ne dovresti andare", it means "you should leave / go away."
target_language_example: Se non ti senti bene, dovresti andare a casa.
native_language_example: If you don’t feel well, you should go home.

meaning: 'you should be' (advice, expectation, or mild reproach).
additional_notes: Formed from the verb "dovere" (to have to/should) in the conditional ("dovresti" = you should) + "essere" (to be). Used to say what someone is expected to be/do, or to give advice: "Dovresti essere a casa" (You should be at home). The negative is "non dovresti essere" (you shouldn’t be): "Non dovresti essere qui" (You shouldn’t be here).
target_language_example: Dovresti essere più gentile con tua sorella.
native_language_example: You should be kinder to your sister.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt about a statement. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo): dubito che vada/sia/abbia…, especially in careful standard Italian.
target_language_example: Dubito che sia una buona idea.
native_language_example: I doubt it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say a duration of time (per due anni = for two years), a time spent somewhere (ha vissuto due anni a...), or an age (ha due anni = she/he is two years old). It can also express an age difference: due anni in più/meno (two years older/younger).
target_language_example: Lavoro qui da due anni.
native_language_example: I’ve been working here for two years.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened two years before now (relative to the moment you’re speaking). It typically comes at the end of the sentence, after the verb.
target_language_example: Ho iniziato a studiare italiano due anni fa.
native_language_example: I started studying Italian two years ago.

meaning: two tickets for / two tickets to.
additional_notes: Used when buying or requesting tickets. With a destination, it means “to” (Due biglietti per Roma). With an event, it means “for” (due biglietti per il concerto). It can also be followed by a category like “adulti/bambini” (“adults/children”). Often followed by “per favore” or “per piacere” (“please”).
target_language_example: Scusi, due biglietti per il museo, per favore.
native_language_example: Excuse me, two tickets for the museum, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (per due giorni = for two days; in due giorni = in two days/within two days) or about time since something started (da due giorni = for two days/for the past two days). You can also use it with dopo to mean “two days later/after” (due giorni dopo).
target_language_example: Resto a Roma per due giorni.
native_language_example: I'm staying in Rome for two days.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened two days before now. It can go at the start or end of the sentence (e.g., “Due giorni fa…” / “…due giorni fa”). Literally “two days” + “ago/back” (fa).
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati a Roma due giorni fa.
native_language_example: We arrived in Rome two days ago.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration with "per" (for two months) or about something happening in the future with "fra/tra" (in two months). Agreement stays the same: "due" doesn’t change, and "mesi" is plural.
target_language_example: Resto a Roma per due mesi.
native_language_example: I’m staying in Rome for two months.

meaning: “two minutes”; often used to mean “just a moment / a minute.”
additional_notes: Common in everyday speech to ask for a short wait or to say you’ll do something very soon: “Dammi due minuti!” = “Give me a minute!” It can also be literal (exactly two minutes), and it’s used with time amounts in general (e.g., “Il mio orologio perde due minuti al giorno” = “My watch loses two minutes a day”).
target_language_example: Aspettami due minuti, arrivo subito.
native_language_example: Wait for me a minute, I’ll be right there.

meaning: two or three; a couple (an approximate small number).
additional_notes: Used to give an approximate quantity, time, or duration (not exact): two or three people/things, around 2–3 o’clock, for about two or three days. Often means “a few” but specifically suggests a small number close to 2–3.
target_language_example: Aspetta due o tre minuti, per favore.
native_language_example: Wait two or three minutes, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for two hours) or a time in the future (in two hours). Often appears with: per due ore (for two hours), da/per circa due ore (for/about two hours), tra/fra due ore (in two hours). Word order stays the same: number + time unit.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo tra due ore.
native_language_example: See you in two hours.

meaning: a short walk; a very short distance away (nearby).
additional_notes: Commonly used in two fixed expressions: (1) "fare due passi" = to go for a short walk, often as a casual suggestion ("Shall we take a short walk?"); (2) "a due passi da" = very close to something ("a stone’s throw from"). It doesn’t mean literally "two steps" in these uses.
target_language_example: Il bar è a due passi da qui: facciamo due passi e prendiamo un caffè.
native_language_example: The café is just a short walk from here: let’s take a quick walk and grab a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to count physical things, often with "di" + food or objects ("due pezzi di pizza", "due pezzi di pane"). On its own ("Due pezzi."), it’s a short answer meaning "Two." In a food context, "un pezzo" can mean a slice/portion; for pizza you may also hear "due fette" (two slices).
target_language_example: Per favore, mi dia due pezzi di torta.
native_language_example: Please give me two pieces of cake.

meaning: two points; (in scores) by two points.
additional_notes: Often used in sports or games to talk about the score difference: “per due punti” = “by two points” / “by 2 points.” It can also mean the punctuation mark “:” (a colon) in contexts like writing or dictation.
target_language_example: Abbiamo vinto per due punti.
native_language_example: We won by two points.

additional_notes: Used to say a duration (per due settimane = for two weeks) or a time distance (a due settimane di distanza = two weeks away). In expressions like "Sono due settimane che...", it means "It’s been two weeks since..." / "for two weeks now".
target_language_example: Restiamo qui per due settimane.
native_language_example: We’re staying here for two weeks.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens in one day. Common with routines and taking medicine. Also: una volta al giorno (once a day), tre volte al giorno (three times a day).
target_language_example: Prendo questa medicina due volte al giorno.
native_language_example: I take this medicine twice a day.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens in the time period of an event or activity. It’s “durante” + the definite article “il” (masculine singular). With other nouns you’ll often see: durante la (f.), durante lo (m. before s+consonant, z, gn, etc.), durante l’ (before a vowel), durante i / gli / le (plural).
target_language_example: Durante il film, per favore spegni il telefono.
native_language_example: During the movie, please turn off your phone.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens within a time period or event: durante la vacanza (during the vacation), durante la riunione (during the meeting), durante la notte (during the night). It must be followed by a feminine singular noun; with masculine you use "durante il/lo" and with plural "durante i/gli/le".
target_language_example: Non ho usato il telefono durante la lezione.
native_language_example: I didn’t use my phone during the lesson.

additional_notes: A time expression used to say something happened in the period when the war was going on. It often refers to a specific war understood from context (e.g., World War II). You can swap in other events: durante la lezione (during the lesson), durante la notte (during the night).
target_language_example: Durante la guerra, molte famiglie hanno lasciato la città.
native_language_example: During the war, many families left the city.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens at some point in the nighttime. It can also mean “overnight” in the sense of happening very quickly (e.g., becoming famous/rich overnight).
target_language_example: Ho sentito un rumore strano durante la notte.
native_language_example: I heard a strange noise during the night.

meaning: during the summer holidays / during summer vacation.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened within the time period of summer vacation. You can use it at the beginning or end of a sentence (e.g., "Durante le vacanze estive..." / "... durante le vacanze estive"). Note: "vacanze" is plural in Italian, so you normally say "le vacanze" (not *la vacanza*) when talking about a holiday period.
target_language_example: Durante le vacanze estive ho visitato i miei nonni.
native_language_example: During the summer holidays I visited my grandparents.

meaning: hard work (physically or mentally demanding work).
additional_notes: Used to describe work that requires a lot of effort or is tiring. Often appears with "fare" (fare un duro lavoro) or in phrases like "grazie per il suo duro lavoro" and "stanco per il duro lavoro".
target_language_example: È stato un duro lavoro, ma ne è valsa la pena.
native_language_example: It was hard work, but it was worth it.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun to say who is bothered: mi dà fastidio (it bothers me), ti dà fastidio, le dà fastidio (formal “to you” / “to her”), gli dà fastidio (to him), ci dà fastidio, vi dà fastidio, gli dà fastidio (to them). Often used with things (noise, light, someone’s presence) or actions, including questions like “Ti dà fastidio se…?” (“Does it bother you if…?”).
target_language_example: Ti dà fastidio se apro la finestra?
native_language_example: Does it bother you if I open the window?

additional_notes: Used on its own to agree or confirm: "D’accordo!" = "Okay!/Agreed!" With essere: "Sono/Non sono d’accordo" = "I (don’t) agree." With andare (molto) + d’accordo + con: "Vado (molto) d’accordo con..." = "I get along (very well) with..." "D’accordo?" can mean "Okay?" or "Agreed?" depending on tone. "Cambio d’accordo" means "I change my mind" (literally "I change agreement").
target_language_example: Va bene, d’accordo: ci vediamo alle otto.
native_language_example: Okay, agreed: see you at eight.

additional_notes: Used to transition to the next point or ask what happens next (often at the start of a question: “E adesso cosa facciamo?”). It can also contrast a past situation with the present: “prima…, e adesso…”.
target_language_example: E adesso che facciamo?
native_language_example: So what do we do now?

meaning: “so…”, “and then…”, or “well then…?” (often to ask “so what/what now?”).
additional_notes: Used to pick up a point and push it forward: asking for the consequence (“So who is he?”), what to do next (“So what do we do?”), or challenging someone (“Well then, why…?”). On its own as a question (“E allora?”) it often means “So what?” or “And then?/What now?”. Tone depends on context and can sound impatient or confrontational.
target_language_example: E allora, che facciamo adesso?
native_language_example: So, what do we do now?

additional_notes: Used to add an extra person/thing/idea, similar to “and also.” Often before what’s being added: “e anche qui” (and here too), “e anche a te” (and to you too), “e anche io” (and I do too/me too). In Italian, pronouns usually follow: “e anche te” = “and you too.”
target_language_example: Vengo domani, e anche mia sorella viene.
native_language_example: I’m coming tomorrow, and my sister is coming too.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the end of the matter: no more additions, explanations, or discussion. Often sounds firm or a bit blunt, like “period.” You can attach it after a verb or statement: “Ho detto di no, e basta.”
target_language_example: Ho deciso così, e basta.
native_language_example: I decided this way, and that's it.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to challenge or protest something said or implied. It’s often rhetorical and can suggest doubt or annoyance: implying that nobody (or not you) will do it/pay/know it, etc. Literal meaning is simply "and who", but the tone is frequently more pointed in conversation.
target_language_example: E chi lo sa?
native_language_example: And who knows? / Who would know that?

additional_notes: Used after a list to mean there are more similar items you’re not naming. Very common in speech and writing; can also describe a repeated sequence of actions or events ("...then this happens, and so on"). Often interchangeable with "ecc." in writing.
target_language_example: Porta penne, quaderni, libri e così via.
native_language_example: Bring pens, notebooks, books, and so on.

additional_notes: Used to add the number 2 after another item (e.g., 'uno ... e due ...' = 'one ... and two ...'). Very common inside expressions meaning 'both': **tutti e due** (both, masculine/mixed) and **tutte e due** (both, feminine). You’ll often see it with pronouns/articles: **tutti e due**, **tutte e due le...**, **tutti e due i...**.
target_language_example: Vorrei due biglietti: uno per me e due per i miei amici.
native_language_example: I’d like two tickets: one for me and two for my friends.

meaning: and the others; and the rest (of them).
additional_notes: Used to add an unspecified group of other people or things along with the ones already mentioned (similar to “and the others/and everyone else”). It can refer to people ("Emet e gli altri" = "Emet and the others") or things ("il fiore... e gli altri" = "the flower... and the others"). Often used after naming one person/thing to include their companions or the remaining items.
target_language_example: Porta questo documento a Marco e gli altri, per favore.
native_language_example: Bring this document to Marco and the others, please.

additional_notes: Used to link items or clauses: e = “and” + i = “the” for masculine plural nouns (usually starting with most consonants), e.g. i progetti, i libri. Before nouns that take gli (like gli amici, gli studenti), you say “e gli…”, not “e i…”.
target_language_example: Prendo il pane e i pomodori.
native_language_example: I’ll take the bread and the tomatoes.

additional_notes: Used after a person’s name or pronoun to add “and their friends.” The possessive (suo/sua/suoi/sue) agrees with the noun, not the owner: amici (plural masculine) → suoi, even if it refers to “her friends.”
target_language_example: Marco e i suoi amici vanno al cinema stasera.
native_language_example: Marco and his friends are going to the movies tonight.

meaning: “and his/its (… )” (also can mean “and her/your-formal (… )” depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to link two people/things: “X e il suo + noun” = “X and his/its + noun.” Italian possessives agree with the thing possessed, so **il suo** is used with a **masculine singular** noun (e.g., *il fratello, il bambino, il naso*). The owner can be **his, her, its, or your (formal)**—context tells you which.
target_language_example: Ho visto Marco e il suo cane al parco.
native_language_example: I saw Marco and his dog at the park.

additional_notes: Used after mentioning something (a name, phone number, partner, etc.) to ask for the other person’s equivalent: "Mi dici il tuo nome... e il tuo (numero)?" = "Tell me your name... and yours (your number)?" It often implies repeating a noun from context (e.g., "numero", "fidanzato", etc.). You can also say "E la tua...?" (feminine) or "E i tuoi...?" (plural).
target_language_example: Io prendo un caffè. E il tuo?
native_language_example: I’m having a coffee. And yours?

additional_notes: Literally means "and I." It is used to add or contrast yourself with what was just said. In speech, especially at the start of a sentence, it can sound emphatic and sometimes mean something like "and me?" or "what about me?" depending on context and intonation. Italian often drops subject pronouns, so using io adds emphasis.
target_language_example: Tutti sono partiti, e io sono rimasto a casa.
native_language_example: Everyone left, and I stayed home.

meaning: "and I don’t…" / "and I can’t…" (introduces what *I* do not do or cannot do).
additional_notes: Used to add a contrasting or emphatic point about yourself, often after something already said: "..., and *I* don’t...". The exact meaning depends on the verb that follows (e.g., non amo = I don’t like, non posso = I can’t, non cedo = I won’t give in). In writing it can be preceded by a comma: ", e io non...".
target_language_example: Voi volete uscire, e io non ho voglia.
native_language_example: You want to go out, and I don’t feel like it.

meaning: “and I am …” (used to add what you are / how you feel / where you are, often in contrast).
additional_notes: Made of e (“and”) + io (“I”) + sono (“am”). Often used to emphasize your own situation after someone else’s: “Lei ha…, e io sono…” = “She has…, and I’m…”. You normally follow it with a noun/adjective/past participle: e io sono stanca (tired), e io sono rimasto qui (I stayed / I ended up here).
target_language_example: Lui è in vacanza, e io sono ancora al lavoro.
native_language_example: He’s on vacation, and I’m still at work.

meaning: 'and my' (before a feminine singular noun) / 'and mine?'
additional_notes: Used to add something to a list ("...and my...") or in questions to mean "What about my ...?". It must agree with the noun: feminine singular = "la mia" (e.g., "la mia pistola", "la mia scarpa"). For masculine singular you’d say "e il mio"; for feminine plural "e le mie"; for masculine plural "e i miei".
target_language_example: E la mia borsa?
native_language_example: And my bag? / What about my bag?

additional_notes: Used to add the person’s family to the subject or object of the sentence. "Sua" agrees with the thing owned (famiglia = feminine singular), not with the owner; it can mean either “his” or “her” depending on context. Often appears after a name: "Tom e la sua famiglia".
target_language_example: Domani viene Maria e la sua famiglia.
native_language_example: Tomorrow Maria and her family are coming.

meaning: “and your …” / “and yours?” (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun: **e la tua mamma** (“and your mom?”), **tu e la tua amicizia** (“you and your friendship”). It can be a follow-up question meaning “and yours?” when the noun is understood from context (usually something feminine, like *mamma*, *casa*, *macchina*). For masculine nouns you use **e il tuo** (e.g., *e il tuo papà?*).
target_language_example: Io sto bene. E la tua famiglia?
native_language_example: I’m fine. And your family?

meaning: “and the” (before feminine plural nouns); also “and” before “le …” in time expressions.
additional_notes: It’s the conjunction **e** (“and”) + the plural feminine definite article **le** (“the”). Use it before feminine plural nouns: **le spose** (“the brides”), **le erbe** (“the herbs”). You also see it in clock-time phrases like **tra le cinque e le sei** (“between five and six o’clock”), where **le** introduces the hour.
target_language_example: Porta il pane e le bevande, per favore.
native_language_example: Bring the bread and the drinks, please.

additional_notes: Used to add a group of female friends to someone: “X e le sue amiche”. **Sue** agrees with **amiche** (feminine plural) and can mean **his** or **her** depending on who owns the friends (it does *not* tell you the owner’s gender). In English you usually drop the article: “and his/her friends.”
target_language_example: Vado al cinema con Marco e le sue amiche.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with Marco and his female friends.

meaning: “and a half” (also: “and a half times” after volte).
additional_notes: Used after numbers to add half: "tre e mezzo" = three and a half. With "volte" (times), it means “X and a half times”: "due volte e mezzo" = two and a half times. It doesn’t mean “and medium”; for that you’d use words like "medio/a".
target_language_example: Ci vogliono due ore e mezzo per arrivare.
native_language_example: It takes two and a half hours to get there.

additional_notes: Used to join two ideas, where the second one is negative. In Italian, non usually comes before the verb: e non offre = 'and does not offer', e non smetto = 'and I do not stop'. With commands, it often corresponds to 'and don't'.
target_language_example: Parla piano e non fare rumore.
native_language_example: Speak quietly and don't make noise.

additional_notes:
This is the start of a negative continuation: **e** (“and”) + **non** (“not”) + **ci**. **Ci** changes meaning by context:
- **ci** = “us/ourselves”: *e non ci chiediamo…* (“and we don’t ask ourselves…”)
- **ci** = “there”: *e non ci è ritornato?* (“and he didn’t go back there?”)
- **ci** = “each other”: *e non ci sentivamo / non ci parliamo* (“and we couldn’t hear each other / we don’t talk to each other”)
- In expressions like **non ci tengo**, **ci** refers to “it/that”: “I don’t care about it.”
target_language_example: Volevano aiutare, e non ci hanno nemmeno provato.
native_language_example: They wanted to help, and they didn’t even try.

additional_notes: Used to connect to what just happened and shift to the present moment, often to ask what happens next (e.g., “E ora che…”, “E ora come…?”, “E ora dove…?”). It can also introduce a consequence or a new situation: “Prima…, e ora…”.
target_language_example: Ho finito il lavoro, e ora che facciamo?
native_language_example: I’ve finished work, so what do we do now?

meaning: “and more / and change” (plus a bit more; approximately).
additional_notes: Used after a number to mean “and some more,” often when the amount is not exact or is being rounded (e.g., ages, prices, quantities): “cinquanta euro e passa” = “fifty euros and change / fifty-something euros.” Colloquial in tone.
target_language_example: Ho aspettato un’ora e passa.
native_language_example: I waited an hour and then some.

additional_notes: Used to link actions/events in sequence. Common in storytelling and instructions: first X, e poi Y. It can also introduce the next point in a list (like “and then/and next”).
target_language_example: Prima mangiamo e poi andiamo al cinema.
native_language_example: First we eat and then we go to the movies.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical idea, worry, or suggestion (“what if…?”). It’s often followed by the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., *avessi, fossimo*) for unreal/hypothetical situations, or sometimes by the imperfect indicative (e.g., *andassi*) in spoken Italian when imagining a possibility.
target_language_example: E se domani piovesse?
native_language_example: What if it rained tomorrow?

meaning: “What if it were…?” / “What if…?” (introduces a hypothetical possibility).
additional_notes: Used to raise a doubt or consider a possible scenario, often with worry or caution. It uses the imperfect subjunctive of essere (fosse = “were/was”), and you can follow it with an adjective, a noun, or a place: E se fosse vero? (What if it’s true?), E se fosse un errore? (What if it’s a mistake?), E se fosse qui? (What if it’s here?).
target_language_example: E se fosse troppo tardi?
native_language_example: What if it were too late?

meaning: "What if ... doesn’t/don’t ...?" (introduces a worry or hypothetical).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to imagine a negative possibility: *E se non + verb...?* It often expresses concern or planning for something that might not happen (or someone who might not do something). Literally it’s “and if not,” but in English it’s usually translated as “what if … doesn’t/don’t …?”
target_language_example: E se non arriva in tempo?
native_language_example: What if it doesn’t arrive on time?

additional_notes: Used to mention someone together with their wife. **Sua** agrees with **moglie** (feminine singular) and can mean “his,” “her,” or sometimes “your” (formal), depending on context. Often follows a name or pronoun: “Marco e sua moglie…”, “Lui e sua moglie…”.
target_language_example: Ho visto Paolo e sua moglie al supermercato.
native_language_example: I saw Paolo and his wife at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Often used to turn a question back to the other person in conversation. In statements, it can also simply mean 'and you', sometimes with contrast or emphasis, as in 'e tu meno di tutti' = 'you least of all'. 'tu' is the singular informal 'you'.
target_language_example: Io resto a casa, e tu?
native_language_example: I'm staying home, and you?

additional_notes: Used to turn a question back to the other person or to ask for their opinion/experience: **E tu cosa + verb?** It often implies “OK, now you tell me.” In speech it’s commonly followed by a verb (capisci, dici, pensi, ecc.).
target_language_example: Io ho finito il lavoro; e tu cosa fai stasera?
native_language_example: I finished work; what about you—what are you doing tonight?

meaning: “and you are …” / “and you?” (often introducing a question or comparison).
additional_notes: Used to shift focus to the other person: to ask who they are, what they are, or to make a comparison ("…and you are like him"). Often appears at the start of a sentence or question and can sound surprised or challenging depending on tone.
target_language_example: Io sono pronto; e tu sei pronto?
native_language_example: I’m ready; and are you ready?

additional_notes: Used in conversation to agree or give in, sometimes with impatience or resignation—similar to “OK, fine.” It can also be repeated for emphasis ("va bene, va bene"). Often comes before changing topic or ending the conversation ("E va bene, ciao!").
target_language_example: E va bene, facciamo come vuoi tu.
native_language_example: All right, we’ll do it your way.

meaning: "here’s what" / "this is what" (introducing what happened, what someone said, or what to do).
additional_notes: Used to introduce information you’re about to explain (a conclusion, a discovery, instructions, etc.). Often comes at the start of a sentence and is followed by a clause: "Ecco cosa + (subject) + verb" (e.g., "Ecco cosa dobbiamo fare").
target_language_example: Ecco cosa ti consiglio: chiamalo domani.
native_language_example: Here’s what I suggest: call him tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or point out the explanation for something (often after giving clues or a cause). “Ecco” is like “here you go / there you have it,” and together with “perché” it emphasizes the conclusion: “there’s the reason.”
target_language_example: Non risponde mai ai messaggi: ecco perché è difficile organizzarsi.
native_language_example: He never answers messages: that’s why it’s hard to make plans.

additional_notes: Used to link “I” to someone/something else: “lei ed io” = “she and I.” The conjunction is “e” (“and”), but it often becomes “ed” before a word starting with a vowel (like “io”) to sound smoother; meaning doesn’t change. Common in more formal/written Italian; in speech you may also hear “e io.”
target_language_example: Domani verranno Marco ed io.
native_language_example: Tomorrow Marco and I will come.

additional_notes: “Ed” is a variant of “e” (“and”) used before words that start with a vowel, especially before “è”, to make pronunciation smoother. It connects two clauses: “..., ed è ...” = “..., and it is ...”. In many cases “e è” is avoided in writing and replaced with “ed è”.
target_language_example: Non è facile, ed è per questo che ti aiuto.
native_language_example: It’s not easy, and that’s why I’m helping you.

meaning: “Hey, don’t …” / “Hey, not …!” (to stop or correct someone).
additional_notes: Used to get someone’s attention and immediately object to what they’re doing/saying, often followed by a verb: “Ehi, non andare via!” It’s a casual, sometimes urgent interruption; tone can range from friendly to annoyed depending on context.
target_language_example: Ehi, non toccarlo: è fragile!
native_language_example: Hey, don’t touch it: it’s fragile!

additional_notes: A friendly, informal way to address a group (usually male or mixed). Often used to call people over, stop them, or start speaking: “Ehi, ragazzi, aspettate!” (“Hey guys, wait!”). You can also use it with a question intonation (“Ehi, ragazzi?”) when checking if they’re listening.
target_language_example: Ehi, ragazzi, un secondo: devo dirvi una cosa.
native_language_example: Hey guys, one second: I have to tell you something.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean “both the …”. It agrees in gender and number: entrambe le figlie (both daughters). With masculine plural: entrambi i / entrambi gli.
target_language_example: Entrambe le strade portano al centro.
native_language_example: Both roads lead to the city center.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “both the …”. It agrees in gender/number with the noun: entrambi i cani = “both (the) dogs”; entrambi i miei gatti = “both my cats”; entrambi i loro fratelli = “both their brothers”. For feminine plural, use “entrambe le” (e.g., entrambe le sorelle). It can refer to two people/things in general (“both”) or specifically “both of the …” when followed by a noun.
target_language_example: Entrambi i miei amici parlano inglese.
native_language_example: Both of my friends speak English.

additional_notes: Used with a place or group/institution you are going into: entrare in casa (enter the house), entrare in quella stanza (go into that room), entrare in una famiglia/college (join/be accepted into a family or college). Often followed directly by a noun; before a definite article it combines: in + il = nel, in + la = nella, in + lo = nello, etc. (e.g., entrare nel bagno).
target_language_example: Posso entrare in ufficio adesso?
native_language_example: Can I go into the office now?

additional_notes: Used to say someone was mad at another person (or at themself). It’s the imperfect tense of essere (era = was) + the adjective arrabbiato (angry) + con (with). For a woman you usually say: era arrabbiata con. You can also change the tense/person: sono arrabbiato/a con (I’m angry with), ero arrabbiato/a con (I was angry with).
target_language_example: Ieri era arrabbiato con me, ma poi abbiamo chiarito.
native_language_example: Yesterday he was angry with me, but then we cleared things up.

meaning: 'he/she/it was so…' or 'it was like that'.
additional_notes: “Era” is the imperfect past of *essere* (to be): *era* = “was” (he/she/it). “Così” means “so / this way / like that.” Very common pattern: **era così + adjective + che ...** (“was so + adjective + that ...”), often followed by a consequence. It can also mean “it wasn’t like that” in contrasts: *Non era così* = “It wasn’t like that.”
target_language_example: Era così freddo che abbiamo deciso di restare a casa.
native_language_example: It was so cold that we decided to stay home.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a past state or quality (imperfetto of *essere* + *davvero*). Often followed by an adjective (e.g., *era davvero bello/noioso/triste*) or a phrase like *a buon mercato* (“cheap”). In questions like *Era davvero necessaria?*, it expresses doubt or surprise: “Was it really necessary?”
target_language_example: Quel ristorante era davvero buono.
native_language_example: That restaurant was really good.

additional_notes: “Era” is the imperfect tense of “essere” (to be), used for ongoing states in the past (“he/she was”). You’ll often see it with extra information: + di + infinitive (Era felice di vederti. = He/She was happy to see you), or with places/contexts (Era felice qui. = He/She was happy here).
target_language_example: Quando l’ho chiamata, era felice di sentirti.
native_language_example: When I called her, she was happy to hear from you.

additional_notes: Used with the imperfect tense of "essere" (era = he/she/it was) plus "il mio" to say someone/something used to be yours or belonged to you in the past. It’s typically followed by a masculine noun (e.g., "era il mio amico"). For a feminine noun, use "era la mia" (e.g., "era la mia amica").
target_language_example: Marco era il mio vicino di casa quando vivevo a Roma.
native_language_example: Marco was my neighbor when I lived in Rome.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (di + verb) to say someone had (or didn’t have) the ability, capacity, or possibility to do something in the past. Often appears in the negative: “non era in grado di …” = “was not able to …”. You can change the tense/person: “sono in grado di” (I am able to), “sarò in grado di” (I will be able to), “sarei in grado di” (I would be able to).
target_language_example: Dopo l’operazione, non era in grado di camminare.
native_language_example: After the surgery, he wasn’t able to walk.

additional_notes: Imperfetto of essere ("era" = "was"), used for describing a past situation/state (often ongoing or background). Can refer to a person or a life: "la sua vita era in pericolo" = "her life was in danger." You can change the tense/person: "sono in pericolo" (I’m in danger), "sei in pericolo" (you’re in danger).
target_language_example: Pensavo che fosse tardi e che lui era in pericolo.
native_language_example: I thought it was late and that he was in danger.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s emotional state in the past. "Era" is the imperfect of "essere" (to be), and it can mean "was" in an ongoing/background sense (how someone was feeling or what they were like at that time). Change the subject pronoun if needed: "io ero infelice" (I was unhappy), "noi eravamo infelici" (we were unhappy).
target_language_example: Quando viveva lì, era infelice.
native_language_example: When he lived there, he was unhappy.

additional_notes: "Era" is the imperfetto (past) of "essere" (to be), used to describe states/conditions in the past. "Molto" usually means "very" before an adjective ("era molto stanco" = "he was very tired") and can also mean "a lot/very much" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ieri era molto stanco dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: Yesterday he was very tired after work.
