native_language_example: He realized his mistake and apologized.

additional_notes: “Suo” is the possessive for a third-person singular owner (his/her/its), and it agrees with the thing owned: il suo gatto (cat, masc. sing.), la sua gatta (female cat), i suoi gatti (cats, masc. pl.), le sue gatte (cats, fem. pl.). It can also mean “your” when speaking formally to someone (Lei).
target_language_example: Dov'è il suo gatto?
native_language_example: Where is his/her cat? (or: Where is your cat? — formal)

additional_notes: "Suo" is a possessive adjective meaning "his/her/its" and also "your" in the formal address (Lei). It agrees with the thing owned: "il suo giardino" (masc. singular), "i suoi giardini" (masc. plural), "la sua casa" (fem. singular), "le sue case" (fem. plural). In Italian, the possessive usually comes with the definite article (il/la/i/le).
target_language_example: Posso vedere il suo giardino?
native_language_example: Can I see your garden?

additional_notes: "Impiego" means a job/position (employment). "Il suo" means "his" or "her" (formal "your" is also possible, but in these examples it’s third person). Often used with verbs like "perdere" (to lose) and "amare" (to love) to talk about someone’s work situation.
target_language_example: Ha trovato un nuovo impiego dopo aver perso il suo impiego.
native_language_example: He found a new job after losing his job.

additional_notes: "Suo" means "his/her" or "your" (formal, to one person: "Lei"). "Indirizzo" can be a home/mailing address; in some contexts it can also mean an email address ("indirizzo email"). Often used in requests and forms: "Il suo indirizzo?" = "Your address?"
target_language_example: Mi può dare il suo indirizzo, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you give me your address, please?

additional_notes: Means “his teacher” or “her teacher” depending on context. Italian possessives usually take an article: il suo insegnante (male teacher, singular). For a female teacher: la sua insegnante. Common with verbs like piacere (“to like”) and can also appear in romantic-crush contexts (avere una cotta per...).
target_language_example: Ha una cotta per il suo insegnante.
native_language_example: He/She has a crush on his/her teacher.

additional_notes: Means “the invitation from him/her” (formal possessive). You’ll often see it with verbs like accettare (to accept) or rifiutare (to refuse), and it can be followed by a + an activity: il suo invito a cena (his/her invitation to dinner).
target_language_example: Grazie, ma devo rifiutare il suo invito.
native_language_example: Thanks, but I have to refuse his/her invitation.

additional_notes: “Il” is the masculine singular definite article (“the”). “Suo/sua/suoi/sue” is a possessive that agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: here “laptop” is masculine singular, so it’s “il suo laptop.” In Italian, “suo” can mean “his” or “her” depending on context; it can also mean “your” in the formal address (Lei).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato il suo laptop in ufficio.
native_language_example: I forgot his/her laptop at the office.

additional_notes: Means “his/her” (or sometimes “its”) “job/work.” "Suo" agrees with the thing owned (here: "lavoro" is masculine singular), not with the owner. In Italian, "suo" can mean both “his” and “her,” so the context tells you which one.
target_language_example: Ha finito il suo lavoro alle sei.
native_language_example: He/She finished his/her work at six.

additional_notes: "Suo" means "his," "her," or "your" (formal). The exact meaning depends on context. With "il" it agrees with the masculine singular noun "libro". Note: in Italian, possessives usually take the definite article (il/lo/la/i/gli/le): "il suo libro" = "his/her/your book."
target_language_example: È il suo libro?
native_language_example: Is it his/her/your (formal) book?

additional_notes: “Moroso” is a common, fairly informal word (especially in Northern Italy) meaning “boyfriend” or “steady boyfriend/partner.” It’s often used with a possessive: il suo moroso (her boyfriend), il mio moroso (my boyfriend). For a female partner you’ll hear “la sua morosa” (her girlfriend).
target_language_example: Stasera esce con il suo moroso.
native_language_example: Tonight she’s going out with her boyfriend.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "suo" with the definite article "il" (common in Italian with possessives). "Suo" agrees with the thing possessed (here "nome" is masculine singular), not with the person who owns it. Depending on context, it can mean "his", "her", or polite/formal "your" (Lei).
target_language_example: Mi scusi, qual è il suo nome?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is your name?

additional_notes: Used to introduce or identify someone by name. "Suo" can refer to 'his' or 'her' (the owner is the person whose name it is). Often followed by a name ("Il suo nome è Marco") or used in questions like "Il suo nome è sulla lista?" = 'Is his/her name on the list?'
target_language_example: Il suo nome è già nel sistema.
native_language_example: His/Her name is already in the system.

additional_notes: Means “the phone number belonging to him/her,” but with formal address it can also mean “your phone number” (to one person you address as Lei). Used in polite requests: “Mi dia…” (Give me…), “Posso avere…?” (May I have…?).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere il suo numero di telefono?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I have your phone number?

additional_notes: Means someone’s new employment/position. "suo" changes with the noun it describes (here masculine singular "impiego"), not with the person who owns it; it can mean either "his" or "her" depending on context. Common verbs with it include "piacere" (to like), "trovare" (to find/consider), and "iniziare/cominciare" (to start).
target_language_example: Sono contenta per Marco: il suo nuovo impiego gli piace molto.
native_language_example: I’m happy for Marco: he really likes his new job.

additional_notes: "Suo" is the possessive used with a noun and agrees with the noun, not the owner: ombrello is masculine singular, so "il suo ombrello". It can mean “his umbrella” or “her umbrella”; context tells you which. With formal/polite "Lei" (you), you also use "suo/sua" (e.g., "È il suo ombrello, signora?").
target_language_example: Scusi, è il suo ombrello o quello di Tom?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is it his/her umbrella or Tom’s?

meaning: his/her/its watch (or clock), referring to the subject’s own.
additional_notes: "Suo" means “his/her/its,” and it usually agrees with the thing owned: "il suo orologio" (masc. sing.), "la sua borsa". In Italian, "suo" often refers back to the subject of the sentence (e.g., Mary… il suo orologio = Mary’s watch). Use "il loro orologio" for “their watch.” "Orologio" can mean a wristwatch or a clock; context tells you which.
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato il suo orologio sul tavolo.
native_language_example: I forgot his/her watch on the table.

additional_notes: "Suo" means "his/her"; in formal address it can also mean "your" (often written with a capital S: "il Suo paese"). "Paese" can mean either a country or a (usually small) town/village; context usually clarifies which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Questo è il suo paese.
native_language_example: This is his/her country (or hometown/village).

additional_notes: "Suo" means "his", "her", or (formal) "your". In requests to a stranger or in official situations (airport, hotel, police), "Mi mostri il suo passaporto" means "Show me your passport". The article "il" = "the" and is commonly used with possessions in Italian (il suo passaporto = literally "the his/your passport").
target_language_example: All'aeroporto mi hanno chiesto di mostrare il suo passaporto.
native_language_example: At the airport they asked me to show my passport (formal: “your passport”).

additional_notes: “Suo” means “his/her/its” (it doesn’t show the gender of the owner—only the thing owned). It agrees with the noun: *piano* (masc. singular) → *il suo piano*. In more formal contexts, *suo* can also refer to “your” (formal *Lei*): *il suo piano* = “your plan (sir/ma’am)”. Note: *piano* in Italian means “plan,” not the musical instrument.
target_language_example: Non conosco ancora il suo piano, ma mi sembra una buona idea.
native_language_example: I still don’t know his/her plan, but it seems like a good idea to me.

additional_notes: "Portatile" is a common way to say "laptop" in Italian (short for "computer portatile"). "Il suo" means "his" or "her" depending on context; Italian uses the same possessive for both. It can be used with verbs like aprire/chiudere (to open/close), accendere (to turn on), and lasciare (to leave).
target_language_example: Non trovo il suo portatile: forse l'ha lasciato in ufficio.
native_language_example: I can't find his/her laptop: maybe they left it at the office.

meaning: her boyfriend / his boyfriend (depending on context).
additional_notes: In Italian, **suo** can mean **his** or **her**—you tell which one from context. It agrees with the thing owned (here: **ragazzo**, masculine singular), not with the owner. Use **il suo ragazzo** for “his/her boyfriend”; for “his/her girlfriend” you’d say **la sua ragazza**.
target_language_example: Ha detto che viene alla festa con il suo ragazzo.
native_language_example: She said she’s coming to the party with her boyfriend.

additional_notes: Means “the report belonging to him/her/it.” In Italian, "suo" agrees with the noun that follows (here: "rapporto" is masculine singular), not with the owner. The owner is understood from context or specified (e.g., "il suo rapporto" = his report / her report). Common with verbs like leggere (to read), consegnare (to hand in/submit), riscrivere (to rewrite).
target_language_example: Devo finire il suo rapporto entro stasera.
native_language_example: I have to finish his/her report by this evening.

additional_notes: Means “the gift” belonging to someone. "Suo" changes with the thing owned (regalo = masculine singular → suo) and can refer to his, her, or your (formal) depending on context. "Il" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”). In polite/formal situations, "il suo" can mean “your” (to one person).
target_language_example: Grazie per il suo regalo, è molto gentile.
native_language_example: Thank you for your gift, that’s very kind.

additional_notes: Means “the secret of him/her” (someone else’s secret). It’s polite/formal; in Italian “suo/sua/suoi/sue” can mean either “his” or “her”, so context tells you which. The article (il/lo/la, etc.) is normally used with possessives: “il suo segreto”, not just “suo segreto”.
target_language_example: Non dirlo a nessuno: è il suo segreto.
native_language_example: Don't tell anyone: it's his/her secret.

additional_notes: Means “the dream of” a person you address with polite Lei (“your dream”), or a third person (his/her dream). In writing, suo/sua can refer to “your” (formal), “his,” or “her,” so context clarifies who it belongs to. Often used when talking about goals or aspirations.
target_language_example: Il suo sogno è aprire un ristorante.
native_language_example: His/Her (or your, formal) dream is to open a restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone else’s smile. "Suo" agrees with the noun: "sorriso" is masculine singular, so it becomes "suo". Italian often uses the definite article with possessives (il suo, la sua, i suoi, le sue), especially when talking about things like a person’s features (smile, eyes, hair). Context tells you whether it means "his" or "her".
target_language_example: Non dimenticherò mai il suo sorriso.
native_language_example: I’ll never forget his/her smile.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "suo" with the definite article: "il suo" + a masculine singular noun ("successo"). "Suo" agrees with the thing possessed (successo), not with the person who has it—so it can mean either "his" or "her" depending on context. Common with verbs like "dovere" (to owe) and "attribuire" (to attribute): "deve il suo successo a...", "ha attribuito il suo successo a...".
target_language_example: Nonostante le difficoltà, il suo successo è arrivato con il tempo.
native_language_example: Despite the difficulties, his/her success came over time.

additional_notes: "Suo" is a possessive adjective that agrees with the noun (telefono = masculine singular → il suo). It usually means “his/her/its” based on context; with "Lei" (formal “you”), it means “your” (e.g., "Utilizzi il suo telefono" = “Use your phone.”). For a feminine noun you’d use "la sua" (e.g., "la sua macchina").
target_language_example: Non trovo il suo telefono: l’ha lasciato sul tavolo?
native_language_example: I can’t find his/her phone—did he/she leave it on the table?

meaning: “his/her time” (often: “(to) take your time”; also: “(to) serve/do one’s time” or “it’s past its prime,” depending on context).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “his/her time.” Most commonly appears in **prendersi il suo tempo** = “to take his/her time” (i.e., not to rush; to take the time one needs). In **ha fatto il suo tempo**, it can mean “he served his time” (e.g., in prison) or more broadly “it has had its day / it’s past its prime.” In **il suo tempo si sta avvicinando**, it can mean “his/her time is approaching” (e.g., a deadline, the moment to act, or—depending on context—end of life). Note that for directly addressing someone, Italian typically uses **il tuo tempo** (informal “your time”) or **il Suo tempo** (formal “your time”), not **il suo tempo**.
target_language_example: Dissi a Mary di prendersi il suo tempo.
native_language_example: I told Mary to take her time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s place in an order (a queue, a sequence of actions, taking turns in conversation or games). Often used with verbs like aspettare (to wait): "Aspetta il suo turno" = "He/She waits for his/her turn." You can also swap the possessive: "il mio turno" (my turn), "il tuo turno" (your turn), "il nostro turno" (our turn).
target_language_example: Adesso è il suo turno di parlare.
native_language_example: Now it’s his/her turn to speak.

meaning: “his/her last” or “his/her latest/most recent” (thing/person mentioned next).
additional_notes: Used before a noun: *il suo ultimo desiderio* (“his/her last wish”), *il suo ultimo romanzo* (“his/her latest novel”), *il suo ultimo marito* (“his/her last/most recent husband”). Meaning depends on context: **ultimo** can mean the final one ever (“last”) or the most recent (“latest”). The article and adjective agree with the noun: *il suo ultimo* (masc. sing.), *la sua ultima* (fem. sing.), *i suoi ultimi*, *le sue ultime*.
target_language_example: Hai letto il suo ultimo libro?
native_language_example: Have you read his/her latest book?

additional_notes: Used to specify someone’s actual name (not a nickname, stage name, or fake name). "Suo" agrees with the thing owned ("nome"), so it can mean either “his” or “her” depending on context. You’ll often see it with verbs like "conoscere" (to know) or phrases like "mi chiedo se..." (I wonder if...).
target_language_example: Non so se questo è il suo vero nome.
native_language_example: I don’t know if this is his/her real name.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s trip to a place. "suo" agrees with the thing owned (viaggio = masculine singular), not with the owner. Choose the preposition based on the destination: "in" is common with most countries/continents (in India, in Australia); with most cities you typically use "a" (il suo viaggio a Roma).
target_language_example: Ha raccontato il suo viaggio in Brasile.
native_language_example: He/She talked about his/her trip to Brazil.

additional_notes: Literally “his/her face.” In Italian, "suo" can mean "his" or "her" depending on who owns the face; the gender of the owner is not shown in the word itself. Used in descriptions of emotions or reactions (e.g., turning red, looking sad) and for recognizing someone.
target_language_example: Ho visto il suo volto e l’ho riconosciuto subito.
native_language_example: I saw his/her face and recognized it right away.

additional_notes: Masculine singular possessive pronoun phrase. It usually means "his/hers" when the noun is understood from context: for example, il suo orologio = "his/her watch", but il suo on its own = "his/hers" or "his/hers one." It can also mean "its" or "theirs" depending on context.
target_language_example: Non trovo il mio libro, quindi prendo il suo.
native_language_example: I can't find my book, so I'll take his/hers.

additional_notes: A masculine noun in Italian: il sushi. Used to talk about sushi as food in general, or as what you’re eating/ordering. In Italian, many loanwords like sushi don’t change in the plural: il sushi / i sushi.
target_language_example: Vorrei il sushi, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like sushi, please.

meaning: the table; also ‘the (restaurant) table’ (the group/seat number).
additional_notes: Most often means a physical table (a piece of furniture): *Il tavolo è pulito.* In restaurants it can refer to the customers seated together or their table number: *Cuocere i soufflé per il tavolo sei* = “for table 6.” Gender/number: *il tavolo* (sing.), *i tavoli* (pl.).
target_language_example: Possiamo spostare il tavolo vicino alla finestra?
native_language_example: Can we move the table near the window?

additional_notes: Italian often uses the definite article with languages: il tedesco, l’italiano, lo spagnolo, ecc. It’s used with verbs like parlare (to speak), capire (to understand), imparare/studiare (to learn/study), insegnare (to teach), amare (to love). It can also mean “the German person/thing” depending on context, but in these examples it clearly means the language.
target_language_example: Sto imparando il tedesco per lavoro.
native_language_example: I'm learning German for work.

additional_notes: Commonly used for both a landline and a mobile phone (depending on context). You’ll often see it with verbs like suonare (“to ring”), rispondere (“to answer”), and prendere (“to pick up/answer”). Note the direct object form is usually lo: «Lo prendo io il telefono» = “I’ll get the phone / I’ll answer it.”
target_language_example: Scusa, non posso parlare adesso: sta suonando il telefono.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk right now: the phone is ringing.

additional_notes: Don't confuse tempo with English tempo. Depending on context, it can mean the weather or time; it can also mean a period or season. With adjectives like bello, brutto, or freddo, it usually refers to weather. In expressions like passare il tempo, it means time.
target_language_example: In primavera il tempo cambia spesso.
native_language_example: In spring the weather changes often.

meaning: "the time to" (do something); sometimes "just enough time to".
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive: "(dare/avere) il tempo di + infinito" = to have/give (someone) time to do something. In storytelling it can be shortened to "Il tempo di + infinito, e..." meaning something happened immediately after, often implying there was barely enough time: "Il tempo di girarmi e..." = "I barely had time to turn around and...".
target_language_example: Mi dai il tempo di finire questo messaggio?
native_language_example: Can you give me time to finish this message?

meaning: the test; the exam; the trial/check.
additional_notes: Used for an exam (school/qualification) or a practical/technical test (e.g., testing a new engine). Common verbs: fare/sostenere un test (take a test), superare un test (pass a test), fallire un test (fail a test), iniziare il test (start the test). In Italian you often keep the English loanword “test” with the masculine article “il”.
target_language_example: Domani ho il test di italiano.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have the Italian test.

meaning: the text (written words; also the lyrics of a song).
additional_notes: Commonly refers to a written passage (in a book, exercise, article, message, etc.). In music, "il testo" can mean the lyrics (the words) as opposed to the melody. Masculine singular: il testo; plural: i testi.
target_language_example: Puoi mandarmi il testo dell’email?
native_language_example: Can you send me the text of the email?

meaning: the title; also: a championship title.
additional_notes: Most commonly means the name of a book, song, film, article, etc. In sports it can mean a “title” as in winning a championship (often with words like mondiale, campione, combattere per). Grammar: masculine singular; plural: i titoli. Common pattern: il titolo di + [thing] (il titolo del libro / della canzone).
target_language_example: Non ricordo il titolo del film, ma mi è piaciuto molto.
native_language_example: I don’t remember the title of the movie, but I liked it a lot.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: **il** + **treno** (masculine singular). Plural: **i treni** (“the trains”). Common with verbs like **prendere il treno** (“to take/catch the train”) and **perdere il treno** (“to miss the train”). You can specify a departure time with **il treno delle otto** (“the eight o’clock train”).
target_language_example: Scusi, dov'è il treno per Firenze?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the train to Florence?

additional_notes: Used to indicate the train whose destination is the place that follows “per”. You’ll often see/hear it in stations and announcements: “Questo è il treno per…” = “This is the train to…”. Related common phrase: “perdere il treno per [città]” = “to miss the train to [city]”.
target_language_example: Scusi, dov’è il treno per Milano?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the train to Milan?

meaning: "the train is" / "the train has" (with a past participle).
additional_notes:
Used to give information about the train’s status or schedule: 
- with an adjective or phrase: "Il treno è in ritardo" (The train is late), "Il treno è in anticipo" (The train is early).
- with a past participle (passato prossimo with essere): "Il treno è arrivato" (The train has arrived).
"Il" = “the” (masculine singular), "treno" = “train”, "è" = “is/has”.
target_language_example: Scusi, il treno è già partito?
native_language_example: Excuse me, has the train already left?

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: il tuo libro = your book. Even though it literally includes the article il, in English you usually just translate it as your. On its own, il tuo can also mean yours for a masculine singular thing.
target_language_example: Dov'è il tuo telefono?
native_language_example: Where is your phone?

additional_notes: Means help coming from the person you’re speaking to (informal singular tu). It’s commonly used with verbs like: mi serve il tuo aiuto (I need your help), grazie per il tuo aiuto (thanks for your help), apprezzo il tuo aiuto (I appreciate your help). For polite/formal singular, use il Suo aiuto; for talking to more than one person, use il vostro aiuto.
target_language_example: Mi serve il tuo aiuto con questo esercizio.
native_language_example: I need your help with this exercise.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male friend of the person you’re talking to: il = “the”, tuo = “your”, amico = “friend (male)”. For a female friend, say “la tua amica”. In Italian, the article (il/la) is often included before possessives (il tuo, la tua, i tuoi, le tue), especially with family/friends and many everyday nouns.
target_language_example: Il tuo amico parla inglese?
native_language_example: Does your friend speak English?

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s love/affection (often romantic, but it can also be deep affection in general). It’s a noun phrase: il (the) + tuo (your) + amore (love). Common in emotional statements and declarations (e.g., “Tutto quello che voglio è il tuo amore”).
target_language_example: Tutto quello che voglio è il tuo amore.
native_language_example: All I want is your love.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s dog, addressing one person informally (tu). The article changes with gender/number: il tuo cane (m. sing.), la tua cagna (f. sing., less common; often people still say "il mio/tuo cane" for a female dog), i tuoi cani (pl.), le tue cagne (pl.). In questions like "Come si chiama...?" it means “What’s your dog’s name?”
target_language_example: Dov'è il tuo cane?
native_language_example: Where is your dog?

meaning: your boss (or your manager/supervisor; depending on context, also “your leader”).
additional_notes: Literally “your head/chief,” but in everyday Italian it most commonly means “your boss” at work. The phrase itself is neutral; it can appear in rude or insulting sentences depending on surrounding words.
target_language_example: Hai già parlato con il tuo capo di questa cosa?
native_language_example: Have you already talked to your boss about this?

additional_notes: Used to talk to someone about their birthday. Often appears with expressions like “Oggi è il tuo compleanno” (Today is your birthday), “Domani è il tuo compleanno” (Tomorrow is your birthday), or “Il tuo compleanno si avvicina” (Your birthday is coming up).
target_language_example: Allora, cosa vuoi fare per il tuo compleanno?
native_language_example: So, what do you want to do for your birthday?

additional_notes: Used to talk directly to someone about how they are acting, often to criticize (“I have problems with your behavior”), but it can also be positive (“your behavior was heroic”). It’s singular masculine: il comportamento; with possessive: il tuo comportamento.
target_language_example: Non mi piace il tuo comportamento in questo momento.
native_language_example: I don’t like your behavior right now.

additional_notes: Used when talking directly to someone about their computer. "Il" is the masculine singular definite article, and "tuo" agrees with the noun (computer is masculine in Italian). Often appears in questions and requests: "Posso usare/prendere in prestito il tuo computer?"
target_language_example: Non posso usare il tuo computer adesso.
native_language_example: I can’t use your computer right now.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective **tuo** with a definite article (**il**) before the noun: **il tuo + noun** (e.g., *il tuo corpo*). The phrase is neutral, but depending on context it can sound intimate/sexual (e.g., talking about someone’s appearance) or can be used in serious contexts (health, injury, even referring to a dead body).
target_language_example: Ascolta il tuo corpo e riposati quando sei stanco.
native_language_example: Listen to your body and rest when you’re tired.

meaning: “your ass” (vulgar; used to tell someone to move/get somewhere).
additional_notes: Very vulgar and often aggressive, used especially in commands like “muovi il tuo culo” / “porta il tuo culo…” (“move your ass / get your ass…”). Can be used jokingly among close friends, but it’s rude in most situations—avoid in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Muovi il tuo culo, siamo in ritardo!
native_language_example: Move your ass, we’re late!

meaning: "your heart" (literally; often meaning your feelings/inner voice).
additional_notes: Used literally for the physical heart (especially with verbs like battere/sentire) and figuratively in expressions like ascoltare/seguire il tuo cuore (“listen to/follow your heart”), meaning to trust your feelings or intuition. In romantic/dramatic contexts, "Dammi il tuo cuore!" can mean “Give me your love/yourself.”
target_language_example: A volte è difficile, ma devi ascoltare il tuo cuore.
native_language_example: Sometimes it’s hard, but you have to listen to your heart.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or give someone’s address (home, mailing, etc.). *Indirizzo* can also mean “direction” (e.g., a street direction) depending on context, but with *tuo* it commonly means someone’s address. Often used with verbs like *dire* (tell), *dare* (give), *scrivere* (write), *chiedere* (ask).
target_language_example: Mi mandi il tuo indirizzo, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you send me your address, please?

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular noun "lavoro" (work/job) with the possessive adjective "tuo" (your). It can refer to your job (employment) or more generally to the work you do, depending on context. Often used after prepositions like "con" (with), "a" (at), or "nel" (in the).
target_language_example: Come va con il tuo lavoro?
native_language_example: How’s it going with your job?

additional_notes: Uses the definite article + possessive: il (the) + tuo (your) + libro (book). In Italian, possessives usually take an article (il tuo, la tua, i tuoi, le tue). Here it’s masculine singular (libro). You can use it in questions or statements when talking directly to someone about their book.
target_language_example: Scusa, dov'è il tuo libro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is your book?

additional_notes: Used to address one person informally (tu). In more formal situations (to a stranger, customer, older person), use “il suo nome” instead. Often appears in questions when asking for someone’s details.
target_language_example: Qual è il tuo nome?
native_language_example: What is your name?

additional_notes: Used when asking for someone’s phone number. You can use it after verbs like: dare (“Dammi…”, give me…), avere (“Posso avere…?”, can I have…), dire (“Mi diresti…?”, would you tell me…). Often paired with “il tuo nome” (your name) in more polite/form-style requests.
target_language_example: Scusa, posso avere il tuo numero di telefono?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have your phone number?

meaning: "your new" (masculine singular, used before a noun).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: il tuo nuovo ragazzo (your new boyfriend), il tuo nuovo vestito (your new outfit/dress), il tuo nuovo animale (your new animal/pet). It must agree in gender/number; for feminine you use la tua nuova, and for masculine plural i tuoi nuovi.
target_language_example: Dov'è il tuo nuovo telefono?
native_language_example: Where is your new phone?

additional_notes: Literally "the your plan". Used when talking about someone’s idea/strategy (un piano) or, in some contexts, someone’s schedule (il piano, e.g., a work plan). Often followed by verbs like è (is), sembra (seems), funziona (works), fallisce (fails).
target_language_example: Il tuo piano è interessante, ma costa troppo.
native_language_example: Your plan is interesting, but it costs too much.

additional_notes: Means “your phone” when talking to one person you address with tu. It’s masculine singular: il (the) + tuo (your) + telefono (phone). Used in everyday situations: losing your phone, it ringing, borrowing it, charging it, or asking how often someone uses it. For “your phone” in the formal singular (Lei), use: il Suo telefono.
target_language_example: Scusa, dov'è il tuo telefono? Sta suonando.
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is your phone? It’s ringing.

additional_notes: Literally means “your time.” Very common with the verb phrase **(prendersi) il tuo tempo** = “to take your time / not rush” (often said as advice or encouragement). It can also mean the time you have available, e.g. **tutto il tuo tempo** = “all your time.”
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: prenditi il tuo tempo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: take your time.

additional_notes: Possessive with the definite article. Used as a possessive pronoun (the noun is understood): "Il tuo e il mio" = "Yours and mine." It agrees with the thing owned (not the owner): il tuo (masc. sing.), la tua (fem. sing.), i tuoi (masc. pl.), le tue (fem. pl.). Common when comparing or emphasizing (e.g., "non il tuo" = "not yours / not your one").
target_language_example: Questo libro è il tuo, non il mio.
native_language_example: This book is yours, not mine.

additional_notes: Means “tea” (the drink). Common patterns: “tè al limone” = lemon tea; “tè con il latte” = tea with milk; “senza zucchero” = without sugar. In “Rimani per il tè”, it can mean staying for tea (the drink/tea time).
target_language_example: Vuoi il tè caldo o freddo?
native_language_example: Do you want hot tea or iced tea?

meaning: the old man; the old one (male).
additional_notes: Literally “the old.” In Italian, an adjective like vecchio can be used as a noun when paired with an article (il, la, i, le). Depending on context it can mean “the old man” or more generally “the old one” (referring to a male person).
target_language_example: Il vecchio vive da solo in quella casa.
native_language_example: The old man lives alone in that house.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun phrase: il (the) + vento (wind). Often used with weather verbs like soffiare (to blow): “Il vento soffia” = “The wind is blowing.” You can modify it with adverbs/adjectives (forte = strong) to describe how windy it is.
target_language_example: Oggi c'è il vento, quindi fa più freddo.
native_language_example: Today it’s windy, so it feels colder.

additional_notes: Usually refers to glass as a material (e.g., something you cut, break, or that can shatter). In some contexts it can also mean a glass pane (like a window or a display case). Often used with verbs like tagliare (to cut), rompere (to break), and against/onto it (contro il vetro).
target_language_example: Attento: il vetro è fragile.
native_language_example: Careful: glass is fragile.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun meaning a trip/journey (travel from one place to another). Often followed by “a/in + place” to say where you’re going (e.g., “il viaggio a Parigi”). Plural: “i viaggi”.
target_language_example: Il viaggio in treno è durato tre ore.
native_language_example: The train trip lasted three hours.

additional_notes: Used for a video clip/movie recording (online or offline). With "video" the singular article is usually "il" (il video), plural "i video". Common with verbs like vedere (to watch), mettere in pausa (to pause), caricare (to upload).
target_language_example: Puoi mandarmi il video?
native_language_example: Can you send me the video?

additional_notes: Literally “the wine” (il = “the”, masculine singular). In Italian, the definite article is often used when talking about something in general: “Mi piace il vino” = “I like wine.” Use “del vino” to mean “some wine.”
target_language_example: A cena vorrei del vino, ma il vino rosso mi piace di più.
native_language_example: For dinner I’d like some wine, but I like red wine more.

additional_notes: Common in restaurants and at home. "Il" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”). You’ll often hear it contrasted with "il vino bianco" (white wine). With preferences you can use: "Preferisco il vino rosso" (I prefer red wine) and comparisons like "Preferisce il vino rosso al vino bianco" (He/She prefers red wine to white wine).
target_language_example: Al ristorante prendo il vino rosso, grazie.
native_language_example: At the restaurant I’ll have red wine, thanks.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun. Used with verbs like suonare (to play) and sapere suonare (to know how to play). Plural: i violini.
target_language_example: Mia sorella studia il violino da due anni.
native_language_example: My sister has been studying the violin for two years.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: "il" (the, masculine singular) + "virus". Used for a disease-causing virus; in Italian, "virus" is invariable in the singular and plural (il virus / i virus).
target_language_example: Secondo il medico, il virus è molto contagioso.
native_language_example: According to the doctor, the virus is very contagious.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: il vostro blog, il vostro impiego. vostro agrees with the noun, not with the person who owns it. In Italian, possessives are often used with a definite article, unlike in English.
target_language_example: Dov'è il vostro albergo?
native_language_example: Where is your hotel?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "vostro" to address more than one person ("your" plural) or to address someone formally ("your" polite). Often used with verbs like "servire" (to need) and "apprezzare" (to appreciate), and in expressions like "senza il vostro aiuto" (without your help).
target_language_example: Grazie per il vostro aiuto: senza di voi non ce l’avrei fatta.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help: without you I wouldn’t have made it.

meaning: "your dog" (addressing more than one person, or using polite/formal 'you').
additional_notes: “Il” is “the” and “vostro” means “your” for plural “you” (voi) or for polite/formal address in some contexts. It agrees with the masculine singular noun “cane” (dog). You can also hear “il cane vostro,” but “il vostro cane” is more common.
target_language_example: Il vostro cane è molto simpatico, ma abbaia troppo.
native_language_example: Your dog is very nice, but it barks too much.

additional_notes: Used when addressing more than one person (‘you all’) or as a polite/formal way to address one person. It agrees with the noun: computer is masculine singular, so it takes il vostro. Common in instructions, tech support, and formal communication.
target_language_example: Il vostro computer sta funzionando correttamente?
native_language_example: Is your computer working properly?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive vostro (“your”) with the article il (“the”). It’s used when speaking to more than one person (you all) or to one person formally (like “your” in a polite context). Common with verbs like dare (to give) and dire (to tell): “Datemi/Ditemi il vostro indirizzo” = “Give/Tell me your address.”
target_language_example: Può scrivermi il vostro indirizzo, per favore?
native_language_example: Could you write me your address, please?

additional_notes: "Vostro" is the possessive for "you" plural (voi) and also a polite/formal "your" when addressing someone (often with titles like Signore/Signora). "Lavoro" can mean both the job/profession and the work someone is doing. Used when talking to a group or speaking formally to one person.
target_language_example: Mi interessa molto il vostro lavoro.
native_language_example: I'm very interested in your work.

meaning: “your book” (addressing more than one person, or one person formally).
additional_notes: “Il” = “the”; “vostro” is the possessive for “your” used with (1) multiple people (“you all/you guys”) or (2) formal “you” in some contexts; it agrees with the noun: libro (masculine singular) → vostro. Often used when talking about something that belongs to the people you’re speaking to or referring to.
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito il vostro libro per un giorno?
native_language_example: Can I borrow your book for one day?

additional_notes: "Vostro" is the formal "your" (to one person you address as "Lei"), or "your" to more than one person ("you all"). It’s often used in polite questions: "Posso chiedere il vostro nome?".
target_language_example: Mi scusi, qual è il vostro nome?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is your name?

additional_notes: Used with the possessive "vostro" to address more than one person ("you all") or, in some contexts, as a formal/polite "your". In everyday conversation with one person, you’ll more often hear "il tuo numero di telefono" (informal) or "il Suo numero di telefono" (formal).
target_language_example: Può ripetere il vostro numero di telefono, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you repeat your phone number, please?

meaning: "your plan" (addressing more than one person, or using formal "you").
additional_notes: "Vostro" agrees with the noun: "il vostro piano" (masc. singular). You can also say "il piano vostro", but "il vostro piano" is much more common. Used when speaking to a group ("your" plural) or to one person in a polite/formal way (Lei).
target_language_example: Capisco il vostro piano, ma credo che serva più tempo.
native_language_example: I understand your plan, but I think we need more time.

additional_notes: "Il" = "the" and "vostro" = "your" when speaking to more than one person (voi) or in formal contexts. Used for giving instructions or addressing a group: "Caricate/Usate/Utilizzate il vostro telefono". Often alternates with "il tuo telefono" (your phone, informal singular).
target_language_example: Per favore, spegnete il vostro telefono durante la riunione.
native_language_example: Please, turn off your phone during the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause, often in more formal or written Italian, as an alternative to “che” or “cui”. It agrees with the noun it refers to: il quale (m. sg.), la quale (f. sg.), i quali (m. pl.), le quali (f. pl.). Often used after prepositions: “con il quale” (with which/whom), “per la quale” (for which), etc.
target_language_example: Ho parlato con il quale avevi lavorato l’anno scorso.
native_language_example: I spoke with the person you had worked with last year.

additional_notes: Used to express an assumption or a guess about something. It’s commonly followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo), especially in more careful/formal Italian: "Immagino che sia...", "Immagino che tu abbia...". In everyday speech you may also hear the indicative, but learners should recognize the subjunctive pattern.
target_language_example: Immagino che tu sia stanco dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: I imagine you’re tired after the trip.

additional_notes: From the verb "imparare" (to learn). "Imparando" is the gerund, commonly used with "stare" to form the present continuous: "sto/stai/sta/stiamo/state/stanno imparando il francese" = "I am/you are/he is/we are/you (pl.) are/they are learning French."
target_language_example: In questo periodo sto imparando il francese online.
native_language_example: These days I’m learning French online.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like volere (to want), piacere (to like), aiutare (to help), or avere bisogno di (to need): e.g., “Voglio imparare il berbero.” “Berbero” is a language name and is capitalized less consistently in Italian than in English; both “berbero” and “Berbero” may be seen.
target_language_example: Sto cercando un corso per imparare il berbero.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a course to learn Berber.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "imparare" (to learn) + the language name with the definite article: "il francese" (French). It often appears with another verb to talk about starting/trying to learn: "iniziare a imparare", "provare a imparare", "cercare di imparare".
target_language_example: Hai già iniziato a imparare il francese?
native_language_example: Have you already started learning French?

additional_notes: Imparare = “to learn”; il tedesco = “German (language)”. Used for talking about studying the German language. You’ll often see it with time questions: “Quanto tempo ti/le serve per…?” (How long do you need to…?), and with “iniziare a…” (to start to…).
target_language_example: Sto cercando di imparare il tedesco per lavoro.
native_language_example: I'm trying to learn German for work.

additional_notes: Used to say something is shown/broadcast on television. With verbs like vedere/guardare (to see/watch): “Vederlo in TV” = “to see him on TV”; “guardare … in TV” = “to watch … on TV.”
target_language_example: Stasera c'è un film interessante in TV.
native_language_example: Tonight there's an interesting movie on TV.

additional_notes: Used to say there is a lot of something. Often appears with "ne" (“some/any of it/them”): "Ne ho in abbondanza" = “I have plenty (of it/them).” Can also follow a noun: "cibo in abbondanza" = “food in abundance.”
target_language_example: Qui l'acqua è in abbondanza.
native_language_example: Here there’s plenty of water.

additional_notes: Used to say you travel using an airplane, or to ask/how long a trip takes by plane. Often used with verbs like andare/viaggiare/arrivare (to go/travel/arrive) and with time questions: Quanto tempo ci vuole in aereo?
target_language_example: Andiamo a Roma in aereo perché è più veloce.
native_language_example: We’re going to Rome by plane because it’s faster.

additional_notes: Used with housing, rooms, cars, etc. to mean something is available to rent (casa in affitto = house for rent) or that someone has it rented/leased (avere una casa in affitto = to rent a house). Common with verbs like "cercare" (to look for), "trovare" (to find), "prendere" (to rent/take), and "dare/mettere in affitto" (to rent out).
target_language_example: Cerco un appartamento in affitto vicino al centro.
native_language_example: I'm looking for an apartment for rent near the city center.

meaning: lying in wait; lurking (ready to attack or happen).
additional_notes: Used for people/animals/enemies waiting to ambush, or for dangers/trouble that may happen suddenly. Common with verbs like "stare/essere" (stare/essere in agguato) and with phrases like "dietro l'angolo" (around the corner).
target_language_example: C'era qualcuno in agguato vicino all'ingresso.
native_language_example: There was someone lurking near the entrance.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a higher position (on a shelf, on a wall, higher up in a building, etc.). Very common in instructions: “Metti le mani in alto!” = “Hands up!” / “Put your hands up!”
target_language_example: Il libro è in alto, sullo scaffale.
native_language_example: The book is up high, on the shelf.

additional_notes: Used for position or direction above you (often with verbs like guardare, puntare, andare). With comparatives it means “higher” (più in alto). Can also describe doing something with greater ambition or aiming higher (mira più in alto).
target_language_example: Metti la scatola in alto, così i bambini non la prendono.
native_language_example: Put the box up high so the kids can’t grab it.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a higher position or direction (opposite of "in basso" = down/below). Common with verbs like "guardare" (to look), "andare" (to go), "mettere" (to put), and "tenere" (to hold): "Guarda in alto" (look up), "Mettilo in alto" (put it up high). Can also describe something located high up: "La finestra è in alto" (the window is up high).
target_language_example: Guarda in alto: c’è un uccello sul tetto.
native_language_example: Look up: there’s a bird on the roof.

additional_notes: Used to restate the same idea more clearly, often to explain the conclusion or the real meaning of what was just said. It can appear at the beginning of a sentence, or after a pause: “..., in altre parole, ...”.
target_language_example: Non può venire oggi; in altre parole, dobbiamo rimandare l’incontro.
native_language_example: He can’t come today; in other words, we have to postpone the meeting.

meaning: in advance; ahead of time; early.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens before the expected time (essere in anticipo = to be early) or before another action/deadline (pagare in anticipo = to pay in advance). Common with apologies: scusarsi in anticipo = “to apologize in advance.”
target_language_example: Per favore, avvisami in anticipo se non puoi venire.
native_language_example: Please let me know in advance if you can’t come.

meaning: apparently; on the surface; in appearance (but not necessarily in reality).
additional_notes: Used to contrast how something seems with how it really is (often followed or implied by "ma in realtà..." = "but in reality..."). It can modify a whole statement ("In apparenza, ...") or come after the verb ("era solo in apparenza"). Common intensifiers: "solo/solamente/soltanto in apparenza" = "only apparently".
target_language_example: In apparenza è gentile, ma in realtà pensa solo a sé.
native_language_example: He seems kind, but in reality he only thinks about himself.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is written, spoken, revealed, or expressed using the Arabic language. Very common with verbs like essere (to be), parlare (to speak), scrivere (to write), and phrases like tutto in arabo (“all in Arabic”). In questions, it often means “in Arabic, what does it mean?”
target_language_example: Puoi scriverlo in arabo, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you write it in Arabic, please?

meaning: in the air; up in the air (e.g., thrown/blown up/raised).
additional_notes: Used for something physically above the ground (throwing something up, a balloon rising, arms raised). It’s also common in expressions like “saltare in aria” (to blow up / go flying) and “far saltare … in aria” (to blow … up). With body parts it means “up/raised,” e.g., “le braccia in aria.”
target_language_example: Ha alzato le mani in aria quando ha visto la polizia.
native_language_example: He raised his hands in the air when he saw the police.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is coming and will arrive soon. Very common for transport or messages (e.g., "posta in arrivo" = inbox), and also as a warning in urgent situations ("È in arrivo..." = "...is coming / incoming"). Often follows the verb "essere" ("è/sono in arrivo"), or is used as a standalone alert ("Evacuazione in arrivo").
target_language_example: Il treno è in arrivo al binario 2.
native_language_example: The train is arriving at platform 2.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "essere" ("sono/sei/siete in ascolto") to say someone is listening, and with "mettersi in ascolto" as an instruction meaning "to start listening / listen carefully". It can also mean being tuned in (e.g., to a radio show) or on standby to hear something.
target_language_example: Ragazzi, siete in ascolto?
native_language_example: Guys, are you listening?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is the highest/strongest when comparing everything possible: "il più ... in assoluto" = "the ...est of all / ever". It can also be used alone as a short confirmation ("In assoluto." = "Absolutely." / "Definitely.").
target_language_example: È il mio film preferito in assoluto.
native_language_example: It’s my favorite movie of all time.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like stare/rimanere/restare “to stay/remain” to mean “to be waiting” or “to stay on hold.” Often followed by di + noun (in attesa di notizie = waiting for news) or che + clause (in attesa che succeda qualcosa = waiting for something to happen). Common in polite instructions: “Rimanga/Resti in attesa” = “Please stay on the line / Please wait.”
target_language_example: Siamo in attesa di una risposta.
native_language_example: We’re waiting for an answer.

additional_notes: Used to say you are waiting for a person, thing, event, or instructions. It often implies you expect it to happen soon or you’re standing by. Common patterns: "essere in attesa di + noun" (Siamo in attesa di notizie) and "essere in attesa di + infinitive" (Sono in attesa di partire).
target_language_example: Siamo in attesa di una risposta.
native_language_example: We’re waiting for an answer.

meaning: by bus (using the bus as transport).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/coming/traveling (and similar) to say you are traveling by bus: andare/venire/arrivare/partire in autobus. Compare: “con l’autobus” is also possible but less common in everyday speech for this meaning. You can add destinations with a or in: “Vado in stazione in autobus.”
target_language_example: Domani andiamo in centro in autobus.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going downtown by bus.

meaning: “by bus or by …” (asking which means of transport).
additional_notes: Used to offer/ask between two travel options. In Italian you often use **in + vehicle** to mean “by (that vehicle)”: *in autobus, in auto, in treno*. This phrase typically continues with a second option: *in autobus o in auto?*
target_language_example: Andiamo in autobus o in metro?
native_language_example: Are we going by bus or by subway?

meaning: in the bathroom; to the bathroom (to use the toilet).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of being/staying to mean you are located in the bathroom (e.g., "Sono/è in bagno" = "I’m/he’s in the bathroom"). With verbs of motion it often means going to the bathroom to pee/poop (e.g., "andare/correre in bagno" = "go/run to the bathroom"). Also used as a polite way to say you need the toilet.
target_language_example: Scusa, devo andare in bagno.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need to go to the bathroom.

meaning: at the bank; (money) in the bank.
additional_notes: Used for being physically at/going to the bank (e.g., “Sono andata in banca”) and for money kept in a bank account (e.g., “ho dei soldi in banca”). With verbs like "andare" it often implies going to the bank building; with amounts of money it means deposited/saved in a bank.
target_language_example: Ho dei soldi in banca, ma oggi devo andare in banca a prelevare.
native_language_example: I have money in the bank, but today I have to go to the bank to withdraw (some).

additional_notes: Used to say something depends on a factor or is judged using a reference/criterion. Very common with "in base a" + noun/pronoun (e.g., in base ai dati, in base al reddito, in base alle circostanze).
target_language_example: La decisione cambia in base alle informazioni che abbiamo.
native_language_example: The decision changes based on the information we have.

additional_notes: Used for physical position (look/sign down at the bottom of a page, lower part of something): "Firma in basso" = "Sign at the bottom." It can also be figurative with "cadere in basso" meaning "to sink so low" (morally/socially or in status).
target_language_example: Il tuo nome è scritto in basso, a destra.
native_language_example: Your name is written at the bottom, on the right.

additional_notes: Used to say the language someone speaks or communicates in. It often goes with verbs like parlare (to speak) and comunicare (to communicate). Capitalization can vary, but you may also see it as “in Berbero”.
target_language_example: Possiamo parlare in berbero a casa.
native_language_example: We can speak in Berber at home.

additional_notes: Used when something is left empty (a form, an answer, a page). Very common with verbs like "lasciare" (to leave) and "riempire" (to fill): "lasciare in bianco" = to leave blank. Also appears in set phrases like "voto in bianco" (blank vote/abstention) and "notte in bianco" (a sleepless night).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato il modulo in bianco.
native_language_example: I left the form blank.

additional_notes: Used to say you are/were located inside a library (often where you study or read). In Italian you can say "in biblioteca" without an article; it’s equivalent to "in the library" in English.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo in biblioteca dopo pranzo.
native_language_example: See you in the library after lunch.

additional_notes: Used to say you travel using a bicycle (like “by car/on foot”). Very common with verbs of movement such as andare, venire, tornare: “Vado in bici.” You can also hear “in bicicletta” (same meaning, more explicit).
target_language_example: Domani andiamo al parco in bici.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to the park by bike.

meaning: 'Good luck!' (especially before a test, performance, interview, etc.).
additional_notes: A very common Italian way to wish someone luck. It literally means “in the mouth of the wolf,” but it’s used like “break a leg.” The traditional reply is “Crepi!” (or the more polite/modern “Crepi il lupo!” / “Viva il lupo!”). Often said on its own or after a goodbye.
target_language_example: Domani hai l’esame? In bocca al lupo!
native_language_example: You have the exam tomorrow? Good luck!

additional_notes: Used to summarize or get to the main point. It can appear at the beginning (“In breve, ...”) or inserted parenthetically (“Il progetto, in breve, ...”). Often corresponds to “long story short” in tone, but it’s neutral (not slang).
target_language_example: In breve, non posso venire stasera.
native_language_example: In short, I can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say someone gives/does something and expects or receives something else back. Common with verbs like dare/offrire (to give/offer), chiedere (to ask), ricevere/avere (to get/have). Often followed by "di" + noun/verb: "in cambio di aiuto" = "in exchange for help".
target_language_example: Ti aiuto con i compiti in cambio di un caffè.
native_language_example: I’ll help you with your homework in exchange for a coffee.

additional_notes: "Camera" means "room" (often specifically "bedroom"), not a photo/video "camera"—that’s "macchina fotografica" or "fotocamera". You’ll also often hear the more standard form "nella mia camera" (= in my room). "In camera mia" can sound a bit more direct/colloquial, especially in speech (e.g., inviting someone).
target_language_example: Studiamo in camera mia dopo cena.
native_language_example: Let’s study in my room after dinner.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located or doing something in their (private) room. "Sua" agrees with the noun "camera" (feminine), and can mean “his” or “her” depending on context (also “your” in formal address: Lei). Note: Italian "camera" means “room/bedroom,” not a “camera” (the device).
target_language_example: È in camera sua a leggere.
native_language_example: He/She is in his/her room reading.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens (“You can eat in your room”) or to tell someone to go back/go there (“Go to your room”). In Italian, "camera" means "room/bedroom" (not a photo camera).
target_language_example: Non fare troppo rumore in camera tua, per favore.
native_language_example: Don’t make too much noise in your room, please.

meaning: in the countryside; out in a rural area.
additional_notes: Used to say someone lives or is located outside the city, in a rural setting (fields, small towns, farmland). Often contrasts with in città (“in the city”).
target_language_example: Nel fine settimana andiamo spesso in campagna.
native_language_example: On the weekend we often go to the countryside.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is imprisoned or will be sent to prison/jail. Often follows verbs like essere (to be), andare (to go), mettere/mandare (to put/send). You can add a place after it: in carcere a Roma / a Boston. In Italian, carcere is more like “prison” (not a vehicle), but it’s also commonly used where English might say “jail.”
target_language_example: È finito in carcere per furto.
native_language_example: He ended up in prison for theft.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is inside their home (location). Common with "essere": "Sono in casa" = "I’m at home / in the house." Contrast: "a casa" often focuses on being at home as a destination or general state ("Vado a casa" = "I’m going home").
target_language_example: Stasera resto in casa.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m staying at home.

meaning: in my house; at my place.
additional_notes: Means inside your home or at your place in general. Often used with surprise or annoyance in questions like "Che fai in casa mia?" (What are you doing in my house?). Can also appear in firmer statements about rules or welcome: "Non sei più il benvenuto in casa mia."
target_language_example: Non fumare in casa mia, per favore.
native_language_example: Don’t smoke in my house, please.

meaning: in case (if it happens / if needed).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a possible situation or condition: "in case" + subjunctive (common in Italian), e.g., "in caso piova / in caso tu venga". Often followed by a full clause ("in caso + [something happens]") or by "di" + infinitive ("in caso di pioggia" = in case of rain). It can also mean "if there are/should be..." as in "in caso ci fossero altre domande".
target_language_example: Porta con te una giacca, in caso faccia freddo stasera.
native_language_example: Bring a jacket with you, in case it gets cold tonight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a possible situation and what to do if it happens, often in instructions or planning. Followed by a noun: "in caso di bisogno/incendio/problemi". With a clause, Italian often uses "nel caso in cui" (e.g., "nel caso in cui piova").
target_language_example: Porta un ombrello in caso di pioggia.
native_language_example: Bring an umbrella in case of rain.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is located in the central area of a town/city, or is going there (movement can be understood from context or the verb). You can also hear it as "in centro città" (in the city center).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo in centro alle sei.
native_language_example: See you downtown at six.

additional_notes: Used with a noun or infinitive to say someone is searching for something (often abstract like "aiuto" or "avventura"). Common with verbs of movement or purpose (andare/venire/partire/essere) and can introduce a motivation: "Siamo qui in cerca di...".
target_language_example: Sono in cerca di lavoro.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a job.

meaning: in a circle; in a circular formation.
additional_notes: Used for people/objects arranged in a ring (e.g., sitting/standing in a circle) or for movement that goes around repeatedly (e.g., birds circling overhead: “girare/volare in cerchio”).
target_language_example: Per favore, mettetevi in cerchio per il gioco.
native_language_example: Please get into a circle for the game.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the way something happens or the manner/reason something is true. Often used in questions to request an explanation or clarification (similar to "how exactly?").
target_language_example: In che modo possiamo risolvere questo problema?
native_language_example: How can we solve this problem?

additional_notes: Means being inside a church (location) or going to church, depending on the verb. With verbs of movement like "andare", it often means "(to go) to church"; with "vedersi", "stare", etc., it means "in/at church". Often used without an article (not *nella chiesa*) when speaking generally about church attendance or the usual place of worship.
target_language_example: Domani vado in chiesa con i miei nonni.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to church with my grandparents.

additional_notes: Used to say someone regularly goes to church on Sundays (often implying a weekly habit, sometimes in a Catholic context). You can change the day: "in chiesa ogni sabato" (every Saturday).
target_language_example: Da piccolo, andavo in chiesa ogni domenica con i miei nonni.
native_language_example: When I was little, I went to church every Sunday with my grandparents.

additional_notes: Means someone/something is located within the city/town limits. Often used to contrast with places outside the city (e.g., in campagna = in the countryside). You can also say: in città ci sono... = there are... in the city.
target_language_example: Domani devo andare in città per fare la spesa.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have to go into town to do the grocery shopping.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens while you are in a classroom during a lesson (studying, speaking, being present, rules like not eating). Often refers to the time/context of the lesson rather than a specific physical place.
target_language_example: Oggi in classe facciamo un quiz.
native_language_example: Today in class we’re doing a quiz.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like "sentirsi" (to feel) or "far sentire" (to make someone feel): "sentirsi in colpa" = to feel guilty, "far sentire (qualcuno) in colpa" = to make (someone) feel guilty (guilt-trip them). Often followed by "per" or "di" to say what you feel guilty about: "in colpa per..." / "in colpa di...".
target_language_example: Non voglio farti sentire in colpa, ma mi hai promesso che saresti venuto.
native_language_example: I don’t want to make you feel guilty, but you promised you would come.

meaning: in common; shared (by two or more people/things).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say something is shared: amici in comune (mutual friends), interessi in comune (common interests), una cosa in comune (one thing in common). Very frequent with avere: Abbiamo molto in comune = We have a lot in common.
target_language_example: Io e mia sorella abbiamo tanti interessi in comune.
native_language_example: My sister and I have many interests in common.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things/situations, often to highlight a difference (e.g., bigger, better, nothing compared to). It can come at the start of the sentence (In confronto a X, ...) or after what you’re describing (… in confronto a X).
target_language_example: In confronto a questo ristorante, quello è molto caro.
native_language_example: Compared to this restaurant, that one is very expensive.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **tenere in considerazione** (to take into account) and **prendere in considerazione** (to consider). You can also say **prendere in considerazione di + infinitive** to mean “to consider (doing something)”.
target_language_example: Dovremmo prendere in considerazione altre opzioni.
native_language_example: We should consider other options.

additional_notes: Used to say you pay with physical money (coins/bills), not by card or bank transfer. Common with verbs like pagare (to pay) and sometimes with “preferisci pagare in contanti o con la carta?”
target_language_example: Posso pagare in contanti?
native_language_example: Can I pay in cash?

meaning: in touch with; in contact with.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like essere (to be), mettersi (to get), entrare (to come), rimanere (to stay) to talk about communicating or having a connection with someone. Common in both everyday and more formal contexts (e.g., emergencies: “mettersi in contatto con…”).
target_language_example: Sono ancora in contatto con i miei ex colleghi.
native_language_example: I’m still in touch with my former colleagues.

additional_notes: Used to say you keep communicating with a man (by phone, messages, email, etc.). Common with verbs like essere/restare/rimanere (“to be/stay/remain”) and mettersi (“to get in touch”): e.g., "Ti sei messa in contatto con lui?" = "Did you get in touch with him?". For a woman, use "con lei"; plural: "con loro".
target_language_example: Sono ancora in contatto con lui, ci scriviamo spesso.
native_language_example: I'm still in contact with him; we message often.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly without stopping, often as a complaint. It can go at the end of the sentence (e.g., “abbaia in continuazione”) or at the beginning for emphasis (“In continuazione, ...”).
target_language_example: Mi chiami in continuazione: che succede?
native_language_example: You keep calling me all the time: what’s going on?

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly or without stopping. In standard Italian you can also say "continuamente" or "sempre". "In continuo" is common in speech but can sound a bit informal/colloquial.
target_language_example: Mi scrive in continuo durante la lezione.
native_language_example: He texts me constantly during the lesson.

additional_notes: Used to say something has started and is happening now (not finished yet). Common with nouns like "lavori" (road/construction work), "indagine" (investigation), "riunione" (meeting), "missione" (mission), "procedura" (procedure). You’ll also see it on road signs: "lavori in corso" = roadworks/construction in progress.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, la riunione è ancora in corso.
native_language_example: Sorry, the meeting is still in progress.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located in the kitchen, or that an action happens there. Often answers questions like “Dove?” (Where?).
target_language_example: Il gatto dorme in cucina.
native_language_example: The cat sleeps in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to say you want (or give) a full, detailed explanation rather than a general summary. Often follows verbs like spiegare (to explain), descrivere (to describe), raccontare (to tell).
target_language_example: Puoi spiegarmelo in dettaglio, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you explain it to me in detail, please?

additional_notes: Used for TV/radio/streaming to mean something is being broadcast or shown at the same moment it’s happening (not recorded). Common in announcements and questions: “Siamo in diretta?” (= Are we live/on air?).
target_language_example: La conferenza stampa è in diretta sul sito.
native_language_example: The press conference is live on the website.

additional_notes: Used with essere/stare: "sono/era in disaccordo". Often followed by "con" + a person ("Sono in disaccordo con lui") or "con" + an idea/decision. You can intensify with adverbs like "del tutto" (completely): "Ne sono del tutto in disaccordo" (I completely disagree with it/that).
target_language_example: Siamo in disaccordo con questa decisione.
native_language_example: We disagree with this decision.

additional_notes:
Used to say something is not settled or is being challenged. Common with verbs like:
- "mettere in discussione (qualcosa/qualcuno)" = to question/challenge (something/someone)
- "essere in discussione" = to be in doubt / up for debate.
Often implies uncertainty or that something’s being called into question, not just casually discussed.
target_language_example: Il suo ruolo nel progetto è ancora in discussione.
native_language_example: His role in the project is still up for debate.

meaning: in doubt; questioned (often in the phrase "mettere in dubbio" = to doubt / to call into question).
additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb "mettere": "mettere in dubbio qualcosa" means to question something’s truth or reliability (similar to "to cast doubt on" / "to call into question"). It can also describe a state of uncertainty: "essere in dubbio" = to be unsure.
target_language_example: Non metto in dubbio quello che dici, ma vorrei vedere le prove.
native_language_example: I’m not doubting what you’re saying, but I’d like to see the proof.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like tagliare/dividere/spezzare to mean splitting something into two parts ("Ha tagliato la mela in due"). It can also describe something being arranged as two parts ("La Terra è divisa in due"). In very vulgar threats/insults it can be used figuratively (avoid using this).
target_language_example: Puoi dividere il panino in due?
native_language_example: Can you split the sandwich in two?

additional_notes: Used to confirm or clarify something, often like English “actually” when you realize something is true or you want to correct/adjust what was said. It can introduce an explanation or reinforcement: “In effetti, …”.
target_language_example: In effetti, hai ragione: è troppo tardi.
native_language_example: Actually, you’re right: it’s too late.

additional_notes: Use "in + language" to say something is done using that language, especially with verbs like parlare (to speak), scrivere (to write), tradurre (to translate), leggere (to read), and sometimes pensare (to think).
target_language_example: Puoi scriverlo in esperanto, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you write it in Esperanto, please?

additional_notes: Used for things happening directly to someone’s face (often with verbs like prendere in faccia = “get hit in the face”, tirare/sputare in faccia = “throw/spit in someone’s face”). It also appears in expressions like vedere qualcuno in faccia (“see someone’s face,” sometimes implying meeting/seeing them clearly).
target_language_example: Mi è arrivata una palla in faccia.
native_language_example: A ball hit me in the face.

meaning: in favor of; in support of.
additional_notes: Used to say you support a person/idea, or that something is done for someone’s benefit. Common with verbs like essere (to be) and votare (to vote): “Sono in favore di…” / “Ha votato in favore di…”. In Italian you’ll also often hear the synonym “a favore di”.
target_language_example: Sono in favore di questa proposta.
native_language_example: I’m in favor of this proposal.

additional_notes: Used to say something is burning (often as an emergency warning): “La casa è in fiamme!” It can also be used figuratively to mean a place is in chaos or violence (e.g., “La città è in fiamme”).
target_language_example: Chiamate i pompieri: il garage è in fiamme!
native_language_example: Call the firefighters: the garage is on fire!

additional_notes: Used to say people should form a line or stand one behind the other. Very common in instructions/commands with verbs like "mettersi" (to get in line): "Mettetevi in fila!" (plural) / "Mettiti in fila!" (singular). You can add numbers to say how many people per row: "in fila per tre" = in rows/lines of three (three abreast).
target_language_example: Siamo già in fila per entrare nel museo.
native_language_example: We’re already in line to enter the museum.

additional_notes: Used mainly for plants/trees/flowers when they have blossoms. Often with the verb essere (è/sono in fiore) or diventare/mettersi (mettersi in fiore). Related expression: di fiore in fiore = “from flower to flower” (as in bees moving between flowers).
target_language_example: In primavera, i mandorli sono in fiore.
native_language_example: In spring, the almond trees are in bloom.

meaning: at the end/bottom; deep down / after all.
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) physical location: “at the end of” a place (a street, a line) or “at the bottom of” something (a hole, a bag). Often followed by “a” + noun (in fondo a una fossa). (2) figurative meaning: “deep down,” “when you think about it,” or “after all,” often commenting on a situation/opinion (In fondo non la conoscevo; Non ci odiavamo, in fondo).
target_language_example: In fondo alla stanza c'è una porta.
native_language_example: At the back of the room there is a door.

meaning: in the form of; also: in shape/fit.
additional_notes: Often used with an adjective or noun to specify the type of form something takes: "in forma anonima" (anonymously), "in forma scritta" (in writing), "in forma digitale" (in digital form). On its own, "essere/tenersi in forma" means to be/stay fit.
target_language_example: Cerco di tenermi in forma andando a camminare ogni giorno.
native_language_example: I try to stay in shape by going for a walk every day.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is said, written, sung, or done using the French language. With school subjects, grades, or ability, it can also mean "in French" as a subject, as in being good at French or getting good marks in French.
target_language_example: Per favore, scrivi questo messaggio in francese.
native_language_example: Please write this message in French.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens quickly or that someone should hurry up. Often with verbs like "fare" (fare in fretta = hurry up) and "dire" (dire in fretta = say quickly). Similar to "velocemente" but more about being rushed/pressed for time.
target_language_example: Scusa, devo andare: sono in fretta.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go: I'm in a hurry.

meaning: 'in the future' (from now on; at a later time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that will happen later than now. Common after verbs like accadere (to happen) and with advice/requests: “in futuro, sii…” = “in the future/from now on, be…”.
target_language_example: In futuro vorrei vivere vicino al mare.
native_language_example: In the future I'd like to live near the sea.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like andare/finire/essere in galera (“go/end up/be in jail”). It’s fairly colloquial; in more formal contexts you may hear in prigione or in carcere.
target_language_example: Se continui così, finirai in galera.
native_language_example: If you keep this up, you'll end up in jail.

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s ability or effectiveness: Sei in gamba! = “You’re really good/competent.” It can describe a person (un tipo/un uomo in gamba) or be said on its own as praise. Literally “on leg,” but the meaning is idiomatic.
target_language_example: La nuova collega è davvero in gamba.
native_language_example: The new colleague is really competent.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something broadly, not a specific case. Common in phrases like "parlando in generale" (= generally speaking) or "in generale" at the start/end of a sentence to soften or generalize a statement.
target_language_example: In generale, preferisco studiare la mattina.
native_language_example: In general, I prefer to study in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is true most of the time or for most people/things (a generalization), not an absolute rule. It can go at the beginning of the sentence ("In genere, ...") or in the middle set off by commas ("..., in genere, ...").
target_language_example: In genere prendo il caffè senza zucchero.
native_language_example: I usually take my coffee without sugar.

meaning: in the garden / in the yard.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located in the garden (outdoors, usually at/behind a house). With verbs like essere/stare it answers “Where?” (Dov’è?). With action verbs it means the action happens there (e.g., piantare in giardino = to plant in the garden).
target_language_example: I bambini stanno giocando in giardino.
native_language_example: The kids are playing in the garden.

additional_notes: Used to describe a position ("essere in ginocchio" = to be kneeling) or as an order ("In ginocchio!" / "Mettiti in ginocchio" = Get down on your knees). Often said by police/authority figures or in dramatic contexts.
target_language_example: È caduto e si è messo in ginocchio per rialzarsi.
native_language_example: He fell and got down on his knees to get back up.

additional_notes: Most often means "at stake" (what could be won/lost or what is at risk): "milioni di dollari in gioco", "l’onore/la vita è in gioco". It can also mean "to come into play / to get involved" in the expression "entrare in gioco" ("Now we come into play").
target_language_example: Con questa decisione, è in gioco la tua carriera.
native_language_example: With this decision, your career is at stake.

additional_notes: Most commonly means being around/out (moving around without a specific destination): "andare in giro" = "to go around / to wander". Very common in the fixed expression "prendere in giro (qualcuno)", which means "to make fun of / to tease (someone)" (not the literal idea of taking someone around).
target_language_example: Sono in giro per la città e torno più tardi.
native_language_example: I'm out around the city and I'll be back later.

additional_notes: Most often used with "essere" + "in grado di" + infinitive: "sono in grado di farlo" = "I’m able to do it". You can also use it alone as a judgment about someone’s ability/fitness in the moment: "Non è in grado!" = "He/She isn’t capable (of it)!" / "He/She can’t do it!".
target_language_example: Non sono in grado di venire stasera.
native_language_example: I’m not able to come tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has the ability/capacity to help. It’s built from: essere in grado di (“to be able to”) + aiutare (“to help”). Often used with different tenses: ero in grado di aiutare (I was able to help), sarai in grado di aiutare (you will be able to help). Similar in meaning to “poter aiutare” (can help), but “essere in grado di” can sound a bit more formal/explicit about capability.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, oggi non sono in grado di aiutare.
native_language_example: Sorry, today I’m not able to help.
