Adding "io" can give emphasis/contrast (e.g., "I bought it (not someone else)"). Common add-ons: "per te" (for you), "a Tom" (for Tom; can also mean "from Tom" depending on context), "ad un prezzo basso" (at a low price), "al negozio" (at the shop).
target_language_example: Io ho comprato quel libro per te.
native_language_example: I bought that book for you.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of dire (“to say/tell”). It’s followed by the person you spoke to, introduced by a: Io ho detto a Maria… (“I told Maria…”). You can then add what you said with che (“that…”) or another clause.
target_language_example: Io ho detto a Laura che arrivavo tardi.
native_language_example: I told Laura that I was arriving late.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "dormire" (to sleep), using the auxiliary "avere": (io) ho dormito. Often used to say you slept (once) in the recent past or to report a completed action. Context can change the meaning: "Ho dormito con X" can mean you slept in the same bed/place with someone, but it can also imply you had sex with them.
target_language_example: Ieri sera io ho dormito otto ore.
native_language_example: Last night I slept eight hours.

meaning: I had to / I have had to (I was forced/required to).
additional_notes: "Ho dovuto" is the passato prossimo of "dovere" (to have to, must). It expresses a necessity/obligation in the past and is typically followed by an infinitive: "(io) ho dovuto + verbo" (e.g., "io ho dovuto aspettare"). In Italian, the subject pronoun is often omitted in everyday speech, so "Ho dovuto..." is more common than "Io ho dovuto...", but using "io" can add emphasis (e.g., contrasting with someone else).
target_language_example: Io ho dovuto cambiare il piano.
native_language_example: I had to change the plan.

additional_notes: “Io” (I) + “ho fatto” is the passato prossimo of fare (to do/make). It’s used for actions completed in the past, often with an object: ho fatto dei piani (I made plans), ho fatto una chiamata (I made a call), ho fatto un sogno (I had a dream), ho fatto molti soldi (I made a lot of money). In everyday Italian, the subject “io” is often omitted unless you want emphasis or contrast: Ho fatto dei piani.
target_language_example: Io ho fatto tutto quello che potevo.
native_language_example: I did everything I could.

additional_notes: Used to say you have already done something. Very common with the passato prossimo (ho + past participle): “Io ho già finito…”. In everyday speech, “io” is often dropped because “ho” already implies “I”: “Ho già finito.”
target_language_example: Io ho già parlato con lei.
native_language_example: I’ve already spoken with her.

meaning: "I met" / "I ran into" (past: passato prossimo of incontrare).
additional_notes: Used to say you met someone or came across someone/something in the past. Literally "I have met" (io + ho + incontrato), but it’s usually translated as simple past in English. You can add where/when: "ieri", "in Europa", etc.
target_language_example: Io ho incontrato un turista alla stazione.
native_language_example: I met a tourist at the station.

meaning: "I left / I have left"; sometimes "I let" (allowed).
additional_notes: First-person singular passato prossimo of lasciare. It can mean to leave something/someone (e.g., leave a place, leave something behind) or to allow/let someone do something, often with an infinitive: “Ho lasciato entrare…” = “I let (someone) in.”
target_language_example: Io ho lasciato le chiavi sul tavolo.
native_language_example: I left the keys on the table.

meaning: “I read” / “I have read” (completed past action of “to read”).
additional_notes: This is the passato prossimo of “leggere”: “(io) ho letto”. In Italian, the subject pronoun “io” is often optional and omitted (“Ho letto…”), but keeping it can add emphasis or contrast (e.g., “Io ho letto, tu no”).
target_language_example: Io ho letto davvero il tuo libro.
native_language_example: I really read your book. / I have really read your book.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo (past tense) of "mangiare" (to eat): "ho" (I have) + "mangiato" (eaten). In Italian, the subject pronoun "io" is often optional, so you’ll also commonly hear just "ho mangiato". Used for a completed action in the past (often with a time like "ieri", "stamattina").
target_language_example: Oggi non ho fame perché io ho mangiato già.
native_language_example: Today I’m not hungry because I already ate.

additional_notes: First-person singular passato prossimo of perdere (“to lose”). Used to say you lost something (often followed by a noun) or that you no longer have a feeling/quality: io ho perso interesse (I lost interest), io ho perso la speranza (I lost hope). In everyday Italian, the subject pronoun io is often omitted (ho perso...), but keeping io can add emphasis or contrast.
target_language_example: Io ho perso le chiavi.
native_language_example: I lost my keys.

meaning: “I took / I got / I had” (past: I got/bought/ordered, depending on context).
additional_notes: First-person singular of the passato prossimo of prendere (“to take”). Used for things you took physically (Io ho preso due bottiglie), things you got/bought (Io ho preso un nuovo cappello), things you ordered/had (Io ho preso una tazza di caffè), and also fixed expressions like prendere una decisione (“to make a decision”). In everyday speech you can often drop the subject “io” because the verb already shows the person: “Ho preso…”.
target_language_example: Io ho preso una tazza di caffè al bar.
native_language_example: I had a cup of coffee at the bar.

meaning: "I tried to / I have tried to".
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (provare a + verb) to say you made an attempt to do something, often without saying whether you succeeded. In everyday English it’s usually translated as “I tried to…”.
target_language_example: Io ho provato a chiamarti ieri, ma non rispondevi.
native_language_example: I tried to call you yesterday, but you weren’t answering.

meaning: "I heard" / "I've heard" (passato prossimo of "sentire": to hear).
additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo: "io" (I) + "ho" (I have) + "sentito" (heard). It can refer to hearing a sound (e.g., a phone ringing) or hearing information/rumors ("io ho sentito che..."). In natural Italian, the subject pronoun "io" is often omitted: "Ho sentito..."
target_language_example: Io ho sentito che domani piove.
native_language_example: I've heard that it's going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: “I found” / “I have found”; also “I found (that)…” (I thought/considered).
additional_notes: Past tense of trovare with the subject “io” (“I”). It can mean finding something physically (“I found your diary”), discovering something (“I found Tatoeba on Google”), or giving an opinion with an adjective (“I found the book interesting” = “I thought the book was interesting”). You can also use it with che + clause: “Ho trovato che…” = “I found that… / I felt that…”. In everyday speech, Italians often drop the subject: “Ho trovato…”.
target_language_example: Io ho trovato questo ristorante per caso e l’ho trovato ottimo.
native_language_example: I found this restaurant by chance and I thought it was great.

meaning: "I saw" / "I have seen" (past of vedere, "to see").
additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo: io + ho (auxiliary avere) + visto (past participle of vedere). Often translates as simple past in English (“I saw”). With another verb (e.g., piangere, attraversare) it can mean “I saw someone/something do ...”.
target_language_example: Io ho visto Marco uscire di casa.
native_language_example: I saw Marco leave the house.

additional_notes: Basic way to say that you possess something or that something is true for you. In Italian, the subject pronoun is often omitted, so ho by itself usually already means "I have". Io is added for emphasis or contrast.
target_language_example: Io ho due fratelli.
native_language_example: I have two brothers.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something (a noun) or you need to do something (verb in the infinitive). In Italian, the subject pronoun is often omitted, so “Ho bisogno di…” is more common than “Io ho bisogno di…”, but using “io” can add emphasis (“I” specifically). With nouns, add articles/quantities as needed: “io ho bisogno di ghiaccio” (some ice), “io ho bisogno di un po’ di tempo” (a bit of time).
target_language_example: Io ho bisogno di controllare qualcosa.
native_language_example: I need to check something.

meaning: “I have some …” (talking about having certain things, in a general/unspecified amount).
additional_notes: Used with a plural noun to say you have some of something: **io ho dei + noun**. **dei** is the partitive article for masculine plural nouns (e.g., *dei dolori, dei parenti*). Variants: **degli** before vowels or certain consonant clusters (e.g., *io ho degli amici*), and **delle** for feminine plural (e.g., *io ho delle idee*). Often in everyday speech you can also omit it: *Ho dolori terribili*.
target_language_example: Io ho dei problemi con la macchina.
native_language_example: I have some problems with the car.

additional_notes: Used with a plural noun to say you possess or have two of something. In Italian, "ho" = "I have" (from *avere*), and "due" means the number 2. Note: Italian "due" can look like English "due" (payable), but it means "two."
target_language_example: Io ho due biglietti per il concerto.
native_language_example: I have two tickets for the concert.

additional_notes: Used to express a personal intention or plan, typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., parlare, studiare, vedere). In everyday speech, Italian often drops the subject pronoun (“ho intenzione di...”), but including “io” adds emphasis or contrast.
target_language_example: Io ho intenzione di parlare con Tom a riguardo.
native_language_example: I intend to talk to Tom about it.

meaning: "I have some / I have a few."
additional_notes: Used to say you have a small number or an unspecified amount of something. With "qualche", Italian typically uses a singular noun ("qualche amico", "qualche idea", "qualche libro") even though the meaning is plural. "Io" is often optional in Italian, so you may also hear just "Ho qualche...".
target_language_example: Io ho qualche minuto per parlare.
native_language_example: I have a few minutes to talk.

additional_notes: Used to say you possess something or you have something (including feelings/conditions), followed by a masculine singular noun. In everyday Italian the subject pronoun is often omitted: "Ho un...". For feminine singular, use "io ho una" / "ho una".
target_language_example: Io ho un leggero dolore al fianco.
native_language_example: I have a slight pain in my side.

meaning: "I have a" (with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you possess or have something. "Una" is the feminine singular form of "a/an" (e.g., una moglie, una sorpresa, una bici). In everyday speech, Italians often drop the subject pronoun "io" and just say "Ho una...". For masculine nouns, use "io ho un" (or "ho un...").
target_language_example: Io ho una domanda.
native_language_example: I have a question.

meaning: “I feel like / I want to (do something).”
additional_notes: Used to say you’re in the mood to do something (often right now or in general). It’s followed by an infinitive verb: io ho voglia di + mangiare/uscire/studiare. The negative is common too: io non ho voglia di… (“I don’t feel like…”). In everyday speech, Italians often omit “io” and just say: ho voglia di…
target_language_example: Oggi io ho voglia di stare a casa.
native_language_example: Today I feel like staying at home.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: it’s just the subject pronoun io (“I”) + the direct object pronoun la (“her” / “it” for a feminine noun). La usually comes before a conjugated verb: io la ammiro (“I admire her/it”), io la penso così (“I think so / I think it this way”). With an infinitive, la can go before the helping verb (io la riesco a fare) or attach to the infinitive (io riesco a farla). In phrases like perché io la compri, the verb is in the subjunctive (compri) after perché when it means “so that / for … to …”.
target_language_example: Io la vedo spesso al lavoro.
native_language_example: I see her often at work.

additional_notes: Used when the person you love is a woman (or a feminine noun) and is the direct object. “La” = “her” (or “it” for a feminine thing), and “amo” is from “amare” (to love). In Italian, the subject pronoun “io” is often omitted, so you’ll commonly hear “La amo.” For a man you’d say “Io lo amo” / “Lo amo.”
target_language_example: Io la amo davvero.
native_language_example: I really love her.

additional_notes: Subject + verb: "io" (I) + "lavoro" (I work). In Italian the subject pronoun is often dropped, so you’ll also hear just "lavoro". It can describe your job in general (Io lavoro in uno zoo) or what you’re doing these days (Io lavoro ancora in Australia). Common patterns: "lavoro a tempo pieno" (full-time), "lavoro per + [person/company]" (I work for), "lavoro sodo" (I work hard), "lavoro velocemente" (I work quickly), "persino (la) domenica" (even on Sunday).
target_language_example: Io lavoro in centro, vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: I work downtown, near the station.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: io means “I” and lo is a masculine singular direct object pronoun placed before the verb. It can refer to a person (“him”), a thing (“it”), or sometimes a whole idea, especially in phrases like lo so (“I know it/that”). Italian often drops io unless it is being used for emphasis or contrast.
target_language_example: Io lo vedo ogni giorno.
native_language_example: I see him every day.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you already knew or suspected. "Lo" is an anticipatory pronoun meaning "it" (referring to the whole following idea), so in English you often just say "I knew (that)…" or, more emphatically, "I knew it!". Word order can vary in real speech (e.g., "Lo sapevo che…", "Sapevo che…").
target_language_example: Io lo sapevo che avrebbe detto di no.
native_language_example: I knew he/she would say no.

additional_notes: Used to say you know something. "Lo" means "it" (referring to a fact, situation, or what was just said). In everyday Italian, the subject pronoun "io" is often dropped ("Lo so"), but keeping it can add emphasis ("I do know"). You can add words like "già" (already) or "bene" (well) for nuance: "Io lo so già" = "I already know".
target_language_example: Tranquillo, io lo so già.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I already know.

additional_notes: "Io" = "I" and "mangio" is the 1st-person singular present of "mangiare" (to eat). In Italian the subject pronoun is often omitted ("Mangio..."), but "io" is used for emphasis or contrast (e.g., "Io mangio carne, ma lei no"). The present tense can mean a habit ("I eat every day") or something happening now ("I'm eating").
target_language_example: Scusa, adesso io mangio e non posso parlare.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm eating right now and I can't talk.

meaning: I'm leaving / I'm going away (from here).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "andarsene" (to go away, to leave). "me ne" are pronouns that go with this verb and often don’t translate word-for-word in English. Commonly used to say you’re leaving a place right now ("Io me ne vado!" can sound firm: "I’m leaving!"), or that you’re leaving at a certain time (e.g., "domani", "dopodomani"). Often you can drop "io" because Italian already implies the subject: "Me ne vado".
target_language_example: Scusa, è tardi: io me ne vado.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s late: I’m leaving.

additional_notes: Used to introduce yourself and say your name. Often shortened to just “Mi chiamo …” (the “io” = “I” is optional because the verb ending already shows who is speaking). “Chiamarsi” is a reflexive verb meaning “to be called.”
target_language_example: Ciao, io mi chiamo Sara.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Sara.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect yes/no question when you’re unsure or curious about something. It’s often followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "se sia", "se siano"), especially in more formal/standard Italian, though in everyday speech you may also hear the indicative.
target_language_example: Io mi chiedo se abbia già chiamato.
native_language_example: I wonder if he/she has already called.

additional_notes: From the verb **sentirsi** (“to feel” in terms of emotions/conditions). **Mi** is reflexive (“myself”), and **sentivo** is the **imperfetto** (imperfect past), used for an ongoing feeling or background situation in the past (“I was feeling…”, “I used to feel…”). It’s commonly followed by an adjective: *a mio agio* (comfortable), *solo/sola* (alone), *isolato/a* (isolated), *indesiderato/a* (unwanted).
target_language_example: Quando sono arrivato in città, io mi sentivo perso.
native_language_example: When I arrived in the city, I felt lost.

meaning: "I feel" (talking about your physical or emotional state).
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb "sentirsi". It’s commonly followed by an adjective ("io mi sento triste" = I feel sad) or by an expression like "a mio agio" (comfortable) or "in cima al mondo" (on top of the world). In everyday speech Italians often drop "io" because it’s understood: "Mi sento stanco".
target_language_example: A volte io mi sento triste.
native_language_example: Sometimes I feel sad.

additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs in the passato prossimo (past tense): io + mi sono + past participle. It often translates as “I have … (myself)” or simply “I …” in English (e.g., io mi sono adattato = “I adapted / I’ve adapted”). The past participle usually agrees with the subject: mi sono adattato (male speaker), mi sono adattata (female speaker). In everyday speech, “io” is often dropped: mi sono adattato/a.
target_language_example: Io mi sono svegliato presto stamattina.
native_language_example: I woke up early this morning.

meaning: “I have some / I have one (of them).”
additional_notes: Used with the pronoun **ne** to mean “of it/of them,” usually when the thing has already been mentioned or is understood. Very common with **numbers and quantities**: *Ne ho uno/una* (I have one), *Ne ho due* (I have two), *Ne ho tanti* (I have many). With **passato prossimo** (e.g., *ne ho visto/a/i/e*), the past participle often **agrees** with the quantity word (*uno/una/tanti/tante*): *Ne ho vista una*, *Ne ho viste tante*.
target_language_example: Hai dei biglietti? Io ne ho due.
native_language_example: Do you have any tickets? I have two.

meaning: “I have some / I have (some) of it/them.”
additional_notes: Used with the pronoun **ne** to replace something introduced with **di** or an implied group/quantity (“of it/them”). Very common with numbers and quantities: **Io ne ho sei** = “I have six (of them)”; **Io ne ho ancora uno** = “I still have one (of them)”; **Io ne ho abbastanza** = “I’ve had enough (of it/that) / I have enough.” Often answers “How many do you have?” without repeating the noun.
target_language_example: Hai delle penne? Sì, io ne ho tre.
native_language_example: Do you have any pens? Yes, I have three.

additional_notes: 'io' means 'I' and 'non' negates the verb. Italian often leaves out subject pronouns, so io non is commonly used for emphasis or contrast: 'I don't...' / 'me, I don't...'. The exact English translation depends on the verb and tense, for example 'I don't', 'I'm not', 'I haven't', or 'I won't'.
target_language_example: Io non mangio carne.
native_language_example: I don't eat meat.

meaning: “I don’t … there / about it / in it” (using **ci** as “there” or “about it”).
additional_notes: **Ci** is a very common little pronoun that often means **“there”** (a place) or **“about it / in it”** (referring to something). In phrases like **io non ci sto** (“I’m not in / I won’t go along with it”), **io non ci credo** (“I don’t believe it”), **io non ci vengo/ci vado** (“I’m not coming/going there”), **io non ci capisco niente** (“I don’t understand anything about it”), the **ci** is necessary in Italian even if English doesn’t always say “there/about it.”
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, io non ci credo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t believe it.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never done something up to now (life experience). Structure: "io" (often omitted) + "non" + "ho" + "mai" + past participle (fatto, detto, visto, ferito, mentito, perso, ecc.). In conversation it’s very common to drop the subject: "Non ho mai...".
target_language_example: Io non ho mai fatto questo prima.
native_language_example: I’ve never done this before.

meaning: “I no longer have” / “I don’t have anymore.”
additional_notes: Uses the pattern **non ... più** to mean “no longer / not anymore.” In natural Italian, the subject pronoun **io** is often omitted (*Non ho più...*), but it can be included for emphasis or contrast. Common continuations: **bisogno** (“need”), **niente/nulla** (“nothing/anything”), or a noun (*Io non ho più una casa*).
target_language_example: Io non ho più niente da perdere.
native_language_example: I don't have anything left to lose.

additional_notes: Used to say you are unable to do something or not allowed to do it. It’s often followed by an infinitive (e.g., *io non posso approvare / toccare*). In the special structure **non posso che + infinitive**, it means “I can only…” (there’s no other option), as in *Io non posso che crederle* = “I can only believe you.”
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, io non posso venire oggi.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I can’t come today.

meaning: "I can't" / "I can’t manage to" (I’m unable to).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (io non riesco a + verb) to say you can’t manage to do something—because it’s too hard, you lack strength/ability, or the situation makes it impossible. Often implies effort or trying, similar to “I can’t manage to…” or “I can’t bring myself to…” in emotional contexts.
target_language_example: Io non riesco a capire questa regola di grammatica.
native_language_example: I can’t understand this grammar rule.

meaning: "I don't know" / "I can't" (depending on what follows).
additional_notes: Literally “I not know.” Often used to say you don’t have information or you don’t know an answer (usually with a clause like “io non so dov’è…” / “io non so che…”). When followed by an infinitive (e.g., “io non so + dormire/farlo”), it can mean “I don’t know how to…” or, in some contexts, “I can’t …” (e.g., “io non so dormire” ≈ “I can’t sleep”). You can also drop the subject and just say “Non so …”, which is more common in conversation.
target_language_example: Scusa, io non so dove sia la fermata dell’autobus.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know where the bus stop is.

additional_notes: Used to negate the verb "essere" (to be) in the first person singular. Often you can drop "io" because the verb form already implies "I": "non sono un uomo" = "I'm not a man." Can also be used before adjectives and nouns: "non sono romantica" (not romantic), "non sono vostro figlio" (not your son).
target_language_example: Io non sono pronto oggi.
native_language_example: I’m not ready today.

additional_notes: Used to refuse or express that you don’t want to do something. Often followed by an infinitive verb: "Io non voglio + verb" (e.g., voglio andare = I want to go; non voglio andare = I don’t want to go). You can drop the subject pronoun in Italian and just say "Non voglio" (common in conversation).
target_language_example: Io non voglio uscire stasera.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go out tonight.

additional_notes: Means “I hate.” In Italian, the subject pronoun (io) is often optional because the verb already shows who is doing the action, so you can also just say “Odio…”. “Odio” is the present tense, 1st person singular of “odiare” (to hate).
target_language_example: Io odio aspettare in fila.
native_language_example: I hate waiting in line.

meaning: “I hate being … / I hate to be …”
additional_notes: Used to say you really dislike being in a certain situation or having a certain quality. It’s followed by the infinitive essere (“to be”) plus an adjective or phrase: io odio essere a casa da solo (“I hate being home alone”). Adjectives and past participles agree with the speaker (stupido/stupida; ingannato/ingannata).
target_language_example: Io odio essere in ritardo.
native_language_example: I hate being late.

meaning: "I hate the" (talking about masculine plural things/people).
additional_notes: Used to say you strongly dislike a category of things or people. "i" is the masculine plural definite article (= "the") and is followed by a masculine plural noun: "i weekend", "i pomodori", "i poliziotti". (For feminine plural you’d use "le": "Io odio le bugie".)
target_language_example: Io odio i compiti.
native_language_example: I hate homework.

meaning: "I hate the" (talking about a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to express very strong dislike: io = I, odio = I hate, il = the (masculine singular). Often sounds harsh in everyday conversation; a softer alternative is "non mi piace" (I don’t like). Change the article depending on the noun: "io odio la..." (feminine), "io odio i/gli..." (masculine plural), "io odio le..." (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Io odio il traffico del lunedì mattina.
native_language_example: I hate Monday morning traffic.

additional_notes: From the verb *parlare* (to speak). In Italian you can usually drop the subject pronoun and just say *parlo*; adding *io* emphasizes "I" (e.g., in contrast with someone else). Often followed by a language (*Io parlo italiano*) or by *in* + language when talking about the language you use in a situation (*Io parlo in francese con Tom*).
target_language_example: Io parlo un po' di italiano, ma capisco bene lo spagnolo.
native_language_example: I speak a little Italian, but I understand Spanish well.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed/assumed in the past (often something that turned out not to be true). After "pensavo che", Italian typically uses the subjunctive (congiuntivo) in the following clause (e.g., "fosse", "fossero").
target_language_example: Io pensavo che fosse già arrivata, ma era ancora in viaggio.
native_language_example: I thought she had already arrived, but she was still on the way.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a personal opinion or belief. In Italian, the subject pronoun io is often omitted, so you will also often hear just penso che. It is commonly followed by the subjunctive in standard Italian, as in the examples.
target_language_example: Io penso che sia una buona idea.
native_language_example: I think that it's a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion (io penso che = “I think that”), followed by an indirect object with a (“to/for [someone]”), e.g., a Tom = “to/for Tom”. After “penso che”, Italian often uses the subjunctive (congiuntivo) in the next verb: “penso che a Tom piacerebbe...”, “penso che a Tom serva...”.
target_language_example: Io penso che a Maria serva un po' di tempo.
native_language_example: I think Maria needs a bit of time.

additional_notes: Means you have the ability or permission to do something. In Italian the subject pronoun is often dropped, so you’ll very commonly hear just "posso" (e.g., "Posso entrare?" = "Can I come in?").
target_language_example: Io posso aiutarti domani.
native_language_example: I can help you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional tense of potere (potrei) to talk about a possibility or something you would be able to do. It’s also common for being polite/less direct than "posso" (e.g., asking permission or making a request). Often followed by an infinitive: "Io potrei + verbo".
target_language_example: Io potrei venire più tardi, se vuoi.
native_language_example: I could come later, if you want.

additional_notes: Used to say what you like better than something else. Often followed by an infinitive (Io preferisco camminare = I prefer walking) or a noun (Io preferisco i film divertenti = I prefer funny movies). For comparisons, use "preferire X a Y" (Io preferisco le automobili inglesi a quelle straniere = I prefer English cars to foreign ones). The subject pronoun "io" is optional and is mainly used for emphasis or contrast.
target_language_example: Io preferisco prendere un caffè invece del tè.
native_language_example: I prefer to have a coffee instead of tea.

meaning: “I can / I manage to …” (I succeed in doing something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: “io riesco a + infinito” (e.g., io riesco a capire = I can understand). It often implies it’s difficult but possible, like “I manage to” rather than simple permission/ability (which is often expressed with “posso”). In everyday speech, Italians often drop “io” and just say “riesco a …”, but including “io” adds emphasis.
target_language_example: Oggi io riesco a finire il lavoro in tempo.
native_language_example: Today I manage to finish the work on time.

additional_notes: First-person singular future tense of essere (to be). Italian often drops the subject pronoun, so sarò is common; io sarò adds emphasis or contrast (e.g., “I will be, not you”). Used to talk about what you will be in the future (a role, a state, availability, etc.).
target_language_example: Domani io sarò a casa tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I will be at home all day.

additional_notes: "Io so" is the 1st-person singular of "sapere" (to know). In Italian the subject pronoun is often omitted, so you’ll very commonly hear just "so" (= "I know"). Use "sapere" for knowing facts/information ("so chi è" = I know who it is; "so già" = I already know). With an infinitive, it means knowing how to do something / being able to: "so suonare la chitarra" = I can play the guitar. You can also say "so di..." / "so di te" (I know about...) and "so molto su..." (I know a lot about...).
target_language_example: Io so come arrivare alla stazione.
native_language_example: I know how to get to the station.

additional_notes: Used to say you have the ability/knowledge to do something, typically followed by an infinitive (e.g., aiutare, gestirlo, parlargli). In conversation you can also omit “io” and just say “so come…”.
target_language_example: Io so come arrivare alla stazione.
native_language_example: I know how to get to the station.

additional_notes: Used to identify yourself or describe who you are, where you're from, or your state/condition. In Italian, io is often omitted because sono already means "I am"; io is mainly added for emphasis or contrast.
target_language_example: Io sono pronto per partire.
native_language_example: I am ready to leave.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "andare" using the auxiliary "essere". "Andata" agrees with the speaker: a woman says "(io) sono andata"; a man says "(io) sono andato". Often followed by a place ("sono andata a Roma"), or by "a" + infinitive to say what you went to do ("sono andata a nuotare", "a vedere"). You can also use "in" for institutions/places like schools ("sono andata in una scuola...").
target_language_example: Ieri io sono andata al supermercato.
native_language_example: Yesterday I went to the supermarket.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "andare" with the auxiliary "essere". The past participle agrees with the subject: a man says "io sono andato"; a woman says "io sono andata". Often "io" is omitted because the verb already shows the person, but it can be used for emphasis or contrast.
target_language_example: Io sono andato al parco ieri.
native_language_example: I went to the park yesterday.

meaning: "I am the" (used before a masculine singular noun/title).
additional_notes: Used to introduce yourself or identify who you are. "Il" is the masculine singular definite article; use "io sono la" for feminine singular. With some masculine words you’ll need "lo" instead of "il" (e.g., "io sono lo studente", "io sono lo zio"). Often the subject "io" is omitted in Italian: "Sono il commissario."
target_language_example: Buongiorno, io sono il responsabile del progetto.
native_language_example: Good morning, I am the person in charge of the project.

additional_notes: Used to say you feel something or have a quality to a strong degree, followed by an adjective (e.g., soddisfatto/a, fiero/a, interessato/a). The adjective often changes ending for gender: -o (masc.) / -a (fem.), and sometimes -i / -e in plural.
target_language_example: Io sono molto stanco oggi.
native_language_example: I am very tired today.

additional_notes: Past tense of *nascere* (to be born), which uses *essere* as the helping verb. It agrees with the speaker’s gender/number: a man says *io sono nato*; more than one woman: *siamo nate*; mixed/men: *siamo nati*. Used to talk about where/when/how you were born or what you were born with (*nata con…*).
target_language_example: Io sono nata a Milano, ma vivo a Londra.
native_language_example: I was born in Milan, but I live in London.

meaning: “I have been / I was” (said by a female speaker).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *essere* for “io” with feminine past participle *stata* (male: *io sono stato*). Used to talk about a past state/situation (*sono stata dentro*, *sono stata impegnata*), feelings/conditions (*sono stata fortunata*), or in the passive voice (*sono stata ingannata*, *sono stata promossa*). Often corresponds to English “I was…”, though Italian also uses *io ero* (imperfetto) for ongoing/background past situations.
target_language_example: Ieri io sono stata molto stanca dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: Yesterday I was very tired after work.

meaning: 'I have been' / 'I was'; also used to form the passive ('I was ...-ed').
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of essere (essere + stato). Used (1) to describe a past state/condition: "Io sono stato impegnato" = "I was/have been busy"; and (2) as the auxiliary in the passive with a past participle: "Io sono stato invitato/ingannato" = "I was invited/deceived." In everyday speech Italians often drop the subject pronoun and just say "Sono stato...".
target_language_example: Io sono stato invitato al loro matrimonio.
native_language_example: I was invited to their wedding.

additional_notes: Used to state what you are (profession, role, identity) with a masculine singular noun/adjective: io sono un + noun (e.g., io sono un medico). For feminine singular, use “io sono una” (io sono una studentessa). “Io” is often omitted in Italian (e.g., “sono un fotografo”), but including it adds emphasis/contrast. If the next word starts with a vowel, feminine often uses “un’ ” (e.g., “io sono un’insegnante”).
target_language_example: Io sono un fotografo freelance.
native_language_example: I am a freelance photographer.

meaning: “I am a …” (female speaker; used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Use to introduce yourself or describe your job/role/identity when you are a woman or using feminine grammar. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (often ending in -a, like dottoressa, fotografa, giornalista, scrittrice). For a male speaker you typically say “io sono un …” (or “io sono uno …” before s+consonant, z, ps, gn, etc.). Often “io” is dropped in natural speech: “Sono una fotografa.”
target_language_example: Io sono una fotografa freelance.
native_language_example: I am a freelance photographer (female).

additional_notes: Used to introduce a hope/wish about something (often something uncertain). In Italian it’s commonly followed by the subjunctive: io spero che Tom cambi idea; io spero che a Tom piaccia…; io spero che abbiate…. In everyday speech you can also just say “Spero che…”.
target_language_example: Io spero che tu possa venire domani.
native_language_example: I hope you can come tomorrow.

meaning: “I was” (used to talk about what you were doing/experiencing at a specific time in the past).
additional_notes: “Io” is often optional in Italian because the verb ending already signals the subject; you’ll commonly just hear/see “stavo.” It’s the imperfect of “stare” and is frequently used with a gerund to express an ongoing past action (io stavo dormendo = I was sleeping; io stavo lavorando = I was working), often as background when something else happened. It can also be used with certain expressions to describe a past state (e.g., io stavo male = I felt ill).
target_language_example: Io stavo dormendo quando è arrivato Mark.
native_language_example: I was sleeping when Mark arrived.

additional_notes: Used with the gerund (-ando/-endo) to describe an action happening right now: "io sto + gerund" = "I’m ...-ing" (io sto aspettando = I’m waiting). Often in real conversation Italians drop the subject "io" and just say "sto aspettando", because "sto" already implies "I".
target_language_example: Io sto studiando per l’esame.
native_language_example: I’m studying for the exam.

additional_notes: A very common combination: **io** = “I” (often omitted in Italian), and **ti** = “you” as an unstressed object pronoun (can mean “you” or “to you,” depending on the verb). **Ti** usually comes right before the verb: *io ti capisco* = “I understand you”; *io ti scriverò* = “I’ll write to you.”
target_language_example: Io ti mando un messaggio dopo.
native_language_example: I’ll text you later.

additional_notes: “Io vado” is the 1st-person singular of andare (“to go”). The subject pronoun io (“I”) is often optional in Italian; you can also just say “vado”. Used for going to a place (vado al mercato), going somewhere regularly (vado a nuotare ogni lunedì), going by a means of transport (vado al lavoro in autobus), or going to do an activity (vado a nuotare). With a letto it means “I go to bed” (vado a letto alle undici).
target_language_example: Scusa, è tardi: io vado a casa.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s late: I’m going home.

additional_notes: "Io" is the subject pronoun "I" and "vivo" is "(I) live" from the verb "vivere." In Italian, the subject pronoun is often optional, so you’ll frequently hear just "Vivo qui" ("I live here"). It’s commonly followed by "con" (with), "in" (in + country/region/city), "qui" (here), or "vicino a" (near).
target_language_example: Io vivo a Roma da due anni.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in Rome for two years.

meaning: "I live in" / "I live at" (followed by a place).
additional_notes: Used to say where you live. With cities and small islands Italians often use **a** (e.g., *a Roma, a Malta*). For most countries they use **in** (*in Italia, in America*). In normal conversation you can just say **Vivo a...** (the subject *io* is often omitted).
target_language_example: Io vivo a Roma, ma lavoro a Milano.
native_language_example: I live in Rome, but I work in Milan.

additional_notes: First-person singular of volere. It is used to express what the speaker wants or intends to do, often followed by an infinitive verb. In Italian, io is often omitted unless it is being emphasized.
target_language_example: Io voglio imparare l'italiano.
native_language_example: I want to learn Italian.

additional_notes:
Used to say you want to go somewhere or leave. Often followed by:
- a destination with **a/in** (“Io voglio andare a casa / in Italia.”)
- a place/activity with **a + infinitive** (“Io voglio andare a mangiare.”)
- a person with **con** (“Io voglio andare con te.”)
In everyday speech, the subject pronoun **io** is often omitted: **“Voglio andare…”**.
target_language_example: Io voglio andare a casa adesso.
native_language_example: I want to go home now.

additional_notes: Used to say what you want to become or what state/role you want to have. Often followed by an adjective or noun (e.g., "felice", "un medico"), or by "sicuro/sicura che..." to mean “I want to be sure/certain that...”. In Italian, the subject pronoun "io" is optional, so you’ll often hear just "voglio essere".
target_language_example: Io voglio essere più organizzato quest'anno.
native_language_example: I want to be more organized this year.

additional_notes: Used to express the desire to eat. In everyday Italian, the subject pronoun “io” is often omitted (“Voglio mangiare…”), but including it adds emphasis (e.g., contrasting with what someone else wants). Common add-ons: “ora” (now), “qui” (here), “fuori” (out/to eat out).
target_language_example: Io voglio mangiare ora.
native_language_example: I want to eat now.

additional_notes: Used to state strongly that you want information or an explanation. Often followed by a question word (chi = who, come = how, perché = why) or by se (“whether/if”) to introduce an indirect yes/no question. In conversation you can also just say “Voglio sapere…” without “Io.”
target_language_example: Io voglio sapere quando inizia la riunione.
native_language_example: I want to know when the meeting starts.

meaning: "I just want to" / "all I want is to".
additional_notes: Used to express a simple or limited desire/goal, often to downplay expectations or emphasize that you don’t want anything else. In everyday Italian you can also omit the subject: "Voglio solo...". It’s typically followed by an infinitive (aiutare, finire, sapere) or sometimes by a noun phrase.
target_language_example: Io voglio solo parlare con te un minuto.
native_language_example: I just want to talk to you for a minute.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to watch/see something. Followed by an infinitive (vedere) and often a person + infinitive action: “Voglio vedere Tom farlo” = “I want to see Tom do it.” In everyday speech, Italians often drop the subject pronoun: “Voglio vedere …”.
target_language_example: Io voglio vedere come funziona.
native_language_example: I want to see how it works.

additional_notes: Means “I want.” In Italian you often drop the subject pronoun, so you’ll very commonly hear just “voglio …”. Note: in the fixed expression “voglio bene a …” it does NOT mean “I want (something)”; it means “I care about / I love (someone)” in a non-romantic or general sense (e.g., family, friends).
target_language_example: Io voglio un caffè, per favore.
native_language_example: I want a coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used to express what you want another person to do. It is normally followed by a verb in the present subjunctive (congiuntivo presente): e.g., che tu venga, che tu faccia, che tu consideri, che tu stia. In everyday speech, some people may use the indicative instead, but the subjunctive is the standard/grammatical form.
target_language_example: Io voglio che tu mi chiami domani.
native_language_example: I want you to call me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express what you want your state/identity/location to be, followed by the infinitive "essere" + a place ("a Boston"), role/relationship ("sua amica"), or an adjective/state. In everyday Italian the subject pronoun is often dropped: "Voglio essere...".
target_language_example: Io voglio essere pronto alle otto.
native_language_example: I want to be ready at eight.

meaning: "I wanted" / "I meant to" (imperfect past of volere).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (volevo) to talk about what you wanted/intended in the past, often as background, an unfulfilled plan, or something you were going to do. In conversation it can introduce an explanation or correction: "Io volevo..." = "What I wanted/was trying to say/do was..." Often the subject "io" is optional in Italian ("Volevo...") but adding it gives emphasis.
target_language_example: Scusa, io volevo solo aiutarti.
native_language_example: Sorry, I just wanted to help you.

meaning: "I would like" (polite way to say what you want).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of "volere" (to want) to sound polite/soft. Often followed by an infinitive: "Vorrei andare..." = "I’d like to go..." You can also use it with a noun: "Vorrei un caffè" = "I’d like a coffee." In conversation, "io" is usually dropped: "Vorrei..."
target_language_example: Io vorrei un caffè, per favore.
native_language_example: I would like a coffee, please.

meaning: "I would like (it) that…" / "I wish that…" (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or desire about a situation. It’s typically followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., fosse, fossero, arrivasse). Often used when you want something to be true or to happen, not as a direct request to someone.
target_language_example: Io vorrei che tu venissi con noi.
native_language_example: I’d like you to come with us.

meaning: “I would like to be…” / “I wish I were…”.
additional_notes: Used to express a desire or wish about what you want to be (often a personal quality or role). It’s polite/neutral. In natural Italian you can often omit the subject pronoun (“Vorrei essere…”), but including “io” adds emphasis. Commonly followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., più spontaneo/a, intelligente, come lei/voi).
target_language_example: Io vorrei essere più spontanea.
native_language_example: I’d like to be more spontaneous.

meaning: jet lag (tiredness and sleep disruption after long-distance travel).
additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb avere: avere il jet lag = “to have jet lag.” Often appears after talking about long flights or changing time zones.
target_language_example: Dopo il volo per Tokyo, avevo un forte jet lag.
native_language_example: After the flight to Tokyo, I had bad jet lag.

additional_notes: In Italian, “duca” means “duke,” and normally you would say **il duca** (masculine). With **la** and capitalized (**La Duca**), it’s most often an **Italian last name** where the article “La” is part of the surname (common in some regions, e.g., Sicily). You typically don’t translate it; you treat it as a proper name.
target_language_example: Ho un appuntamento con la signora La Duca alle tre.
native_language_example: I have an appointment with Mrs. La Duca at three.

additional_notes: Common ingredient used for bread, pasta, cakes, etc. Often used with quantities: "un chilo di farina" (a kilo of flour), or with the partitive: "della farina" (some flour). In shops you might see types like "farina 00" (very fine flour) or "farina integrale" (whole wheat flour).
target_language_example: Mi serve della farina per fare una torta.
native_language_example: I need some flour to make a cake.

meaning: "the Fat one" (a nickname, especially for Bologna, referring to its rich food).
additional_notes: Used as part of the traditional nickname for Bologna: "Bologna la Grassa". It’s a feminine form (because it refers to "Bologna", which is feminine in Italian). You may also see it alongside other nicknames like "la Dotta" (learned) and "la Rossa" (red).
target_language_example: Bologna è chiamata anche "la Grassa" per la sua cucina.
native_language_example: Bologna is also called “the Fat one” because of its cuisine.

additional_notes: Used as a respectful way to refer to a woman teacher. In schools, kids often call their teacher "Maestra!" (without "la"). With "la" it usually means "the teacher" when talking about her (e.g., to parents). It can also mean a female "maestro" in music/arts, but in everyday Italian it commonly means "teacher".
target_language_example: La Maestra oggi non è a scuola.
native_language_example: The teacher isn’t at school today.

additional_notes: Literally “the morning.” With the definite article (la), it’s often used to talk about mornings in general or a routine (“La mattina bevo un caffè”). For a specific morning, context usually makes it clear (“La mattina del 3 maggio…”). You can also say “di mattina” to mean “in the morning.”
target_language_example: La mattina vado al lavoro in autobus.
native_language_example: In the morning I go to work by bus.

meaning: "the Stone" (a specific stone, often an important/special object).
additional_notes: Pietra normally means “stone,” but the capital letter ("la Pietra") often signals a particular, named object (e.g., in a story or game). It’s feminine singular, so it takes la and pronouns like la (e.g., “Prendila!” = “Take it!”).
target_language_example: Dov'è la Pietra? Devo prenderla subito.
native_language_example: Where is the Stone? I have to take it right away.

additional_notes: Usually written la porta unless it is capitalized at the start of a sentence or in a name/title. la is the feminine singular word for "the," and porta means "door." It can also sometimes mean "gate" depending on context.
target_language_example: Chiudi la porta, per favore.
native_language_example: Close the door, please.

meaning: the Queen (a female monarch; also a ‘queen’ in titles).
additional_notes: Used as a title for a queen or reigning female monarch. It can be followed by a name ("la Regina Vittoria") or used alone when the context is clear ("La Regina vive..."). In some historical/formal titles it can mean someone’s rank or claim ("la Regina di Acri...").
target_language_example: La Regina Elisabetta II ha regnato per molti anni.
native_language_example: Queen Elizabeth II reigned for many years.

additional_notes: Most often you’ll see it as the common noun phrase "la rosa" = "the rose". In writing, a capital R ("la Rosa") can indicate a proper name (e.g., a woman named Rosa or a family name). In sports/news, "la rosa" can also mean a team’s roster/squad (e.g., "la rosa della squadra" = "the team roster").
target_language_example: Questa è la rosa che preferisco.
native_language_example: This is the rose I like best.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: a wheel (of a bike, car, cart, etc.). In some contexts, especially when capitalized ("la Ruota"), it may refer to a specific named wheel (e.g., part of a title like "La Ruota della Fortuna" or a particular wheel in a game/lottery).
target_language_example: Devo cambiare la ruota della macchina.
native_language_example: I have to change the car’s wheel.

additional_notes: Often refers to the main room in a home where people sit and relax (similar to "il salotto"). In other contexts it can mean a specific room or hall in a building (e.g., a waiting room, a cinema/theater hall, or a meeting room).
target_language_example: La sala è grande e luminosa.
native_language_example: The living room is big and bright.

meaning: "the plug" (electrical plug); also "the thorn/spine" depending on context.
additional_notes: Most commonly in everyday situations it means an electrical plug: mettere la spina (to plug in), togliere/staccare la spina (to unplug). In other contexts spina can mean a thorn (una spina) or, in set phrases, spine/backbone (e.g., spina dorsale). Capitalization ("Spina") may also be part of a name (surname, place, business), depending on where you saw it.
target_language_example: Puoi staccare la spina, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you unplug it, please?

additional_notes: Common noun: *stella* = “star” (in the sky). It can also be a proper name (*Stella*) for a person or the name of a place/business, in which case Italian still uses the article in some contexts (e.g., *La Stella* as a restaurant name). Plural: *le stelle* (“the stars”).
target_language_example: Guarda la Stella più luminosa nel cielo.
native_language_example: Look at the brightest star in the sky.

additional_notes: Common in everyday Italian. You use it both for the device (turn it on/off, lower the volume) and for watching television in general (guardare la TV = to watch TV). It’s feminine singular: la TV.
target_language_example: Stasera guardiamo la TV dopo cena.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re going to watch TV after dinner.

additional_notes: Used as a proper noun for our planet, so it’s usually capitalized (la Terra). It often appears with the definite article “la” in Italian. In some contexts, “terra” (lowercase) can also mean “land/soil/ground,” but “la Terra” refers specifically to the planet.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo proteggere la Terra.
native_language_example: We must protect the Earth.

additional_notes: Used as a regular noun phrase with the definite article: la torre (feminine singular). It can refer to a tower/building (e.g., a castle tower) and in chess it means the rook.
target_language_example: La torre è molto alta.
native_language_example: The tower is very tall.

additional_notes: Literally the feminine form of “old” (vecchia) with the feminine singular article (la). Often written lowercase in normal sentences (la vecchia). Capitalized (la Vecchia) can also be a title or nickname in specific contexts (e.g., referring to a particular person or something personified), so the exact reference depends on context.
target_language_example: La vecchia del paese racconta storie ai bambini.
native_language_example: The old woman in the village tells stories to the children.

additional_notes: Common noun phrase for the animal (usually written lowercase: "la volpe"). It can also be used figuratively to describe a crafty/cunning person. Gender: feminine (la volpe / una volpe). Plural: le volpi.
target_language_example: Nel bosco ho visto la volpe.
native_language_example: In the woods I saw the fox.

meaning: the (little) girl; a young female child.
additional_notes: "Bambina" is the feminine form of "bambino" (boy/child). With "la" it usually means a specific girl already known from context ("the girl"). It can also be used figuratively to tell an adult woman she’s acting childish: "Smetti di fare la bambina!" (Stop acting like a little girl!).
target_language_example: La bambina sta giocando in giardino.
native_language_example: The little girl is playing in the garden.

additional_notes: Used for a place/company that handles money (accounts, loans, payments). Common with verbs like aprire/chiudere (to open/close), rapinare (to rob), and avere bisogno di (to need): “La banca ha bisogno della sua firma” = the bank needs your signature.
target_language_example: La banca è chiusa domenica.
native_language_example: The bank is closed on Sunday.

additional_notes: Used for a country's flag or any flag/signal flag. Common verbs: alzare/la bandiera (to raise the flag), cambiare la bandiera (to change/switch the flag), tenere la bandiera (to hold the flag), salutare la bandiera (to salute the flag). Colors can be used as adjectives: la bandiera è nera (the flag is black).
target_language_example: Durante la cerimonia, hanno alzato la bandiera italiana.
native_language_example: During the ceremony, they raised the Italian flag.

additional_notes: Used with the definite article in Italian: “ha la barba” = “he has a beard.” You can add an adjective to describe it (e.g., lunga = long, corta = short, folta = thick).
target_language_example: Mio fratello ha la barba lunga.
native_language_example: My brother has a long beard.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “the drums” (the percussion instrument set), especially with verbs like *suonare* (“to play”). It can also mean “the battery” (e.g., a phone battery), so context matters.
target_language_example: Non posso ascoltare musica: la batteria del telefono è quasi scarica.
native_language_example: I can’t listen to music: my phone’s battery is almost dead.

additional_notes: Used to give information about the library. Common patterns: **la biblioteca è + location** (a destra, in centro, in fondo alla strada), **la biblioteca è + adjective** (aperta, piccola), or **la biblioteca è stata + past participle** to form the passive in the past (e.g., *è stata fondata* = “was founded”).
target_language_example: Scusi, la biblioteca è vicino alla stazione?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is the library near the station?

additional_notes: Noun; feminine singular. Often used with verbs like piacere (A lei piace la birra? = Do you like beer?), or to talk about a specific beer in context (Porta la birra = Bring the beer). You can add adjectives like artigianale (craft) or fredda (cold).
target_language_example: Preferisco la birra fredda.
native_language_example: I prefer cold beer.

additional_notes: Means the physical mouth. Common with verbs like aprire la bocca (“open your mouth”) and chiudere la bocca (“close your mouth”), which can also be used to tell someone to be quiet (“shut up”). Polite request: "Apra la bocca"; informal: "Apri la bocca".
target_language_example: Non riesco a parlare: ho la bocca secca.
native_language_example: I can’t speak: my mouth is dry.

meaning: your mouth shut; (figuratively) quiet / not telling anyone.
additional_notes: Most often used with the verb "tenere" ("tenere la bocca chiusa") meaning "to keep quiet" or "to keep a secret." In the imperative ("Tieni/tenete la bocca chiusa!") it can sound harsh, like “Shut up!” or “Keep your mouth shut!”
target_language_example: Puoi venire, ma tieni la bocca chiusa su questa cosa.
native_language_example: You can come, but keep your mouth shut about this.

additional_notes: Commonly means a bag you carry (especially a handbag/purse). It’s feminine: la borsa (plural: le borse). In other contexts, borsa can also mean “stock exchange” (la Borsa), but in these sentences it clearly means a bag.
target_language_example: Ho lasciato la borsa in macchina.
native_language_example: I left my bag in the car.

additional_notes: Used for a container (glass/plastic) for drinks or liquids. Common verbs with it: rompere (break), far cadere (drop), aprire (open), passare (hand/pass). Feminine noun: la bottiglia; plural: le bottiglie.
target_language_example: Puoi passarmi la bottiglia, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the bottle, please?

meaning: 'the room' (often a bedroom or hotel room).
additional_notes: In everyday Italian, *la camera* usually refers to a bedroom or a hotel room (e.g., *La camera è libera* = “The room is available”). It can also mean a general room in a building, depending on context. Be careful: it looks like English “camera,” but the device is *la macchina fotografica* (or informally *la fotocamera*).
target_language_example: Scusi, la camera è pronta?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is the room ready?

additional_notes: Used for a (typically button-up) shirt. With clothing in Italian you usually use the definite article (la) where English often uses a possessive: e.g., "si tolse la camicia" = "he/she took off his/her shirt."
target_language_example: Devo stirare la camicia per domani.
native_language_example: I have to iron the shirt for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Usually means “meat” as food. In other contexts, it can also mean “flesh” (the human/animal body). Often used as a general, uncountable category (“I like meat” = “Mi piace la carne”).
target_language_example: Non mangio la carne.
native_language_example: I don't eat meat.

additional_notes: "La carne" means "the meat" and "è" is "is" (present tense of essere). It’s commonly followed by an adjective to talk about doneness (cotta, al sangue/medio-al sangue), quality (squisita), or amount/availability (scarsa).
target_language_example: La carne è troppo cotta per me.
native_language_example: The meat is too well-done for me.

meaning: paper; a card (e.g., a credit/debit card).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “paper” in everyday contexts: *la carta taglia* (paper cuts), *finire la carta* (to run out of paper, e.g., in a fax/printer), *piegare la carta* (to fold paper). In other contexts, *la carta* can mean “card,” especially when talking about paying: *pagare/fare con la carta* (“to pay/by card”). The exact meaning depends on what’s happening in the sentence.
target_language_example: Mi sono tagliato con la carta mentre aprivo la busta.
native_language_example: I got a paper cut while opening the envelope.

additional_notes: A very common phrase. casa can mean both a physical house and, in many contexts, home. la is the feminine singular definite article, meaning 'the'.
target_language_example: La casa è vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: The house is near the station.

additional_notes: Used to describe the state, quality, location, or ownership of a house. Pattern: **La casa è + adjective** (La casa è bianca/fredda), **+ prepositional phrase** (La casa è in fiamme), or **+ possessive** (La casa è sua = The house is his/hers).
target_language_example: La casa è molto vecchia.
native_language_example: The house is very old.

additional_notes: Refers to the main meal in the evening. Common with verbs like preparare (to prepare), cucinare (to cook), mangiare (to eat), and saltare (to skip). Used with the definite article la because cena is feminine singular.
target_language_example: Stasera facciamo la cena alle otto.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re having dinner at eight.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a physical key. It's often followed by di / del / della to say what the key is for: la chiave di casa, la chiave della stanza. More generally, chiave can also mean the key to a problem or idea in other contexts.
target_language_example: Non trovo la chiave di casa.
native_language_example: I can't find the house key.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article "la" because "chitarra" is feminine singular. Often used with the verb "suonare" (to play an instrument): "suonare la chitarra" = "to play the guitar". In Italian, you typically include the article when talking about playing an instrument.
target_language_example: Sto imparando a suonare la chitarra.
native_language_example: I’m learning to play the guitar.

meaning: the belt; also the seat belt.
additional_notes: Usually refers to a belt you wear (for pants or as part of clothing). In contexts like cars or safety (“Metti la cintura”), it means the seat belt (“cintura di sicurezza” is the full term). It can also mean a martial-arts belt, often specified by color (e.g., “cintura nera” = black belt).
target_language_example: In macchina metti sempre la cintura.
native_language_example: In the car, always wear your seat belt.

additional_notes: Common way to refer to a specific city already known from context. It’s feminine singular: la città; plural: le città. The accent on "città" stays the same in singular and plural.
target_language_example: La città è piena di turisti in estate.
native_language_example: The city is full of tourists in the summer.

meaning: 'the city is…' (used to describe a city).
additional_notes: "La città" means "the city" and "è" is the verb "is" (from *essere*). Use it to start a description: *La città è piccola/rumorosa/sporca* (adjectives) or with place/condition phrases: *La città è nel caos / in fiamme / circondata da…*. Often followed by an adjective or by *famosa per* + noun.
target_language_example: La città è molto bella, ma è anche trafficata.
native_language_example: The city is very beautiful, but it’s also busy with traffic.

additional_notes: Means the morning meal (“breakfast”). Common collocations include: “fare colazione” (to have breakfast), “preparare la colazione” (to prepare breakfast), “portare la colazione” (to bring breakfast), and “mangiare la colazione” (to eat breakfast). Often paired with items like “caffè”, “cornetto”, “pane”, “marmellata”.
target_language_example: A che ora vorresti la colazione?
native_language_example: What time would you like breakfast?

meaning: the blame; fault (responsibility for something bad).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like **dare la colpa (a qualcuno/qualcosa)** = “to blame (someone/something)”, and **prendersi la colpa** = “to take the blame.” Common pattern: **la colpa di + noun** (“the blame for/of …”).
target_language_example: Ha dato la colpa del suo fallimento alla malattia.
native_language_example: He blamed his failure on illness.

additional_notes: Used literally for a rope/cord you can grab (afferrare), pull (tirare), or cut (tagliare). In idioms, "avere la corda al collo" means being in serious trouble/under heavy pressure (literally “with a rope around one’s neck”), and "tagliare la corda" can also mean “to run away / get out of here” (more informal).
target_language_example: Puoi tenere ferma la corda mentre la taglio?
native_language_example: Can you hold the rope still while I cut it?

meaning: the race; the run (a scheduled trip/service).
additional_notes: Most often means a race/competition (e.g., running, cycling). It can also mean a run of a bus/train/tram or a scheduled trip: "Hai saltato la corsa" = "You missed the bus/train (that run)."
target_language_example: Chi ha vinto la corsa?
native_language_example: Who won the race?

additional_notes: A general way to refer to a thing, situation, issue, or fact when the exact noun is unknown, obvious, or unimportant. Very common in patterns like "la cosa importante/strana è che..." = "the important/strange thing is that...".
target_language_example: La cosa migliore è aspettare domani.
native_language_example: The best thing is to wait until tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the morally correct or most appropriate action or words in a situation. Common with verbs like fare (“do”) and dire (“say”): fare la cosa giusta = do the right thing; dire la cosa giusta = say the right thing.
target_language_example: Non so qual è la cosa giusta da fare.
native_language_example: I don’t know what the right thing to do is.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the best option, the best part, or the best experience in a situation. Often followed by "è" + infinitive ("la cosa migliore è + verb") or by a relative clause ("la cosa migliore che...").
target_language_example: La cosa migliore è chiedere aiuto.
native_language_example: The best thing is to ask for help.

additional_notes:
Used to highlight what matters most in a situation (“Wait—the most important thing!”) or in general statements about life/values. Often followed by:
- “è + infinitive” (La cosa più importante è essere felici.)
- “nella vita” (La cosa più importante nella vita...)
You can change gender/number to match what you mean: “il fatto più importante” (the most important fact), “le cose più importanti” (the most important things).
target_language_example: Per me, la cosa più importante è la salute.
native_language_example: For me, the most important thing is health.

additional_notes: Most commonly means the room where you prepare food ("the kitchen"). It can also mean cooking as an activity or a style of food ("cuisine"), especially with an adjective like "la cucina francese" (French cuisine). Feminine noun: la cucina; plural: le cucine.
target_language_example: La cucina è al piano di sotto.
native_language_example: The kitchen is downstairs.

meaning: “the difference” (a distinction; what makes things not the same).
additional_notes: Used to compare two things or to point out a distinction: "Qual è la differenza fra A e B?" = "What’s the difference between A and B?" It can also mean “to make a difference” (= to have an important effect): "fare la differenza". Common verbs: capire/vedere/spiegare la differenza (understand/see/explain the difference).
target_language_example: Non vedo la differenza tra queste due foto.
native_language_example: I don’t see the difference between these two photos.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “the question” (e.g., in conversation, school, interviews): *Ricordi/Si ricorda la domanda?* In other common everyday uses, *domanda* can also mean an “application” or “request” (e.g., a job application), but in the examples here it clearly means “question.”
target_language_example: La domanda è: perché sei in ritardo?
native_language_example: The question is: why are you late?

additional_notes: With days of the week, Italian often uses the definite article (la/il) to mean a general habit: "la domenica" = "on Sundays" (every Sunday). Without the article, "domenica" often refers to a specific Sunday (e.g., this/next Sunday).
target_language_example: La domenica andiamo al parco.
native_language_example: On Sundays we go to the park.

additional_notes: Feminine singular noun phrase: "la" = "the" (used before most feminine singular nouns), and "donna" = "woman". Used to talk about a specific woman known from context or previously mentioned.
target_language_example: La donna parla con il medico.
native_language_example: The woman is talking with the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing which woman you mean (che = “who/that” for people and things). It can be followed by a verb (e.g., che mente) or by a pronoun + auxiliary (e.g., che ti ha donato…).
target_language_example: La donna che vive qui accanto è molto gentile.
native_language_example: The woman who lives next door is very kind.

additional_notes: Literally the physical face (often with verbs like lavarsi/asciugarsi/coprirsi/toccarsi la faccia). In some expressions it refers to pride or reputation: "perdere la faccia" = "to lose face" (be embarrassed/lose respect). "Ho la faccia da…?" means "Do I look like…?" (often rhetorical).
target_language_example: Non voglio perdere la faccia davanti a tutti.
native_language_example: I don’t want to lose face in front of everyone.

additional_notes: Means a family (a group of relatives), often referring to a specific family unit or household. It can also mean a “family” as a group/side you belong to (e.g., in a conflict: “protect the family”). Gender/number: singular feminine; plural is "le famiglie".
target_language_example: Stasera ceno con la famiglia.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m having dinner with the family.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere la febbre" = "to have a fever". Often refers to being sick with a temperature (e.g., from a cold or flu).
target_language_example: Ho la febbre, quindi oggi resto a casa.
native_language_example: I have a fever, so I'm staying home today.

additional_notes: A common noun usually used with the definite article (la) when talking about happiness in general or as an abstract idea (e.g., la felicità non si compra). It’s also used in wishes: Ti auguro la felicità (“I wish you happiness”).
target_language_example: Cerco la felicità nelle piccole cose.
native_language_example: I look for happiness in the little things.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a party or celebration event (often with food, music, guests). It can also mean a holiday or feast day (e.g., una festa nazionale = a national holiday). Used with verbs like fare/organizzare una festa (to throw/organize a party), annullare la festa (to cancel the party), rimandare la festa (to postpone the party), lasciare la festa (to leave the party).
target_language_example: Domani organizziamo la festa a casa mia.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re having the party at my house.

meaning: "the end" (literally or figuratively: "it’s over / that would be the end of us").
additional_notes: Used for the literal end of something (a movie, a story, an event) and very often in a figurative/dramatic sense: "È la fine" = "It’s the end" / "We’re finished". Common structures: "alla fine" means "in the end / finally" (different phrase). Note: Italian "fine" means "end", not English "fine" (= okay/good) and not "a fine" (= a penalty).
target_language_example: Se ci scoprono, è la fine.
native_language_example: If they find us out, it’s the end.

meaning: "the end of the world"; (figuratively) "a disaster / the worst thing".
additional_notes: Often used literally in dramatic contexts (apocalypse), but very commonly used figuratively to mean something is not a huge problem. Common set phrase: "Non è la fine del mondo" = "It’s not the end of the world." You can also say "Sembra la fine del mondo" (It feels like the end of the world).
target_language_example: Dai, non è la fine del mondo se arriviamo in ritardo.
native_language_example: Come on, it’s not the end of the world if we arrive late.

additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like aprire/chiudere (to open/close) and with prepositions like attraverso (through) and dalla (from the). Also used in polite requests/commands: “Chiuda la finestra, per favore” (formal you).
target_language_example: Puoi aprire la finestra? Fa caldo qui.
native_language_example: Can you open the window? It’s hot in here.

meaning: the crowd; the mass of people.
additional_notes: Used for a large group of people gathered in a place (at a match, concert, on the street, etc.). It’s a feminine singular noun, but it refers to many people, so verbs are typically singular in Italian: “La folla applaude / grida”. Common uses: “tra la folla” (in/among the crowd), “la folla impazzisce” (the crowd goes wild), “accontentare la folla” (to please the crowd).
target_language_example: Non mi piace camminare in mezzo alla folla.
native_language_example: I don’t like walking in the middle of the crowd.

additional_notes: Often used for physical strength ("Mi manca la forza") or inner strength/courage ("dammi la forza"). You can add a possessive: "la mia/tu(a) forza" (my/your strength). Common emphatic phrase: "Tutta la forza che hai!" = "With all your strength!".
target_language_example: Non ho più la forza di continuare.
native_language_example: I don’t have the strength to continue anymore.

meaning: 'the strength/energy to' (do something); or 'the strength/force of' (someone/something).
additional_notes: Common patterns: **(non) avere / trovare la forza di + infinitive** = to (not) have / find the strength (or courage) to do something: *Non ho la forza di parlarne.* It can also be followed by a noun to mean **the strength of**: *la forza di tua sorella*, *la forza di una luna crescente*.
target_language_example: Non ho la forza di continuare oggi.
native_language_example: I don't have the strength to keep going today.

additional_notes: "Foto" is short for "fotografia" and is very common in everyday speech. It’s feminine singular: la foto; plural: le foto. Used with verbs like avere (ho la foto = I have the photo), vedere (vedere la foto = to see the photo), mostrare (mostrare la foto = to show the photo), fare una foto (to take a photo).
target_language_example: Mi mandi la foto, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you send me the photo, please?

additional_notes: Most commonly means “the sentence” in grammar or writing exercises (e.g., complete/correct/change/translate the sentence). It can also mean a “phrase” (a short group of words), but in school-type contexts Italian often uses frase for a whole sentence. Feminine singular: la frase; plural: le frasi.
target_language_example: Puoi tradurre la frase in inglese?
native_language_example: Can you translate the sentence into English?

additional_notes: “Frutta” is a feminine singular noun used as an uncountable/category word in Italian, so you often use the singular article: “la frutta” = “fruit” (in general). For specific pieces, Italian usually uses “un frutto” (a fruit) or names the type (una mela, una banana). Common in shopping/food contexts (washing it, having some at home, fruit in season: “frutta di stagione”).
target_language_example: Preferisci la frutta o il dolce?
native_language_example: Do you prefer fruit or dessert?

additional_notes: Means a (human/animal) leg. In Italian, with body parts you often use the definite article (la) instead of a possessive: "Mi fa male la gamba" = "My leg hurts." It can also refer to a "leg" of an object (e.g., a table), but the example here is about pain/injury.
target_language_example: Mi fa male la gamba, quindi oggi cammino piano.
native_language_example: My leg hurts, so today I’m walking slowly.

additional_notes: Used to specify the left leg (sinistra = left). With injuries/medical events, Italian often uses the definite article (la) with body parts: "si è rotta la gamba" = "she broke her leg." You can also say "mi fa male la gamba sinistra" (my left leg hurts).
target_language_example: Mi fa male la gamba sinistra.
native_language_example: My left leg hurts.

additional_notes: "Gatta" is the feminine form of "gatto" (male cat). In everyday Italian, "gatto" can also be used generically for “cat,” but "gatta" specifies a female cat. "La" is the definite article (“the”).
target_language_example: La gatta dorme sul divano.
native_language_example: The (female) cat sleeps on the couch.

additional_notes: Used to describe a female cat (la gatta) with the verb essere (“to be”). Follow it with an adjective (La gatta è affamata. = The cat is hungry) or a place expression (La gatta è in cucina. = The cat is in the kitchen). Note: for a male cat you usually say il gatto è. In the past tense with movement verbs, the participle agrees: La gatta è corsa… (“The cat ran…”).
target_language_example: La gatta è sotto il tavolo.
native_language_example: The (female) cat is under the table.

additional_notes: Usually refers to people in general or to the public. In Italian, gente is grammatically singular, so it normally takes a singular verb: la gente è, not la gente sono.
target_language_example: La gente qui è molto gentile.
native_language_example: People here are very kind.

meaning: “People say that…” / “they say that…” (a rumor or general opinion).
additional_notes: Used to report what is commonly said or rumored, without saying who specifically said it. Often introduces hearsay and can imply “apparently” or “according to people.” Grammar: it’s followed by a clause with che + verb (e.g., La gente dice che è vero).
target_language_example: La gente dice che questo ristorante è il migliore in città.
native_language_example: People say that this restaurant is the best in town.

additional_notes: A common clothing noun. Used for everyday jackets (e.g., a military-style jacket) and in set phrases like "giacca di salvataggio" (life jacket). With verbs like mettere (to put on), sbottonare (to unbutton), or piacere (to like).
target_language_example: Fa freddo: prendi la giacca e usciamo.
native_language_example: It’s cold: take your jacket and let’s go out.

meaning: the day (as a whole day’s time; one’s day).
additional_notes: Used when talking about how you spend or start a day (e.g., "spend the day", "start the day"). It can also mean a specific day dedicated to something: "la giornata di/della ..." (e.g., garbage day, a holiday/event day).
target_language_example: Come hai passato la giornata?
native_language_example: How did you spend the day?

additional_notes: Most commonly means the physical throat, especially in health/comfort phrases: "avere la gola infiammata" (to have a sore/inflamed throat) and "avere la gola secca" (to have a dry throat). It can also be used figuratively for appetite or craving (often for food), e.g. "seguire la gola" = to give in to your appetite. In threats, "tagliare la gola" means "to cut (someone’s) throat."
target_language_example: Ho la gola secca: mi porti un bicchiere d’acqua?
native_language_example: My throat is dry: can you bring me a glass of water?

additional_notes: Means “war” in general or a specific war understood from context. Often used with common expressions like “dopo la guerra” (after the war) and “è scoppiata la guerra” (war broke out).
target_language_example: Dopo la guerra, la città era molto cambiata.
native_language_example: After the war, the city had changed a lot.

additional_notes: Most often means “the law” in general (the legal system/rules): rispettare la legge = “obey the law”; seguire la legge = “follow the law.” It can also refer to a specific law, especially with context or an adjective (es. la legge italiana). “È ancora in vigore” means it is still valid/in force.
target_language_example: È contro la legge parcheggiare qui.
native_language_example: It’s against the law to park here.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a written letter/message (paper or formal correspondence). It can also mean “letter (of the alphabet)” in other contexts, but in these examples it’s a letter you write, send, receive, read, translate, etc.
