additional_notes: Used to ask someone for information. It’s made of puoi (“can you”) + dirmi (“tell me”). Often followed by a question word like come (how), chi (who), cosa (what), quale (which), or by an indirect question.
target_language_example: Puoi dirmi dove si trova la stazione?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where the station is?

meaning: "can you do" / "you can do" (asking or saying someone is able/allowed to do something).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to do something (request): "Puoi fare una cosa per me?" It can also mean permission/possibility: "Non puoi fare così" (= you can’t do it like that / you’re not allowed to). Often followed by a noun ("puoi fare il sushi…") or by something like "qualcosa" ("puoi fare qualcosa in più?").
target_language_example: Puoi fare una prenotazione per domani sera?
native_language_example: Can you make a reservation for tomorrow evening?

additional_notes: Formed by "puoi" (you can) + "venire" (to come). It can be a question (“Puoi venire…?” = Can you come…?) or a statement (“Puoi venire.” = You can come.). Often followed by a place (qui/here, là/there) or direction (da questa parte/this way), and can be used to make a polite request.
target_language_example: Puoi venire con me un attimo?
native_language_example: Can you come with me for a moment?

additional_notes: Used for a figure made of snow, typically built by children in winter. Plural: "pupazzi di neve". You can say "fare un pupazzo di neve" (to build a snowman).
target_language_example: Dopo la nevicata, i bambini hanno fatto un pupazzo di neve in giardino.
native_language_example: After the snowfall, the children built a snowman in the garden.

meaning: just to / even if only to (do something), often implying a sacrifice.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (pur di + verb) to say someone does something with a strong purpose, sometimes “at all costs” or “even if it means” something negative. Common with verbs like riuscire, ottenere, vedere, parlare: “Farebbe di tutto pur di riuscire.”
target_language_example: Ha accettato quel lavoro pur di pagare l’affitto.
native_language_example: He accepted that job just to be able to pay the rent.

additional_notes: Common food/dish name on menus and at home. Often served as a side dish (contorno). You may also see it written as “purè di patate” or simply “purè”.
target_language_example: Per contorno prendo il purè di patate.
native_language_example: For a side dish, I’ll have the mashed potatoes.

additional_notes: Formed with può ("can") + aiutare ("to help"). It is used for a third-person subject like "he/she/it can help," but in polite speech it can also mean "can you help?" because Italian often uses the formal Lei with third-person verb forms: Mi può aiutare? = "Can you help me?".
target_language_example: Forse Marco può aiutare con i bagagli.
native_language_example: Maybe Marco can help with the luggage.

additional_notes: Literally “it can go,” but very often used to say something is acceptable even if it’s not perfect (similar to “va bene,” but a bit more like “it’ll do”). You can also use it in the literal sense (“it can go”).
target_language_example: Alle 7 è un po’ presto, ma può andare.
native_language_example: 7 o’clock is a bit early, but that works.

meaning: “can have / may have” (is able to have; it’s possible/allowed to have).
additional_notes: From potere (can/may) + avere (to have). Used to express possibility, ability, or permission related to possessing/obtaining something. Common in negatives (non può avere… = “can’t have…/may not have…”) and in general statements (Non si può avere tutto = “You can’t have everything”). With object pronouns or choices it can mean being given/allowed to take something (Può avere entrambe = “You can have both”).
target_language_example: Può avere tutto quello che vuole.
native_language_example: He/She can have anything he/she wants.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility/uncertainty (like “maybe”). It’s commonly followed by the subjunctive: può darsi che + (io) sia, (tu) abbia, (lui/lei) venga, etc. It can also be used alone: “Può darsi.” = “Maybe / It’s possible.”
target_language_example: Può darsi che oggi piova, quindi porto l’ombrello.
native_language_example: It might rain today, so I’m bringing an umbrella.

meaning: "can (you/he/she/it) say/tell" (polite form with Lei: "can you tell me?").
additional_notes: "Può" is the present of potere (“can/may”), and "dire" means “to say/tell.” It’s very common in polite questions to ask for information: "Mi può dire...?" = “Can you tell me...?” With an object pronoun it becomes: "Lo può dire" (He/She can say it / tell it). In negative form: "Non può dire nulla" = “He/She can’t say anything.” Impersonal: "Non si può dire" = “You can’t say / one can’t say.”
target_language_example: Scusi, mi può dire che ore sono?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you tell me what time it is?

additional_notes: Literally “can be” (3rd-person singular). Used to express possibility/uncertainty: “Può essere.” = “Maybe / It could be.” Also common in polite questions/requests: “Può essere più precisa?” (“Could you be more specific?”). With a past infinitive, it refers to a possible past event: “può essere stato/a…” (“may/might have been…”). It’s also used in passive constructions: “Può essere fatto?” (“Can it be done?”).
target_language_example: Può essere che abbia sbagliato indirizzo.
native_language_example: It could be that I wrote the wrong address.

additional_notes: Literally "(it) can be." Used to express possibility or uncertainty: with a question to ask what something might be ("Sai cosa può essere?"), or as a short standalone reply meaning "Maybe" / "Could be" ("Può essere."). Often refers to an implied subject like "it".
target_language_example: Non ne sono sicuro, ma può essere una buona idea.
native_language_example: I'm not sure, but it could be a good idea.

meaning: “can do” / “is able to do” (he/she/it can do).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase “potere” (can/to be able to) + “fare” (to do/to make). It’s used to talk about ability or possibility, often in questions (e.g., “Può fare questo lavoro?” = “Can he/she do this job?”). The subject is often clear from context or a name/pronoun nearby (Tom può fare…, lei può fare…). For politeness when speaking directly to someone, you can also use it like a request: “Può fare…?” (“Could you do…?”).
target_language_example: Può fare una prenotazione per domani?
native_language_example: Can you make a reservation for tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is able/allowed to do something. "Può" is the present tense of "potere" (can/may) for he/she/it, and also for formal "you" (Lei). "Farlo" = "fare" (to do/make) + "lo" (it). Word order can change in questions: "Può farlo?" = "Can you do it?"
target_language_example: Non so se può farlo oggi.
native_language_example: I don't know if he/she can do it today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that is possible (often unexpected) in general or in a specific situation. It can stand alone as a comment meaning “That can happen.” You’ll also see it with: **può succedere di tutto** (“anything can happen”), **può succedere di + infinitive** (“it can happen that…”), and **può succedere a qualcuno** (“it can happen to someone”).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: può succedere a chiunque.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it can happen to anyone.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is allowed to come (permission) or is able to come (possibility). Often used with a person as the subject ("Tom può venire") or in the impersonal form "non si può venire" = "you can’t come / it’s not allowed to come".
target_language_example: Stasera Luca può venire alla festa.
native_language_example: Tonight Luca can come to the party.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the inside of the place/container you are currently in or pointing to. Often interchangeable with **qui dentro** (more neutral), while **qua** can sound a bit more conversational. Typically placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence (e.g., *C’è qualcuno qua dentro?*).
target_language_example: C’è qualcuno qua dentro?
native_language_example: Is there someone in here?

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is close to your current location. Common in speech; "qua" is a more conversational form of "qui". You’ll also hear "qui vicino" with the same meaning. Can refer to places (un ristorante qua vicino) or people (abito qua vicino), and it can be used after a verb as an adverb (Siediti qua vicino = Sit down near here/close by).
target_language_example: C’è una farmacia qua vicino?
native_language_example: Is there a pharmacy nearby?

additional_notes: used to ask for the identity, meaning, title, or correct choice of a masculine singular noun. It combines qual(e) + è + il. Often translated as either 'what is the' or 'which is the' depending on context. Written qual è, without an apostrophe.
target_language_example: Qual è il tuo film preferito?
native_language_example: What is your favorite movie?

additional_notes: Used to ask what the difficulty/issue is. Often appears both as a direct question (Qual è il problema?) and inside a longer sentence after verbs like sapere/capire/dire (e.g., so qual è il problema). Sometimes it can sound a bit confrontational depending on tone; for a softer version you can say: Qual è il problema? / C’è un problema? / Qual è il problema esattamente?
target_language_example: Non capisco: qual è il problema?
native_language_example: I don’t understand: what’s the problem?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s preference or a specific item, introducing a noun: “Qual è il suo + [noun]…?”. “Suo” is a possessive meaning “your” (formal) or “his/her/its,” and it changes to match the noun: suo (m. sing.), sua (f. sing.), suoi (m. pl.), sue (f. pl.). You often see it with “Lei” (formal you).
target_language_example: Qual è il suo indirizzo email?
native_language_example: What is your email address?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s choice or to identify something that belongs to them. Often followed by a noun: “Qual è il tuo animale preferito?” = “What’s your favorite animal?” The possessive “tuo” agrees with what follows (tuo/tuoi/tua/tue): “Qual è la tua macchina?” “Quali sono i tuoi amici?”
target_language_example: Qual è il tuo numero di telefono?
native_language_example: What’s your phone number?

additional_notes: Used to ask “which/what … is yours?” when speaking to more than one person (“your” plural) or politely/formally to one person (like “your” in emails or customer service). It must be followed by a noun: Qual è il vostro problema/indirizzo/compositore preferito? With a feminine noun, use: “Qual è la vostra …?”
target_language_example: Scusate, qual è il vostro numero di telefono?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is your phone number?

meaning: "what is the" / "which is the" (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask for information or to choose/identify something. It’s made of **qual** (“which/what”) + **è** (“is”) + **la** (“the”, feminine singular). You use it before feminine singular nouns: *Qual è la data? Qual è la risposta?* (With masculine singular nouns: *Qual è il...*).
target_language_example: Qual è la tua domanda?
native_language_example: What is your question?

meaning: "what is your (formal)" / "which one is yours (formal)" (female noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask about something that belongs to or relates to the person you’re addressing politely (Lei). "Sua" agrees with a feminine noun (e.g., data, squadra, villa, vocale, soluzione). Often followed by the noun: "Qual è la sua data di nascita?" If the noun is masculine, use "Qual è il suo ...?" or "Qual è il suo?"
target_language_example: Scusi, qual è la sua email?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is your email address?

meaning: "what is your ...?" (asking which one belongs to you).
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s choice, preference, or information related to them. It must be followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., destinazione, offerta, vocale) or by an implied feminine noun understood from context. In speech it’s often used as part of a longer question: "Qual è la tua destinazione?" = "What’s your destination?"
target_language_example: Qual è la tua scelta?
native_language_example: What is your choice?

additional_notes: Used to ask for information about something belonging to or associated with the person you’re speaking to, when addressing more than one person (you all) or using polite/formal “you” (voi). It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., canzone, destinazione, nazionalità, offerta, squadra). For masculine singular, use “Qual è il vostro …?”; for feminine plural, “Quali sono le vostre …?”
target_language_example: Qual è la vostra richiesta?
native_language_example: What is your request?

additional_notes: Used when you want to say you have a small number of questions (not specific). Common in polite requests: “Posso fare qualche domanda?” / “Potrebbe rispondere a qualche domanda?”. Note: in standard Italian you usually say “fare qualche domanda” (ask a few questions) or “porre qualche domanda”; “chiedere qualche domanda” is less natural than “fare/porre” + “domanda” (or “chiedere” + “informazione/delucidazioni”). “Qualche” is followed by a singular noun (“domanda”) but the meaning is plural.
target_language_example: Scusi, posso fare qualche domanda?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask a few questions?

additional_notes: Used to mean an unspecific small number of days. Often appears with prepositions: “fra/tra qualche giorno” (in a few days), “da qualche giorno” (for a few days/for some days), “di qualche giorno” (by a few days, e.g., extend/delay by a few days). Can also be a short answer meaning “for a few days.”
target_language_example: Resterò a Roma ancora qualche giorno.
native_language_example: I’ll stay in Rome for a few more days.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened a small number of days in the past (not exact). Often placed at the end of the sentence (but it can appear earlier for emphasis).
target_language_example: Ci siamo sentiti qualche giorno fa, ma non ho ancora risposto.
native_language_example: We talked a few days ago, but I still haven’t replied.

additional_notes: Used when you need or offer a small amount of information. "Qualche" means “some/a few” and is followed by a singular noun (qualche + singular), even though the meaning is plural-ish. Common with verbs like "avere" (to have), "trovare" (to find), "servire" (to need/be needed), and "avere bisogno di" (to need). Works in polite questions too: "Lei ha trovato...?"
target_language_example: Mi può dare qualche informazione su questo museo?
native_language_example: Can you give me some information about this museum?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a small, non-specific amount of time. In Italian, "qualche" is followed by a singular noun ("minuto"), even though the meaning is plural in English ("minutes"). It often appears with verbs like "avere bisogno di" (to need) or "servire" (to be needed), and can also be used in time expressions like "qualche minuto più tardi" (a few minutes later).
target_language_example: Aspettami qui qualche minuto, torno subito.
native_language_example: Wait here a few minutes, I’ll be right back.

meaning: some problem(s); a bit of trouble.
additional_notes: Used to say there is at least one issue, without specifying exactly what or how many. Often sounds softer/less direct than "un problema" (a specific problem). Common in questions like "Ha qualche problema?" (= "Is something wrong?/Do you have a problem?") and with qualifiers like "tecnico" (technical) or "grave" (serious).
target_language_example: Scusi, c’è qualche problema con l’ordine?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is there some problem with the order?

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens from time to time, without a fixed schedule. It can be placed at the end of the sentence (common) or near the verb: “Qualche volta vado al cinema.”
target_language_example: Vengo qui qualche volta, quando ho tempo.
native_language_example: I come here sometimes, when I have time.

meaning: something about it/that; something regarding it/that.
additional_notes: Used when referring back to a topic already mentioned ("about it/that matter"). Often appears with verbs like dire (to say), leggere (to read), sapere (to know), ricordare (to remember), negare (to deny): e.g., "Hai detto qualcosa a riguardo?" = "Did you say anything about it?"
target_language_example: Se sai qualcosa a riguardo, dimmelo.
native_language_example: If you know something about it, tell me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes or identifies a thing. Often followed by a verb: "qualcosa che posso fare" (something I can do), "qualcosa che appartiene a me" (something that belongs to me). In casual speech it can also mean “anything that…” depending on context (especially in questions).
target_language_example: Cerco qualcosa che mi aiuti a studiare italiano.
native_language_example: I'm looking for something that helps me study Italian.

meaning: "something that doesn’t..." / "something that isn’t..." (introduces a negative description).
additional_notes: Used when you start describing a thing in a negative way, usually followed by a verb: e.g. "qualcosa che non va" (something’s wrong), "qualcosa che non torna" (something doesn’t add up), "qualcosa che non riguarda..." (something that doesn’t concern...). Often implies that there is a problem or mismatch, especially with "non va" and "non torna".
target_language_example: C’è qualcosa che non va con questo computer.
native_language_example: There’s something wrong with this computer.

additional_notes: Used to offer, ask for, or request a drink in general (not a specific beverage). Common with verbs like offrire (to offer), dare (to give), and avere bisogno di (to need). The structure is qualcosa (“something”) + da bere (“to drink”).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere qualcosa da bere?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have something to drink?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone wants to speak or has a comment/opinion. Common in questions like “Hai qualcosa da dire?” or on its own (“Qualcosa da dire?”) which can sound direct or challenging depending on tone/context. Literally “something to say/to tell.”
target_language_example: Se avete qualcosa da dire, parlate adesso.
native_language_example: If you have something to say, speak now.

additional_notes: Common with verbs like avere/volere (“to have/want something to do”) and dare (“to give someone something to do” = to assign a task). The structure “qualcosa + da + infinitive” means “something to [verb]” (a thing that needs doing).
target_language_example: Non ho molto tempo, ma ho qualcosa da fare prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I don’t have much time, but I have something to do before going out.

meaning: something to read; something to read (for you).
additional_notes: Used to offer or ask for reading material (a book, magazine, document, etc.). "Qualcosa" = "something" and "da leggere" literally means "to read" / "for reading" (something intended for you to read). You can swap the verb: "qualcosa da mangiare" (something to eat), "qualcosa da bere" (something to drink).
target_language_example: Se hai tempo, ti mando qualcosa da leggere stasera.
native_language_example: If you have time, I’ll send you something to read tonight.

additional_notes: Used when you want food in general (not a specific dish). Often follows verbs like volere (to want), prendere (to get), or dare (to give): "Voglio/prendo/Le dia qualcosa da mangiare".
target_language_example: Abbiamo qualcosa da mangiare in frigo?
native_language_example: Do we have something to eat in the fridge?

additional_notes: Used to refer to an event/experience similar to the one being talked about, often with surprise or emphasis. Very common in questions like "Come può capitare qualcosa del genere?" (= "How can something like that happen?") and after negatives like "non era mai successo" (= "it had never happened").
target_language_example: Non mi aspettavo qualcosa del genere.
native_language_example: I wasn’t expecting something like that.

additional_notes: Used when qualcosa is followed by an adjective or another descriptive phrase: qualcosa di interessante, qualcosa di più forte. In this pattern, di usually is not translated directly into English.
target_language_example: Vorrei qualcosa di caldo da bere.
native_language_example: I'd like something hot to drink.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified bad event, situation, or problem. Common with verbs like "succedere" and "capitare": "È successo/capitato qualcosa di brutto" = "Something bad happened." Depending on context, it can also imply a serious problem (often health-related): "Sapevo di avere qualcosa di brutto".
target_language_example: Le è successo qualcosa di brutto.
native_language_example: Something bad happened to her.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified good thing. Often means “something tasty” when talking about food (e.g., what to eat), but it can also mean “something good” in general (good news, a good event, a good sign). With events you’ll also hear: “È successo/capitato qualcosa di buono?” = “Has something good happened?”
target_language_example: Dopo una giornata difficile, ho bisogno di qualcosa di buono da mangiare.
native_language_example: After a difficult day, I need something good to eat.

additional_notes: Used to say you have a different idea/plan, or you want an alternative to what was suggested. It’s often followed by “da + infinitive” (e.g., “qualcosa di diverso da fare” = “something different to do”).
target_language_example: Vorrei qualcosa di diverso da mangiare stasera.
native_language_example: I’d like something different to eat tonight.

additional_notes: Used when you want to introduce information you think matters or is serious. Often followed by an infinitive with da (e.g., “qualcosa di importante da dirti” = “something important to tell you”). It can be a statement or a question (È qualcosa di importante? = Is it something important?).
target_language_example: Devo parlarti: c’è qualcosa di importante.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you: there’s something important.

additional_notes: Used to ask if there is anything interesting, to say you want to do something interesting, or to hint that you’re looking for news/updates. Pattern: qualcosa di + adjective (e.g., qualcosa di nuovo = something new).
target_language_example: Hai letto qualcosa di interessante oggi?
native_language_example: Have you read something interesting today?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or mention new information, news, updates, or a new thing to see/try. Often followed by an infinitive or extra detail (e.g., "qualcosa di nuovo da mangiare/da dire").
target_language_example: Cerco qualcosa di nuovo da leggere.
native_language_example: I'm looking for something new to read.

additional_notes: Used when you want an additional thing or a stronger/better/different option than what is being discussed. Often followed by an adjective to specify the comparison: “qualcosa di più economico” (something cheaper), “qualcosa di più semplice” (something simpler), “qualcosa di più serio” (something more serious). The “di” is required before “più” in this structure.
target_language_example: Cerco qualcosa di più interessante da leggere.
native_language_example: I’m looking for something more interesting to read.

additional_notes: Used to say there is an unusual, suspicious, or unexpected thing/situation. Common after verbs like vedere (to see), trovare (to find), notare (to notice), pensare (to think), or dire (to say/tell). Literally: qualcosa (something) + di (of) + strano (strange).
target_language_example: C'è qualcosa di strano qui: la porta è già aperta.
native_language_example: There’s something strange here: the door is already open.

additional_notes: Used to say that a very bad thing happened, or that someone did a very bad action. Common with verbs like: è successo/capitato qualcosa di terribile (something terrible happened) and ho fatto qualcosa di terribile (I did something terrible). "Qualcosa" = something; "di" links it to the adjective; "terribile" = terrible.
target_language_example: Ho paura che sia successo qualcosa di terribile.
native_language_example: I'm afraid something terrible happened.

additional_notes: Used to say you feel that a situation is not OK, or to ask someone if there’s a problem. Often used as a question: “Qualcosa non va?” You can also add details with "in/nel...": “Qualcosa non va in questa storia” (Something’s not right in this story). Literal meaning is “something doesn’t go (well),” but in English you usually say “something’s wrong.”
target_language_example: Aspetta un attimo: qualcosa non va con questo computer.
native_language_example: Wait a second: something’s wrong with this computer.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or request something intended for the speaker (a gift, a message, a task, a song, etc.). With “Hai qualcosa per me?” it often means “Do you have something for me?” (e.g., news, a note, a present). With “È qualcosa per me,” it means “It’s something meant for me / for my benefit.”
target_language_example: C'è un pacco: è qualcosa per me?
native_language_example: There’s a package— is it something for me?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a different person from the one already mentioned or expected. Often comes after the verb (e.g., "Può rispondere qualcun altro?") or after a noun/pronoun to mean “another person” (e.g., "da qualcun altro" = "by someone else").
target_language_example: Se non puoi venire tu, può venire qualcun altro?
native_language_example: If you can’t come, can someone else come?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing an unspecified person. Very often followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo), especially after expressions like "cercare" (to look for): "Cerco qualcuno che sappia..." = "I’m looking for someone who knows...".
target_language_example: Cerchiamo qualcuno che parli inglese.
native_language_example: We’re looking for someone who speaks English.

additional_notes: Used to say that a task or responsibility is necessary and will fall to some person (often implied: “someone has to do it,” sometimes meaning “I/you will have to”). Followed by an infinitive (qualcuno deve fare...) or by avere + past participle to express a logical assumption about the past (qualcuno deve avere visto... = “someone must have seen...”).
target_language_example: Qualcuno deve chiamare il medico.
native_language_example: Someone has to call the doctor.

meaning: "one of you" / "any of you" (someone among you).
additional_notes: Used to ask or state that at least one person in the group you’re speaking to is involved. Common in questions (e.g., asking if anyone knows/has seen someone). It can also be used in statements, often with a conditional or hypothetical tone.
target_language_example: Qualcuno di voi può aiutarmi?
native_language_example: Can any of you help me?

meaning: "which of the two" (asking to choose between two people/things).
additional_notes: Used when there are exactly two options. It can refer to people or things (e.g., due fratelli, due libri). The verb is usually singular because you’re asking about one choice: “Quale dei due è…?” You can change it for other numbers: “quale dei tre / dei quattro…”.
target_language_example: Ho due giacche: quale dei due preferisci?
native_language_example: I have two jackets: which of the two do you prefer?

additional_notes: Used to ask about a specific choice within a known or limited set of books. "Quali" is the plural form of "quale" and agrees with the plural noun "libri"; it’s used in questions like "Quali libri...?" (Which books...?).
target_language_example: Quali libri vuoi comprare?
native_language_example: Which books do you want to buy?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a list or identification of multiple things. It’s the plural form of the question "qual è?" (= what/which is?). Usually followed by a plural noun: "Quali sono gli svantaggi?" It can also appear in indirect questions: "Sapete quali sono le regole?"
target_language_example: Quali sono le opzioni disponibili?
native_language_example: What are the available options?

additional_notes: Used with the formal address Lei. “i suoi / le sue” means “your” (formal) and agrees with the noun that follows: i suoi (masc. plural: orari, passatempi, piani, sintomi, sogni), le sue (fem. plural: idee, preferenze). Often used in questions to ask about someone’s things, plans, preferences, etc.
target_language_example: Quali sono i suoi dati di contatto?
native_language_example: What are your contact details?

additional_notes: Means “anything/whatever” in a very general sense. It can be used on its own (often as a question: “Qualsiasi cosa?” = “Anything?”) or followed by a verb/relative clause: “qualsiasi cosa voglia” (whatever she wants), “qualsiasi cosa mi capiti” (anything that happens to me). Often used to invite questions: “Chiedimi qualsiasi cosa!” = “Ask me anything!”
target_language_example: Puoi chiedermi qualsiasi cosa, non è un problema.
native_language_example: You can ask me anything, it’s not a problem.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified thing, with the idea of “no matter what (thing)”. Common in offers/availability (e.g., “if you need anything”), and in general statements. It can be followed by a clause, often with “che” (e.g., “qualunque cosa (che) dici…” = “whatever you say…”).
target_language_example: Se vuoi cambiare idea, puoi dirmi qualunque cosa.
native_language_example: If you want to change your mind, you can tell me anything.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time something was bought. "Quando" = when; "ha comprato" is the passato prossimo of "comprare" (to buy) for "lui/lei" and also "Lei" (formal you). Often followed by the object (e.g., "Quando ha comprato queste uova?").
target_language_example: Quando ha comprato questo telefono?
native_language_example: When did you (formal)/he/she buy this phone?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time or date of an event ("Quando è?" = "When is it?"). In questions with the auxiliary "è" + past participle (passato prossimo), it asks when something happened (e.g., "Quando è arrivato?" = "When did he arrive?"). Often followed by a verb or a subject: "Quando è il concerto?"
target_language_example: Scusa, quando è la riunione?
native_language_example: Excuse me, when is the meeting?

additional_notes: Used to specify the age someone had at the time something happened in the past. Common in storytelling, biographies, and narration. The verb is the imperfect of "avere" (aveva) and typically refers to a third-person subject (he/she). You can change the age: "quando aveva dieci anni", "quando aveva vent'anni", etc. For first person you would use "quando avevo ... anni".
target_language_example: Tom cominciò a giocare a golf quando aveva tredici anni.
native_language_example: Tom started playing golf when he was thirteen.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a period in someone’s past. "Era" is the imperfect tense of "essere" (to be), common for describing ongoing states/habits in the past. It can refer to a man or a woman; the subject is understood from context (e.g., "lui" or "lei").
target_language_example: Mio nonno viaggiava molto quando era giovane.
native_language_example: My grandpa traveled a lot when he was young.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a time in the past, followed by a description/state in the imperfect tense (ero = 'I was' from essere). Often used for childhood memories: quando ero piccolo/bambino/ragazzino.
target_language_example: Quando ero studente, vivevo vicino alla scuola.
native_language_example: When I was a student, I lived near the school.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your past (often with the imperfect tense): describe habits, repeated actions, or ongoing situations in your youth. You can expand it (e.g., “quando ero più giovane” = “when I was younger”) or change the person (“quando eri giovane” = “when you were young”).
target_language_example: Quando ero giovane, andavo al mare ogni estate.
native_language_example: When I was young, I used to go to the sea every summer.

meaning: “when I was little” / “when I was a child” (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened or was true in your childhood. It often introduces a memory or past habit; you can place it at the beginning or end of the sentence. If you’re a man, you say “quando ero piccolo”.
target_language_example: Quando ero piccola, passavo tutte le estati dai nonni.
native_language_example: When I was little, I spent all my summers at my grandparents’ place.

meaning: “when I was little/when I was a child.”
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened in your childhood. It often introduces a past habit or belief, so it’s commonly followed by the imperfect tense (e.g., amavo, credevo, ero). You can place it at the beginning (Quando ero piccolo, ...) or after the main clause (... quando ero piccolo).
target_language_example: Quando ero piccolo, giocavo sempre in strada.
native_language_example: When I was little, I always played in the street.

meaning: "when I am" / "when they are" (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause with the verb *essere* (to be). *Sono* is present tense and can mean **I am** or **they are**; the subject is often understood from context (or made clear with a pronoun like *io* or *loro*). It’s typically followed by an adjective/noun (*quando sono felice* = when I’m happy) or by a past participle to form the *passato prossimo* (*quando sono tornata* = when I came back).
target_language_example: Quando sono stanco, vado a letto presto.
native_language_example: When I’m tired, I go to bed early.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the time an event happened, often in the past. Common with the imperfetto for an ongoing action interrupted by a completed action in the passato prossimo (e.g., “Stavo dormendo quando è arrivato…”). Change the ending to match the person: quando è arrivata (she), quando sono arrivati (they, masc./mixed), quando sono arrivate (they, fem.).
target_language_example: Quando è arrivato Paolo, stavamo già mangiando.
native_language_example: When Paolo arrived, we were already eating.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the number of languages someone speaks/knows/recognizes or that exist somewhere. You’ll often see it with verbs like parlare (to speak), conoscere (to know), riconoscere (to recognize), or imparare (to learn). Can be a direct question (Quante lingue parli?) or an indirect question after verbs like chiedere (Mi chiese quante lingue parlassi = “He/She asked me how many languages I spoke”).
target_language_example: Scusi, quante lingue parla?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how many languages do you speak?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the number of apples. "Quante" agrees with the noun: it’s the feminine plural form of "quanto" because "mele" (apples) is feminine plural. You can swap in another plural noun (e.g., "Quanti libri?" = how many books?). Often used on its own as a short question: "Quante mele?"
target_language_example: Quante mele vuoi comprare?
native_language_example: How many apples do you want to buy?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a number of people. Since "persone" is feminine plural, "quante" agrees (not *quanti*). Often followed by "ci sono" (there are) or a verb like "sono" / "contribuiscono".
target_language_example: Scusa, quante persone vengono alla festa?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how many people are coming to the party?

additional_notes: Used to ask the number of times something happened (in the past, present, or future). It agrees with the feminine plural noun "volte" (times). Often followed by a clause with a verb: "Quante volte hai…?"
target_language_example: Quante volte sei stato in Italia?
native_language_example: How many times have you been to Italy?

meaning: "how many (of them)" / "as many as (of them)" (feminine plural).
additional_notes: Used when you’re talking about a quantity of previously mentioned feminine plural items (e.g., mele, cose). "Ne" means “of them / some (of it/them)” and refers back to what was mentioned. Common patterns: "più ... di quante ne ..." = “more ... than (the number) of them that ...”; "Quante ne vuoi?" = “How many (of them) do you want?” It must agree in gender/number: masculine plural "quanti ne"; singular "quanta ne" (f.), "quanto ne" (m.).
target_language_example: Prendine quante ne vuoi.
native_language_example: Take as many (of them) as you want.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s (or something’s) age. It literally means “how many years does he/she/it have?”, so you’ll often add the subject after it: “Quanti anni ha tuo fratello?” You can also use it for places/things to mean “How old is this place/this building?”
target_language_example: Scusi, quanti anni ha sua figlia?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how old is your daughter?

additional_notes: A common, neutral way to ask someone’s age. Italian uses the verb "avere" (to have): literally "how many years do you have?" You can add "Tu" for emphasis: "Tu quanti anni hai?"
target_language_example: Scusa, quanti anni hai?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how old are you?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the number of hot dogs. "Quanti" is the plural form (used with masculine plural nouns like "hot dog"). In Italian you’ll also see the spelling "hotdog". Word order is flexible: you can also say "Quanti hot dog hai comprato?"
target_language_example: Scusa, quanti hot dog servono per la festa?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how many hot dogs do we need for the party?

additional_notes: Used to ask about an amount of money. Grammatically it’s plural because "soldi" is plural in Italian, so you use "quanti" (not "quanto"). Often followed by a verb like "deve" (owes), "dona" (donates), "spende" (spends), etc.
target_language_example: Quanti soldi devi al proprietario?
native_language_example: How much money do you owe the landlord?

additional_notes: Used when asking about a quantity of something already mentioned or understood. The particle “ne” means “of it/of them” and replaces the noun (e.g., “Quanti ne vuoi?” = “How many (of them) do you want?”).
target_language_example: Quanti ne vuoi, di biscotti?
native_language_example: How many cookies do you want?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a topic and comment on it, often contrasting it with something else. Common in more formal or written Italian. Typically followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., “Quanto a me, …”, “Quanto al prezzo, …”).
target_language_example: Quanto a me, preferisco restare a casa stasera.
native_language_example: As for me, I’d rather stay home tonight.

additional_notes: Used to ask the price of something. Often followed by the thing you’re asking about: “Quanto costa questo/questa…?” or “Quanto costa + noun?” You can also just ask “Quanto costa?” while pointing at an item.
target_language_example: Scusi, quanto costa questo panino?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how much does this sandwich cost?

additional_notes: Used to ask about frequency (how many times in a given period). Often followed by the present tense: Quanto spesso vai in palestra? You can place it at the start of the question or after the subject (Tu quanto spesso...?). Common answers use frequency words like: sempre (always), spesso (often), qualche volta (sometimes), raramente (rarely), mai (never), or expressions like due volte a settimana (twice a week).
target_language_example: Quanto spesso vai al cinema?
native_language_example: How often do you go to the movies?

additional_notes: Used in questions before an adjective or adverb to ask about degree or extent. In English, this is usually translated simply with 'how': 'Quanto è stanco?' = 'How tired is he/she?' Not literally 'how much is'.
target_language_example: Quanto è difficile questo esercizio?
native_language_example: How difficult is this exercise?

meaning: as much as needed; just enough.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the necessary amount (money, food, ingredients, etc.), often implying “no more than needed.” In recipes it can mean “to taste / as needed” (e.g., sale quanto basta). Said alone, it can also mean “that’s enough / just enough.”
target_language_example: Metti il sale quanto basta e poi assaggia.
native_language_example: Add as much salt as needed and then taste.

additional_notes: Used to compare yourself (or someone/something) with the person you’re talking to. It follows an adjective or an expression of amount: e.g., "alto quanto te" (as tall as you), "sorpreso/a quanto te" (as surprised as you), "(non) ne so quanto te" ((I don’t) know as much as you). With "quasi": "quasi quanto te" = "almost as … as you".
target_language_example: Non ho tanti amici quanto te.
native_language_example: I don’t have as many friends as you do.

additional_notes: Used for the central office or main base of an organization (company, police, military, etc.). Often appears as "il quartier generale" (the headquarters) or "al/dal quartier generale" (at/from headquarters).
target_language_example: Domani devo andare al quartier generale per una riunione.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have to go to headquarters for a meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very rarely. It’s often used with a negative verb (e.g., “non … quasi mai”), but it can also be used without “non” depending on context. Position is flexible, but it commonly goes after the verb.
target_language_example: In inverno esco quasi mai la sera.
native_language_example: In winter I hardly ever go out in the evening.

meaning: almost every day; nearly every day.
additional_notes: Used to talk about habits or routines that happen very often, but not literally every single day. Common in the present tense to describe regular actions.
target_language_example: Vado in palestra quasi ogni giorno.
native_language_example: I go to the gym almost every day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (per quattro anni = for four years), a sentence length (quattro anni di prigione = four years in prison), an age difference (quattro anni in meno/di più = four years younger/older), or age (Quando aveva quattro anni = When he/she was four). With age you’ll often hear: avere quattro anni = to be four years old.
target_language_example: Ho vissuto a Milano per quattro anni.
native_language_example: I lived in Milan for four years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (per quattro giorni = for four days), a time needed (ci vogliono quattro giorni = it takes four days), or a delay/time difference (quattro giorni più tardi = four days later). It can also be used alone as a short answer or to confirm/ask: “Quattro giorni.” / “Quattro giorni?”
target_language_example: Resto a Roma per quattro giorni.
native_language_example: I’m staying in Rome for four days.

additional_notes: Masculine plural demonstrative meaning “those” (usually people/things not close to the speaker, or used for emphasis). The form **quegli** is used before masculine plural nouns that start with a vowel (like **uomini**) and also before certain consonant clusters (e.g., s+consonant, z, gn). Compare: **quei ragazzi** (“those boys”), **quegli studenti** (“those students”), **quegli uomini** (“those men”).
target_language_example: Non voglio parlare con quegli uomini.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk to those men.

additional_notes: Used to point out or talk about two specific people (often) or things that are not close to the speaker. It’s made of "quei" (those, masculine plural) + "due" (two). You can also use it on its own as a subject: "Quei due si assomigliano" = "Those two look alike." Sometimes you’ll hear "quei due là" to emphasize “those two over there.”
target_language_example: Non fidarti di quei due: stanno mentendo.
native_language_example: Don’t trust those two: they’re lying.

additional_notes: Used to point to specific books that are not near the speaker (or already known from context). "Quei" is the masculine plural form of "quel" and is used before many consonant sounds (e.g., quei libri, quei ragazzi). For feminine plural, use "quelle" (quelle riviste).
target_language_example: Puoi mettere quei libri sul tavolo, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you put those books on the table, please?

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective “quei” (plural masculine of “quel”) before a noun starting with most consonants (ragazzi). It points to specific boys/guys who are not here/are not the speaker’s group, often already known from context. For mixed groups you can still use masculine plural (“ragazzi”) in Italian; “quelle ragazze” = “those girls.”
target_language_example: Non ascoltare quei ragazzi: stanno scherzando.
native_language_example: Don’t listen to those guys: they’re joking.

additional_notes: "Quei" is the masculine plural form of "quel" (= that/those), used before a noun like "soldi" (money). It points to specific money already known from context (e.g., the money you mentioned, were given, or are asking for). In English you often say "that money" (even though "money" is uncountable).
target_language_example: Non voglio accettare quei soldi.
native_language_example: I don’t want to accept that money.

meaning: “that bastard” (a very strong insult for a man).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific man you’re angry at or despise (“that guy”). Very offensive/vulgar; avoid in polite situations. Can be said on its own as an outburst (“Quel bastardo!”). Also common: “quel bastardo di + nome” = “that bastard + name” (e.g., “quel bastardo di Mustafà”).
target_language_example: Non riesco a credere che quel bastardo mi abbia mentito.
native_language_example: I can’t believe that bastard lied to me.

additional_notes: Used to point out or refer to a specific dog (usually one that’s visible, nearby, or already mentioned). "Quel" is the masculine singular demonstrative meaning "that"; it becomes "quello" before s+consonant or z (e.g., "quello zaino").
target_language_example: Non toccare quel cane: ha paura.
native_language_example: Don’t touch that dog: he’s scared.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective "quel" (= "that") with the masculine singular noun "cappello". It's used to point out a particular hat that both speakers can identify (by seeing it or from prior context). Often implies a bit of emphasis: “that hat (we’re talking about)”.
target_language_example: Mi piace quel cappello, ti sta benissimo!
native_language_example: I like that hat, it suits you really well!

additional_notes: Used before a noun to insult, complain, or show strong frustration (similar to “that damn/that fucking …”). It’s extremely offensive because it uses the swear word *cazzo* (“dick”), so avoid it in polite or public situations. Less vulgar alternatives: *quel cavolo di…*, *quella stupida…*, *quella dannata…*.
target_language_example: Dov’è finito quel cazzo di telecomando?
native_language_example: Where did that fucking remote go?

meaning: “that son of a bitch” (very offensive insult).
additional_notes: Very strong profanity used to insult or express anger toward a specific man ("quel" = "that" for masculine singular). Often said as an exclamation or added at the end of a sentence for emphasis. Avoid in polite situations; it can easily start a fight. For a woman you’d hear "quella figlia di puttana."
target_language_example: Quel figlio di puttana mi ha rubato il portafoglio!
native_language_example: That son of a bitch stole my wallet!

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective "quel" (from "quello") to point to a specific movie already mentioned or understood from context. Usually refers to something not right here/now (otherwise you might hear "questo film" = "this movie"). "Film" is masculine singular, so it takes "quel".
target_language_example: Non voglio rivedere quel film.
native_language_example: I don't want to watch that movie again.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific day in the past or future that’s already known from context (often a memorable or important day). "Quel" is the masculine singular form of "quello" (that).
target_language_example: Non dimenticherò mai quel giorno.
native_language_example: I will never forget that day.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific book that’s not the one right here (or that has already been mentioned). "quel" is the masculine singular form of "quello" used before most consonants (e.g., quel libro). You’ll see other forms depending on the next sound: quello zaino, quello studente (s+consonant), quell’amico (before a vowel).
target_language_example: Non ho letto quel libro, ma ne ho sentito parlare.
native_language_example: I haven’t read that book, but I’ve heard about it.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective "quel" (short form of "quello") to point to a specific shop that’s already known, previously mentioned, or indicated (e.g., “that one over there”). "Quel" is used before a masculine singular noun starting with most consonants (negozio).
target_language_example: Andiamo in quel negozio vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: Let’s go to that shop near the station.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective quel (= that) with posto (= place/spot/seat/job position). It can refer to a physical location ("that place") or, depending on context, a position such as a job/role ("that position"). Often used when the place/position is already known or has been mentioned.
target_language_example: Non voglio tornare in quel posto.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go back to that place.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific male person (often someone already known or mentioned). "Quel" is the masculine singular demonstrative adjective (“that”) used before most masculine singular nouns (e.g., quel ragazzo, quel libro). In everyday speech it can mean “that guy” as well as “that boy.”
target_language_example: Chi è quel ragazzo con la giacca nera?
native_language_example: Who is that guy in the black jacket?

meaning: "that guy" / "that man" (referring to a particular person).
additional_notes: Used to point out or refer to a specific male person, often when you don’t know his name or don’t want to say it. It can sound neutral (“that guy over there”) or slightly negative/annoyed depending on tone and context (e.g., *Quel tipo mi infastidisce*). For a woman you’d say *quella tipa* (more casual) or *quella donna* (more neutral/formal).
target_language_example: Chi è quel tipo vicino alla porta?
native_language_example: Who is that guy near the door?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific category or sort of person/thing already known, mentioned, or implied. It agrees with the noun it refers to: quel tipo di (masc. sing.), quel genere di; that kind of usually stays singular in Italian even if the following noun is plural (e.g., quel tipo di cose = that kind of things).
target_language_example: Non mi piace quel tipo di musica.
native_language_example: I don't like that kind of music.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male person in an imprecise or slightly dismissive way (like “that guy”). Often used when you don’t know the person’s name or don’t want to say it. Can sound rude depending on tone/context. Also appears as just “tizio” (“a guy/some guy”).
target_language_example: Non parlare con quel tizio.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to that guy.

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific dress that’s not right here or not the one you’re holding. "Quel" is the masculine singular form of "quello" and goes before a noun. For a feminine noun like "gonna" (skirt), you’d say "quella gonna". Common with "stare bene": "Quel vestito ti/le/vi sta bene" = “That dress looks good on you/her/you (plural/formal).”
target_language_example: Ti piace quel vestito nero in vetrina?
native_language_example: Do you like that black dress in the shop window?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a thing or action you’re referring to: “quel che faccio” = “what I do”. Very common in set phrases like “Per quel che ne sappiamo” = “as far as we know / for all we know”. Often interchangeable with “quello che” (slightly more explicit).
target_language_example: Dimmi quel che vuoi mangiare stasera.
native_language_example: Tell me what you want to eat tonight.

meaning: “that song” (a specific song, not this one).
additional_notes: Used to point to a particular song that both speakers can identify from context (e.g., one mentioned before, playing on the radio, or known to both). The demonstrative adjective agrees with the noun: quella (feminine singular) + canzone. You can also use this as a lead-in to ask about a song: “Sai chi canta quella canzone?” (“Do you know who sings that song?”).
target_language_example: Non sopporto quella canzone: la sento dappertutto.
native_language_example: I can’t stand that song: I hear it everywhere.

additional_notes: Uses the feminine singular demonstrative adjective "quella" (that) with "casa" (house) to point to a specific house that’s not here/near the speaker, often one already known from context (e.g., previously mentioned or visible at a distance).
target_language_example: Non mi piace quella casa.
native_language_example: I don’t like that house.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an object, creature, event, or concept when you don’t know the name, don’t want to say it, or assume the listener knows what you mean from context. Often has a slightly vague or ominous tone depending on the situation. Grammar: feminine singular (quella + cosa); plural: “quelle cose”; for masculine “that thing” you’ll often hear “quello (lì)” or “quel coso”.
target_language_example: Non toccare quella cosa: non sappiamo cos’è.
native_language_example: Don’t touch that thing: we don’t know what it is.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective “quella” (feminine singular of “quel/ello”) to point out or refer back to a specific woman, often someone not close to the speaker (or psychologically more “distant”). It can be used with location words like “lì / laggiù” (“there / over there”).
target_language_example: Non conosco quella donna.
native_language_example: I don’t know that woman.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific woman who is not close to the speaker (quella = “that”, vs questa = “this”). Follow it with an adjective (bella, forte), a noun (un'insegnante), or a pronoun (lei). Italian adjectives must agree with donna (feminine singular), e.g., bella/forte, not bello/forto. In questions you can keep the same word order and use rising intonation: “Quella donna è…?”
target_language_example: Quella donna è un'insegnante molto brava.
native_language_example: That woman is a very good teacher.

additional_notes: Very vulgar and aggressive. Used to refer contemptuously to something (an object, a mess, drugs, etc.). Often appears as **quella merda di + noun** (“that shitty + noun” / “that piece of shit of a + noun”), e.g. **quella merda di droga**.
target_language_example: Non voglio più vedere quella merda in casa mia.
native_language_example: I don’t want to see that shit in my house anymore.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific night in the past (or one already known from context). Often used to set the time in a story or when talking about an event: "quella notte" = on/that night.
target_language_example: Quella notte non abbiamo dormito molto.
native_language_example: That night we didn’t sleep much.

additional_notes: Used to point out a particular word already mentioned, heard, or understood from context. Agree it with the noun: quella parola (feminine singular), quel/quel­lo termine (masculine singular), quelle parole (feminine plural), quelle/quei termini (masculine plural). Often used when asking where someone learned a word or commenting that a word is hard to pronounce/translate.
target_language_example: Non usare quella parola con me, per favore.
native_language_example: Don’t use that word with me, please.

meaning: "that part" / "that area" (a specific part of something).
additional_notes: Refers to a particular part/section/aspect already known or pointed out from context. Often used for a physical area (e.g., *quella parte di Boston* = “that part of Boston”) or for an aspect of something (e.g., “that part is frustrating”). *Quella* is the feminine singular form of “that,” agreeing with *parte* (feminine).
target_language_example: Non mi piace quella parte del film.
native_language_example: I don’t like that part of the movie.

meaning: “that person” (someone you’re pointing out or referring to).
additional_notes: Uses the feminine singular demonstrative “quella” to refer to a specific person at some distance (physically or in the conversation). It can be used even if the person is male when you’re speaking generally about “a person” (“persona” is grammatically feminine). Often clarified with “lì / là” (e.g., “quella persona lì” = “that person there”).
target_language_example: Scusi, conosce quella persona vicino alla porta?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you know that person near the door?

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific door that’s not close to the speaker (feminine singular: quella + porta). You’ll often see it with prepositions like “da quella porta” (“through/from that door”) or as an object in commands: “Chiudete quella porta!” (“Close that door!”). Note: “porta” can also be a form of the verb “portare” (“(he/she) carries/brings”), but in this phrase it’s the noun “door.”
target_language_example: Non entrare da quella porta.
native_language_example: Don’t go in through that door.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective “quella” to point out a particular girl, often someone already known or mentioned. “Quella” agrees with the feminine singular noun “ragazza.” It can sound neutral or judgmental depending on tone/context (e.g., “Quella ragazza è pazza!”).
target_language_example: Non parlare male di quella ragazza: è una brava persona.
native_language_example: Don’t speak badly about that girl: she’s a good person.

meaning: 'that stuff/that thing' (often said vaguely or dismissively).
additional_notes: Used when you don’t want to name something precisely, or when you’re talking about it in a casual/negative way. "Roba" can refer to objects, things, or even ideas/beliefs. With "tutta" it means "all that stuff".
target_language_example: Non mi interessa quella roba.
native_language_example: I'm not interested in that stuff.

meaning: 'that box' (a specific box over there / not near the speaker).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective "quella" (feminine singular of "quel/quello") + the noun "scatola" (box). It refers to a particular box identified by context, often at some distance from the speaker. For "this box" (near the speaker), use "questa scatola".
target_language_example: Puoi portarmi quella scatola, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you bring me that box, please?

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific chair that’s not right next to the speaker (often “that one”). *Quella* is the feminine singular form of the demonstrative (“that”), matching *sedia* (feminine). For a chair near you, you often hear *questa sedia* (“this chair”).
target_language_example: Puoi spostare quella sedia vicino alla finestra?
native_language_example: Can you move that chair near the window?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific evening in the past or in a story that both speakers know or have mentioned. Often used when asking or talking about what happened on that particular evening.
target_language_example: Ci siamo incontrati al bar quella sera.
native_language_example: We met at the bar that evening.

additional_notes: Used to point out or identify a specific feminine thing/person and introduce a relative clause with che. It contrasts with questa/quella (this/that) and changes with gender/number: quello che (masc.), quelli che (masc. pl.), quelle che (fem. pl.). Often corresponds to English “the one that…” or “the one you…”.
target_language_example: È quella che cercavi ieri?
native_language_example: Is that the one you were looking for yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to point out or identify something at a distance or already mentioned. "Quella" is the feminine singular of "quello" (that), and it can refer to a feminine noun (e.g., "quella stanza" = that room) or a feminine idea/thing understood from context. It contrasts with "questa è" (this is).
target_language_example: Quella è la mia borsa?
native_language_example: Is that my bag?

meaning: "that is a" (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to point out or identify something: **Quella** = “that (one)” feminine singular, **è** = “is”, **una** = “a/an” feminine singular. It’s followed by a **feminine singular noun** (e.g., *una menzogna*, *una zebra*). With a masculine noun you usually use **Quello è un…**; with a feminine noun starting with a vowel you may hear **Quella è un’…** (e.g., *Quella è un’idea*).
target_language_example: Quella è una buona idea.
native_language_example: That is a good idea.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective **quelle** (feminine plural of *quello*) + **cose** (“things”). It points to specific things already known from context, often “over there”/not close to the speaker (physical or figurative distance). For masculine plural you’d use **quei/quelli** (e.g., *quei libri* = “those books”).
target_language_example: Non voglio parlare di quelle cose adesso.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about those things right now.

additional_notes: "Quelle" is the feminine plural demonstrative meaning “those” (far from the speaker, or already mentioned). In Italian, "informazioni" is plural, but in English we usually say "that information" (uncountable) rather than *"those informations". Often used when referring back to specific information someone has or needs.
target_language_example: Non dovevi condividere quelle informazioni con nessuno.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t have shared that information with anyone.

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific group of people at a distance (physically or in the conversation). "Quelle" is the feminine plural of "quello" and agrees with "persone" (feminine plural). For people nearby you’d usually say "queste persone" (these people).
target_language_example: Non conosco quelle persone.
native_language_example: I don’t know those people.

additional_notes: "Quelle" is the feminine plural form of the demonstrative adjective "quel/quella" and agrees with "scarpe" (feminine plural). It’s used to point to shoes that are not near the speaker, or shoes already known/mentioned in the conversation. In spoken Italian it can also be repeated or placed at the end for emphasis (e.g., "Le avete pagate quelle scarpe?").
target_language_example: Mi piacciono quelle scarpe, ma sono troppo care.
native_language_example: I like those shoes, but they’re too expensive.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific group of feminine plural people/things already known from context: "quelle" = "those" (fem. plural) + "che" = "that/which/who". Often followed by a verb clause (e.g., "quelle che sono presenti..."). For masculine plural, you’ll usually see "quelli che".
target_language_example: Prendi quelle che preferisci.
native_language_example: Take the ones you prefer.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific group of people previously mentioned or understood from context, followed by a relative clause with che (e.g., quelli che abitano..., quelli che prendono...). It agrees in number/gender: quelli che (masc. plural or mixed), quelle che (fem. plural), quello che (masc. singular), quella che (fem. singular).
target_language_example: Quelli che arrivano in ritardo devono avvisare.
native_language_example: Those who arrive late have to let us know.

additional_notes: Very rude/vulgar. Used to insult a man or refer to him with contempt. Agreement changes with the person: **quello stronzo** (that asshole, masc.), **quella stronza** (fem.), **quegli stronzi / quelle stronze** (plural). Literally *stronzo* is “turd,” but in everyday speech it means “asshole/jerk.”
target_language_example: Non parlare con quello stronzo.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to that asshole.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a thing or action in a general way: quello che dici = what you say / what you're saying. It can also mean the one who/that in some contexts, depending on what follows.
target_language_example: Quello che dici è vero.
native_language_example: What you're saying is true.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something previously said by “you” in the polite/plural form (voi). Common in reported speech, questions, and statements about the content of someone’s words. It can take an indirect object (e.g., a me, alla polizia) and can be the subject of a sentence (e.g., Quello che avete detto non ha senso).
target_language_example: Non ho capito quello che avete detto.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what you said.

additional_notes: Literally “that which (he/she) says.” Used to refer to the words/opinion of a person or source. The subject can change: quello che dice tua madre = “what your mother says”, quello che dice la Bibbia = “what the Bible says”. Also common after comparisons: più … di quello che dice (di essere) = “more … than (he/she) says (he/she is)”.
target_language_example: Non credere a tutto quello che dice Marco.
native_language_example: Don’t believe everything Marco says.

additional_notes: Used to refer to (and often react to) someone’s words or opinion. Common in statements that criticize or disagree: “È ridicolo quello che dici” (What you’re saying is ridiculous). You can also say “Quello che dici è…” or “Non sai quello che dici” (You don’t know what you’re talking about).
target_language_example: Capisco quello che dici, ma non sono d’accordo.
native_language_example: I understand what you’re saying, but I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Literally "that which I say." Used to point to the content of your words, often in reminders or warnings (e.g., "Listen carefully to what I’m saying"). Can also appear as part of longer sentences: "quello che dico è importante" (what I’m saying is important).
target_language_example: Per favore, credi a quello che dico.
native_language_example: Please, believe what I'm saying.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of someone else’s words (often “they” = other people in general, like friends, society, “gli altri”). It can introduce a clause: “quello che dicono + subject” = “what + subject + say.” Similar to “ciò che dicono,” which is a bit more formal.
target_language_example: Non ascoltare quello che dicono: fai quello che ti rende felice.
native_language_example: Don’t listen to what they say: do what makes you happy.

meaning: "what he/she does" (the thing that someone does).
additional_notes: Uses the pattern "quello che" + verb to mean "what/that which". "Fa" is from *fare* (to do/make). Often followed by a subject for clarity: "quello che fa lui" (what he does), "quello che fa lei" (what she does). It can also mean "what someone usually does" depending on context (e.g., "quello che fa sempre" = what he always does).
target_language_example: Non capisco quello che fa Marco.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what Marco is doing.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your actions, activities, or your job/work in general. Literally means “that which I do,” and it often follows verbs like amare/piacere (to love/like) or sapere (to know), or is used as the subject of the sentence: “Quello che faccio è…”
target_language_example: Non capisci quello che faccio ogni giorno.
native_language_example: You don’t understand what I do every day.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s activity, behavior, or job (often implied by context). It can sound neutral (“Tell me what you do”) or accusatory (“Do you like what you do to others?”). Literally “that which you do.”
target_language_example: Puoi spiegarmi meglio quello che fai al lavoro?
native_language_example: Can you explain to me better what you do at work?

meaning: "what they do" / "the thing that they do".
additional_notes: Uses the structure "quello che" + verb to mean "what/that which" (a relative clause). Here, "fanno" is 3rd person plural of "fare" (they do/make). You’ll often see it after verbs like "piacere": "Mi piace quello che fanno" = "I like what they do."
target_language_example: Non capisco quello che fanno ogni giorno.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what they do every day.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to someone’s words. Literally “that which (he/she) has said.” Common with a name: “quello che ha detto Tom” = “what Tom said.” The verb changes with the subject: “quello che ho detto” (what I said), “quello che hai detto” (what you said), “quello che hanno detto” (what they said).
target_language_example: Tom si è scusato per quello che ha detto.
native_language_example: Tom apologized for what he said.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an action done by someone (often already known from context). The subject (he/she) is implied by the verb form “ha fatto” (= “has done/did”). You can add the person to be clearer: “quello che lui/lei ha fatto”. Often used when judging, praising, or discussing someone’s behavior.
target_language_example: Non riesco a dimenticare quello che ha fatto ieri.
native_language_example: I can’t forget what he did yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific statement the other person made. It can introduce a clause that acts like a noun phrase (subject or object): e.g., "Quello che hai detto mi ha ferito" = "What you said hurt me." Often followed by a time reference (ieri, stamattina) or context (in questo caso).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma quello che hai detto non è vero.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but what you said isn’t true.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to your own previous words. Often follows verbs like sentire/ascoltare (to hear/listen) and dimenticare (to forget). You can adjust the tense/person: quello che hai detto (what you said), quello che ho detto (what I said).
target_language_example: Non fraintendere quello che ho detto: volevo solo aiutarti.
native_language_example: Don’t misunderstand what I said: I just wanted to help you.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to an event or information the speaker witnessed. It’s built from "quello che" (“what/that which”) + "ho visto" (past: “I saw / I have seen”). Often appears after verbs like "dire" (to say/tell) or as the subject of a sentence: "Quello che ho visto...".
target_language_example: Non posso dimenticare quello che ho visto ieri.
native_language_example: I can’t forget what I saw yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to someone’s words. The subject isn’t specified in the phrase itself, so it depends on context (he/she/you). In indirect speech it often corresponds to English “what … told me” or “that … told me.”
target_language_example: Non dimenticherò quello che mi ha detto ieri.
native_language_example: I won’t forget what he/she told me yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s opinion or thoughts. It often follows prepositions like di/da/a prescindere da: “da quello che pensa” = “regardless of what (he/she) thinks”. The person who thinks can be stated after it (e.g., “quello che pensa mio padre” = “what my father thinks”). In comparisons, “più … di quello che pensa” means “more … than he/she thinks.”
target_language_example: Non mi importa quello che pensa la gente.
native_language_example: I don’t care what people think.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or thoughts, especially after verbs like dire (to say), dire a qualcuno (to tell someone), lasciami/mi lasci dire (let me say), or sapere (to know). It can refer to your general opinion (“what I think” in general) or your current thoughts (“what I’m thinking”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Voglio dirti quello che penso, con sincerità.
native_language_example: I want to tell you what I think, honestly.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the information you know (often as the object of a verb like dire “to say/tell”): Ho detto… quello che so = “I told… what I know.” Literally “that which I know.”
target_language_example: Ti dirò quello che so appena lo scopro.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you what I know as soon as I find out.

additional_notes: Used to refer to events or the situation (often something that is happening now or in general). Common after verbs like importare (to matter), sapere (to know), capire (to understand), or in patterns like “È quello che succede quando…” (“That’s what happens when…”). It can also take an indirect object: “quello che succede a Tom” = “what happens to Tom.”
target_language_example: Dimmi quello che succede, per favore.
native_language_example: Tell me what’s going on, please.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause about “you,” often followed by a verb: quello che ti piace (what you like), quello che ti serve (what you need), quello che ti hanno detto (what they told you). It refers to a specific thing/idea understood from context (“the thing that…”).
target_language_example: Dimmi quello che ti preoccupa.
native_language_example: Tell me what worries you.

additional_notes: Used to stress that someone should listen carefully and follow your advice or instructions. Often appears with verbs like ascolta/senti/aspettare (e.g., “listen to what I’m telling you”). Can sound firm or insistent depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Ascolta quello che ti dico: è importante.
native_language_example: Listen to what I’m telling you: it’s important.

additional_notes: Quello che = “what / that which” and introduces a clause (often the subject or object of the sentence). Vogliamo is “we want” (volere). You can replace the verb to match the subject: quello che vuoi (you want), quello che vogliono (they want). Sometimes it refers to a person: Tom è quello che vogliamo = “Tom is what we want.”
target_language_example: Questo è quello che vogliamo davvero.
native_language_example: This is what we really want.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the specific thing(s) you want. It can sound demanding or strong, especially in sentences like "Devi darmi quello che voglio". Literally "that which I want" (quello che = what/that which; voglio = I want). Often used with verbs like ottenere (to get) or dare (to give).
target_language_example: Non sempre ottengo quello che voglio, ma ci provo.
native_language_example: I don’t always get what I want, but I try.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something unspecified that satisfies another person’s wishes/requests. It’s often used after verbs like avere (to have), dare (to give), fare (to do): Hai quello che vogliono? / Dai loro quello che vogliono. You can change the verb to match the subject: quello che voglio (what I want), quello che vuoi (what you want), quello che vuole (what he/she wants), quello che vogliamo (what we want), quello che volete (what you all want), quello che vogliono (what they want).
target_language_example: Non hanno ancora quello che vogliono.
native_language_example: They still don’t have what they want.

meaning: "whatever you want" / "what you want" (addressing you plural or formal).
additional_notes: Uses the polite/plural form "volete" (you all want / you want, formal). It refers to an unspecified thing or action chosen freely: "Do/choose/eat/drink whatever you want." Often used to give permission or say you don’t mind what someone chooses.
target_language_example: Scegliete quello che volete dal menu.
native_language_example: Choose whatever you want from the menu.

meaning: "what he/she wanted" / "the thing that he/she wanted".
additional_notes: Uses "quello che" (= "what" / "that which") + the imperfect "voleva" ("wanted"). It refers to an object or thing someone desired, usually understood from context. The subject of "voleva" depends on the sentence (he/she). You can change it: "quello che volevo" (what I wanted), "quello che volevi" (what you wanted).
target_language_example: Alla fine ho comprato quello che voleva mia sorella.
native_language_example: In the end I bought what my sister wanted.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the thing someone wants. Often appears after a verb like essere: “È quello che vuoi?” = “Is that what you want?” It can also be used in statements like “Fai quello che vuoi” = “Do whatever you want.”
target_language_example: È davvero quello che vuoi?
native_language_example: Is that really what you want?

additional_notes: Uses **quello che** (“what/that which”) + **vuole** (“wants”). It can refer to a man or a woman (the subject of **vuole** is understood from context). Often used after verbs like **dare** (to give), **comprare** (to buy), **fare** (to do): *Dagli quello che vuole* = “Give him what he wants.”
target_language_example: Non capisco perché gli dai sempre quello che vuole.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why you always give him what he wants.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a past event, often something important or upsetting. Common after verbs like dire/sapere/sentire/raccontare: "Dimmi quello che è successo" = "Tell me what happened." Can also be followed by time details: "quello che è successo quella notte" (what happened that night).
target_language_example: Non voglio parlare di quello che è successo ieri.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about what happened yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to point out or identify something: "quello" = "that" (masculine singular), "è" = "is", "il" = "the" before most masculine singular nouns (e.g., il passato). The article can change depending on the noun (e.g., "quello è lo...", "quello è l'..."). Often used when showing something or talking about something at a distance (physical or figurative).
target_language_example: Quello è il mio libro.
native_language_example: That is my book.

meaning: 'that is a' (pointing out or identifying something masculine singular).
additional_notes: Used to identify something at a distance or already mentioned: "Quello" = "that" (masculine singular), "è" = "is", "un" = "a/an". Often used in questions to ask what something is. Use "quella è una" for feminine singular; use "questo/questa" for "this".
target_language_example: Quello è un animale pericoloso?
native_language_example: Is that a dangerous animal?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific song that is close in context (the one you’re listening to now, the one you just mentioned, etc.). "Questa" agrees with the feminine singular noun "canzone" (so it’s "questa canzone").
target_language_example: Non conosco questa canzone, ma mi piace molto.
native_language_example: I don’t know this song, but I like it a lot.

additional_notes: Means a specific house that’s close to the speaker or being pointed out. "questa" is the feminine singular form of "this" and it agrees with the noun "casa" (feminine). For "these houses," use "queste case."
