additional_notes: Means “a woman” (indefinite: one/any woman). Often used to introduce someone new or describe an unknown/unspecified woman. Compare: “la donna” = “the woman”. “Donna” can also mean “lady” depending on context.
target_language_example: In treno ho parlato con una donna molto simpatica.
native_language_example: On the train I talked to a very nice woman.

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: used to talk about “a/one family” in general or an unspecified family. For a specific one, you’d typically use “la famiglia” (“the family”).
target_language_example: Ha una famiglia numerosa.
native_language_example: He/She has a big family.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has many people in their family, often implying many children or siblings. You can change the article depending on context (e.g., "ho una famiglia numerosa" = I have a big family; "vengo da una famiglia numerosa" = I come from a big family).
target_language_example: Vengo da una famiglia numerosa: siamo in sette.
native_language_example: I come from a big family: there are seven of us.

additional_notes: Means “a party” (a social event). Often followed by “di + event/holiday” (una festa di Halloween = a Halloween party) or “a casa di…” / “a casa sua” (una festa a casa sua = a party at his/her place).
target_language_example: Stasera c'è una festa a casa mia.
native_language_example: Tonight there's a party at my place.

additional_notes: Used to say what kind of party it is or what it’s for: una festa di Halloween (a Halloween party), una festa di addio (a farewell/goodbye party), una festa di strada (a street party). The “di” links the party to its theme/purpose.
target_language_example: Domani facciamo una festa di compleanno per mia sorella.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re having a birthday party for my sister.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has a (female) child. You’ll often see it after the verb avere (to have): Ho una figlia. It can be followed by details with che (who/that) or called/named: una figlia che si chiama…, una figlia chiamata…. Article changes with context (e.g., mia figlia = my daughter; due figlie = two daughters).
target_language_example: Ho una figlia di otto anni.
native_language_example: I have an eight-year-old daughter.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or offer a fork (a piece of cutlery), especially at the table or in a restaurant. Feminine noun: una forchetta; plural: due/le forchette.
target_language_example: Scusi, mi dà una forchetta, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you give me a fork, please?

meaning: (1) good luck; a lucky thing. (2) a fortune (a very large amount of money).
additional_notes: Common with essere: "È una fortuna" = "It’s lucky / it’s a good thing." Also used with costare: "costa una fortuna" = "it costs a fortune" (very expensive). Context makes the meaning clear: luck/fortunate situation vs. lots of money.
target_language_example: È una fortuna che tu sia arrivato in tempo.
native_language_example: It’s lucky that you arrived on time.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech. Often used with verbs like fare una foto (take a photo), scattare una foto (snap/take a photo), and farsi fare una foto (have someone take a photo of you). You can specify the subject with di (una foto di Roma = a photo of Rome) or the person/thing being photographed with a (ha scattato una foto alla mia casa = he took a photo of my house).
target_language_example: Mi fai una foto, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you take a photo of me, please?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the subject of a photo (the person/thing shown). Often followed by a noun or a possessive phrase: “una foto di mia nonna”, “una foto di sua madre”.
target_language_example: Hai una foto di tuo fratello sul telefono?
native_language_example: Do you have a photo of your brother on your phone?

additional_notes: Most commonly means “a sentence” in everyday Italian (a complete unit with a subject/verb), especially in learning contexts: *capire una frase*, *leggere una frase*. It can also mean “a phrase/wording” (how something is expressed), often with qualifiers like *una frase del genere* (“a phrase/sentence like that”).
target_language_example: Puoi ripetere una frase, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you repeat a sentence, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about one (unspecified) leg, often in accidents/injuries: "rompersi una gamba" = "to break a leg". With "a" after a verb (e.g., "sparare a una gamba"), it means "shoot (someone) in the leg". If you mean a specific leg, use the article: "la gamba" (the leg).
target_language_example: Mi sono fatto male a una gamba giocando a calcio.
native_language_example: I hurt one of my legs playing soccer.

meaning: a day (often emphasizing what the day was like or how it was spent).
additional_notes: Common with adjectives to describe the day (una giornata bella/calda/fredda/orribile/speciale). Also used in phrases like “prendere una giornata libera” = to take a day off. Can refer to a specific day (e.g., Monday) or a day in general.
target_language_example: Domani sarà una giornata lunga, quindi vado a dormire presto.
native_language_example: Tomorrow will be a long day, so I’m going to bed early.

meaning: "a great / big" (emphatic form of *una grande* before a noun/adjective).
additional_notes: *Gran* is a shortened form of *grande* used before another word to add emphasis (similar to “a really great/big…”). It’s common in fixed patterns like **una gran bella casa** (“a really beautiful house”) or **una gran cosa** (“a great thing”). For masculine you’ll see **un gran** (e.g., *un gran problema*).
target_language_example: È stata una gran sorpresa!
native_language_example: It was a big (great) surprise!

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., una grande famiglia = “a big family”). "grande" can describe physical size (big/large) or importance/quality (great). It agrees with the noun: un grande (masc. sing.), una grande (fem. sing.), grandi (plural).
target_language_example: Ho avuto una grande idea per il progetto.
native_language_example: I had a great idea for the project.

meaning: a big/large family; (figuratively) one big family.
additional_notes: Literally refers to a family with many members. It can also be used figuratively for a close-knit group (e.g., a school, workplace, or community) that treats each other like family: "come una grande famiglia" = "like one big family." The adjective agrees with the noun: una grande famiglia (feminine singular), una grande famigliare? (not here), una famiglia grande is also possible but slightly different emphasis.
target_language_example: Nel nostro ufficio siamo come una grande famiglia.
native_language_example: In our office we’re like one big family.

additional_notes: Refers to a (written) letter/message on paper. Common with verbs like scrivere (to write), spedire/inviare (to send), ricevere (to receive), and leggere (to read). With an indirect object you’ll often see: "scriverti una lettera" = "to write you a letter". "Lettera" is feminine; plural: "lettere".
target_language_example: Domani ti mando una lettera.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’ll send you a letter.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition “a” + a person’s name to indicate the recipient of the letter: “una lettera a Judy” = “a letter to Judy.” Often appears with verbs like scrivere (to write), consegnare (to deliver), and spedire (to send).
target_language_example: Ho scritto una lettera a mia nonna ieri sera.
native_language_example: I wrote a letter to my grandma last night.

additional_notes: Used when saying who a letter is from. With places, it can mean a letter sent from that place (e.g., “una lettera da Boston”). Often follows verbs like ricevere (to receive), leggere (to read), arrivare con (to arrive with).
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto una lettera da mia nonna ieri.
native_language_example: I received a letter from my grandmother yesterday.

additional_notes: Use it for (1) a teaching session (a lesson/class/lecture): “una lezione di storia”, “tenere una lezione su…”; and (2) a life lesson or a harsh experience that teaches you something: “La vita mi ha dato una lezione.” Also in the expression “insegnare una lezione (a qualcuno)”, meaning “to teach someone a lesson” (often in a negative/punishing sense).
target_language_example: Domani ho una lezione di italiano alle nove.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have an Italian class at nine.

additional_notes: Used for a spoken language in general. After "una lingua" you can add an adjective: "una lingua difficile" (a difficult language), "una lingua nuova" (a new language). Also common in menus or settings: "Scelga una lingua" = "Choose a language."
target_language_example: Sto imparando una lingua straniera.
native_language_example: I'm learning a foreign language.

additional_notes: Used to say someone wrote/sent a letter that is long (often implying detailed or lengthy). The adjective *lunga* agrees with *lettera* (feminine singular), so it’s *una lunga lettera*.
target_language_example: Ti ho scritto una lunga lettera ieri sera.
native_language_example: I wrote you a long letter last night.

meaning: a car; (also) a machine (depending on context)
additional_notes: In everyday Italian, "una macchina" most often refers to "a car" (especially with verbs like guidare "to drive", noleggiare "to rent", parcheggiare "to park"). Depending on context, it can also mean "a machine" (e.g., industrial equipment). "Una" is the feminine singular indefinite article ("a/an").
target_language_example: Vorrei noleggiare una macchina.
native_language_example: I’d like to rent a car.

additional_notes: Used for a device that takes photographs. Often just "macchina fotografica" without the article. In everyday speech you may also hear "fotocamera". Plural: "macchine fotografiche".
target_language_example: Hai una macchina fotografica? Vorrei fare qualche foto.
native_language_example: Do you have a camera? I’d like to take a few photos.

additional_notes: Literally means “a hand” (the body part), as in "con una mano" = “with one hand.” Very commonly used in the expression "dare una mano (a qualcuno)" = “to give someone a hand / to help someone.” With pronouns: "dammi una mano" (help me), "dagli una mano" (help him).
target_language_example: Mi dai una mano a portare queste valigie?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand carrying these suitcases?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a physical or digital map. Often followed by "di/del/della" to specify what kind of map it is (e.g., "una mappa della città" = a city map; "una mappa del tesoro" = a treasure map).
target_language_example: Hai una mappa della città?
native_language_example: Do you have a map of the city?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a single pencil. "Una" is the feminine form of "a/an"; plural: "delle matite" (some pencils) or "matite" (pencils). Often paired with "una penna" (a pen).
target_language_example: Mi serve una matita per scrivere.
native_language_example: I need a pencil to write.

additional_notes: "Una" is the feminine singular form of the indefinite article "a/an" and can also mean "one" in some contexts. Used when asking for, offering, or referring to a single apple.
target_language_example: Posso avere una mela, per favore?
native_language_example: Can I have an apple, please?

additional_notes: Used to introduce or mention one of your female friends. It’s a very common way to say “a friend of mine” (not necessarily your best friend). For a male friend: “un mio amico”. You can also use it with names: “Rita, una mia amica” = “Rita, a friend of mine.”
target_language_example: Stasera esco con una mia amica.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going out with a friend of mine.

meaning: a mission; an important task/assignment (often with a specific goal).
additional_notes: Used for an official or organized assignment (military, diplomatic, rescue, space, etc.) or, more generally, a personal goal you feel you must accomplish. Often followed by "per" + infinitive to say the purpose (e.g., "una missione per trovare...").
target_language_example: Siamo partiti per una missione di soccorso.
native_language_example: We left on a rescue mission.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has a wife or to describe a woman as a wife. "Una" is the feminine singular indefinite article (“a”), and the plural is "due/tre mogli" (“two/three wives”). With negation: "non ho una moglie" = “I don’t have a wife / I’m not married.”
target_language_example: Marco ha una moglie e due bambini.
native_language_example: Marco has a wife and two kids.

additional_notes: Used for a single coin (loose change). It can also mean “a currency” in general when talking about money systems, but with “una” it usually means one physical coin.
target_language_example: Hai una moneta da un euro?
native_language_example: Do you have a one-euro coin?

meaning: a mosque (a Muslim place of worship).
additional_notes: Feminine noun: la moschea / una moschea. Plural: le moschee. Used with common verbs like andare in (to go to), pregare in (to pray in), visitare (to visit), vivere accanto a (to live next to).
target_language_example: C'è una moschea vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: There is a mosque near the station.

meaning: a move; a step/action (also used to mean “a quick move” in expressions like darsi una mossa = to hurry up).
additional_notes: Literally “a move.” Common in games (chess, cards, etc.) meaning “one move/turn”: Non ripetere mai una mossa… (“Never repeat a move…”). In everyday speech it’s often part of the phrase darsi una mossa / darsi una mossa! (or plural: datevi una mossa!) meaning “to hurry up!” / “Get a move on!” (informal/colloquial).
target_language_example: Se vogliamo arrivare in orario, dobbiamo darci una mossa.
native_language_example: If we want to arrive on time, we have to hurry up.

additional_notes: Indefinite phrase: "una" = "a/one" (feminine singular) + "mucca" = "cow". Used to talk about an unspecified cow. For a male, use "un toro" (a bull).
target_language_example: C'è una mucca nel campo.
native_language_example: There’s a cow in the field.

additional_notes: "Nave" is a feminine noun (la nave / una nave). It usually means a large ship (bigger than a "barca"), and it can also mean a spacecraft in phrases like "nave spaziale".
target_language_example: Dal porto si vede una nave enorme.
native_language_example: From the port you can see a huge ship.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (or a feminine adjective used as a noun). It agrees in gender/number with what follows: una nuova scuola = “a new school”, una nuova fase = “a new phase”. For masculine you use un nuovo (e.g., un nuovo problema).
target_language_example: Abbiamo bisogno di una nuova idea.
native_language_example: We need a new idea.

additional_notes: Used to talk about buying, needing, or choosing a new car. "Una" is the feminine singular indefinite article (“a”), "nuova" means “new,” and "auto" means “car” (feminine in Italian).
target_language_example: Stiamo cercando una nuova auto per la famiglia.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a new car for the family.

meaning: a new house; a new home.
additional_notes: Used when talking about building, buying, or moving into a different house/home. "Casa" can mean both the physical house and the idea of a home; "una" is feminine singular (“a”), and "nuova" agrees with "casa".
target_language_example: Stiamo cercando una nuova casa vicino al lavoro.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a new home near work.

meaning: a new life; a fresh start.
additional_notes: Used when someone starts over or begins a different chapter in life (after moving, changing jobs, recovering from a difficult period, etc.). Often with verbs like cominciare/iniziare (to begin) or avere (to have).
target_language_example: Dopo il divorzio, ha deciso di cominciare una nuova vita in un'altra città.
native_language_example: After the divorce, he decided to start a new life in another city.

meaning: a ball (a round object used for playing; also used for spherical shapes).
additional_notes: Literally “a ball.” Used for a physical ball you throw/kick (e.g., in sports). It can also describe something that is round/spherical: “La Terra è una palla blu” = “The Earth is a blue ball.”
target_language_example: Mi presti una palla per giocare in spiaggia?
native_language_example: Can you lend me a ball to play with at the beach?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a single word in general or in a text. In negative expressions it often means “a word” = “anything”: "non dire una parola" / "non mi ha detto una parola" = “don’t say a word / he didn’t say a word.”
target_language_example: Non dire una parola, per favore.
native_language_example: Don’t say a word, please.

meaning: a break; a pause (a short rest).
additional_notes: Used for a short rest from an activity (work, walking, cooking, etc.). Common with verbs like fare una pausa (to take a break), prendersi una pausa (to take a break for yourself), and dare una pausa (to give someone a break / let them rest). It can also mean a pause in speaking or action.
target_language_example: Facciamo una pausa di dieci minuti.
native_language_example: Let’s take a ten-minute break.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: the animal. "Pecora" is a feminine noun, so it uses "una" in the singular (una pecora) and "pecore" in the plural (due pecore). It can also be used figuratively to mean someone who is very naive or who follows others blindly (like "a sheep").
target_language_example: Al mercato ho comprato una pecora.
native_language_example: At the market I bought a sheep.

additional_notes: Used when asking for or referring to a pen. With the indefinite article "una" (feminine singular), it means “a pen”; the plural is "delle penne". Often appears with verbs like "avere" (to have), "prendere" (to take), and "prendere in prestito" (to borrow).
target_language_example: Mi presti una penna, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you lend me a pen, please?

additional_notes: Used to say an activity, meeting, lesson, etc. wasn’t useful or worth doing. Often follows “è stata” (it was) or “è” (it is): “È/È stata una perdita di tempo.”
target_language_example: Aspettare qui senza informazioni è una perdita di tempo.
native_language_example: Waiting here with no information is a waste of time.

meaning: “a person who …” (used to describe someone by what they do/are).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that defines or describes someone: una persona che + verb (e.g., fuma, disegna, è…). It’s singular; plural is “delle persone che” / “persone che.” Often used for general statements and definitions.
target_language_example: Cerco una persona che parli bene inglese.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a person who speaks English well.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (una + feminine adjective piccola) to describe something small in size, amount, or importance (e.g., una piccola sorpresa, una piccola somma, una piccola busta). With some nouns it can imply “just a little” in a polite or minimizing way (e.g., asking for a tip: Una piccola mancia?). The masculine form is "un piccolo".
target_language_example: Posso avere una piccola informazione, per favore?
native_language_example: Could I have a little bit of information, please?

additional_notes: Literal meaning: a (small) stone you can pick up (raccogliere) or throw (tirare) at something/someone. In comparisons like "come una pietra" it can mean "like a stone" (very hard, heavy, still, or emotionally cold depending on context).
target_language_example: Ho trovato una pietra interessante sulla spiaggia.
native_language_example: I found an interesting stone on the beach.

additional_notes: Means a pistol/handgun (a small gun). The article changes with gender/number: un/una (a), la (the), delle pistole (some pistols). Often used with verbs like comprare (to buy), possedere (to own), dare (to give).
target_language_example: Non voglio avere una pistola in casa.
native_language_example: I don’t want to have a gun at home.

additional_notes: Used to order or choose food. With "andare" (e.g., "A me va una pizza"), it means "A pizza works for me / I'd like a pizza."
target_language_example: Per me, una pizza margherita, grazie.
native_language_example: For me, a margherita pizza, please.

additional_notes: Used for a commitment you make to do (or not do) something. Common collocations: fare una promessa (to make a promise), mantenere una promessa (to keep a promise), infrangere una promessa (to break a promise). Also used in expressions like È una promessa! (“It’s a promise!”).
target_language_example: Te lo prometto: è una promessa.
native_language_example: I promise you: it’s a promise.

meaning: “a matter of …” / “an issue of …” (it depends on …).
additional_notes: Used to say what something is really about, or what the deciding factor is: *È una questione di + noun* (“It’s a matter of + noun”). Often emphasizes that it’s not about something else: *non è una questione di X, ma di Y* (“it’s not a matter of X, but of Y”). You can also use it for the reason behind something: *per una questione di lavoro* (“for work reasons”).
target_language_example: Non è una questione di soldi, ma di fiducia.
native_language_example: It’s not a matter of money, but of trust.

additional_notes: Most literally means “a girl” (a young female person). In context (especially with verbs like avere: “Ho una ragazza”), it commonly means “a girlfriend.” Use “la mia ragazza” for “my girlfriend.”
target_language_example: Ho conosciuto una ragazza al corso di italiano.
native_language_example: I met a girl at the Italian course.

meaning: a relationship; also a connection (with someone).
additional_notes: Most commonly used for a romantic relationship (“una relazione seria”, “avere una relazione con…”). It can also mean a personal connection/bond that isn’t romantic, including family relationships (“una relazione difficile con suo padre”) or a special bond (“una relazione speciale”). You can add details like “a lunga distanza” (long-distance).
target_language_example: Non voglio una relazione a lunga distanza.
native_language_example: I don’t want a long-distance relationship.

meaning: an answer; a reply (to a message/request).
additional_notes: Used for both answering a question and replying to an email/message or giving an official response. Common with verbs like avere (to have): “Hai una risposta?”, dare (to give): “Mi dia una risposta”, mandare (to send): “mandare una risposta”. You can add adjectives to specify the type: “una risposta definitiva” (a final/definitive answer).
target_language_example: Mi può dare una risposta entro domani?
native_language_example: Can you give me an answer by tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used for an appointment where people get together to discuss something (work, school, town hall, etc.). Common with verbs like avere/essere in/andare a/partecipare a: “Ho una riunione” (I have a meeting), “Tom è in una riunione” (Tom is in a meeting), “andare a una riunione” (to go to a meeting).
target_language_example: Scusa, non posso parlare adesso: sono in una riunione.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk right now: I’m in a meeting.

additional_notes: Used for a container, usually made of cardboard, wood, or plastic. Often followed by “di” to say what’s inside or what it contains: “una scatola di mele” = “a box of apples.” You can also describe it with adjectives like “piena di …” (full of …): “una scatola piena di mele.”
target_language_example: Puoi mettere questi biscotti in una scatola?
native_language_example: Can you put these cookies in a box?

meaning: a choice; an option; a decision.
additional_notes: Used for choosing between options (“fare una scelta” = to make a choice). You can also “dare una scelta (a qualcuno)” = to give someone a choice. Often paired with adjectives like “una scelta saggia” (a wise choice).
target_language_example: Hai una scelta: restare qui o venire con noi.
native_language_example: You have a choice: stay here or come with us.

additional_notes: Used literally for the animal. It can also be used as an insult or to say someone looks/behaves like a monkey (often childish and can be offensive). Common patterns: "sembra una scimmia" (he/she looks like a monkey), "si comporta come una scimmia" (he/she behaves like a monkey), "imitare una scimmia" (to imitate a monkey).
target_language_example: Lui sembra una scimmia.
native_language_example: He looks like a monkey.

additional_notes: Most often means “an excuse” (a reason you give to explain/justify something), especially with verbs like inventare/si è inventato una scusa (“to make up an excuse”). With verbs like dovere (Gli/Le dovete una scusa), it means “to owe someone an apology.” The plural is scuse (“excuses/apologies”).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace: ti devo una scusa.
native_language_example: I’m sorry: I owe you an apology.

additional_notes: Used to ask for, offer, or refer to a single chair. Often appears with verbs like "dare" (to give), "portare" (to bring), and "sedere/siedere" (to sit).
target_language_example: C'è una sedia libera vicino alla finestra.
native_language_example: There’s a free chair near the window.

meaning: a series of; a number of.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “a sequence/collection of things,” often translating naturally as “a number of.” Very common with “tutta una serie di” = “a whole series of / all sorts of.”
target_language_example: Devo fare una serie di telefonate prima di partire.
native_language_example: I have to make a series of phone calls before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for one week) or a point in time in the future with "fra/tra" (= in a week). Can also mean "per una settimana" (= for a week) depending on context.
target_language_example: Resto a Roma per una settimana.
native_language_example: I’m staying in Rome for a week.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to a single cigarette. With verbs like "fumare" (to smoke), "accendere" (to light), and with items like "un accendino" (a lighter). In requests you’ll often hear: "Posso avere una sigaretta?" (Can I have a cigarette?).
target_language_example: Scusa, hai una sigaretta?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have a cigarette?

meaning: a solution; a way to solve a problem.
additional_notes: Used for an answer or practical way to fix/resolve a problem (“trovare una soluzione” = to find a solution). Also used for a possible option/approach (“una soluzione migliore” = a better solution). Feminine noun: la soluzione / una soluzione; plural: le soluzioni.
target_language_example: Cerchiamo una soluzione insieme.
native_language_example: Let’s look for a solution together.

additional_notes: Used to say something unexpected happens or to keep something secret until the moment (e.g., a gift, a party, news). With the verb "essere": "È/È stata una sorpresa" = "It’s/It was a surprise."
target_language_example: Il regalo per tuo padre deve restare una sorpresa.
native_language_example: The gift for your father has to stay a surprise.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the person who will receive the surprise: "una sorpresa per + [person]". You can add a verb like "Ho una sorpresa per te" (I have a surprise for you) or "È una sorpresa per mia sorella" (It’s a surprise for my sister). The article can change (una/un/una grande, etc.) depending on the noun and context.
target_language_example: Ho una sorpresa per te.
native_language_example: I have a surprise for you.

meaning: 'a kind of' / 'sort of' (used to describe something approximately).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean something is similar to that thing, but not exactly (or you don’t want to be too precise): "una sorta di celebrità" = "a sort of celebrity." Often used when you’re unsure, simplifying, or being intentionally vague. Can also introduce an approximate explanation/idea ("una sorta di spiegazione").
target_language_example: È una sorta di problema, ma possiamo risolverlo.
native_language_example: It’s kind of a problem, but we can solve it.

additional_notes: Used to describe something approximately or loosely: it’s similar to X, but not exactly X. Very common in spoken Italian. It can also soften what you’re saying (making it less direct). Usually followed by a noun: "una specie di test", "una specie di crisi".
target_language_example: È una specie di scusa, ma non mi convince.
native_language_example: It’s kind of an excuse, but it doesn’t convince me.

additional_notes: "Spia" is a feminine noun; "una spia" refers to a female spy or uses the feminine form as the default. For a male spy you often hear "una spia" as well, but you can also say "una spia (uomo)" or more commonly "un agente segreto". It can also mean an indicator light (e.g., on a car dashboard): "una spia rossa".
target_language_example: In quel film lei è una spia.
native_language_example: In that movie she is a spy.

additional_notes: Used when you want a reason or clarification for something. Often followed by "per" (for) to explain what it’s about: "una spiegazione per ciò" / "una spiegazione per il suo errore". "Hai una spiegazione?" is a common way to ask "Do you have an explanation?"
target_language_example: Puoi darmi una spiegazione, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you give me an explanation, please?

meaning: a room (in a house, building, hotel, etc.).
additional_notes: Commonly used for any kind of room: a bedroom, an office, a waiting room, etc. In hotels, you’ll often hear it with details: "una stanza con doccia" (a room with a shower), "una stanza pulita" (a clean room), "una stanza sul retro" (a room in the back). Don’t confuse with "uno stanzo" (not used) or "la stanza" (the room).
target_language_example: Scusi, vorrei una stanza per due notti.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I’d like a room for two nights.

meaning: “a room for …” (used to say who/what the room is for, or how long you need it).
additional_notes: Common when booking accommodation. After per you can add: (1) the purpose/people: per gli ospiti (“for guests”), per due persone (“for two people”); or (2) the length of stay: per sei notti (“for six nights”). In questions you’ll often hear: Avete/Hai una stanza per …? (“Do you have a room for …?”).
target_language_example: Avete una stanza per due persone per tre notti?
native_language_example: Do you have a room for two people for three nights?

additional_notes: Often means “a story” (a tale someone tells or reads), but it can also mean “history” (the past of a place/people), especially in phrases like “una storia ricca.” Context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Mi racconti una storia prima di dormire?
native_language_example: Will you tell me a story before I go to sleep?

additional_notes: Common in everyday requests and orders. Use it with verbs like voglio (I want), mi piacerebbe (I’d like), ordinare (to order), and versare (to pour). You can change the article: una tazza di caffè (a cup), due tazze di caffè (two cups), la tazza di caffè (the cup). In many cafés you might also hear just un caffè for an espresso.
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere una tazza di caffè, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a cup of coffee, please?

additional_notes: Used when ordering or offering a drink. Common with polite requests like (Mi) dia / Datemi… per favore (“Please give me…”) and with offers/questions like Vuoi/Volete…? or Vorresti/Vorreste…? (“Would you like…?”).
target_language_example: Potrei avere una tazza di latte caldo, per favore?
native_language_example: Could I have a cup of warm milk, please?

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for offering or talking about a drink. Often used with verbs like preparare (to prepare), portare (to bring), versarsi (to pour oneself), and with offers/questions like Vuoi una tazza di tè? (Do you want a cup of tea?).
target_language_example: Dopo cena, prendo sempre una tazza di tè.
native_language_example: After dinner, I always have a cup of tea.

additional_notes: Used with fare/ricevere: "fare una telefonata" = to make a phone call; "ricevere una telefonata" = to receive a phone call. Can be modified (e.g., "una telefonata urgente" = an urgent phone call).
target_language_example: Scusa, devo fare una telefonata veloce.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to make a quick phone call.

additional_notes: Noun phrase: the indefinite article "una" (a/an) + feminine singular noun "tigre". Used when talking about a tiger in general or an unknown tiger. In questions like "Ha mai visto..." it often means "Have you ever seen...".
target_language_example: Ho visto una tigre allo zoo.
native_language_example: I saw a tiger at the zoo.

additional_notes: Used for a sweet cake (e.g., banana cake, Christmas cake). Common patterns: "una torta alla ..." (a ...-flavored cake, like banana), "una torta di ..." (a ... cake, often for an occasion or style, like Christmas), and "tagliare una torta in due" (to cut a cake in half).
target_language_example: Per il suo compleanno ho comprato una torta al cioccolato.
native_language_example: For her birthday I bought a chocolate cake.

meaning: a tragedy; (also figuratively) a disaster / a very bad situation.
additional_notes: Used for a real serious tragic event (death, accident, catastrophe): "È avvenuta una tragedia." It’s also common as an exaggerated reaction meaning “it’s awful/terrible”: "No, una tragedia." In the expression "farne una tragedia" it means “to make a big deal out of it / to overreact”: "Perché ne stai facendo una tragedia?"
target_language_example: Ho perso il treno: per me è stata una tragedia!
native_language_example: I missed the train: for me it was a disaster!

additional_notes: Literally a device used to catch animals or pests (e.g., a mousetrap). Figuratively, it means a plan to trick someone or lure them into danger ("It could be a trap"). Often used with "essere" (è/era/sarebbe una trappola) or "tendere una trappola" (to set a trap for someone).
target_language_example: Non fidarti: potrebbe essere una trappola.
native_language_example: Don’t trust it: it could be a trap.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for time off from work/school for rest or travel. Often used with verbs like fare (to take/go on) and avere bisogno di (to need): fare una vacanza, avere bisogno di una vacanza. Plural: vacanze.
target_language_example: Quest’estate voglio fare una vacanza al mare.
native_language_example: This summer I want to take a vacation at the seaside.

additional_notes: Feminine singular form of *vecchio* (“old”). Often used before a feminine noun: *una vecchia bici* (“an old bike”), *una vecchia storia* (“an old story”). When used on its own as a noun, *una vecchia* usually means “an old woman” (can sound blunt depending on context; *un’anziana* is more neutral/polite).
target_language_example: In autobus c’era una vecchia che chiedeva informazioni.
native_language_example: On the bus there was an old woman asking for information.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to emphasize that something is genuine or truly has a quality: una vera amica (a true friend), una vera festa (a real party). It’s the feminine form of the adjective vero; compare: un vero amico (masculine), una vera amica (feminine), dei veri amici / delle vere amiche (plural).
target_language_example: Vorrei una vera pizza napoletana.
native_language_example: I’d like a real Neapolitan pizza.

meaning: a visit (an appointment/visitor; or the act of visiting).
additional_notes: Used for both formal and casual visits. Common patterns: "fare una visita a [someone/place]" = to pay a visit to; "passare a fare una visita" = to stop by for a visit; "avere una visita" can mean "to have a visitor" (e.g., at home, at the office, in a hospital). In some contexts (like reception/phone calls), "Ha una visita" means someone is here to see you.
target_language_example: Domani pomeriggio ho una visita, quindi non posso uscire.
native_language_example: Tomorrow afternoon I have a visitor/appointment, so I can’t go out.

additional_notes: Usually refers to someone’s life ("una vita lunga e felice" = “a long and happy life”). In phrases like "sembra/sentirsi come se fosse passata una vita", it’s often used more loosely to mean “a very long time / ages,” even if not literally a whole lifetime. "I risparmi di una vita" means “a lifetime’s savings” (money saved over many years).
target_language_example: Ho aspettato una vita per questo momento.
native_language_example: I’ve waited ages for this moment.

additional_notes: Common phrase meaning a life that is generally happy and satisfying. Used with verbs like vivere (to live), aver(e) avuto (to have had), and condurre (to lead): vivere/condurre una vita felice. In questions, it can ask whether someone’s life overall has been happy.
target_language_example: Spero che tu possa vivere una vita felice.
native_language_example: I hope you can live a happy life.

additional_notes: Usually means "once" or "one time" when talking about how many times something happened. In other contexts, especially with past descriptions, it can mean "once" in the sense of "formerly" or "used to".
target_language_example: Ci sono andato una volta.
native_language_example: I went there once.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens (frequency). It commonly goes after the verb: "Ci vediamo una volta al mese". Related patterns: "una volta alla settimana" (once a week), "due volte al mese" (twice a month).
target_language_example: Faccio la spesa una volta al mese.
native_language_example: I do the grocery shopping once a month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency. It can go at the beginning or end of the sentence (often after the verb): “Ci vediamo una volta alla settimana.” Similar patterns: “una volta al giorno” (once a day), “due volte alla settimana” (twice a week).
target_language_example: Vado in palestra una volta alla settimana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym once a week.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition in time: after something happens or is completed, then the next thing will happen. Often followed by a verb in the present tense for future meaning (e.g., “Una volta che mi dai…, chiamerò…” = “Once you give me…, I’ll call…”). Similar to “dopo che” (“after”), but “una volta che” emphasizes “as soon as/once it’s done.”
target_language_example: Una volta che finisci il lavoro, possiamo uscire.
native_language_example: Once you finish the work, we can go out.

meaning: once in a while; every now and then.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens occasionally, not regularly. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis, but it can also go after the verb (e.g., "Gioco a tennis una volta ogni tanto").
target_language_example: Una volta ogni tanto prendo un caffè al bar.
native_language_example: Once in a while I have a coffee at the café.

meaning: once and for all; for good (finally, permanently).
additional_notes: Used to say you want to end or settle something definitively, so it won’t come back (a problem, argument, situation, or person). Often appears with verbs like finire (to stop), sistemare (to fix), liberare (to free), risolvere (to solve), or in a slightly threatening tone: la pagherai una volta per tutte (“you’ll pay for it once and for all”).
target_language_example: Chiudiamo questa discussione una volta per tutte.
native_language_example: Let’s end this discussion once and for all.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens (or should happen) a single time. Common in warnings or firm statements ("I’ll say it only once") and to mean you’ve done something only one time in your life ("We went there only once").
target_language_example: Te lo ripeto: lo spiego una volta sola.
native_language_example: I’ll repeat it: I’ll explain it only once.

additional_notes: Used to pick one item/person out of a group of feminine plural nouns: una delle ragazze (one of the girls), una delle cose (one of the things), una delle spiagge (one of the beaches). For masculine plural, use “uno dei” (uno dei ragazzi = one of the boys). Often followed by a superlative: una delle più belle = one of the most beautiful.
target_language_example: Questo è uno dei miei ristoranti preferiti, ma quella è una delle mie pizzerie preferite.
native_language_example: This is one of my favorite restaurants, but that is one of my favorite pizzerias.

additional_notes: Used to pick one item/person from a group of feminine plural nouns (e.g., amiche, cose, magliette). It’s the feminine form; compare masculine “uno dei”. Often followed by a superlative: “una delle più + adjective” = “one of the most + adjective”.
target_language_example: Vorrei una delle tue borse, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like one of your bags, please.

meaning: “one of us” (referring to a female person).
additional_notes: Used to say that a woman/girl belongs to your group (“one of us”). With a male person or a mixed group, you typically use **uno di noi**. You can also specify a smaller group: **una di noi due** = “one of the two of us.”
target_language_example: Giulia è una di noi, quindi può venire alla riunione.
native_language_example: Giulia is one of us, so she can come to the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific item or person belonging to a previously mentioned or implied group of feminine plural things/people (“quelle”). Often followed by a noun (e.g., "una di quelle candele" = “one of those candles”) or used more generally about a type of person (“una di quelle donne” = “one of those women”). For masculine, use "uno di quelli".
target_language_example: Puoi passarmi una di quelle bottiglie, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you pass me one of those bottles, please?

meaning: "one of those" (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to pick out or ask for one item from a group already known/pointed out in context (e.g., items on a shelf). It agrees with the noun: una (feminine singular). Variations: "uno di quelli" (masculine singular), "una di queste" (feminine, "these"), "uno di questi" (masculine, "these"). Often follows verbs like comprare (to buy), prendere (to take), volere (to want), avere (to have).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere una di quelle borse, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have one of those bags, please?

meaning: "one of these" (referring to a feminine thing).
additional_notes: Used to pick one item from a group indicated by "queste" (“these”, feminine plural). It agrees with the noun: for masculine you say "uno di questi"; for plural “some of these” you can say "alcune di queste" (fem.) / "alcuni di questi" (masc.). Often used in questions like "Hai mai usato una di queste?" (“Have you ever used one of these?”).
target_language_example: Posso provarne una di queste?
native_language_example: Can I try one of these?

additional_notes: “Sbirro” is an informal slang word for a police officer and can sound distrustful or insulting depending on context and tone. In neutral/polite situations, prefer “un poliziotto / una poliziotta” or “un agente (di polizia)”. “Uno” is the masculine indefinite article used before s+consonant (sb-, sp-, st-, etc.), z, gn, ps, x, y: e.g., “uno sbirro”, “uno studente”.
target_language_example: Secondo me è uno sbirro, quindi stai attento a quello che dici.
native_language_example: I think he’s a cop, so be careful what you say.

additional_notes: Used to say something is meant as humor or not serious: "È/era solo uno scherzo" (“It’s/it was just a joke”). Often appears in the negative to stress seriousness: "Non è uno scherzo!" / "Questo non è uno scherzo" (“This is no joke”).
target_language_example: Scusa, era solo uno scherzo.
native_language_example: Sorry, it was just a joke.

additional_notes: Used for a male person; for a female scientist, say “una scienziata”. “Uno” is used (instead of “un”) because “scienziato” starts with “s” + consonant (sc-). Often used with “diventare” (to become) or “essere” (to be).
target_language_example: Da grande, vuole diventare uno scienziato.
native_language_example: When he grows up, he wants to become a scientist.

additional_notes: "Scoiattolo" is masculine; before most words it takes the article "uno" (e.g., uno scoiattolo, uno studente). The plural is "scoiattoli" ("due scoiattoli"). You’ll often hear it in exclamations when you spot one: "Guarda, uno scoiattolo!"
target_language_example: Nel parco ho visto uno scoiattolo.
native_language_example: In the park I saw a squirrel.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s job or identity is “a writer,” often with adjectives (e.g., uno scrittore famoso) or with “di…” to add details (e.g., uno scrittore di grande talento). For a female writer, say “una scrittrice.”
target_language_example: Mio fratello è uno scrittore e lavora da casa.
native_language_example: My brother is a writer and works from home.

additional_notes: Used for looking briefly at something (dare uno sguardo = to take/have a look) or for an exchanged look between people (scambiarsi uno sguardo). It can also mean a meaningful look (a look can “say” something).
target_language_example: Puoi dare uno sguardo a questo documento?
native_language_example: Can you take a look at this document?

meaning: a specialist; an expert (often a doctor or professional).
additional_notes: Used for someone with specialized knowledge in a field. Often followed by **di** (area of expertise) or **in** (field), e.g., *uno specialista di sicurezza / in sicurezza*. In medical contexts it means a specialist doctor (*vedere uno specialista* = to see a specialist). The feminine form is **una specialista**.
target_language_example: Devo prendere un appuntamento con uno specialista.
native_language_example: I need to make an appointment with a specialist.

additional_notes: Used for a small bite between meals. Very common with the verb "fare": "fare uno spuntino" = "to have a snack". You can also offer it politely: "Vuole uno spuntino?" (formal) / "Vuoi uno spuntino?" (informal).
target_language_example: Ho fame: facciamo uno spuntino prima di cena.
native_language_example: I’m hungry: let’s have a snack before dinner.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “a foreigner” (a person from another country): *Tom è uno straniero.* It can also be used more figuratively as “a stranger/someone unfamiliar” to a situation or idea: *La morte resterà per lui sempre uno straniero* (“death will always remain something unfamiliar to him”). Masculine singular; the feminine is *una straniera*.
target_language_example: Per uno straniero è facile perdersi in questa città.
native_language_example: For a foreigner, it’s easy to get lost in this city.

meaning: a jerk / an asshole (a very offensive insult).
additional_notes: Very vulgar and insulting. Used to call someone a terrible, unpleasant person (usually a man; for a woman you’d say “una stronza”). Commonly used after “Sei…” (“You’re…”) or “Sei stato…” (“You’ve been…”). Avoid in polite situations; use only if you understand the social consequences.
target_language_example: Sei proprio uno stronzo, signor Berg.
native_language_example: You’re really an asshole, Mr. Berg.

meaning: a tool; an instrument (especially a musical instrument).
additional_notes: Used for something you use to do a task (a tool) or to achieve a goal (“a powerful tool”, “a tool for improving…”). With music verbs like "suonare" it usually means a musical instrument: "suonare uno strumento" = "to play an instrument". It can also be used figuratively to mean someone is being used as a means to an end (and can sound insulting, e.g. "uno strumento inutile").
target_language_example: Questo sito è uno strumento utile per imparare l’italiano.
native_language_example: This website is a useful tool for learning Italian.

additional_notes: "Uno" is the masculine singular indefinite article used before words starting with s + consonant (st-, sp-, sc-, etc.), z, ps, pn, or gn (e.g., "uno studente"). With "a" (to) you often see the combined form "a uno" → "ad uno" in more formal/written Italian, though in everyday speech "a uno studente" is also common.
target_language_example: In casa con me vive uno studente di medicina.
native_language_example: A medical student lives in my house with me.

meaning: 'one, two!' (counting to start or keep a rhythm).
additional_notes: Used to count off before starting something (e.g., music, dancing, exercise) or to keep a steady rhythm. Often repeated ("uno, due, uno, due") and may be followed by "e tre" ("and three").
target_language_example: Pronti? Uno, due!
native_language_example: Ready? One, two!

additional_notes: Used to pick one item/person from a plural group. It agrees with the noun you’re talking about: uno dei + masculine plural noun (uno dei luoghi, uno dei tori). For feminine nouns use: una delle (una delle cose). Often followed by a superlative or adjective phrase: uno dei più + adjective ("one of the most...").
target_language_example: Questo è uno dei ristoranti più buoni della zona.
native_language_example: This is one of the best restaurants in the area.

additional_notes: Used to describe a type of person by adding a relative clause with **che**: **uno che + verb** (“someone who…”). It often comments on someone’s character or habits (sometimes with a judgment). It changes with gender/number: **una che** (a woman who), **uno che** (a man who / someone), **quelli che** (those who).
target_language_example: Non sono uno che si arrende facilmente.
native_language_example: I’m not someone who gives up easily.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a single person or thing belonging to a group: "uno" + "dei" (plural "di + i" = "of the"). The noun after it is usually plural: "uno dei suoi figli" = "one of his sons". For feminine/plural forms you’ll also see: "una delle" (one of the [fem. pl.]), "uno/una degli/delle" depending on gender/number.
target_language_example: Marco è uno dei miei migliori amici.
native_language_example: Marco is one of my best friends.

meaning: "one of my" (followed by a plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to say a single person/thing from your group: uno dei miei + plural noun (libri, cani, denti, amici, zii). It agrees with what “one” is: uno (masc. singular); una delle mie (fem. singular). You can also use plural: due dei miei = “two of my.”
target_language_example: Uno dei miei vicini parla inglese.
native_language_example: One of my neighbors speaks English.

meaning: one of ours; one of our (people/things).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something belongs to “us” or is part of our group/category (family, team, club, students, pets, favorite places, etc.). It’s usually followed by a noun ("uno dei nostri bambini") or a plural category ("uno dei nostri testimoni"), and it agrees in gender/number: "una delle nostre" (feminine), "uno dei nostri" (masculine), "una dei nostri" is not used.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: è uno dei nostri studenti.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’s one of our students.

additional_notes: Used to pick one item/person from a group that belongs to someone. The possessive "suoi" agrees with what is owned (masculine plural): "uno dei suoi libri" = one of his/her books. For feminine plural, use "una delle sue" (e.g., "una delle sue amiche"). For masculine singular, "uno dei suoi" often appears as part of a longer phrase (e.g., "uno dei suoi studenti").
target_language_example: Questo è uno dei suoi film preferiti.
native_language_example: This is one of his/her favorite movies.

meaning: “one of them” (referring to a group of people).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is one person among a group. It agrees with gender/number: uno di loro (masc.), una di loro (fem.), uno/una di voi (“one of you”), uno/una di noi (“one of us”). Often follows “essere” (to be): essere uno di loro = to be one of them.
target_language_example: Non voglio essere uno di loro.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be one of them.

additional_notes: Used to say someone belongs to a group (often to show solidarity, protection, or shared identity). It can also be used with suspicion/accusation depending on context (e.g., pointing out a traitor or someone who’s secretly part of the group). You can specify the group: "uno di noi due" = "one of the two of us."
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: è uno di noi.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’s one of us.

meaning: "one of those" (one item/person from a group already understood).
additional_notes: Used to point to or refer back to a specific thing (or person) among several, usually something visible or already mentioned. Agree it with what you mean: uno di quelli (masc. sg.), una di quelle (fem. sg.), uno di quelle (mixed/unspecified group; often for people), una di quelli (rare).
target_language_example: Non so quale scegliere: prendo uno di quelli in vetrina.
native_language_example: I don’t know which one to choose: I’ll take one of those in the window.

meaning: one of these days; sometime soon.
additional_notes: Used to mean an unspecified day in the near future (often as a friendly suggestion or vague plan). It can also be used as a warning/threat: “One of these days, I’ll…”. As a stand-alone phrase (“Uno di questi giorni.”) it implies “someday soon / I’ll do it soon,” often without committing to a specific date.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo prenderci un caffè uno di questi giorni.
native_language_example: We should grab a coffee one of these days.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a single item within a group of things that are present, shown, or understood from context. It often appears with questions like Avete mai…? (“Have you ever…?”) and with Ti serve… (“You need…”). You can change gender/number depending on what you’re referring to: una di queste (feminine), uno di quelli / una di quelle (“one of those”).
target_language_example: Vuoi provare uno di questi?
native_language_example: Do you want to try one of these?

additional_notes: Common breakfast dish. Used with the plural noun phrase "le uova strapazzate"; in polite offers/questions you’ll often hear "Vuole/Volete delle uova strapazzate?" (some scrambled eggs?).
target_language_example: Per colazione prendo le uova strapazzate e un caffè.
native_language_example: For breakfast I’ll have scrambled eggs and a coffee.

additional_notes: Used for an egg boiled in its shell until the yolk and white are firm. Contrast: “uovo alla coque” (soft-boiled). Plural: “uova sode”.
target_language_example: Vuoi un uovo sodo per colazione?
native_language_example: Do you want a hard-boiled egg for breakfast?

additional_notes: Commonly used for going out socially with someone, and often implies dating/romantic interest depending on context. It’s followed by a person: uscire con lui/lei, uscire con i miei amici. In invitations it can mean “go out (together)”: Vuoi uscire con me stasera?
target_language_example: Non voglio uscire con lui perché beve troppo.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go out with him because he drinks too much.

meaning: to get out of here / to leave this place.
additional_notes: Used to say you want (or need) to leave the current place. Often expresses urgency or frustration, especially with adesso (“now”) or with an exclamation. It can be used literally (leaving a room/building) or more generally (leaving a situation).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo uscire da qui prima che sia troppo tardi.
native_language_example: We have to get out of here before it’s too late.

meaning: to get out of here; to leave this place.
additional_notes: Used when you want to leave a place, often urgently or because you feel trapped or unsafe. Common with dovere (Dobbiamo uscire di qui subito. = We have to get out of here right away) and with imperative forms to ask/command someone to let you out: Fammi uscire di qui! (Let me out of here!).
target_language_example: Non mi sento al sicuro: dobbiamo uscire di qui adesso.
native_language_example: I don’t feel safe: we have to get out of here now.

additional_notes: "Utilizzare" means "to use" (a bit more formal than "usare"). "Il suo" is a polite/formal way to say "your" (to one person, Lei), and it can also mean "his" or "her" depending on context. Often used with verbs like "permettere" or "lasciare" to ask/allow someone to use a computer.
target_language_example: Potrei utilizzare il suo computer per un minuto?
native_language_example: Could I use your computer for a minute?

additional_notes: Form of the verb andare (“to go”): va = “he/she goes” or “you (formal) go.” Use va a + place/destination (va a Boston, va a casa) or va a + activity/event (va a un picnic, va a caccia). Often answers “Where is he/she going?” (Dove va?). In questions, Italian may omit the subject: Va a Londra? = “Is he/she going to London?”
target_language_example: Va a scuola in bici.
native_language_example: He/She goes to school by bike.

additional_notes: Formed from andare (to go): va = 'he/she goes' + a scuola = 'to school'. Used to talk about someone attending school or going there regularly (often as part of a routine). You can add how someone goes (in autobus, in bicicletta) or when (il sabato). For 'I go to school' you say: vado a scuola.
target_language_example: Mia sorella va a scuola ogni giorno.
native_language_example: My sister goes to school every day.

meaning: (He/she) goes to school on foot (walks to school).
additional_notes: Common way to say someone goes somewhere walking. Structure: andare + a + place (a scuola) + a piedi (“on foot”). Conjugate "andare" for the subject: vado/va/andiamo/vanno a scuola a piedi.
target_language_example: Mia sorella solitamente va a scuola a piedi.
native_language_example: My sister usually walks to school.

additional_notes: Very common informal filler in speech. Used to accept something, end a topic, or move on (similar to “anyway”). Often written as “vabbè” or “vabbè,” especially in informal texting.
target_language_example: Va beh, allora ci vediamo domani.
native_language_example: Alright then, I’ll see you tomorrow.

additional_notes: A very common expression used to agree, accept, say something is fine, or ask for confirmation. At the end of a sentence, va bene? often means "okay?" or "is that okay?". Literally it is something like "it goes well," but that is not how it is usually translated.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle sette, va bene?
native_language_example: We'll see each other at seven, okay?

additional_notes: Used to accept something while adding a limitation, condition, or concern right after. Often followed by a question (Va bene, ma come?) or a restriction (…ma solo lì / …ma dopo / …ma prima). In speech it can sound like “Alright, but…”.
target_language_example: Va bene, ma non oggi: domani.
native_language_example: Okay, but not today: tomorrow.

meaning: “Is it okay if…?” / “Is it alright if…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for permission or check if something is acceptable. Often followed by a verb phrase (usually in the present tense): “Va bene se entro adesso?” = “Is it okay if I come in now?” You can also use it without “se”: “Va bene se…?” is a very common spoken pattern.
target_language_example: Va bene se pago con la carta?
native_language_example: Is it okay if I pay by card?

additional_notes: From the verb andare (to go). "Va" is the present tense for lui/lei/Lei (he/she/you-formal). Often followed by a purpose: "per + infinitive" (per leggere = to read) or "a + infinitive" (a studiare = to study). You can swap the subject: "Io vado in biblioteca", "Noi andiamo in biblioteca".
target_language_example: Oggi va in biblioteca per studiare.
native_language_example: Today he/she goes to the library to study.

additional_notes: From the verb andare (to go): va = “goes” (also used for “you go” in the formal Lei form). In everyday use it often means attending church services (e.g., on Sundays, at Christmas), not just physically entering the building. For “I go,” say vado in chiesa; for “we go,” andiamo in chiesa.
target_language_example: Mio padre va in chiesa ogni domenica.
native_language_example: My dad goes to church every Sunday.

additional_notes: Used to check if a situation is okay (often as a question). Literally it’s like “everything goes well,” but in English you usually say “is everything okay?” You can use it about home, relationships, work, etc. As a reassurance/statement, it’s often said as “va tutto bene.”
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare, va tutto bene.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything’s fine.

additional_notes: Refers to holidays taken in the summer. Often used with possessives: le mie/le tue/le nostre vacanze estive. Common verbs: passare/trascorrere le vacanze estive (to spend your summer vacation).
target_language_example: Quest'anno le nostre vacanze estive saranno in Sicilia.
native_language_example: This year our summer vacation will be in Sicily.

meaning: Go easy / take it easy (with something or someone).
additional_notes: Colloquial imperative (to one person: tu). Often used as a warning to tell someone to slow down, calm down, or not overdo it. Very common with **con/col** + noun/person: **Vacci piano con gli insulti** = “Go easy on the insults,” **Vacci piano con lui** = “Go easy with him.” Can also be used alone: **Vacci piano!** = “Easy!” / “Take it easy!”
target_language_example: Vacci piano con il sale, è già abbastanza salato.
native_language_example: Go easy on the salt, it’s already salty enough.

meaning: "go away" / "leave" (formal/polite: to someone you address as Lei).
additional_notes: Uses the Lei form (formal/polite) of the verb: "vada" = (that you) go. Often used as a command: "Vada via!" = "Go away!" It can also appear after "che" to express a wish/order: "Voglio/Che vada via" = "I want/Make sure he/she goes away."
target_language_example: Mi scusi, ma deve andare: vada via, per favore.
native_language_example: Excuse me, but you have to go: please leave.

additional_notes: From the verb "andare" (to go): "vado" = "I go" / "I’m going". Common patterns: (1) "vado a" + place = "I go to" (often implies movement): "vado a casa" = "I’m going home". (2) "vado a" + infinitive = "I’m going to" (to do something): "vado a spegnere la radio" = "I’m going to turn off the radio".
target_language_example: Scusa, vado a prendere un caffè.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going to get a coffee.

meaning: I’m going home / I’m going to (my) house.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re leaving and heading home. Often said on its own as a simple statement (like “I’m going home.”). In Italian you usually don’t need a possessive: “a casa” commonly means “home” (your own). You can add details like time or who you’re with: “Vado a casa, è tardi” (I’m going home, it’s late) or “Vado a casa con…” (I’m going home with…).
target_language_example: Scusa, vado a casa: domani lavoro presto.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going home: I work early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re going to bed / going to sleep, often with a time (alle dieci = at 10). It’s the 1st-person singular of andare a letto (to go to bed).
target_language_example: Sono stanco: vado a letto.
native_language_example: I’m tired: I’m going to bed.

meaning: I'm going to go get/pick up (something/someone).
additional_notes: Used when you leave to fetch something or pick someone up. It’s the present tense of "andare a" + infinitive: "(io) vado a" = "I’m going to" and "prendere" = "to take/get". Common with objects (le cose, del cibo) and people (i bambini) and often implies you’ll come back soon.
target_language_example: Aspetta qui: vado a prendere un caffè e torno.
native_language_example: Wait here: I'm going to get a coffee and I'll be back.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "andare" (to go), used to tell someone to go home. Often said as an instruction or order. You can add details like "vai a casa da tua moglie" (go home to your wife) or combine it with another command: "vai a casa e cambiati" (go home and change).
target_language_example: È tardi: vai a casa.
native_language_example: It’s late: go home.

additional_notes: From andare (to go) + a + dormire (to sleep). It can be a statement (“you go to bed”) or, very often, an imperative telling someone to go to bed (“Go to sleep!”). For questions you’ll also see: «Quando vai a dormire?» (“When do you go to bed?”).
target_language_example: È tardi: vai a dormire!
native_language_example: It’s late: go to bed!

additional_notes: Extremely offensive and aggressive. Used to tell someone off or dismiss them with contempt. Usually addressed directly to a person (“Vai a farti fottere!”). Avoid in polite or everyday situations; it can easily start a fight.
target_language_example: Se non ti sta bene, vai a farti fottere.
native_language_example: If you don’t like it, go f**k yourself.

additional_notes: Imperative form addressed to one person (tu): a common way to tell someone to go to bed (often a child). Related questions use the same phrase: “A che ora vai a letto?” = “What time do you go to bed?” You can add time words like adesso/ora (now) or in orario (on time).
target_language_example: Dai, è tardi: vai a letto!
native_language_example: Come on, it’s late: go to bed!

additional_notes: Common instruction using vai (you go) + a + prendere (to take/get). Used for fetching items (food, drinks, objects) or picking up a person (e.g., by car or to go bring them). In speech it can also be shortened to "vai a prenderlo/la/li/le" (go get him/her/them) or "vai a prenderne" (go get some).
target_language_example: Vai a prendere le chiavi e poi torniamo a casa.
native_language_example: Go get the keys and then we'll go home.

additional_notes: Imperative (tu) form of "andare avanti". Used to tell someone to continue speaking or doing something ("Vai avanti con la tua storia"), to proceed without you ("Vai avanti da solo"), or to encourage someone to do something/confirm permission ("Vai avanti, spara" = "Go ahead, shoot/say it"). Can also mean to move forward physically ("go on ahead").
target_language_example: Se vuoi, vai avanti: io ti ascolto.
native_language_example: If you want, go ahead—I’m listening.

meaning: “go like that / like this” (also: “that’s it, keep going!”).
additional_notes: Literally “you go like this/that.” Used (1) as a question showing surprise/criticism: “You’re leaving like that?” (e.g., without saying goodbye, without getting ready), and (2) as an encouraging exclamation meaning “That’s the way! Keep it up!” Repeating it (“Vai così, vai così!”) can sound like a chant to cheer someone on.
target_language_example: Dai, vai così: stai facendo progressi!
native_language_example: Come on, keep it up: you’re making progress!

meaning: “you go to / you go into” (vai in + place).
additional_notes: Used with andare (“to go”) + in to talk about going to a place, especially countries/continents (in Europa), and many locations like church/theater (in chiesa, in teatro). With specific places you may also see an article: in questa chiesa (“in this church”). Note: in insults like “Vai in culo” it’s very rude (literally “go in [your] ass,” meaning “fuck off”).
target_language_example: Vai in Italia quest’estate?
native_language_example: Are you going to Italy this summer?

additional_notes: Imperative form of **andare via** (“to go away/leave”). It can be a firm order and may sound rude depending on tone and context (especially when shouted). Often used with **da qui** (“from here”) or **subito** (“right away”): *Vai via da qui!* / *Vai via subito!* You can also use it more neutrally in urgent situations (e.g., “get out/leave now”).
target_language_example: C'è pericolo: vai via subito!
native_language_example: It’s dangerous: leave right away!

additional_notes: Used to say that an action or experience is worth the effort, time, or cost. Often followed by an infinitive: "Vale la pena + verb" (e.g., "Vale la pena vedere..."). In the negative: "non vale la pena" = "it’s not worth it".
target_language_example: Non vale la pena discutere adesso.
native_language_example: It’s not worth arguing right now.

meaning: to be worth it; to be worth the effort.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is worthwhile. Commonly appears with the particle "ne" ("Ne vale la pena" = "It’s worth it"), but the base multi-word term is "valere la pena". You can also use it with an infinitive: "Vale la pena provare" = "It’s worth trying." In questions/negatives: "Ne vale la pena?" / "Non ne vale la pena."
target_language_example: Visitare questo museo può valere la pena, perché è bellissimo.
native_language_example: Visiting this museum can be worth it, because it’s beautiful.

additional_notes: A common household item: the tub you fill with water to take a bath. Often used with verbs like fare il bagno (to take a bath) or pulire (to clean).
target_language_example: C'è una vasca da bagno in questo hotel?
native_language_example: Is there a bathtub in this hotel?

additional_notes: Combination of pronouns placed before the verb: **ve** = “to you” (to you all, or formal to one person), **lo** = “it” (masculine singular; often stands for a whole idea). Common with verbs like **dire** (to tell), **chiedere** (to ask), **assicurare** (to assure): *Ve lo dico* = “I’m telling you (it).” If the "it" is feminine, you’ll hear **ve la** instead.
target_language_example: Ve lo spiego domani.
native_language_example: I’ll explain it to you tomorrow.

meaning: "to you" + "of it/them" or "from there" (a common pronoun combo).
additional_notes: It’s a combination of two pronouns placed before the verb: **ve** = “to you (plural)” (also used as the polite **you** in some regions), and **ne** = “of it/of them/some” or “from there/away.” Very common with **andarsene** (“to go away/leave”): *Ve ne state andando?* = “Are you leaving?” It’s also used with quantities: *Ve ne posso prendere di più* = “I can take more (of them/it),” and with *una* meaning “one (thing)” in *Ve ne dobbiamo una* = “We owe you one.”
target_language_example: Ve ne posso dare due, se volete.
native_language_example: I can give you two of them, if you want.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the past in a nostalgic way. Often appears in phrases like "per amore dei vecchi tempi" (for old times’ sake) or "in nome dei vecchi tempi" (in the name of the old times), meaning you do something because of shared history or memories.
target_language_example: Facciamolo per amore dei vecchi tempi.
native_language_example: Let’s do it for old times’ sake.

meaning: “my old friend/buddy” (affectionate way to address someone).
additional_notes: Used as a familiar, often affectionate form of address (usually to a male friend). It can sound warm and friendly, and sometimes mildly ironic depending on tone. Often placed at the end of a sentence (e.g., “Ciao, vecchio mio”) or said on its own.
target_language_example: Come va, vecchio mio? È da tanto che non ci vediamo.
native_language_example: How’s it going, buddy? We haven’t seen each other in a long time.

meaning: to see the light; to finally understand/realize (also: to be born / to come out).
additional_notes: Often used figuratively to mean someone finally understands the truth or changes their mind after a long time. It can also be used more literally to mean “to be born” (a baby) or “to be released/published” (a project, book, idea) — i.e., to “see the light of day.” Common pattern: "finalmente ha iniziato a vedere la luce".
target_language_example: Dopo tante spiegazioni, finalmente ha iniziato a vedere la luce e ha capito il problema.
native_language_example: After so many explanations, they finally started to see the light and understood the problem.

meaning: to see a doctor (to go for medical help).
additional_notes: Common way to say you should go to a doctor for advice or treatment. "Vedere" here means "to consult/visit" (not just "to look at"). Often used with "dovresti/dovrebbe" (you should/he should).
target_language_example: Se hai la febbre da due giorni, devi vedere un dottore.
native_language_example: If you’ve had a fever for two days, you need to see a doctor.

additional_notes: Used to suggest trying something, checking what happens, or testing whether something works. It’s the 1st-person plural of *vedere* (“to see”), often used inclusively like English “let’s…”. Common before a verb: *Vediamo se funziona* (“Let’s see if it works”).
target_language_example: Vediamo se domani hai tempo per un caffè.
native_language_example: Let’s see if you have time for a coffee tomorrow.

additional_notes: Usually used in the expression "essere di vedute ristrette" to describe a person who is not open to new ideas, different lifestyles, or other opinions. Often has a negative, critical tone.
target_language_example: Non voglio lavorare con persone di vedute ristrette.
native_language_example: I don’t want to work with narrow-minded people.

additional_notes: "Vendere" means "to sell". "La sua" means "his/her" (and can also mean formal "your" in contexts like "la Sua"). "Automobile" is understood, but in everyday Italian people often say "macchina" or "auto". Whose car it is (his vs. her) is usually clear from context.
target_language_example: Mary sta provando a vendere la sua automobile.
native_language_example: Mary is trying to sell her car.

additional_notes: “Vendette” is the passato remoto (simple past) of *vendere* (“to sell”), common in written stories and in some regions; in everyday speech you’ll often hear *ha venduto*. “La sua” means “his/her/its” referring to a feminine singular thing (e.g., *la macchina, la casa, l’azienda*). The owner’s gender is not shown here—*sua* can mean “his” or “her.”
target_language_example: Ieri vendette la sua macchina e comprò una bicicletta.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she sold his/her car and bought a bike.

additional_notes: "Venga" is the formal (Lei) command form of "venire" (to come). It’s often followed by an infinitive to say what you want the person to come and do: "venga a vedere" (come and see), "venga a parlare" (come and speak). Use with people you address as "Lei" (e.g., strangers, customers, officials).
target_language_example: Signora, venga a sedersi qui, per favore.
native_language_example: Ma’am, please come sit here.

additional_notes: Uses the formal command form (imperative with "Lei"): "venga" from "venire". It’s used when speaking politely to one person (a stranger, customer, older person, etc.), often with "Prego". Informal version to a friend: "Vieni con me".
target_language_example: Mi scusi, venga con me, per favore.
native_language_example: Excuse me, please come with me.

additional_notes: "Venga" is the formal (Lei) imperative of "venire" (to come). It’s used to address someone politely (e.g., a customer, a stranger, an older person) or in formal situations; it can also sound firm/authoritative depending on tone. "Qui" means “here,” and you can add adverbs like "immediatamente" (immediately) or "lentamente" (slowly), or "per favore" (please).
target_language_example: Dottore, venga qui un momento, per favore.
native_language_example: Doctor, come here for a moment, please.

additional_notes: Used to say where you are from (a city/country), or your origin/background. With places: "Vengo da Roma" = I’m from Rome. With distance: "Vengo da lontano" = I’ve come from far away. With family/background: "Vengo da una famiglia..." = I come from a ... family. From the verb "venire" (to come) + "da" (from).
target_language_example: Ciao! Vengo da New York, ma vivo a Milano.
native_language_example: Hi! I’m from New York, but I live in Milan.

additional_notes: Used when the movement is toward the speaker’s home or the place thought of as “home.” Italian often uses the preposition "a" (“to”) with "casa" in this expression (literally “to come to home”), where English typically just says “come home.”
target_language_example: Puoi venire a casa stasera?
native_language_example: Can you come home tonight?

meaning: to be born; to come into the world.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s birth (often in a slightly poetic or formal tone). Common in the past tense: "è venuto/a al mondo" (he/she was born). You can add a place or date: "è venuto/a al mondo a Roma" (was born in Rome).
target_language_example: Mia nonna è venuta al mondo nel 1945: in un'Italia che stava cambiando.
native_language_example: My grandmother was born in 1945, in an Italy that was changing.

meaning: to come with us / to join us.
additional_notes: Used to invite someone to accompany your group. Often appears as a question ("Vuoi/Vorresti venire con noi?") or with plans/intentions ("voglio venire con voi/voi"). Note: the object changes with the group: con me (with me), con te (with you), con voi (with you all).
target_language_example: Se vuoi, puoi venire con noi a cena stasera.
native_language_example: If you want, you can come with us to dinner tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you will accompany someone (the person addressed: "te" = "you" singular/informal). With verbs like "devo" (I have to), "voglio" (I want), or "potremmo" (we could) to express obligation, desire, or possibility.
target_language_example: Posso venire con te al supermercato?
native_language_example: Can I come with you to the supermarket?

meaning: 'to come out' / 'to come outside'; also 'to come up' or 'to turn out (to be revealed)'.
additional_notes: Used literally for leaving a place (Venire fuori di casa = to come out of the house). Very common figuratively to mean something appears, emerges, or is discovered (È venuto fuori un problema = a problem came up; La verità è venuta fuori = the truth came out). In the past, it often uses essere: è venuto/venuta fuori, sono venuti/venute fuori.
target_language_example: Può venire fuori la verità, prima o poi.
native_language_example: The truth can come out, sooner or later.

additional_notes: A straightforward phrase meaning movement toward the speaker's location. In the examples it appears after dire + di, as in dire a qualcuno di venire qui ('to tell someone to come here'). For a direct command to one person, Italian usually says vieni qui.
target_language_example: Puoi venire qui un momento?
native_language_example: Can you come here a moment?

meaning: to come up; to rise; (people/children) to grow up.
additional_notes: Common uses: (1) something physically rises/appears: “Mi viene su un nodo in gola” (a lump comes up in my throat), “Mi viene su un bernoccolo” (a bump comes up). (2) children growing up: “È venuto su in campagna” (he grew up in the countryside). (3) cooking/food: “La torta viene su” (the cake rises). Also in “venire su bene/male” = to turn out well/badly (especially about how someone grows up).
target_language_example: La torta non riesce a venire su bene.
native_language_example: The cake can’t manage to rise well.

meaning: to come off / come away; (also) to leave (with someone).
additional_notes: Often used when something detaches or comes loose: "La macchia non viene via" = "The stain won’t come out"; "Il tappo viene via" = "The cap comes off". With a person (often with "con me/te/lui...") it can mean to go away/leave together: "Vieni via con me" = "Come away/come with me".
target_language_example: Devo far venire via questa etichetta.
